title: [Radix Cache] Sync Rust TreeCore and make it the default
author: Jialin
body:
Use Rust as the default unified tree core and resolve unsupported configurations to Python in one central place. Synchronize these Python behaviors:

| Original Python PR | Rust change |
| --- | --- |
| [#38356 — Logical-page placement](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/38356) | Preserve `rotation_base` through insertion and splitting, and reject incompatible grafts before transferring KV ownership. |
| [#37503 — HiCache accounting](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/37503) | Count every unbacked Full-KV eviction within a native step, including cascades, and report `tracked_unbacked_tokens`. |
| [#37795 — Eviction-policy configuration](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/37795) | Forward SLRU's `protected_threshold` and validate policy parameters. The cutoff orders probationary nodes before protected nodes while preserving LRU order within each segment; the original policy came from [#18843](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/18843). |
| [#34012 — T-LRU eviction](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/34012) | Port tail-first eviction with integer or floating-point `threshold` and `next_prompt_estimate`, preserving Python’s arithmetic order and exact integer/float comparisons. Track path depth and branch high-water history through device/host insertion and splits, retaining history after eviction so repeated trimming stops at the original budget. |
| [#33777 — Write-back host pressure](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/33777) | Preserve insertion order when reclaiming Full host duplicates, including removals and new backups. Register new copies at acknowledgment so pending internal splits publish their prefix before their suffix. Retain device-resident SWA host backups under SWA pressure, matching Python's Full-only duplicate prepass; ordinary host-only SWA eviction remains available. |
| [#38462 — Host-duplicate reclamation](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/38462) | Honor `SGLANG_HICACHE_SKIP_HOST_DUPLICATE_RECLAIM` in native eviction. |
| [#38269 — SWA layout-aware reuse](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/38269) | Use the allocator's actual request-ring capability for SWA matching. This preserves ring prefix reuse without HiCache and rejects paged-SWA hits without the required window, including DSV4.1 encoder replay + DSpark + HiCache configurations from [#38798](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/38798). |
| [#39283 — SWA buffer-mode prefetch](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39283) | Port `swa_tombstone_ranges` and `attach_swa_window`, including repairs that split existing nodes, preserving KV ownership, locks, pending write-through actions and namespace/page offsets. |
| [#37507 — Unified-memory HiCache](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/37507) | Preserve exact Full-row anchors for SWA load-back, including resident-row holes, and resolve current physical SWA rows before backup after compaction. |
| [#40680 — Internal Mamba write-back](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40680) | Back up internal Mamba state before eviction, wait for acknowledgment and retain resident Full KV. Reclaim host-state capacity first; preserve the legacy drop on allocation failure and device state on submission/acknowledgment exceptions. |
| [#40712 — Internal SWA write-back](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40712) | Preserve eligible internal SWA windows before eviction. Pause for the controller to reclaim capacity for the whole unbacked window and finish its host backup, then resume safely after success or allocation failure. |
| [#41092 — Drain pending backups before internal Mamba write-back](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41092) | Reuse the shared pre-backup ACK drain from native internal eviction; run the pending-SWA/internal-Mamba regression on both backends and preserve allocation-failure behavior. |
| [#41276 — Component eviction cursors and lock receipts](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41276) | Preserve main's component-indexed cursors and device/host lock-receipt maps in the rebased adapter and parity tests, including missing-receipt error handling. |
| [#41325 — Extensible sliding-window caching](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41325) | Expose per-component protected sizes and release an SWA window's receipt independently, retaining peer Full/Mamba locks and the root/skipped-component behavior. |
| [#41328 — Per-cache backend selection and LMCache cursors](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41328) | Honor each cache's backend override before the centralized compatibility fallback, preserving environment defaults for other caches and main's LMCache cursor fix. |

Centralized Python fallback applies to both default and explicit Rust selection for:

- Session-aware caching.
- C128 or other unsupported components.
- Custom component overrides.
- Non-Linux platforms.
- PyTorch versions outside 2.11–2.13, or unrecognized versions.
- Devices other than CPU or CUDA.
- Installations containing neither the Rust extension nor its sources.
- Source builds with a missing or unusable Rust toolchain.

Trusted bundled extensions need no compiler. Supported configurations continue to surface build, import and runtime errors. Rust exports return `PyResult`: ordinary Python errors pass through unchanged, and unexpected native panics become `RuntimeError` in the binding. The Python adapter holds the concrete binding directly. Panic handling stays outside the mutex scope, so a core interrupted by a panic remains poisoned and subsequent calls refuse to reuse it. Production, inspection, bigram, constructor and tensor-return paths are covered.

T-LRU supports integer and floating-point parameters with Python's operation order, rounding and exact integer/float comparisons, including NaN and infinity. Integer-only parameters retain the exact tail-budget path. Mixed integer estimates must fit i128; larger values raise `OverflowError` at construction, and checked native addition panics on overflow. Priority evaluation uses native scalar arithmetic without allocation or Python callbacks. T-LRU adds two counters per node (16 bytes on 64-bit platforms); its ancestor history walk runs only for T-LRU and costs O(path nodes).

One insertion-ordered `NodeSet` serves device leaves, host leaves and Full host duplicates. It preserves constant-time membership/removal, amortized constant-time insertion and exact-size iteration. Leaf eviction still ranks candidates in its policy heap; Full duplicate reclamation follows Python's insertion order.

Auxiliary eviction respects each component's own transfer/request locks. An unrelated Full load or expanded SWA backup must not pin independently restored auxiliary state. Actual transfer sources/destinations and Full leaf guards remain protected. Deferred Mamba and SWA eviction revalidate the victim after the controller's backup attempt, preserve device state on submission/acknowledgment exceptions, and retain progress when host allocation fails. For built-in Mamba and SWA, both Python and Rust return internal backup requests to the shared controller, then resume through the same required finish methods. Python components return immutable backup requests containing the victim and required host capacity; the core owns pending-request validation, without adding backup bookkeeping to `TreeComponent`. Python preserves its session-aware cursor ordering; both cores consume pending requests and report frees and eviction counts through the same interface. Custom SWA component types retain their inherited Python behavior.

Hybrid transfer plans cross the binding in Python's component order, removing native HashMap nondeterminism. The shared host allocator now follows main's pool-name ordering from #40512; paired host-pressure expectations follow that order. Main's unified-memory decode host pools (#39478) use the shared controller path and need no separate native port.

The real default-cache test exercises construction, insertion and matching without factory mocks. Shared inspections replace native-specific test skips. This update removes the internal-SWA Rust skip and five obsolete Full+SWA+Mamba HiCache skips, enabling the now-supported hybrid fixtures. Legitimate configuration-applicability guards remain. Session cases in a Rust-selected run exercise centralized Python fallback. External backends implement the abstract SWA repair and internal-eviction finish methods. The README covers usage, supported configurations, builds and the controller/core contract; parity-port history remains in this PR description.

Validation of head `85e244caa9`, based on main `fc9e1c8d29`:

- Local CPU: **531 tests and 43 subtests passed**, with one existing CUDA-only skip. Includes direct component-response coverage, phase/session/custom-component/missing-pool cases, full core/registry/error/inspection/session coverage, and submission/ACK failure restart checks. All **36 actual shared write-back scenarios passed** across Python/Rust: 12 Mamba, 20 SWA and four pending-SWA/internal-Mamba (#41092) cases.
- Rust core and binding sources are unchanged from `f705c05736`, which passed 918 native tests and both configured and binding-enabled Clippy checks. The Python checks use that same native implementation for differential coverage.
- Pinned Python lint/format/import checks and patch whitespace checks passed; the preceding README cleanup passed spelling checks. Independent review found no blocker in the response ownership, common finish contract, accounting, session cursor order or failure cleanup.
- Fresh NVIDIA CI at `85e244caa9`: [Lint](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/36300095687) passed. [Base](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/36300096014) completed successfully on attempt 1: **721 CPU files across 11 shards**, GPU Stage A (**63 passes; two existing FA3 hardware skips**), **all 19 Stage B GPU jobs (320 files)**, **all 15 Stage C GPU jobs (47 files)**, and the final workflow gate passed. Both shared cache GPU suites passed (**1,289 passes and 1,494 unchanged applicability skips each**); the Rust-requested total includes intentional Python session fallbacks, while supported SWA/Mamba write-back cases assert the resolved backend. [Extra](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/36300095825) completed successfully on unchanged-head attempt 3: **all 19 GPU shards, 163 files, 919 passing test executions**, and its final workflow gate passed. The repeated GLM5.3 Flash H200 accuracy failure recovered with **HighThroughput 0.936 and LowLatency 0.950**, both without a built-in retry. The earlier 0.926→0.928 failure also occurred in an independently verified [Python-backed control](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/36254948158/job/108517021499) with the same test and model. Successful executions were retained across the two failed-jobs reruns; no code, thresholds, or skips were changed. These runs tested merge `bf722e6a1a8c7d243703d306b9b6a00dc8834ab0`, combining this head with main `df1fc6ab6441abbdf21944958b131c03e0921253`. Later main [#41281](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41281) received a static compatibility review; it was not executed by these runs.

The preceding head `f705c05736` passed [Base](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/36263883045) and [Extra](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/36263882854): all 720 CPU files, 36 Base GPU jobs and 18 Extra GPU jobs; Lint also passed. Both shared cache suites ran 2,783 cases, with 1,289 passes and 1,494 matching applicability skips. Base required one unchanged-code Inkling retry with a different runner/input sample; no thresholds or skips changed. These are baseline results; the Python refactor requires its own CI run.

Local tests use CPU Torch and simulated transfer boundaries; they do not establish GPU numerical equivalence. Rotation has simulated-rank/core coverage. Session-aware/C128 fallback and hardware/configuration applicability guards remain explicit. Validation is focused on NVIDIA; unrelated platform workflows are not claimed green.

title: dsv4.1: Top-k kernels and candidate selection
author: hnyls2002
body:
## Summary
- Add the DeepSeek-V4.1 sparse-indexer kernels that sit beside Top-k v2: a bf16 small-row top-k, the two-level indexer's block-max keys and sorted block table, and a cluster-occupancy probe.
- Rework Top-k v2's edge handling and cluster dispatch (details below); the existing suite still passes and two new regression cases pin the fixed `-inf` tie behaviour.

## New kernels
- `topk_bf16_small` (`topk_transform_bf16_small`): bf16 top-k for rows of at most 16384 scores, two radix passes over the raw bf16 bytes, fused with the page-table transform; adapted from DeepSelect's init-window select.
- `block_amax` (`amax8_varlen`): level-one keys of the two-level indexer, the max of each 8-score block with the row's newest block forced to `+inf`.
- `candidate_block_table` (`sort_candidate_blocks`): counting sort of a row's selected blocks over a bitmap plus the page transform, in place.
- `jit/utils/occupancy.py` (`get_max_active_clusters`): asks `cudaOccupancyMaxActiveClusters` how many clusters of a given width fit at a given occupancy; sizes the Top-k v2 persistent pool at JIT time.
- `attention/dsv4/candidate_table.py` hosts the two indexer helpers; `topk.py` keeps only the top-k entry points.

## Top-k v2 changes
- Padding uses NaN instead of `-FLT_MAX`, so inactive entries never displace valid `-inf` scores (`test_topk_v2_negative_infinity_ties`, `test_topk_v2_ragged_negative_infinity`); the padding bin is taken from `extract_coarse_bin(padding_value())`, so the histogram correction does not depend on the platform's NaN encoding.
- `coarse_bin_lower_bound` steps the midpoint up on odd-significand bins (fp32 -> fp16 rounds to nearest even) and returns `+/-inf` at the key-space edges.
- Cluster path: `TopKCluster<N>` for N = 8 and 16, inputs interleaved across ranks, rank 0 owns the histogram and threshold behind release/acquire cluster barriers; the persistent-pool size and the cluster-16 small-batch cap come from the occupancy probe, with per-arch defaults as fallback; `topk_plan_cluster` carries per-arch candidate tables.
- `SUPPORT_CLUSTER` limits the cluster path to sm90/sm100; sm120 and ROCm take the streaming path.
- `plan_topk_v2(static_threshold)`: a negative value selects the heuristic (was `0`); no in-tree caller passes the argument.
- The #32830 mitigation (`__builtin_assume` in the small-batch cluster epilogue) is dropped: the restructured epilogue compiles with nvcc 13.1 through 13.4 for sm_90a, while the previous code still segfaults cicc without it.
- `TieHandleSmem` no longer over-aligns its counters; `topk_v2_plan_is_written` replaces the test kit's use of the private JIT module.

## Verification
- `test_topk_v2.py`: 288 cases pass on SM90 and SM100.

title: dsv4.1: compression, KV I/O, and metadata kernels
author: hnyls2002
body:
## Summary
- Add `KVLayout` (`kernels/ops/attention/dsv4/kv_layout.py`, `include/sgl_kernel/deepseek_v4/kv_layout.cuh`): the paged FlashMLA main-KV formats as one enum with their per-token data / scale bytes, tile size and page alignment. `V4` is the existing 584-byte layout (448 fp8 nope + 64 bf16 rope + ue8m0 scales); `V41` (528 B, every dim fp8 with one ue8m0 scale per 32) and `V41_FP4` (288 B, e2m1 codes with one e4m3 scale per 16) are the DeepSeek-V4.1 formats. `PagedKV<layout, page_bits>::row` gives every writer the same address arithmetic, and `v41::store_row` is the single quantizer for the V4.1 rows.
- Thread `layout` through the existing cache writers and reader: `fused_store_cache` (with an optional in-kernel RoPE for the V4.1 layouts), `compress_norm_rope_store`, `fused_k_norm_rope_flashmla`, `dequantize_k_cache_paged`. The default stays `V4`, so current callers are unchanged.
- Add the ratio-1 / ratio-2 decode compressors (`csrc/deepseek_v4/c1.cuh`, `c2.cuh`, `ops/attention/dsv4/low_ratio_compress.py`): pair-pooling (ratio 2), RMSNorm, RoPE and the main-KV write in one launch, returning the pre-RoPE latent; `out_loc == 0` marks a padded graph row.
- Add the V4.1 dequantizers (`dequant_k_cache.py`), `fp4_utils.cuh` (e2m1 fake-quant helpers next to the existing `fp8_utils.cuh`), the pure-torch reference quantizer (`torch_quant.py`), and two small-batch metadata builders (`build_page_table_positions_small`, `build_low_ratio_metadata`).
- Model call sites (pool layout selection, the low-ratio compressor path) are in #38798.

## Changes to existing kernels
- `csrc/deepseek_v4/store.cuh`, `fused_norm_rope_v2.cuh`, `main_norm_rope.cuh`: the V4 path now addresses pages through `PagedKV`; same bytes as before. The kernel templates gain a `KVLayout` parameter.
- `csrc/deepseek_v4/c_plan.cuh`: `ragged_id` is a zero-based uint16, so a 65536-token batch is valid; `batch_size` must stay below 65535 because `pack_w(65535, 65535)` is the invalid-write sentinel. `test_deepseek_v4_compress_plan_bounds.py` covers both bounds and the sentinel collision.
- `get_paged_mqa_logits_metadata` accepts page size 128 as well as 64 (the schedule depends only on the sequence lengths).

## Verification
- JIT builds of every layout variant of the touched kernels (c1, c2, store, compress norm-rope, main-K norm-rope) succeed.
- Existing tests on the modified kernels are rerun on this PR: `test_c4_v2.py`, `test_c128_v2.py`, `test_deepseek_v4_compress_state_runtime_shapes.py`, `test_fp4_indexer.py`, `test_paged_mqa_metadata.py`, plus `test_deepseek_v4_compress_plan_bounds.py`.

title: dsv4.1: communication kernels and wrappers
author: hnyls2002
body:
## Summary
- Add NVLink collectives on the `CustomAllReduceV2` push and pull planes: all-reduce, all-gather and reduce-scatter, each as a push (Lamport slot) and a pull (multicast) kernel, with an optional residual folded into the reduction (`csrc/distributed/nvlink_comm.cuh`, `ops/communication/nvlink_comm.py`).
- Add a fused deferred-MoE finalize -> one-shot push all-reduce kernel with optional shared-expert add and RMSNorm epilogue (`csrc/distributed/all_reduce_fusion.cuh`, `ops/communication/all_reduce_fusion.py`); the rank-local finalize is computed in registers and pushed straight into the peers' slots, keeping the unfused path's bf16 rounding points.
- Add the DeepSeek-V4.1 mHC variants of that kernel: post-mixing, post-mixing + RMSNorm, and post-mixing + RMSNorm + fp8 quantization with ue8m0 group scales (`ops/communication/all_reduce_mhc.py`).
- Add `VocabGather` (`srt/distributed/device_communicators/vocab_gather.py`): one `[rows, local] -> [rows, world_size * local]` interface with local, NCCL and NVLink transports; the NVLink transport takes the push kernel while the slice fits a push slot, the pull kernel into a symmetric-memory output beyond that, and the NCCL ring otherwise.
- Add `sharded_greedy_step` (`ops/speculative/dspark/sharded_greedy.py`): each rank reduces its vocab shard to (value, index) partials and only those cross the transport.
- Model call sites (finalize-fusion admission, communicator registration, the DSpark draft head) are in #38798.

## Changes to existing kernels
- `csrc/distributed/custom_all_reduce.cuh`: the one-shot push kernel maps warps to blocks round-robin instead of block-major, so the tail CTAs keep work in the size band where `choose_block_size` moves past 512 threads before 1024 threads fill the grid. No numerical change.
- `include/sgl_kernel/distributed/ptx.cuh`: the bulk `multimem` loads and stores name the `.global` state space (`ST.E.128` becomes `STG.E.128`). No measured change.

Both changes, and the collectives themselves, are the shared-kernel part of #36720; the Kimi K3 migration in that PR is not included here.

## Verification
- JIT builds of every module in this PR (push, pull, finalize fusion, mHC, mHC + quant) and the Triton kernels succeed.
- Existing tests on the modified shared kernels and headers are rerun on this PR: `test_custom_all_reduce.py`, `test_deterministic_reduce_scatter.py`, `kimi_k3/test_collectives.py`, `kimi_k3/test_ar_fusion.py`, `test_symm_mem_all_gather.py`.

title: dsv4.1: RoPE and FP4 packing kernels
author: hnyls2002
body:
## Summary
- Fused RoPE and FP4 packing kernels for the DeepSeek-V4.1 low-ratio indexer: keys and queries are rotated, fake-quantized to the per-32 UE8M0 FP4 grid and packed into the 68-byte index-K format (64 e2m1 bytes plus four block exponents) that the paged FP4 MQA logits kernel reads.
- `fp4_indexer_rope.cuh` / `fp4_indexer_rope.py`: one warp per row. `index_k_norm_rope_pack_store` fuses RMSNorm, RoPE at the group's first position, both quantization stages and the paged cache store (slot 0 publishes nothing); `index_q_rope_pack_weights` does the query side and computes the indexer head weights in the same launch.
- `fp4_rope_fake_quant.py`: Triton RoPE tail plus FP4 fake-quant for the torch-shaped path, per-32 UE8M0 by default and per-16 E4M3 for compressed KV, preserving the bf16 round-trip after RoPE and round-half-to-even.
- `fp4_indexer.py`: `_index_k_rope_pack_kernel` / `index_k_rope_pack`, the Triton RoPE + fake-quant + pack + store kernel for the prefill path; `_fp4_e2m1_code_rne` and an `rne` flag on `quantize_fp4_indexer_tensor` / `store_fp4_index_k_cache` for the reference's round-to-nearest-even; `INDEX_K_SLOT_BYTES` names the slot size the store kernel already asserted.

## Changes to existing kernels
- `fp4_indexer.py`: `rne` defaults to `False`, so the existing C4 indexer path keeps its threshold rounding; the kernel gains an `RNE` constexpr branch and nothing else.

## Verification
- The CUDA kernels, the Triton pack kernel and the fake-quant + existing packer path agree byte for byte: 504/504 comparisons over rows in {1, 5, 64, 300}, input scales {1, 40, 1e-3} plus zero, subnormal and exact half-way rows, compress ratios {1, 2, 4} and int32/int64 positions, covering the packed payload, the block-exponent words, the paged cache pages with slot-0 suppression, and the fp32 head weights.
- `test_fp4_indexer.py` guards the unchanged default rounding of the existing kernel.

title: dsv4.1: Hopper FP8 matmul kernels and tuning
author: hnyls2002
body:
## Summary
- Add a Hopper variant of the block-FP8 Triton matmul, `_w8a8_block_fp8_matmul_hopper`, with two tuning knobs read from the per-shape config: `SWAP_AB` transposes the MMA so the weight tile occupies the M dimension for tiny M, and `SPLIT_K` splits the K loop over a second grid axis into fp32 partials that `_reduce_block_fp8_split_k` sums.
- `w8a8_block_fp8_matmul_triton` selects the Hopper kernel only on sm90 and only when the chosen config entry carries one of those keys; every other config keeps the existing kernel selection, grid and output buffer.
- Seven H200 tuning files for `fp8_w8a8` with `block_shape=[32, 32]` (N,K in {1152,5120}, {1792,5120}, {25600,6144}, {4096,1280}, {5120,2048}, {5120,576}, {8192,1280}). Their `"1"` entries use `SWAP_AB` and `SPLIT_K` in {1, 2, 4, 8, 16}; the `"2"` entries are plain, so M >= 2 runs the existing kernel and bs=1 rows differ from bs>=2 rows by the fp32 accumulation order (one bf16 rounding step at most).

## Changes to existing kernels
- None. Configs without the two keys, including all existing `[128, 128]` H200 files, take exactly the previous path.

## Verification
- For all seven shipped configs at M in {1, 2, 3}: the Hopper kernel and the existing kernel agree bit for bit at M >= 2; at M = 1 they agree on 97-99% of outputs and differ by one bf16 rounding step on the rest, with the same maximum relative error against an fp64 dequantized reference (2.3e-3 to 3.4e-3).
- CUDA-graph replay of the `SWAP_AB` and `SPLIT_K` paths matches eager execution for all seven shapes.
- `test_fp8_kernel.py` covers the unchanged default path.

title: dsv4.1: mHC computation and compensated projections
author: hnyls2002
body:
## Summary
- Batch-invariant mHC mixing statistics for DeepSeek-V4.1's hyper-connection layers, in `mhc.py`: `hc_mix_stats` computes the per-row mixing projections and sum of squares over a fixed number of K slices with `tf32x3` dots, so a row's result is bitwise identical whether computed alone or in a batch; `hc_mix_stats_sinkhorn` fuses the slice reduction with the sinkhorn normalisation that `hc_split_sinkhorn` performs.
- Two compensated variants of the same projection for large batches, keeping the fp32 weight exact on the tensor cores: `hc_mix_stats_sinkhorn_bf16x3` (Triton, three bf16 weight components, one activation read) and `hc_mix_stats_sinkhorn_deepgemm` (tf32 high part plus fp32 residual through DeepGEMM), with `split_bf16_hc_weight` / `split_tf32_hc_weight` preparing the weight parts. Both accumulate over `_HC_MIX_COMPENSATED_SLICES` and share the sinkhorn reduce kernel; sizes come from the input shapes and `hc_mult`.
- `hc_split_sinkhorn` answers an empty batch directly instead of launching a zero-sized grid, which the TileLang backend rejects.

## Changes to existing kernels
- `hc_split_sinkhorn`: the empty-batch return only. Its existing caller already returns before reaching it with no tokens, so results on existing models are unchanged; the guard is for callers that do not pre-check.

## Verification
- Sinkhorn arithmetic (eps placement, iteration count, RMS scaling order) matches the existing Triton `hc_split_sinkhorn` port and the reference implementation.
- The two compensated variants produce bitwise identical outputs to their previous standalone-module versions for M in {4096, 5000, 8192} (bf16x3) and {128, 1000, 4096} (DeepGEMM) at K = 20480.
- `test_mhc_kernels.py` and `test_hc_combine.py` cover the untouched kernels of the module.

title: dsv4.1: candidate indexer library
author: hnyls2002
body:
## Summary
- Add the two-level candidate indexer for DeepSeek-V4.1 low-ratio decode: one layer scores every reachable compressed position and publishes its `candidate_topk_blocks` best blocks of 8, the layers after it score and select only inside those blocks.
- `candidate_indexer.py`: `IndexerInputs` as the per-layer operand bundle, `make_candidate_indexer`, and the mask helpers (`CandidateMasks`, `select_candidate_blocks`, `mask_topk_scores`) the Hopper decode and prefill paths select through.
- `candidate_indexer_deep_gemm.py`: `DeepGemmCandidateIndexer` (`publish_decode` / `select_decode`), the Blackwell implementation on DeepGEMM's paged sparse MQA logits. Publishing runs the block selection (`candidate_row_lens`, `amax8_varlen`, `sort_candidate_blocks`, DeepGEMM schedule) on a side stream behind the layer's own top-k; the published `SparseBlockTable` carries a `ready` event and `record_stream`s its buffers for the main-stream consumers.
- `indexer.py`: `deep_gemm_fp4_paged_mqa_logits` and `topk_transform_paged_from_metadata` join the existing wrapper block; existing definitions unchanged.
- `configurer.py`: `DEEPGEMM_PAGED_SPARSE_MQA_LOGITS` probes the installed DeepGEMM for `get_paged_sparse_mqa_logits_metadata` / `fp8_fp4_paged_sparse_mqa_logits`; on Blackwell `make_candidate_indexer` requires them (sgl-deep-gemm 0.2.0, the pinned version, has both) instead of falling back.

title: [DSV4.1] Use native 16-head attention for small TP4 decode batches
author: BBuf
body:
## Motivation

For DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash TP4 decode, each rank has 16 actual attention heads, but the current FlashMLA path receives a query buffer padded to 64 heads. Small DSpark verify batches also leave little parallel work when KV tiles are processed sequentially.

This PR adds a native 16-head Blackwell attention path for small query batches. On 4×GB300, BS1 decode speed increases from **1074.8 to 1153.3 tok/s** in one independent start pair and **1046.2 to 1166.6 tok/s** in another, using fixed 4K/1K requests and simulated mean acceptance length 5.5. Real-acceptance model evaluations and the C64 regression comparison are reported below.

## Modifications

- Put the real heads on the MMA **N** dimension, using Gluon `tcgen05_mma`:

  ```text
  K[64, 512] @ Q.T[512, 16] -> scores[64, 16]
  V.T[512, 64] @ P[64, 16] -> partial[512, 16]
  ```

  One CTA handles one query and one 64-token KV split. A second Triton kernel merges the FP32 partial numerator, maximum and denominator, and includes the attention sink exactly once. The caller's allocation can remain padded; the MMA computes only the 16 real heads.
- Read the existing V4 packed cache directly: 448 FP8 channels with UE8M0 scales, plus 64 BF16 RoPE channels. Respect physical page strides, sparse token indices and per-query valid lengths, including the optional extra cache.
- Represent softmax probabilities as a BF16 high part plus a BF16 residual for two PV products. Keep FP32 accumulation and partials, the existing BF16 attention-output boundary, and the existing separate inverse-RoPE operation. This changes floating-point evaluation order and is **not bitwise equivalent to FlashMLA**.
- Dispatch only for SM100/SM103, 16 actual heads, BF16 Q, head/value dimensions 512, the existing scale `512**-0.5`, V4 cache layout (584 bytes/token), and **1–8 query tokens** in decode, target-verify or draft-extend-v2 mode. This token limit is not a request-concurrency limit. Other shapes and layouts retain the existing dispatch. V4.1 FP8/FP4 cache layouts and 64-head DPA are outside this fast path. No new environment variables.
- Add packed-cache, masking, sink, physical-stride and dynamic CUDA Graph replay tests against an independent FP64 reference.

The speedup comes from both avoiding padded-head computation and parallelizing KV tiles. In the pinned FlashMLA build, SM100 disables split-KV when `topk + extra_topk <= 640`; all 32 captured inputs fall in that range. This implementation instead processes 64-token splits in parallel and merges them.

## Accuracy Tests

All model-score tests below use **real DSpark acceptance**, concurrency 1, identical frozen prompts/evaluators and the same model/package environment for both versions. Synthetic acceptance is disabled.

| Evaluation | Baseline | Candidate |
|---|---:|---:|
| GSM8K, 5-shot, all 1,314 held-out questions, temperature 0 | 1,280/1,314 | 1,281/1,314 |
| AIME26, temperature 0, three server-seed blocks | 85/90 | 86/90 |
| AIME26, temperature 1, four full rounds per server-seed block | 348/360 | 350/360 |

The AIME totals repeat the **same 30 questions**, not 90/360 independent questions. All AIME runs use a 65,536-token output limit, `top_p=0.95`, and the same thinking/reasoning settings. GSM8K uses a 4,096-token output limit.

Full AIME breakdown, including the initial unfavorable sampling result:

| Server seed | Greedy baseline → candidate | Four sampling rounds baseline → candidate |
|---|---:|---:|
| 42, initial comparison | 28 → 29 / 30 | **119 → 117 / 120** |
| 43 | 29 → 29 / 30 | 117 → 117 / 120 |
| 44 | 28 → 28 / 30 | 112 → 116 / 120 |

The initial sampling decrease triggered diagnostics and a fixed follow-up plan, written before the new requests: baseline 43, candidate 43, candidate 44, baseline 44. All 20 follow-up lanes completed; no question removal, seed replacement, early stopping, or candidate code change. The initial block ran GSM8K before AIME, whereas the follow-up blocks started with AIME, so their RNG histories differ.

All requests completed without request errors. Truncations remain counted as incorrect: GSM8K 1/1, AIME greedy 4/4, AIME sampling 11/10 (baseline/candidate). Changed answers and finish reasons were reviewed. Request seeds do not pin DSpark's global CUDA RNG sequence; `SGLANG_SPEC_TP_SYNC=rng` synchronizes ranks, not independent requests. These are repeated sampling evaluations, not common-random-number paired trials.

**No aggregate score regression was observed over the complete fixed evaluation. Individual answers and per-start scores vary; these results do not establish universal accuracy equivalence.**

Operator validation:

- 32 captured serving inputs: finite outputs and 100 static CUDA Graph replays each. Compensated output error is close to the BF16 output-rounding floor against an independent FP64 oracle.
- Both new GPU test methods pass, without skips. Coverage includes query counts 1/5/6/8, varied page sizes, extra-cache sizes up to 1,024, partial tiles, empty rows, invalid indices, poisoned padding, strided metadata, attention sinks, and 12 replays with changing queries/indices/lengths.
- Compute Sanitizer **memcheck and synccheck: 0 errors**, both executing the two GPU test methods.

```bash
PYTHONPATH=python python test/registered/kernel/attention/dsv4/test_swapab_attention.py
PYTHONPATH=python compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck --error-exitcode 1 \
  python test/registered/kernel/attention/dsv4/test_swapab_attention.py
PYTHONPATH=python compute-sanitizer --tool synccheck --error-exitcode 1 \
  python test/registered/kernel/attention/dsv4/test_swapab_attention.py
```

## Speed Tests and Profiling

**BS1:** 4×GB300, TP4/EP1, fixed 4,096 input / 1,024 output tokens, DSpark block size 5, static verify, simulated acceptance target 5.5 (`match-expected`), `SGLANG_SPEC_TP_SYNC=rng`. Each fresh server start has one warmup and six measured requests, flushing the cache before each request. Profiling is separate from timing.

| Independent start pair | Baseline median tok/s | Candidate median tok/s | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 1,074.79 | 1,153.28 | +7.30% |
| B | 1,046.21 | 1,166.58 | +11.51% |

The metric is `(final completion tokens - tokens in first streamed event) / (last event time - first event time)`, excluding TTFT. Requests use temperature 0 and `ignore_eos=true`. Acceptance 5.5 is a target mean, not a literal per-cycle token count. The six measurements within a start are not six independent starts.

Captured-input microbenchmarks: long target attention is approximately 19–20 µs → 9 µs; target SWA is approximately 8.7 µs → 7.7 µs. Short first-token inputs have little improvement. A serving trace of 20 verify cycles contains 860 partial kernels, 860 combine kernels and 860 existing inverse-RoPE kernels, confirming 43 attention invocations per cycle use the intended path.

**C64 regression check:** TP4/EP4, simulated acceptance 5.4, 1,024 fixed 4K/1K requests per start, concurrency 64, 64 warmup requests, identical frozen benchmark client, four fresh starts in ABBA order. All 4,096 requests succeeded with the intended lengths.

| Start | Output tok/s | Median TTFT (ms) | Median TPOT (ms) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Baseline A | 7,894.56 | 2,558.43 | 5.56498 |
| Candidate A | 7,903.22 | 2,564.12 | 5.57230 |
| Candidate B | 7,901.31 | 2,564.36 | 5.56415 |
| Baseline B | 7,885.24 | 2,569.24 | 5.58879 |

Two-start mean throughput changes +0.157%; the mean of start-median TTFTs changes +0.016%. No material regression observed; these differences are not evidence of a C64 speedup.

<details>
<summary>BS1 server command and tested versions</summary>

Run from the repository root in a clean benchmark environment; set `MODEL_PATH` to the local DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash checkpoint. The default V4 KV layout is used.

```bash
export MODEL_PATH=/path/to/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
export SGLANG_RAGGED_VERIFY_MODE=static
export SGLANG_SIMULATE_ACC_LEN=5.5
export SGLANG_SIMULATE_ACC_METHOD=match-expected
export SGLANG_SPEC_TP_SYNC=rng
```

title: [Kernel] Coalesce the KDA CuTe DSL decode state transpose: ~3x faster, bit-identical
author: yekerr
body:
## Motivation

The CuTe DSL KDA decode kernels (`kda_kernel_small_batch`, `kda_kernel_small_batch_varlen`,
`kda_kernel_large_batch`, `kda_kernel_large_batch_varlen` in
`python/sglang/kernels/ops/attention/cutedsl_kda.py`) stage the recurrent state through shared
memory with a `global (V, K) <-> shared (K, V)` transpose, once to load the state and once to write it
back. The thread -> element mapping for that transpose uses **V as the fast-varying index**:

```python
k_load = flat_idx // TILE_V
v_load = flat_idx % TILE_V
```

But the state tensor is `(pool_size, HV, V, K)` with **K contiguous** and V strided by
`K * sizeof(fp32) = 512 B`. So the 32 lanes of a warp hit 32 *different* 32-byte sectors and use
4 bytes out of each one — roughly 28 sectors per request where ~4 is the ideal for 32 x 4 B. The
same strided pattern is repeated on the write-back. Since the decode step is state-bandwidth-bound
(every token reads and writes the full fp32 `[HV, V, K]` state), this dominates kernel time.

## Modifications

Swap the two index expressions in each of the 8 transpose sites (one load pair + one write-back pair
per kernel variant) so that **K is the fast-varying index**:

```diff
-                    k_load = flat_idx // TILE_V
-                    v_load = flat_idx % TILE_V
+                    k_load = flat_idx % TILE_K
+                    v_load = flat_idx // TILE_K
```

(`TILE_V_SMALL` -> `TILE_K` in the two small-batch kernels, `TILE_V` -> `TILE_K` in the two
large-batch kernels; the `k_write` / `v_write` pairs change identically.)

`flat_idx` ranges over exactly `[0, TILE_K * TILE_V)` in every loop, so both the old and the new
expression are bijections onto the same `(k, v)` tile: the same elements land in the same shared-memory
slots, the existing `if k_load < TILE_K` guards and `v_global < v.shape[3]` bounds checks are
untouched, and no barrier, loop trip count or arithmetic order changes. Consequently the kernel's
**output tensor and the in-place fp32 state update are bit-identical** before and after (verified
below). Nothing else in the file is modified (16 lines, 8 two-line pairs).

Now a warp's 32 lanes read/write 32 consecutive fp32 along K = 128 contiguous bytes = 4 sectors.

### Known tradeoff (shared memory)

The new mapping trades a global-memory win for a shared-memory regression in the transpose itself.
`TILE_V_PADDED = 36` was chosen so the *compute* loop is bank-conflict-free: there a warp covers
`8 k x 4 v` (`k_local = in_warp_tid // V_PER_WARP`, `v_local = in_warp_tid % V_PER_WARP`), and
bank `(36*k + v) % 32 = (4*k + v) % 32` hits 32 distinct banks. In the transpose, however, the new
mapping walks 32 consecutive `k` at fixed `v`, and `(4*k + v) % 32` takes only 8 distinct values —
a 4-way bank conflict on the staging loads/stores. Nsight Compute confirms it (b=32, large-batch
kernel): shared-load bank conflicts 29.6 K -> 4.74 M, shared-store 5.7 K -> 4.74 M, LSU shared
wavefronts 10.9 M -> 15.6 M (ld) and 3.3 M -> 8.0 M (st). The kernel is still ~3x faster end to end,
which bounds the cost of the shared side.

No single padding constant fixes both patterns: the transpose wants `gcd(P, 32) = 1` (odd `P`), the
compute loop wants `P == 4 (mod 32)`. The remaining lever is a swizzled shared-memory layout or a
128-bit vectorized load of 4 consecutive `k` per thread — not a padding tweak. Left as a follow-up to
keep this PR a pure, bit-identical index swap.

## Accuracy Tests

Because the change is a permutation of the thread -> element assignment with no arithmetic change,
the expected result is bit-exactness, and that is what is observed.

A standalone check ran `cutedsl_fused_sigmoid_gating_kda_update` on the stock and patched kernel
across 9 cases covering all four kernel variants, three input classes, and the `pool_idx < 0` pad
path, hashing (sha256) the raw bytes of the bf16 output and of the updated fp32 state, and also
comparing both arms to an independent from-scratch fp32 PyTorch reference of the recurrent step
(`H=HV=96`, `K=128`, non-zero initial state so the load half of the transpose is exercised):

| case | kernel variant | inputs | out sha256 equal | state sha256 equal | rel err vs fp32 ref (out / state) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| b=32,  dv=128 | dense large-batch | randn | yes | yes | 3.1e-3 / 6.6e-4 |
| b=128, dv=128 | dense large-batch | randn | yes | yes | 2.9e-3 / 6.3e-4 |
| b=32,  dv=256 | dense large-batch | randn | yes | yes | 2.3e-3 / 6.7e-4 |
| b=16,  dv=128 | dense small-batch | randn | yes | yes | 3.8e-3 / 6.3e-4 |
| b=64,  dv=128 | varlen large-batch | randn | yes | yes | 2.9e-3 / 6.6e-4 |
| b=8,   dv=128 | varlen small-batch | randn | yes | yes | 2.3e-3 / 6.7e-4 |
| b=32,  dv=128 | dense large-batch | all zeros | yes | yes | 0 / 1.0e-3 |
| b=32,  dv=128 | dense large-batch | range stress (q, k magnitude ~64; v ~256; g from -1e-6 to -40; beta from 1e-6 to 1-1e-6) | yes | yes | 3.2e-3 / 1.6e-6 |
| b=32,  dv=128 | dense large-batch | randn + every 7th `pool_idx = -1` | yes | yes | 2.8e-3 / 5.9e-4 |

All 9 cases: output **and** state bit-identical stock vs patched; reference errors are identical on
both arms (bf16 output rounding), all values finite.

Existing CI coverage of this kernel is thinner than the file name suggests — no registered test calls
`cutedsl_fused_sigmoid_gating_kda_update`:

- `test/registered/kernels/ops/attention/test_kda_fused_decode.py` exercises the Triton `fla.fused_recurrent` decode path, not this kernel;
- `test/registered/attention/test_kda_prefill_cutedsl.py` covers the CuTe DSL *prefill* kernel (4-gpu-b200 suite);
- the GDN sibling `test_cutedsl_gdn.py` currently has its precision test skipped.

I have not run the sglang test suite locally. If maintainers want in-tree coverage for the decode kernel, I can add
`test/registered/kernels/ops/attention/test_cutedsl_kda.py` (CuTe DSL decode vs. the Triton `fused_sigmoid_gating_recurrent`
reference, modeled on `test_cutedsl_gdn.py`) to this PR or as a follow-up.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Kernel-only timing via CUPTI (10 warmup + 10 timed launches per config), bf16, `dqk = dv = 128`,
`qo_len = 1`, recurrent decode step, single-GPU. `h = 96` (Kimi-K3). All rows are within-box A/B comparisons with **unlocked SM clocks**; the A/B/A protocol
(stock -> patched -> stock) bounds the clock/thermal noise (A-vs-A drift <= 0.03 % on every row,
orders of magnitude below the effect).

The numbers come from a standalone CUPTI harness rather than the in-tree
`benchmark/bench_linear_attention/bench_cutedsl_kda_decode.py` (#21203, Triton vs. CuTe DSL); I can append
that script's stock-vs-patched output on request.

### NVIDIA B200 PCIe

`h = 96`, `dv = 128`; median of 3 per phase.

| batch | stock (us) | patched (us) | delta | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 32  | 476.5  | 152.0  | -68.1 % | 3.14x |
| 128 | 1817.7 | 584.5  | -67.9 % | 3.11x |
| 512 | 7171.1 | 2309.5 | -67.8 % | 3.11x |

A wider sweep on the same B200 (`b in {1, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 512} x dv in {128, 256, 512}`, both
dense kernel variants) showed a consistent ~-67.8 %.

Only the two **dense** variants are exercised by these shapes (b >= 32 -> `kda_kernel_large_batch`;
the b=16 accuracy case -> `kda_kernel_small_batch`). The two **varlen** variants are covered by the
bit-exactness check above but were not timed; the same 8-lane swap applies to them and the access
pattern is identical.

### Mechanism (Nsight Compute)

B200, `b = 32`, `h = 96`, `kda_kernel_large_batch`, one profiled launch, `--cache-control all`.

| metric | stock | patched |
|---|---|---|
| global load sectors / request (`l1tex__average_t_sectors_per_request_pipe_lsu_mem_global_op_ld`) | 28.39 | 3.68 |
| global store sectors / request (`..._op_st`) | 30.18 | 3.82 |
| L1TEX sectors total (`l1tex__t_sectors.sum`) | 101.0 M | 12.9 M (7.8x fewer) |
| L1TEX throughput (% peak) | 83.75 | 65.79 |
| long-scoreboard stalls / issue | 17.48 | 4.10 |
| DRAM bytes read (`dram__bytes_read.sum`) | 204,564,736 | 204,542,208 (unchanged) |
| DRAM throughput (% peak) | 9.54 | 29.83 |
| registers / thread | 128 | 124 |
| kernel duration | 480.9 us | 151.7 us |

DRAM traffic is unchanged: the kernel already moved exactly the bytes the state-update model
predicts, it was just delivering them through ~8x more L1 sectors than necessary. The predicted
mechanism (sectors/request collapse, L1TEX pressure drops, DRAM bytes flat, DRAM utilization rises
toward the bandwidth roof) is what moved.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit). (`ruff format --check`, `ruff check --select=F401,F821,UP037`, `isort --check-only` and `codespell` at the pre-commit-pinned versions (ruff 0.15.1, isort 7.0.0, codespell 2.4.1) report no changes; `git diff --check` clean.)
- [ ] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests). (No new test in this revision; see Accuracy Tests for the current coverage gap of the CuTe DSL decode kernel. I can add `test_cutedsl_kda.py` on request.)
- [ ] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations). (N/A — kernel-internal change.)
- [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed).
- [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance).

title: [DSV4.1] Reduce mHC, metadata and small-batch router overhead
author: BBuf
body:
> Retargeted to `main` at `a6cf05817f11d22023fd951a76255ef50fb09f49`, after #38798 and #40039 landed. The diff contains only this PR's optimizations (15 files), including the router PDL change previously consolidated from #39941.
>
> Conflict resolution preserves main's `post_experts_all_reduce` topology handling and the DSPARK fused-argmax opt-in, while retaining the mHC overlap/fusion changes. Local validation: all pre-commit checks on the changed files passed, including Python syntax, Ruff, formatting, C++ formatting, and CI test registration. GPU correctness/performance measurements below are historical; they have not been rerun on this new main-based revision. CI is being triggered on the updated head.

## Motivation

DeepSeek-V4.1 DSpark verify batches at concurrency 32/64 contain up to 192/384 rows. This reduces mHC boundary, communication, indexer quantization and speculative metadata overhead for those workloads without changing the deployment command.

## Modifications

- Extend deferred MoE finalize/all-reduce to 384 rows using a separate communicator with 4 MiB push slots and 512 row counters. Fuse mHC post and next-input combine while preserving BF16 intermediates; medium batches retain the original standalone RMSNorm.
- Fuse supported prefill post/combine/RMSNorm and schedule mHC statistics on the existing model-wide stream immediately before sublayer all-reduce. Invalidate cross-layer inputs at Engram and row-selection boundaries.
- Batch FP4 indexer quantization by eight rows per CTA and reduce each 32-element scale group directly, retaining exact FP4 codes and UE8 scales.
- Extend integer metadata kernels to 384 rows and use a vocabulary-split argmax for medium speculative logits, preserving NaN/Inf and first-index tie behavior.

This builds on #39370. Compensated mHC and existing small-row paths are retained. There are no new environment variables or CLI flags, and no attention arithmetic changes. The experimental medium RMSNorm/MXFP8 fusion is excluded from this PR.

## Accuracy Tests

Unset both `SGLANG_SIMULATE_ACC_*` variables before launching each evaluation server; their absence is also verified in the serving process environment. All other deployment settings remain identical. Frozen prompts/datasets/clients are shared between arms. GSM8K: 1,314 held-out test problems after excluding five few-shot examples, temperature 0, seed 0, max output 4,096. AIME 2026: all 30 problems. GPQA Diamond: all 198 problems. AIME/GPQA: thinking enabled, reasoning effort max, temperature 0, seed 0, top_p 0.95, max output 65,536. Client concurrency is 64 (AIME has only 30 distinct requests). Two independent starts per arm, with all scores, truncations, request errors and per-question transitions retained.

Correct answers from **both** fresh-server runs (a / b):

| Suite | Base | Candidate | Mean accuracy: base → candidate | Difference |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| GSM8K, 1,314 problems | 1278 / 1278 | 1278 / 1277 | 97.260% → 97.222% | −0.038 pp |
| AIME 2026, 30 problems | 28 / 28 | 29 / 27 | 93.333% → 93.333% | 0 pp |
| GPQA Diamond, 198 problems | 174 / 165 | 166 / 171 | 85.606% → 85.101% | −0.505 pp |

All evaluation requests completed without errors. Output-limit truncations (a / b):

| Suite | Base | Candidate |
|---|---:|---:|
| GSM8K | 2 / 1 | 0 / 0 |
| AIME 2026 | 2 / 2 | 1 / 3 |
| GPQA Diamond | 15 / 18 | 19 / 17 |

The GPQA paired difference reverses from −8 to +6 questions; its two-run mean is one question lower, while the baseline itself varies by nine questions. This does **not** establish accuracy equivalence. Per-question inspection found 11 losses / 3 gains in pair a and 1 loss / 7 gains in pair b. GPQA question 8 was lost in both pairs with candidate truncation; two nontruncated wrong choices in pair a (85 and 127) are correct in candidate run b. All counts, including truncations, remain in the reported scores. All 198 GPQA problems are included in each run.

Additional real-acceptance control: submit the same frozen 4,096-token input IDs in one native `/generate` batch, temperature 0 / sampling seed 0, flush between two 1,024-token replays. Exact full-sequence matches:

| Batch | Base repeat 0 vs 1 | Candidate repeat 0 vs 1 | Base vs candidate, replay 0 / 1 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 32 | 25/32 | 25/32 | 25/32; 25/32 |
| 64 | 45/64 | 46/64 | 46/64; 46/64 |

The cross-version mismatch count is comparable to within-version variation in this control. Among sequences that are identical across both replays within **each** arm (25 at BS32 and 42 at BS64), none differ between arms. Grouped input reduces arrival differences but does not force identical physical batches at every decoding step; this is a token-sequence diagnostic on a frozen corpus, not an additional accuracy benchmark or proof of equivalence.

The earlier rebased head `c797adea1e` passed all 397 retained GPU test cases and a fresh-server real-acceptance check: BS32 and BS64, two grouped 1,024-token replays each, all requested prompts/output lengths verified and full-batch decode observed. Conflict-file pre-commit, syntax and CI registry checks also passed. The frozen A/B scores above are not relabeled as measurements of this rebased commit.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Output throughput, tokens/s; both measurements are retained:

| Concurrency | Base runs a / b | Candidate runs a / b | Base median | Candidate median | Gain |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 32 | 6111.52 / 6113.84 | 6436.61 / 6418.06 | 6112.68 | 6427.33 | **5.15%** |
| 64 | 7817.12 / 7833.92 | 8283.62 / 8263.03 | 7825.52 | 8273.32 | **5.72%** |

Every run completed all 1,024 requests and generated 1,048,576 output tokens. Even the slowest candidate exceeds the fastest baseline by 4.98% at C32 and 5.48% at C64.

Original CPU+GPU profiler traces were checked on all four ranks using launch correlation and 80 mHC sinkhorn anchors to identify a complete target graph. Kernel counts per target launch fall from 1,835 to 1,581 at C32 and from 1,834 to 1,580 at C64. Active CUDA streams stay **5 → 5** on every rank. The two profiled MoE BMM kernel names and their 40 calls each also match between arms. Profiled graph wall time is not used as serving latency.

### Performance protocol and command

TP4/EP4/DP1, unchanged static DSpark block size 5, simulated acceptance length 5.4. 1,024 measured requests, each 4,096 input / 1,024 output tokens, concurrency 32 or 64, matching warmup count, all output tokens required. Two fresh starts per arm/batch with reversed order on the repeat; retain every measurement. These throughput results use simulated acceptance and are separate from the real-acceptance accuracy evaluations.

Server (both arms):

```bash
export MODEL_PATH=/path/to/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3
export MAX_JOBS=16
export PYTHONPATH="$PWD/python"
export SGLANG_SPEC_TP_SYNC=rng
export SGLANG_RAGGED_VERIFY_MODE=static
export SGLANG_SIMULATE_ACC_LEN=5.4
export SGLANG_SIMULATE_ACC_METHOD=match-expected
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --trust-remote-code --model-path "$MODEL_PATH" \
  --served-model-name deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash \
  --tp 4 --ep-size 4 --mem-fraction-static 0.8 \
  --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --speculative-dspark-block-size 5 \
  --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 64 --reasoning-parser auto --tool-call-parser auto \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 30021
```

title: [HiCache] Add the page-unified KV load-back JIT kernel
author: Shunkangz
body:
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->

## Motivation
The load-back half of the page-unified HiCache layout, and the mirror of the staged write-back added in #39606. That PR writes a device pool out into host pages ordered

  MHA: (page, head_group, layer, 2, page_size, head_in_group, dim), K=0 V=1
  MLA: (page, layer, page_size, dim)

but stops at write-back; nothing could read those pages back. This kernel does, for one layer at a time.

Per-layer and unstaged, unlike its write-back mirror. The two directions are not symmetric in how the runtime drives them: write-back moves a whole page at once, so staging it on the device and handing the bulk copy to the copy engine costs nothing extra. Load-back is walked layer by layer by the L2 transfer engine, which unblocks the forward pass one layer at a time, so staging whole pages per layer would move num_layers times the bytes the layer actually needs. Instead the SMs read the pinned host mapping in place, the way every other layout's per-layer load already does.

Each thread moves 16 bytes; the linear index runs dim-fastest then item, so a warp's lanes read consecutive host bytes for the tokens of one (head group, layer, K/V) cell. The grid is capped by kBlockQuota as in HiCacheKernel: the load overlaps a forward pass, so extra blocks buy bandwidth by taking SMs from it.

Note that head_group == 1 is NOT page_first_direct's byte order -- the K/V axis sits inside the page block here, not outside the pool. The HG=1 cases in the test pin that.

Correctness: 123 cases pass on B200 -- 3 geometries x {uint8, fp16, bf16} x {int32, int64} indices x {0, 1, 8} tokens, for MHA and MLA, each sweeping every layer, compared for exact equality against a PyTorch-indexing reference including the rows that must keep their sentinel. Payload is seeded noise, not a counter: a counter is periodic in the layer stride, so a layer mix-up would compare equal.

Round-trip against #39606: running that PR's write-back and then this kernel over 9 configurations (including the head-cut cases) returns the device pool bit-identical, which is the actual contract between the pair.

Performance (B200, PCIe gen5, 61 layers x 8 kv heads x 128 dim, bf16, page_size 64, one layer of K+V, payload counted once):

block_quota | 1 group | 2 groups | 4 groups | 8 groups
-- | -- | -- | -- | --
2 | 15.4-16.2 GB/s | 16.2-17.1 GB/s | 16.7-17.8 GB/s | 17.3-18.2 GB/s
16 | 39.7-47.8 GB/s | 39.7-47.8 GB/s | 39.7-47.8 GB/s | 39.7-47.8 GB/s


against a 53.8 GB/s contiguous cudaMemcpyAsync ceiling. Bandwidth is flat in head-group count -- the run length does not matter, the grid cap does. The shipped default stays at 2; raising it is a measurement-led change that wants an end-to-end number, not a new-kernel PR.

title: [Fix] disaggregation: Clean-up and optimize the KV checksum implementation
author: ShangmingCai
body:
## Motivation

With `--disaggregation-enable-kv-checksum` on, a mismatch on one TP rank hangs the decode engine, and healthy traffic is aborted on several supported configurations. This PR fixes those paths so the flag can be turned on.

## Modifications

**All-reduce the mismatch decision.** Corruption is per rank, so a rank-local drop left the TP peers building different batches and hanging on the next collective. The drop set is MAX-reduced over `attn_tp_cpu_group` with `all_reduce_flags` before any request is aborted.

**Verify once.** The digest covers whole pages, and after a retraction the restored row's last page holds tokens the decode wrote, so re-verifying on resume was a false mismatch at `page_size > 1`. A request is digested when it first enters a batch and its expectation is then cleared.

**Ship a layout signature with the digest.** `kv_layout_signature(kv_args)` hashes the page size and the per-page KV and state item lengths; the prefill writes it into slot 1 of the `kv_checksum` row. A prefill with another TP width or a PP stage is admitted unverified with one warning instead of aborting every request. A prefill that wrote no digest is skipped silently.

**Refuse the decode-side radix cache.** The digest covers `[0, seq_len)` while the prefill then sends only `[decode_prefix_len, seq_len)`, so every prefix hit looks like corruption. The decode logs once at startup and runs without the checksum.

**Survive a metadata buffer count mismatch.** The aux buffers pair positionally, and the Mooncake and NIXL send loops walked the decode's list (Mori's TCP loop the prefill's), so an engine with one more buffer than its peer was an `IndexError` in a transfer thread. The loops stop at the shorter list and the prefill logs an error at registration naming the optional buffers that can differ. The decode resets the checksum row together with the bootstrap room when a metadata slot is freed, so a later occupant whose prefill writes no digest cannot read the previous one.

**Test hook.** `SGLANG_TEST_DISAGG_KV_CHECKSUM_MISMATCH_PROB` flips a decode rank's computed digest with that probability, drawn from a per-rank generator (the global `random` is seeded identically on every TP rank, so the ranks would otherwise inject the same requests). The in-CI raise is suppressed while it is set.

## Accuracy Tests

- `test/registered/unit/disaggregation/test_kv_checksum.py`: new cases for the signature, the slot reset, verify-once, the reduced drop set, the signature in the prefill's metadata write, and the injector not tripping the in-CI raise. The CPU-only cases pass on a CPU box; the CUDA cases need a runner.
- `test/registered/disaggregation/test_disaggregation_kv_checksum.py` (new, `base-c` / `4-gpu-h100`): TP2 on both sides, because at TP1 the reduce is a no-op. Mismatches injected per decode rank at p=0.3 over 16 requests with a multi-chunk prompt: some must abort, some must complete, and both engines must stay up.

No GPU here; the CUDA unit cases and the e2e test need a runner.

title: Skip fully-masked KV tiles in sliding-window extend attention
author: jiaqiang-dot-liu
body:
## Motivation

On a sliding-window layer, the stage-2 loop in `_fwd_kernel` sweeps the extend KV from 0:

```python
for start_n in range(0, extend_end, BLOCK_N):
```

The window mask inside that loop keeps `(q, kv)` only when `q <= kv + SLIDING_WINDOW_SIZE`, so every tile lying entirely below `cur_block_m * BLOCK_M - SLIDING_WINDOW_SIZE` is fully masked and contributes nothing.

Those tiles do not read K/V and do not run the dot — `SKIP_TILE` already guards that. What they still pay, once per tile, is the cost of establishing that they contribute nothing: building `final_mask` (the causal compare, the window compare, the `&`), and then the `[BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N]` cross-wave `tl.max` reduction that computes `SKIP_TILE` itself.

On a long extend with a small window that is the majority of the loop. At `extend_len = 8192` and `W = 127`, the last M block's floor sits at roughly `8192 - 127`, so almost every iteration is spent proving that the tile is empty.

### Where this kernel runs by default

The Triton backend is the default attention backend, without any flag, for:

- **Gemma 4** (`Gemma4ForConditionalGeneration`): its model override selects `triton` whenever `--attention-backend` is unset, on ROCm and on CUDA other than SM100 (which gets `trtllm_mha`). The server logs `Use triton as default attention backend for Gemma4`. 25 of the 30 layers of `gemma-4-26B-A4B-it` are sliding-window layers (`W = 1024`, `head_dim = 256`).
- **OLMo 3** (served as `Olmo2ForCausalLM`) and **EXAONE 4.0** checkpoints with a sliding-window pattern (e.g. `EXAONE-4.0-32B`): `triton` by default on ROCm and on CUDA below SM80.

It also runs for any sliding-window model served with `--attention-backend triton`.

## Modifications

Start the loop at the `BLOCK_N`-aligned tile that contains the window floor:

```python
extend_start = 0
if SLIDING_WINDOW_SIZE > 0:
    extend_start = (
        tl.maximum(cur_block_m * BLOCK_M - SLIDING_WINDOW_SIZE, 0) // BLOCK_N
    ) * BLOCK_N
for start_n in range(extend_start, extend_end, BLOCK_N):
```

The bound is derived from the mask predicate rather than estimated. The kernel returns early when `cur_block_m * BLOCK_M >= cur_seq_len_extend`, so `offs_m = 0` is always a live row and the smallest query index in the block is exactly `m0 = cur_block_m * BLOCK_M`. A skipped tile satisfies `start_n + BLOCK_N <= floor_aligned <= m0 - W`, hence its largest key index `start_n + BLOCK_N - 1 < m0 - W`, so the window mask is false for every one of its elements.

It is also tight at tile granularity: the preceding tile would need `floor_aligned >= m0 - W + 1` to hold a surviving element, which contradicts `floor_aligned <= m0 - W`. Nothing that can contribute is skipped, for any `BLOCK_M`/`BLOCK_N`.

`SLIDING_WINDOW_SIZE` is a `tl.constexpr`, so a full-attention layer loses the branch at trace time and its loop is unchanged. `extend_start` is a multiple of `BLOCK_N`, so `tl.multiple_of(start_n, BLOCK_N)` stays valid. A custom mask or the non-causal path only adds conjuncts, which narrow the mask further, so the bound remains sound there. Under the HIP compact grid `cur_block_m` is still the per-sequence tile index, so the derivation is unaffected.

`test/registered/attention/unittests/swa/test_triton.py` gains three cases with extend lengths above `BLOCK_M` and windows below it — no prefix; a prefix with a window that is not a tile multiple; a window landing exactly on a tile boundary — so some query tile starts past the window and the bound takes effect. Every pre-existing SWA extend case keeps the extend length under `BLOCK_M`, where the loop always starts at tile 0.

## Accuracy Tests

MI355X (gfx950, 256 CU), ROCm 7.2.0, torch 2.9.1, Triton 3.7.0. sglang `main` @ `7ff3a11284` with `sglang-kernel` 0.4.9 built from the same tree and transformers 5.19.0.

**Unit tests.** `test/registered/attention/unittests/swa/test_triton.py` and `.../dense/test_triton.py`: 15 passed, 2 skipped, 58 subtests passed.

**Kernel output is bitwise identical.** 21 configurations (12 sliding-window, 4 full-attention, 5 where the bound never fires) at `B=32, H_Q=64, H_KV=8, D=128`, bf16, causal. Each run hashes its inputs as well as `o_extend`, so the output comparison is only accepted when the inputs provably matched: **21/21 inputs identical, 21/21 outputs bitwise identical.**

**End to end, `gemma-4-26B-A4B-it`, default server args** (no `--attention-backend`; the server resolves `triton`):

- Greedy parity: 32 chat requests sent one at a time to a `main` server and a server with this PR, prompts of 3,968–18,164 tokens (all longer than the 1024-token window, so the bound fires), 128 output tokens, temperature 0. **Outputs identical: 32/32.**
- GSM8K, `python -m sglang.test.run_eval --eval-name gsm8k` (chat API, 5-shot, greedy), all 1319 questions, two runs per server:

| | Run 1 | Run 2 |
|---|---|---|
| `main` | 0.960 | 0.959 |
| This PR | 0.954 | 0.956 |

The per-question standard deviation is 0.20, so the standard error of one run is about 0.0055 and the gap is within run-to-run noise. Concurrent batches change the numerics of other kernels between runs; the parity check above runs one request at a time and shows identical outputs.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

### Kernel

`triton.testing.do_bench(warmup=100ms, rep=500ms, return_mode="median")`, minimum over 7 repetitions, one idle GPU. Inputs come from `_build_batch` in `benchmark/kernels/sliding_window_attention_triton/bench_triton_swa_kernel.py`; `extend_attention_fwd` is called the way `triton_backend` calls it, including `extend_seq_lens_cpu`, so the HIP compact ragged grid is exercised. (That file's own `_run_triton` predates the `k_scale`/`v_scale` parameters, and `sglang.benchmark.bench_utils` imports `flashinfer`, which has no ROCm build.) The baseline was measured before and after this PR; **maximum run-to-run drift was 0.30%**.

| N_CTX | window | `main` (ms) | This PR (ms) | Delta |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8192 | 127 | 16.8079 | 10.2546 | **−39.0%** |
| 8192 | 256 | 17.8121 | 11.8463 | **−33.5%** |
| 8192 | 512 | 19.8016 | 14.9416 | **−24.5%** |
| 4096 | 127 | 6.0625 | 4.4068 | −27.3% |
| 4096 | 256 | 6.5597 | 5.1879 | −20.9% |
| 4096 | 512 | 7.6096 | 6.6472 | −12.6% |
| 2048 | 127 | 2.0704 | 1.7548 | −15.2% |
| 2048 | 256 | 2.3996 | 2.1685 | −9.6% |
| 2048 | 512 | 2.9883 | 2.8848 | −3.5% |
| 1024 | 127 | 0.7139 | 0.6697 | −6.2% |
| 1024 | 256 | 0.8551 | 0.8332 | −2.6% |
| 1024 | 512 | 1.0639 | 1.0535 | −1.0% |

The gain tracks the fraction of the loop below the floor: it grows with sequence length and shrinks with the window.

**Full-attention control.** At `sliding_window_size = -1` the branch is constexpr-eliminated:

| N_CTX | `main` (ms) | This PR (ms) | Delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1024 | 0.6606 | 0.6597 | −0.1% |
| 2048 | 2.4420 | 2.4376 | −0.2% |
| 4096 | 8.1296 | 8.1287 | −0.0% |
| 8192 | 22.9057 | 22.9425 | +0.2% |

All within drift. Full-attention models and the global-attention layers of hybrid models are unaffected.

**Where the bound never fires.** A sliding-window layer whose every M block satisfies `m0 <= W`: `extend_start` evaluates to 0, the trip count is unchanged, and the computation still runs. `_build_batch` draws extend lengths from `randint(1, N_CTX // 2)`, so `W >= N_CTX / 2` makes the bound inert (`max_len_extend <= W` checked per configuration). Drift 0.47%.

| N_CTX | window | max_len_extend | `main` (ms) | This PR (ms) | Delta |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1024 | 1024 | 466 | 1.1159 | 1.1043 | −1.0% |
| 1024 | 2048 | 466 | 1.1189 | 1.1059 | −1.2% |
| 2048 | 2048 | 913 | 4.3393 | 4.2786 | −1.4% |
| 4096 | 4096 | 1884 | 14.9175 | 14.6701 | −1.7% |
| 8192 | 8192 | 4072 | 42.4523 | 41.9583 | −1.2% |

No configuration regresses. The small consistent gain is above drift, but I do not have an explanation for it, so I am reporting it rather than claiming it.

**Register pressure.** Compiled AMDGCN at `N_CTX=8192, W=127`:

```
sgpr_count:        106 -> 106
vgpr_count:        204 -> 204
sgpr_spill_count:   76 ->  80
vgpr_spill_count:    0 ->   0
shared:          16384 -> 16384
```

Four more SGPR spills. They do not show up in any measurement here, but I would rather flag them than assert the bound is free.

### End to end: prefill latency

`gemma-4-26B-A4B-it`, `python -m sglang.bench_one_batch` with default server args (the attention backend resolves to `triton`), `--output-len 4`, one MI355X. Minimum of 4 alternating runs per arm.

| Batch | Input len | `main` (s) | This PR (s) | Delta |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2048 | 0.0505 | 0.0496 | −1.7% |
| 1 | 8192 | 0.2064 | 0.1952 | −5.4% |
| 1 | 16384 | 0.5389 | 0.4952 | **−8.1%** |
| 1 | 32768 | 1.5027 | 1.3333 | **−11.3%** |
| 4 | 2048 | 0.1584 | 0.1571 | −0.8% |
| 4 | 8192 | 0.7822 | 0.7470 | −4.5% |
| 4 | 16384 | 1.9825 | 1.8370 | **−7.3%** |

This is whole-model prefill, MoE included, so the attention-only share of the gain is larger. The 2048 rows are small because the sliding layers have `head_dim = 256`, so `BLOCK_M = 128` here, and against a 1024 window the bound only starts skipping tiles at `cur_block_m >= 9`, i.e. for query tiles from token 1152 on.

### End to end: serving

Same model and default server args (`chunked_prefill_size = 16384`). `python -m sglang.bench_serving --backend sglang --dataset-name random-ids --random-range-ratio 1.0 --random-output-len 16`, 16 prompts at concurrency 1 and 32 at concurrency 4, prefix cache flushed before each run. The `main` and PR servers ran on two separate MI355X GPUs; the run was repeated with the GPU assignment swapped, and the table reports the mean of the two rounds.

| Input len | Concurrency | Median TTFT `main` (ms) | Median TTFT this PR (ms) | Delta | Input throughput |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8192 | 1 | 237.2 | 226.1 | −4.7% | +1.7% |
| 8192 | 4 | 897.9 | 841.6 | −6.3% | +6.6% |
| 16384 | 1 | 604.5 | 559.3 | −7.5% | +6.0% |
| 16384 | 4 | 1947.0 | 1890.9 | −2.9% | +7.8% |
| 32768 | 1 | 1378.3 | 1293.2 | −6.2% | +5.4% |
| 32768 | 4 | 4153.0 | 3872.2 | −6.8% | +6.9% |

A 32k prompt is prefilled in two 16k chunks here, so its gain is smaller than the single 32k extend in `bench_one_batch`. At concurrency 4 the median TTFT includes queueing and varies between rounds (−6.9% and +1.2% at 16k); input throughput is the steadier measure there.

### Reproduce

```bash
MODEL=google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it

# prefill latency
python -m sglang.bench_one_batch --model-path $MODEL \
  --batch-size 1 4 --input-len 2048 8192 16384 --output-len 4

# serving
python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path $MODEL --port 30000
python -m sglang.bench_serving --backend sglang --port 30000 --model $MODEL \
  --dataset-name random-ids --random-input-len 16384 --random-output-len 16 \
  --random-range-ratio 1.0 --num-prompts 16 --max-concurrency 1

# accuracy
python -m sglang.test.run_eval --port 30000 --eval-name gsm8k --num-examples 1319
```

Only MI355X was measured. The change is not ROCm-specific, so CUDA runs of the Triton backend take the same bound; their correctness is covered by the unit tests above in CI.

title: tokenizer perf optimization
author: BingooYang
body:
## Motivation

`OpenAIServingBase.handle_request` performs request conversion inline on the serving event loop. That conversion is not cheap: for `/v1/chat/completions` it runs the message processor and the chat template (jinja) and produces the full tokenized prompt. For a 100k+ token prompt this occupies the event loop for hundreds of milliseconds.

While the loop is blocked, everything else the server is doing stalls with it:

- new connections are not accepted,
- already-open streaming responses are not flushed, so unrelated in-flight requests see their inter-token latency spike,
- health/liveness endpoints sharing the loop stop responding.

The component that does the heavy part is the Rust tokenizer, which releases the GIL while encoding, so this work can genuinely overlap with the event loop instead of serializing behind it. The jinja render is still Python and still competes for the GIL, but the loop keeps running instead of waiting for the whole conversion to finish.

## Modifications

Single file, `python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/openai/serving_base.py`:

- In `handle_request`, `_convert_to_internal_request` is now awaited through `loop.run_in_executor(None, ...)` instead of being called inline.

The conversion logic itself is untouched, and the returned `adapted_request` /`processed_request` are the same objects as before — only the thread they are produced on changes. The surrounding flow is unchanged: validation still runs on the loop, `received_time` is still stamped before dispatch, and the streaming / non-streaming branches below are unaffected. The default executor is used, matching the existing pattern in `http_request_decompression.py`.

## Accuracy Tests

Not applicable. This PR does not touch the model forward path, kernels, sampling, or the tokenizer itself. The same conversion runs on the same inputs, so model outputs are unchanged; the only difference is which thread executes it.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Deployment: DeepSeek-V4-Flash, PD-disaggregated `dwdp` serving config,
`--max-running-requests 480`.

Workload: long-context, average input length 265k tokens.

- QPS: **+3%** with this patch (same node, same server args).

The gain comes from the event loop no longer serializing on prompt conversion: with 265k-token inputs, jinja rendering plus full-prompt tokenization holds the loop for long enough that accepting new requests and flushing in-flight streams are both delayed, so the server is not saturated on the compute side even at max-running-requests 480.

3. Trigger CI tests with [comments](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#how-to-trigger-ci-tests) or contact authorized users to do so.
