title: [Perf] [XPU] diffusion: Use the AOT SYCL fused residual-norm-scale-shift kernel
author: ckvermaAI
body:
## Motivation

On XPU, `ScaleResidualLayerNormScaleShift.forward_xpu` runs a triton kernel that blocks regional `torch.compile` of a Wan2.2 DiT block. Inductor re-lowers the kernel and Intel triton fails to compile the result:

```
triton/backends/intel/compiler.py: make_llir -> RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed
```

This happens in the first denoise step, so compiled Wan2.2 cannot run on XPU today. sgl-kernel-xpu ships an AOT SYCL kernel for the same op (sgl-project/sgl-kernel-xpu#497), in the `sglang-kernel-xpu` 0.4.0 wheel already pinned in `pyproject_xpu.toml`. It is a registered custom op, so inductor keeps it opaque and compiled regions call it unchanged.

## Modifications

- `kernels/ops/diffusion/norm/scale_residual_norm_scale_shift_sycl.py` (new): the SYCL backend, exported through the `ops.diffusion` facade.
  - `can_use_fused_scale_residual_norm_scale_shift_sycl` reuses the triton eligibility check for shape, device and contiguity, and adds the kernel's dtype rule. Gate, weight and bias must share one dtype. Scale and shift are cast to it only when the cast is exact (same dtype, or an upcast to fp32); any other mix stays on triton.
  - `fused_scale_residual_norm_scale_shift_sycl` calls `torch.ops.sgl_kernel` directly, so operands are validated once by the op's C++ checks.
  - A `register_fake` companion lets Dynamo trace the op, since sgl-kernel-xpu registers only the XPU implementation.
- `layernorm.py`: `forward_xpu` prefers the SYCL kernel, then triton, then `forward_native`. The import sits in the existing `_is_xpu` block next to `fused_inplace_qknorm_rope`, so other platforms never load it.

No model code changes. Wan's self-attention site passes bf16 1-element null shift/scale next to an fp32 gate and fp32 affine parameters. The exact upcast keeps that site on the SYCL path, so other devices see no change.

## Accuracy Tests

<!-- Wan2.2-I2V-A14B, same command and seed as the speed tests. Outputs compared frame by frame:

| Comparison | Result |
|---|---|
| Same commit, two runs (before, and after) | bit-identical |
| Before (triton) vs after (SYCL), eager | 29.5 dB PSNR, pixel std 65.7 in both |
| After, compiled vs eager | 30.8 dB PSNR, pixel std 65.7 in both |

The cross-backend gap is expected numerical drift between two fp32-math kernels over 20 denoise steps, not a quality change. At the kernel level, at the Wan shape `[1, 17160, 5120]` bf16 with fp32 parameters, the max abs error against `forward_native` is 0.062 on `y` and 0.053 on the residual output.
-->

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Wan2.2-I2V-A14B, TP=4 on 4x Arc Pro B60, 832x480 resolution, 21 frames, 20 steps, warm caches, first run of the session discarded:

```bash
CCL_ZE_IPC_EXCHANGE=pidfd sglang generate \
  --model-path Wan-AI/Wan2.2-I2V-A14B-Diffusers --num-gpus 4 --tp-size 4 \
  --text-encoder-cpu-offload --pin-cpu-memory \
  --image-path <i2v_input.JPG> --prompt "<prompt>" \
  --height 480 --width 832 --num-frames 21 --num-inference-steps 20 --seed 42 \
  [--enable-torch-compile --regional-compile]   # SGLANG_TORCH_COMPILE_MODE=default
```

| Mode | Denoise before (s) | Denoise after (s) |
|---|---|---|
| eager | 100.43 / 100.10 | 100.10 / 100.05 |
| regional compile | fails at step 0 | 82.74 / 82.74 |

- Eager is unchanged. Both kernels cost about 1.8 ms per call on the GPU at the Wan shape, and the host queues all steps well ahead of the device.
- Regional compile now runs, and its denoise time is 17% below eager (1.21x).
- Compiled end-to-end time is still higher than eager because `--enable-torch-compile` also compiles `vae.decode`. That is unrelated to this PR.

## Motivation

`prepare_mlp` tries fused kernels that complete the attention output's all-reduce together with the residual add and the post-attention norm. The candidates were bare callables:
- what each one completes was stated only in a docstring;
- aux hidden-state capture learned whether a kernel may return a new residual by checking whether the base entry's bound method was in the list.

## Modifications

- **New `FusedMlpInput`** (msgspec struct) for each candidate:
  - `completes`: the group whose sum it completes;
  - `run`: the kernel;
  - `may_return_new_residual`: whether it may hand back a new residual.

  `run(hidden_states, residual, forward_batch)` returns None only before it touches its inputs or starts a collective.
- **`_select_mlp_input_fusions()`** returns these entries:
  - the base aiter / flashinfer entry completes `SumGroup.ATTN_TP`;
  - CuteDSL's kernel completes `SumGroup.TP`.

  Both may return a new residual.
- **Declared path:** `_select_ffn_input` returns the steps and the candidates it bound. It binds a candidate only where the steps are that sum, the add and the norm (nothing gathered or sliced), and only if the candidate completes the sum the attention output owes.
- **Scatter-mode path:** it still binds every candidate, so CuteDSL's kernel, which reduces over the TP group, keeps its place where that group is the attention-TP group.
- **Aux capture:** `_mlp_input_may_fuse` becomes `_mlp_input_may_return_new_residual`, read from the chosen candidates on both paths. Whether capture may keep its reference to the residual (`_post_attn_residual_is_read_only`) follows from it.
- **Notes:** on the scatter-mode path the flag now means "some bound candidate may return a new residual" instead of "the base entry is bound". The two differ only for CuteDSL with a norm that has no `forward_with_allreduce_fusion`. There the predicate is also gated by `apply_flashinfer_allreduce_fusion`, which is False under CuteDSL.
- **Tests:** `TestFusedKernelsTakeOnlyTheStepsTheyComplete` checks three things:
  - a kernel over another group is not chosen;
  - no kernel is chosen where rows are gathered;
  - aux capture follows the chosen kernels.

  The CuteDSL test builds its entry as a `FusedMlpInput`.

## Accuracy Tests

No behavior change is intended.
- **Call sequences, parent vs change:** all eight comparisons are identical, including 169,344 cases through the real constructor, where even the entry that chose the steps is the same.
- **Unit tests:** the 85 related unit files pass.
- **Mutants:** both are caught:
  - dropping the `completes` filter;
  - deriving the aux flag from "a kernel was chosen".
- **GPU (B200):** bit-identical to the parent with FlashInfer all-reduce fusion on, 4 greedy requests × 32 tokens, decode CUDA graph on:
  - Qwen3-0.6B TP2;
  - Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 TP2.
- These results were measured before the stack was rebased onto main after #41257.

The whole stack was also compared with main at its tip; the results are in #41443.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

No kernel or collective changes. The candidates are built once at construction.

Decode latency, time to first token and memory for the whole stack against main are in #41443.

title: [Refactor] Run two-batch-overlap layers on the declared boundaries
author: ch-wan
body:
This PR is part of a stack (oldest at bottom):

* #41443
* #41442
* #41441
* #41440
* #41439
* #41438

* #41436
* #41435
* #41434
* #41433
* #41432
* #41431
* #41430
* #41429
* #41428
* #41427
* __->__ #41426
* #41425
* #41424
* #41423
* #41422
* #41421
* #41420
* #41419
* #41418
* #41417

## Motivation

Under two-batch overlap, a dense MLP on every rank (`moe_dense_tp_size=1`) gathers its output over attention TP before a sparse layer, so the split cuts the attention's rows.
- The declarations could not say so. With attention TP > 1, every layer of such a model went back to the scatter-mode steps.
- The split chose its two moves from scatter modes the model passed in (`input_data_scatter_mode`), plus the first overlapped layer's input mode.

## Modifications

- **`LayerScatterModes.is_next_layer_sparse`** records whether the next layer is sparse, as `is_previous_layer_sparse` records the previous one. It is None when the modes are given directly.
- **The declarations derive the gather from these facts.** Under two-batch overlap:
  - a dense layer on every rank that is followed by a sparse layer hands on the attention's rows: it writes the residual in, then gathers over attention TP (`hands_on_attention_rows`);
  - the sparse layer takes its input there.

  The exclusion of these models from the declarations is removed.
- **New `LayerCommunicator.input_rows`:** the rows a layer's input and residual arrive on, for a batch that runs its ordinary steps. It comes from the declarations. For a layer still on the scatter-mode steps it comes from its input mode, as the rows of a batch that holds every token on each CP rank, so that the split's moves match main's under attention CP.
- **New `tbo_split_moves(layer_input_rows)`:** the split chooses its two moves from the first overlapped layer's input rows. They are the identity pair, or `_gather` / `_scatter` when that layer takes each rank's attention-TP slice; other rows are rejected.
- **`model_forward_maybe_tbo` drops `input_data_scatter_mode`.** The split reads `layers[0].layer_communicator.input_rows`, and only when it runs. The nine call sites are updated: DeepSeek-V2, Dots3, GLM-4-MoE, GLM-4-MoE-Lite, GLM5-Next, MiMo-V2, MiniMax-M2, MiniMax-M3, Qwen2-MoE.
- **Notes:** out-of-tree callers of `model_forward_maybe_tbo` must drop the `input_data_scatter_mode` argument.
- **Tests:**
  - `TestTwoBatchOverlap`: the dense layer before the split hands on the attention's rows; the split moves from the first layer's rows; a layer off the declarations takes its rows from its modes, including under attention CP.
  - The MHC two-batch-overlap test now expects the declared gather.
  - `test_tbo_unreduced_input.py` passes the rows.

## Accuracy Tests

No behavior change is intended.
- **Call sequences through the real constructor**, with a two-batch-overlap axis (off / next layer sparse / next layer dense, for dense-on-every-rank layers under attention DP > 1): 256,128 cases. 251,520 are identical. 4,608 differ only in the recorded entry (the parent took the scatter-mode tables, the change the declarations); their calls are identical.
- **Other comparisons and tests:** the eight other call-sequence comparisons are identical, and 176 related unit files pass. The CP tests' stubs gain the next-layer fact and the overlap flag.
- **Mutants:** three are caught:
  - the dense layer not gathering early for the split;
  - the sparse layer still taking the slice;
  - the split not slicing back. Only the unit test catches this one, since the call-sequence comparison does not run the split.
- **GPU (H200 × 8):**
  - Setup: 4-layer DeepSeek-V3 (bf16, 3 dense + 1 sparse), TP8 × DP4 (attention TP 2), DeepEP + deep_gemm, `moe_dense_tp_size=1`, two-batch overlap.
  - Requests submitted one at a time: parent vs parent is 8 / 8 bit-identical, and parent vs change is 8 / 8 bit-identical.
  - Submitted as one batch, the parent does not reproduce itself (8 of 8 differ between two parent runs with overlap, 4 without), because the batch composition depends on arrival time. So batched runs are not used as a comparison.
  - A runtime audit on the change counted 4 / 4 layers on the declared path per rank, and 20 splits.
- These GPU results were measured before the stack was rebased onto main after #41257, on a configuration without attention CP.
- **At the stack's tip against main** (4-layer DeepSeek-V3, H200): TP8 × DP8 × EP8 with DeepEP and `moe_dense_tp_size=1`, and TP8 × DP4 × EP8 with DeepEP, both with two-batch overlap, are bit-identical. DeepSeek-V2-Lite with DeepEP was not run: unquantized DeepEP supports only low-latency mode, on main as well. Under attention CP the split is covered by `TestTwoBatchOverlap`.

The whole stack was also compared with main at its tip; the results are in #41443.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

No kernel or collective changes. The split's two moves are chosen once per overlapped forward from a layout comparison.

Decode latency, time to first token and memory for the whole stack against main are in #41443.

title: [Refactor] Move CuTe DSL-fused layers onto the declared boundaries and FFN-exit kernel entries
author: ch-wan
body:
This PR is part of a stack (oldest at bottom):

* #41443
* #41442
* #41441
* #41440
* #41439
* #41438
* #41437
* #41436
* #41435
* #41434
* #41433
* #41432
* __->__ #41431
* #41430
* #41429
* #41428
* #41427
* #41426
* #41425
* #41424
* #41423
* #41422
* #41421
* #41420
* #41419
* #41418
* #41417

## Motivation

The CuTe DSL all-reduce fusion (`CuteDSLFusionLayerCommunicator`) was the last communicator that still worked from scatter modes, and its deferred MoE finalize had only one possible reader:
- It opted out of the declared boundaries (`_takes_declared_boundaries = False`), so its layers chose their steps from the scatter modes. Its fusion eligibility read `layer_input_mode` and `mlp_mode` too.
- A MoE that defers its finalize hands the next layer a `MoeFinalizeHandoff`. Only the fused finalize + AR + add + norm kernel could consume it. `reduce_output` passed it through unchanged, so any other reader (the layer-stack exit, the TBO split) would have received a non-tensor. The fused entry also raised when its own kernel declined the batch.
- The FFN exit made its decision through two overridable methods, `should_defer_moe_finalize` and `should_fuse_mlp_allreduce_with_next_layer`. The CuTe DSL overrides read three attributes that `install_cutedsl_fusion` wrote onto each layer after construction.

## Modifications

- **CuTe DSL layers take the declared boundaries.** The opt-out flag and its check in `_declared_sides` are removed.
  - The FFN input's CuTe DSL AR + add + norm entry declares that it completes `SumGroup.ATTN_TP`. It already required the attention-TP group to be the TP group, which is what its workspace sums over.
  - Eligibility reads the declared rows. The entry needs the layer input off `ATTN_TP_SCATTER`. The finalize and the AR need the batch's FFN input rows off `ATTN_TP_SCATTER`: not a2a, the fp4 all-gather, DWDP or a dense MLP on every rank. `cutedsl_ar_fusion.py` no longer imports `ScatterMode`.
- **Any reader can complete a handoff.**
  - New `HandoffOutput`: an output that still owes work only its producer knows how to do. `reduce_output` calls its `complete()`.
  - `MoeFinalizeHandoff` is a `HandoffOutput`. `from_flashinfer(..., reduce=)` takes the MoE's own sum: `post_experts_all_reduce` in DeepSeek-V2, `reduce_moe_output` in Qwen2-MoE. `complete()` runs the MoE's unfused tail: finalize with the shared output, then that sum.
  - The fused attention-input entry only asks whether its own kernel takes the batch. When the kernel declines, the attention input completes the handoff and reads as usual, instead of raising.
  - `finish_layer_stack(..., final_norm_takes_handoff=)` passes a handoff on as it is only to a final norm that does the handoff's work. Qwen3.5 sets it on the last pipeline rank. Every other handoff is completed.
- **The FFN exit tries fused kernels as entries.**
  - `FfnExitFusion` (`DEFER_MOE_FINALIZE`, `NEXT_INPUT`) says what the exit does when a kernel of the next layer's input takes its sum.
  - `LayerCommunicator._select_ffn_exit_fusions()` returns the entries in the order they are tried. The base class has one entry, the aiter / flashinfer check `should_fuse_mlp_allreduce_with_next_layer`, which `MixerExit` also uses. `_select_ffn_completion` takes the first entry that accepts the batch. It asks the unfused condition only when no entry does.
  - `install_cutedsl_fusion` calls `install(service, hands_off_finalize=, next_input_absorbs=, output_is_replicated=)` once per layer. `install` puts the deferred finalize and the absorbed all-reduce that apply in front of the base entry.
- **Removed:** `LayerCommunicator.should_defer_moe_finalize`; the CuTe DSL overrides of it and of `should_fuse_mlp_allreduce_with_next_layer`; `_can_absorb_post_moe_all_reduce`; and the attributes `may_defer_moe_finalize`, `successor_absorbs_all_reduce` and `owes_local_reduction`. No in-tree code reads them.
- **Tests:**
  - `test_cutedsl_ar_fusion.py` adds tests for:
    - fusion only on the FFN's full rows;
    - the exit's entry order (handoff, absorb, base);
    - a handoff completed exactly once by any other reader;
    - `from_flashinfer` completing with the MoE's own sum;
    - a handoff the kernel declines being completed, then normed;
    - the layer-stack exit handing a handoff only to a final norm that takes it.
  - `test_communicator_ffn_exit.py` checks that the next input's fused kernel is tried before the unfused condition.
- **Notes:**
  - On a CuTe DSL layer, `should_fuse_mlp_allreduce_with_next_layer` now gives the base class's answer, because the CuTe DSL decisions are now exit entries. No model calls it directly.
  - A handoff that reaches any reader other than a kernel that takes it is now completed. The fused paths don't change: every configuration that defers also has a consumer whose kernel takes the batch.
  - `complete()` runs the MoE's own sum. That sum skips itself while an FFN exit publishes `fuse_mlp_allreduce` / `mlp_reduce_scatter`, but every reader today runs outside an FFN exit.

## Accuracy Tests

No behavior change is intended on any configuration that runs today.
- **New call-sequence comparison for CuTe DSL communicators, 89,088 cases.** It builds CuTe DSL communicators through the real constructor, at attention DP 1. The axes:
  - TP size, sparse or dense layer, first or last layer;
  - a2a, the fp4 all-gather, DWDP or a dense MLP on every rank;
  - input-scattered attention, quantized communication, the base fused kernels and the forward mode;
  - whether the norm can fuse, whether the kernel takes the batch size, and the three facts `install_cutedsl_fusion` sets.

  Each case records `prepare_attn` on a complete, an owed and a handoff input, plus `prepare_mlp`, `ffn_exit`, the public predicates and `finish_layer_stack`.
  - **First commit (declared boundaries):** identical to the parent. The nine other comparisons are identical too, including the declared-boundary one (256,128 cases).
  - **Second commit (completable handoff):** 35,264 cases are identical. The other 53,824 differ only where a handoff enters the attention input and the kernel does not take it. There the parent raised (`received deferred MoE output on an ineligible path` or `requires a fusable RMSNorm flavour`), and this PR completes the producer's tail and reads as usual. The attention-input comparison shows the same difference in 192 of 50,688 cases, and the other comparisons are identical.
  - **Third commit (exit entries):** every executed step is identical. Only two public predicates differ: `should_defer_moe_finalize`, which is removed, and `should_fuse_mlp_allreduce_with_next_layer`, where the CuTe DSL override had answered True in 6,664 cases. The FFN-exit decision table (64 cases) is identical.
- **Unit tests:** after each commit, the 125-file CPU unit suite gives the same results as the parent. On both trees, only three files that need a GPU fail. 89 related unit files pass. The mutant tests catch 3, 5 and 4 mutants of the three commits.
- **GPU (B200):** parent vs change, 4 greedy requests × 32 tokens, decode CUDA graph on, all bit-identical.
  - First commit: Qwen3-0.6B and DeepSeek-V2-Lite TP2, with the fused AR + norm kernel on and off.
  - Second and third commits together, against the first: those four configurations, plus these eight:
    - Qwen3-0.6B TP4 × DP2, TP4 × DP4 and TP2 × DP2;
    - DeepSeek-V2-Lite TP2 × DP2, TP4 × DP2 and TP4 × DP4 × EP4;
    - GLM-5.3-Flash (MHC) TP4 × DP2 and TP4 × DP4.

    These cover the paths every layer shares with this PR: `reduce_output`, the attention input, the layer-stack exit and the FFN exit.
- **Not covered on GPU:**
  - The CuTe DSL kernels themselves, which need multi-node MNNVL.
  - A CuTe DSL communicator built under attention DP, an a2a backend or input-scattered attention has no eligible kernel and runs the base steps. The CuTe DSL comparison is DP 1 only, so those shapes rely on the base-class comparisons.

The whole stack was also compared with main at its tip; the results are in #41443.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

No kernel or collective changes. The FFN exit now walks a short tuple of entries per FFN, and CuTe DSL eligibility looks up the batch's steps. Both are Python-only.

Decode latency, time to first token and memory for the whole stack against main are in #41443.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).
- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).

- [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed).
- [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance).

1. Ping Merge Oncalls to start the process. See the [PR Merge Process](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/.github/MAINTAINER.md#pull-request-merge-process).

title: [Refactor] Give a layer its CuTe DSL kernels at construction instead of a subclass
author: ch-wan
body:
This PR is part of a stack (oldest at bottom):

* #41443
* __->__ #41442
* #41441
* #41440
* #41439
* #41438
* #41437
* #41436
* #41435
* #41434
* #41433
* #41432
* #41431
* #41430
* #41429
* #41428
* #41427
* #41426
* #41425
* #41424
* #41423
* #41422
* #41421
* #41420
* #41419
* #41418
* #41417

## Motivation

The CuTe DSL all-reduce fusion still needed its own `LayerCommunicator` subclass, `CuteDSLFusionLayerCommunicator`:
- it overrode the three fused-kernel selections: attention input, FFN input and FFN exit;
- its `install()` rewrote the built communicator's exit kernels after the model was constructed;
- DeepSeek-V2 and Qwen3.5 had to pick the communicator class when building each layer.

## Modifications

- **`LayerFusions`** is a protocol for the fused kernels a backend gives a layer, bound to that layer. They are tried before the layer's own kernels at its attention input, FFN input and FFN exit. `LayerCommunicator(..., fusions=)` takes one, and its three selections put the backend's kernels first.
- **`CuteDSLFusion`** (in `cutedsl_ar_fusion.py`), one per layer, holds:
  - the model's CuTe DSL service;
  - what `install()` chose from the next layer: `hands_off_finalize`, and `next_input_absorbs`, which already excludes a replicated output.

  Its kernels read these when they run, so installing leaves the built communicator as it is. An exit kernel that `install` did not choose declines every batch before touching the service.
- **Public facts only:** the CuTe DSL kernels read `layer.ffn.entry(forward_batch).input_rows`, `layer.input_rows`, the layer's norms, and the TP size from `get_parallel()`.
- **Installing:** `install_cutedsl_fusion` and `prepare_cutedsl_fusion` find layers by `communicator.fusions`.
- **Models:** DeepSeek-V2 and Qwen3.5 build a plain `LayerCommunicator` with `fusions=CuteDSLFusion()`, under the same condition that used to pick the subclass. In Qwen3.5, `_layer_communicator_class` becomes `_layer_fusions`.
- **Removed without an alias:** `CuteDSLFusionLayerCommunicator`.
- **Tests:** `test_cutedsl_ar_fusion.py` builds layers with the new construction.

No behavior change.

## Accuracy Tests

- **Call-sequence comparisons:** six are identical to the parent. The two CuTe DSL comparisons build layers with `LayerCommunicator(fusions=CuteDSLFusion())` on this tree: CuTe DSL boundaries (89,088 cases) and the FFN exit decisions (64).
- **Unit tests:** the CPU unit suite (129 files) gives the same per-file results as the parent, and `test_cutedsl_ar_fusion.py` passes (22 tests). A mutant that gives the attention input no CuTe DSL kernels is caught.
- **GPU (B200):** parent vs this PR, 4 greedy requests × 32 tokens, decode CUDA graph on. Qwen3-0.6B and DeepSeek-V2-Lite at TP2, with the fused AR + norm kernel on and off, are bit-identical.
- **Not covered:** the GPU runs cover layers without CuTe DSL. The CuTe DSL kernels need multi-node MNNVL and were not run.

The whole stack was also compared with main at its tip; the results are in #41443.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

No kernel or collective changes. A CuTe DSL layer now calls two exit entries per FFN that return immediately when `install` did not choose them.

Decode latency, time to first token and memory for the whole stack against main are in #41443.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).

title: [KDA] Enable the ptx_kda prefill backend on SM100 (B200 / GB200)
author: yuan-luo
body:
## Motivation

`--linear-attn-prefill-backend ptx_kda` only runs on SM103 (B300 / GB300) today: the extension is built with `-gencode arch=compute_103a,code=sm_103a` and `PtxKDAKernel.supports_prefill` checks for compute capability (10, 3). On B200 / GB200 the backend silently falls back to Triton.

Nothing in the kernel needs SM103:
- All of its inline PTX is available on sm_100a:
  - tcgen05 `cta_group::1`: alloc, ld, st, mma (`kind::f16` and `kind::tf32`), commit, wait and fence.
  - TMA (`cp.async.bulk.tensor`), mbarrier, `mma.sync`, `ldmatrix`, `cp.async`, `prefetch`.
- There is no `ld.red` or other sm_103-only instruction.
- The route and piece-budget cost model reads `multiProcessorCount` at runtime.

On B200 the kernel gives the same speedup over the default Triton path as it does on B300.

## Modifications

- `kernels/ops/attention/linear/kda_ptx_prefill/__init__.py`:
  - Add `SM_ARCHS = {(10, 0): "100a", (10, 3): "103a"}`.
  - Build for the running device's arch. Arch-specific cubins do not run across the two.
  - Name the JIT extension per arch (`kda_prefill_ptx_sm100a` / `kda_prefill_ptx_sm103a`), so a shared `TORCH_EXTENSIONS_DIR` can keep both.
- `srt/layers/attention/linear/kernels/kda_ptx.py`: `supports_prefill` is true on SM100 and SM103.
- `srt/layers/attention/linear/kda_backend.py`: update the fallback and error messages.
- `kernels/jit/csrc/attention/kda_prefill.cu`: update the build comment only. The kernel code is unchanged.
- `test/registered/kernels/ops/attention/test_kda_prefill.py`:
  - The two ptx cases now also run on SM100.
  - The B200 runner now JIT-builds the extension, so its `est_time` goes from 180 to 300 s. The measured time on B200 is 146 s, including the build.

The default KDA prefill backend is unchanged (`triton`). `ptx_kda` stays opt-in.

## Accuracy Tests

B200 (SM100), this branch:

```
test_kda_prefill.py::TestKdaPrefill::test_nvidia_prefill PASSED
test_kda_prefill.py::TestKdaPrefill::test_ptx_padded_raw_beta PASSED
test_kda_prefill.py::TestKdaPrefill::test_ptx_prefill PASSED
3 passed in 146.12s
```

The ptx cases compare both the output and the final state with Triton. The raw-beta case also exercises the wrapper's padding path.

## Benchmarking and Profiling

- Hardware: B200 (148 SMs), torch 2.13 + cu130, triton 3.7.1.
- Method: `PtxKDAKernel.extend` against `TritonKDAKernel.extend`, called the way `KDAAttnBackend.extend` calls them.
- Inputs:
  - q, k, v and the raw gate are bf16 with shape `[1, B·T, H, 128]`.
  - beta is raw (the kernel applies the sigmoid).
  - `A_log` and `dt_bias` follow the Mamba/KDA init.
  - The state pool is fp32.
- Timing: CUDA events including wrapper overhead, median of 10 runs. Latency is in µs.
- "Max diff" is the maximum absolute difference from the Triton output.

With `lower_bound = -5` (safe gate, as in Kimi-K3):

| B × T × H | triton | ptx_kda | speedup | max diff |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 × 8192 × 32 | 968 | 761 | 1.27× | 3e-2 |
| 1 × 32768 × 32 | 3442 | 2498 | 1.38× | 3e-2 |
| 1 × 32768 × 8 | 1835 | 766 | 2.40× | 3e-2 |
| 1 × 32768 × 4 | 1583 | 510 | 3.10× | 3e-2 |
| 4 × 8192 × 32 | 2884 | 1677 | 1.72× | 3e-2 |
| 16 × 2048 × 32 | 2675 | 1798 | 1.49× | 3e-2 |
| 4 × 8192 × 8 | 965 | 808 | 1.19× | 3e-2 |

For comparison, B300 with the same script gives 1.09–2.98×. The absolute ptx_kda times on B200 and B300 are within ±6% of each other.

Without `lower_bound` (plain softplus gate, as in Kimi-Linear), ptx_kda is 1.34–3.21× faster than triton on the same shapes. One shape produces NaN, see Notes.

The biggest gains are at few heads per GPU (TP-sharded) with long prompts. There the Triton `chunk_h` recurrence is latency-bound, taking about 2.3–2.4 µs per 64-token chunk on B200 whether H = 32 or H = 4. ptx_kda splits the sequence into pieces and composes their affine state maps.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the pre-commit hooks (isort 7.0.0, ruff 0.15.1 check and format are clean on the changed Python files).
- [x] Add unit tests (existing ptx cases now run on SM100).
- [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results.

title: [KDA+Kimi K3] Speed up LTX-2.3 QK norm and split RoPE on H200
author: BBuf
body:
## Motivation and changes

Speed up LTX-2.3's QK RMSNorm + split RoPE on H200 using the **KDA + Codex CLI + Kimi K3** candidate. The SM90 implementation combines Q and K into one launch for the measured workloads and uses aligned BF16 vector loads/stores with specialized 64/128 head dimensions. It preserves the original reduction order, intermediate BF16 rounding, public API, custom-op/fake interface and Hopper quality gate.

The change is limited to `ltx2_qknorm_split_rope`: one SM90 CUDA header, its JIT dispatch, and regression tests. Unaligned pointers, odd RoPE strides and other supported head dimensions retain scalar handling; Q and K select their paths independently, including empty sides. Other architectures continue to use the original header.

Baseline: `0bc074db83286449b96198eb340dacdf89041650`. Candidate: `8b4fed70dfec11e1d4483527903cb2ecdf54251b`. The final CUDA preparation only changes comments, formatting and include ordering relative to the timed overlay; the Python dispatch is byte-identical. [Source equivalence](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/blob/9b37400b330ba5e30aa632f36a2cae26e48316e4/diffusion-prs/kda-ltx2-h200-20260927/source-equivalence.json) · [Source patch](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/blob/9b37400b330ba5e30aa632f36a2cae26e48316e4/diffusion-prs/kda-ltx2-h200-20260927/source.patch) · [KDA provenance](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/blob/9b37400b330ba5e30aa632f36a2cae26e48316e4/diffusion-prs/kda-ltx2-h200-20260927/provenance.json).

## Kernel validation

NVIDIA H200, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130 / CUDA 13.0. Three independent processes with fresh input values; CUPTI cold-L2 timing. Speedup is baseline latency / candidate latency. Every frozen workload is retained.

| Workloads | Cases | Three geometric-mean speedups | Worst ratio across all repeats |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| Frozen LTX QK norm + split RoPE suite | 5 | **2.5814× / 2.5932× / 2.6146×** | **1.9177×** |

All measured cases improve in all three repeats; this covers the tested workloads, not arbitrary inputs. [Raw kernel results](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/blob/9b37400b330ba5e30aa632f36a2cae26e48316e4/diffusion-prs/kda-ltx2-h200-20260927/kernel-benchmarks.json) · [Workload shapes and strides](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/blob/9b37400b330ba5e30aa632f36a2cae26e48316e4/diffusion-prs/kda-ltx2-h200-20260927/kernel-workloads.json).

**14 tests pass on the final H200 source**, with 4 Blackwell-specific skips. Coverage includes the Hopper quality gate, BF16 numerical checks, 11 aligned/unaligned/odd-stride/mixed-path/empty-side cases compared byte-for-byte with original CUDA, changed-input CUDA Graph replay, and `torch.compile(fullgraph=True)`. Pre-commit checks pass. A separate real LTX request checks **1,340 Q/K calls** against the unchanged CUDA implementation; all outputs are byte-exact. [Tests](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/blob/9b37400b330ba5e30aa632f36a2cae26e48316e4/diffusion-prs/kda-ltx2-h200-20260927/tests.log) · [Formatting checks](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/blob/9b37400b330ba5e30aa632f36a2cae26e48316e4/diffusion-prs/kda-ltx2-h200-20260927/pre-commit.log) · [Real-model kernel checks](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/blob/9b37400b330ba5e30aa632f36a2cae26e48316e4/diffusion-prs/kda-ltx2-h200-20260927/real-model-kernel-checks.json).

## Isolated end-to-end results

Model: `Lightricks/LTX-2.3`, revision `7caa482d5cd10a2eae6b34cb48f093ebc45a263e`; one H200; 768×512, 121 frames, 30 steps, guidance 3, seed 42, 24 FPS, `high` quality. Prompt: `A beautiful sunset over the ocean`. Eager native SGLang backend, request warmup, fixed checkpoint and settings in both arms.

Two independent **A–B–B–A groups**, eight full saved requests total. Each cell compares two baseline requests with two candidate requests. Saved E2E includes scheduler wait and output saving; model loading and separately captured profiling runs are excluded.

**Measurement condition:** both arms use the same validation-only deterministic audio-decode context. During audio VAE decode and vocoder calls it disables TF32 and cuDNN benchmarking, enables cuDNN deterministic, and restores settings afterward. This helper is outside the production patch. Default audio decode already varied between baseline self-repeats, so the E2E timing and output-identity claims below are conditional on this symmetric setting. [Exact helper](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/blob/9b37400b330ba5e30aa632f36a2cae26e48316e4/diffusion-prs/kda-ltx2-h200-20260927/repro/sitecustomize.py) · [Reproduction command](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/blob/9b37400b330ba5e30aa632f36a2cae26e48316e4/diffusion-prs/kda-ltx2-h200-20260927/repro/run-one.sh).

| Quality | Saved E2E group 1 | Saved E2E group 2 | Actual before/after |
|---|---|---|---|
| high | 43.735 → 43.285 s (**−1.03%**) | 43.765 → 43.260 s (**−1.15%**) | ![Actual before/after](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BBuf/sglang/9b37400b330ba5e30aa632f36a2cae26e48316e4/diffusion-prs/kda-ltx2-h200-20260927/models/high/comparison.gif) |

Across both groups, mean saved-request latency is **43.7500 → 43.2725 s**, a **1.09% reduction** (about 0.48 s). All eight MP4s are file-byte identical; decoded-frame mean/worst SSIM is 1 and PSNR is infinite across all 121 frames. The GIF shows baseline left and candidate right.

[Baseline MP4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BBuf/sglang/9b37400b330ba5e30aa632f36a2cae26e48316e4/diffusion-prs/kda-ltx2-h200-20260927/models/high/baseline.mp4) · [Candidate MP4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BBuf/sglang/9b37400b330ba5e30aa632f36a2cae26e48316e4/diffusion-prs/kda-ltx2-h200-20260927/models/high/candidate.mp4) · [Eight-run timing](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/blob/9b37400b330ba5e30aa632f36a2cae26e48316e4/diffusion-prs/kda-ltx2-h200-20260927/models/high/abba.json) · [Output-quality audit](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/blob/9b37400b330ba5e30aa632f36a2cae26e48316e4/diffusion-prs/kda-ltx2-h200-20260927/models/high/quality-metrics.json) · [Environment](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/blob/9b37400b330ba5e30aa632f36a2cae26e48316e4/diffusion-prs/kda-ltx2-h200-20260927/environment.json).

A separate two-step profile confirms the changed device path executes: target launches **2,680 → 1,340**, cumulative target GPU time **95.90 → 46.20 ms**. The target accounts for 3.15% of baseline CUDA kernel-duration sum; this is not an E2E critical-path fraction. [Profile summary](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/blob/9b37400b330ba5e30aa632f36a2cae26e48316e4/diffusion-prs/kda-ltx2-h200-20260927/profile-summary.json) · [Artifact hashes](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/blob/9b37400b330ba5e30aa632f36a2cae26e48316e4/diffusion-prs/kda-ltx2-h200-20260927/artifact-manifest.json).

title: [Perf] Tune SM90 GDN recurrent verify launch for small batches
author: anthonyhe-bot
body:
## Motivation

Speculative target verify on Gated DeltaNet hybrids (Qwen3.5, Qwen3-Next with MTP / EAGLE / DFlash) runs `fused_sigmoid_gating_delta_rule_update_kernel` once per linear-attention layer. On CUDA, the shared Triton wrapper always launches a 32-column value tile with one warp: `(V / 32) * HV * N` programs. For Qwen3.5-4B (HV=32, V=128) at batch 1, that is 128 single-warp programs on a 132-SM H200, and each program walks the draft tokens sequentially, so the kernel is latency-bound at the small batches where speculative decoding is used.

#39987 tuned this launch for Qwen3.5 TP4 on AMD gfx950 and kept CUDA unchanged. This PR is the SM90 counterpart. Narrowing the value tile to 4 columns (one warp) makes the verify kernel 2 to 3 times faster at batch 1 on H100 and H200, and it is never slower up to batch 64. Value columns are independent and the K reduction stays inside a program, so outputs and cached states are bit-identical.

## Modifications

- `_select_recurrent_launch_config()` gains a `target_verify` flag. The launcher sets it when `intermediate_states_buffer` is passed.
- On CUDA SM90, for non-KDA GDN with K=V=128, target verify and batch 1 to 64, select BV=4 with one warp.
- Everything else keeps the existing launch byte-for-byte: decode (T=1), KDA, other head dims, batches above 64, non-SM90 CUDA (including Blackwell, where smaller tiles are faster but not bit-identical), and the gfx950 branch.
- `test_fused_verify_triton_gdn.py`: launch-envelope assertions, plus 16 bit-exactness cases (batch 1/3/16/64, T 4/16, H/HV 16/32 and 4/16) that compare the tuned launch with BV=32 using `torch.equal` on outputs and intermediate states.

## Accuracy Tests

The change only alters how value columns are split across programs, so results are expected to be bit-identical.

- **Kernel:** the 16 new cases compare the tuned launch against BV=32 with `torch.equal` on outputs and all intermediate states. The full `test_fused_verify_triton_gdn.py` passes on H100 and H200 (33 passed, 1 gfx95 skip). On B200 it passes 16, and the new SM90-only cases skip.
- **Serving, per call:** Qwen3.5-4B with MTP (`--speculative-algorithm NEXTN`, 3 steps / top-k 1 / 4 draft tokens), 1xH200, eager mode, 32 concurrent greedy requests. A debug wrapper reran every verify call with BV=32 and compared. About 840 calls at batches 1 to 32 were all bit-identical.
- **Serving, end to end:** in CUDA-graph mode, 32 greedy requests sent one at a time produce identical token IDs on main and this PR (32/32). Batched outputs can differ between any two server launches for scheduling reasons, independent of this change (main with graphs vs main eager: 31/32).
- **GSM8K**, 200 questions, few-shot, same MTP setup, three runs per arm:

| Configuration | Accuracy | Invalid |
|---|---:|---:|
| main | 0.870 / 0.875 / 0.880 | 0.000 |
| This PR | 0.880 / 0.875 / 0.880 | 0.000 |

## Speed Tests and Profiling

### GDN target-verify microbenchmark

`fused_sigmoid_gating_delta_rule_update` with the target-verify intermediate-state write, BF16 activations, FP32 recurrent state. Each timing replays a CUDA graph of 20 back-to-back calls, so no host launch cost is included. "Tuned" is BV=4 / one warp.

title: [AMD] Add opt-in MiniMax-M3 TP4 indexer context partitioning
author: ThomasNing
body:
## Motivation

Under TP4, MiniMax-M3's four index-query heads are split across ranks while the index-K cache is replicated. Each rank scans the full index cache for its head. This PR adds an opt-in decode path that partitions the block reads across those four ranks and scores all heads while each K tile is resident.

The measured benefit is in the **indexer chain**, including communication: at batch 32 / 128K context, latency falls from 109.84 to 41.63 µs (62.1% lower latency, 2.64× speedup). Short contexts and small batches regress, so the feature defaults off. Full-model serving gains have not been measured.

## Modifications

- Add `SGLANG_MINIMAX_M3_INDEXER_CP=1`, default `0`, for gfx950 TP4 ordinary decode with attention CP/DP size 1, four index heads, four main KV heads, dimension 128, 128-token blocks, max scoring, and top-k 16. Unsupported run configurations log a reason and retain the existing path.
- Gather existing post-RoPE queries through the attention TP communicator, then let rank `r` read blocks `r, r+4, r+8, ...` for all four heads. The cache remains replicated; this reduces read traffic, not cache capacity.
- Use Triton kernels for shard scoring, local top-16 selection per head, and final merging. Keeping 16 candidates on every shard preserves global top-16 even when all winners belong to one shard. Initial/recent block priorities and native ROCm score/ID ordering are preserved.
- Exchange packed score/ID keys through SGLang's communicator, using AITER custom all-gather when supported and the existing fallback otherwise. Keys use FP32 **bitcast views for copying**, without numeric conversion. Warm both collective paths before graph capture; merge directly from the received layout.
- Keep the implementation in two new modules with small backend/dispatch changes. Existing top-k reuse is checked first. Prefill, index-value layers, model projections, checkpoint loading, and main sparse attention retain their existing paths.
- Add a manual four-rank correctness/timing harness, reproduction instructions, and all raw timing samples under `test/manual/minimax_m3/indexer_cp/`.

The initial scope excludes speculation, TBO, HiSparse, FP8 queries, and dense sparse decode. There is no automatic batch/context crossover policy. It does not require a main-attention backend change.

## Accuracy Tests

Completed on four MI355X / gfx950 GPUs:

- **8/8 cases passed on all ranks:** BF16 and FP8 E4M3 index caches × random scores, ties, winners concentrated on one shard, and mixed lengths.
- Exact selected-ID comparisons against native SGLang and an independent FP32 PyTorch reference, including empty rows and partial blocks.
- Changed sequence lengths after graph capture, including short, partial-block, and empty rows; replay matched both references.
- All **17 timing shapes** additionally passed native-versus-CP selected-ID parity in eager execution and graph replay.
- Repository pre-commit hooks passed for all changed files. The scorer, runtime helper, and benchmark script are byte-identical to the files used for the successful GPU run.

**Validation still outstanding:** runtime feature-gate/backend dispatch through a loaded server, full-model accuracy, serving TPS/TTFT/TPOT, and measurements with the fallback collective. The harness directly invokes the indexer helper. The shape gate also accepts FP16 queries and other FP8 cache variants, which were not covered by this run.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Four MI355X GPUs, BF16 queries, FP8 E4M3 index cache, AITER custom gather available. Both gathers are included; projections and main attention are excluded. Eight indexer calls per HIP graph, 100 replays per round, seven rounds alternating baseline/CP order. Each sample uses the slowest rank; reported values are the median of seven samples.

Inputs/cache are repeatedly reused and warm, without an L2 flush or rotating-layer protocol. These are microbenchmark results and cannot be interpreted as model throughput gains.

| Context | Batch | Native TP (µs) | CP (µs) | CP latency change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 8K | 1 | 9.40 | 15.40 | +63.8% |
| 8K | 8 | 7.72 | 18.32 | +137.3% |
| 8K | 32 | 12.12 | 19.58 | +61.5% |
| 32K | 16 | 20.80 | 20.04 | -3.7% |
| 32K | 32 | 30.41 | 24.38 | -19.8% |
| 128K | 1 | 12.71 | 15.93 | +25.4% |
| 128K | 8 | 32.85 | 24.02 | -26.9% |
| 128K | 16 | 51.71 | 32.08 | -38.0% |
| 128K | 32 | 109.84 | 41.63 | -62.1% |
| One 128K row, remaining 1K | 16 | 40.76 | 27.82 | -31.7% |
| One 128K row, remaining 1K | 32 | 68.89 | 34.62 | -49.7% |

Negative latency change is an improvement. All tested 8K shapes and batches 1–2 at 128K regress. The small 32K/batch-16 gain needs independent repetition. The README contains the complete 17-shape table, runtime versions, source hashes, and the reproduction command; `results-gfx950.json` contains every round.

## Checklist

- [x] Format changed files with repository pre-commit hooks.
- [x] Add reproducible four-rank correctness and speed checks (manual GPU harness).
- [x] Document enablement, supported configurations, results, and limitations.
- [x] Provide indexer-level accuracy and speed measurements, including regressions.
- [ ] Validate full-model accuracy and serving performance with CP off/on.
- [ ] Integrate the multi-GPU checks into registered CI.

title: [ROCm] Use the fused MLA absorb + RoPE + KV-write kernel for decode-sized forward modes only
author: jiaryang
body:
## Motivation

On gfx950, `fused_fp8_bmm_rope_cat_and_cache_mla` (#38340) replaces the absorbed q BMM and the
RoPE / cat / KV-write kernel with one launch. At decode and verify sizes this is a clear win, because
neither separate kernel fills the CUs. At prefill shapes (8k tokens x 4) the two separately tuned
kernels are faster. This PR keeps the fused kernel for decode-sized forward modes and uses the
two-kernel path that main already has for EXTEND, MIXED and SPLIT_PREFILL.

## Modifications

- In `forward_absorb_rocm_prepare()` (`forward_mla_rocm.py`), the fused kernel is now also gated on
  `not forward_mode.is_extend_or_draft_extend_or_mixed()`. That is false for EXTEND, MIXED and
  SPLIT_PREFILL, so DECODE, TARGET_VERIFY and DRAFT_EXTEND_V2 keep the fused kernel. `is_extend()` is
  not used because it includes TARGET_VERIFY, which is extend-shaped but decode-sized.

No new numerical path: the prefill modes take the same two-kernel path main uses whenever the fused
kernel is not selected. CUDA graphs are captured for DECODE and TARGET_VERIFY only, so the captured
graphs still contain the fused kernel.

## Accuracy Tests

title: [Diffusion] Fix concurrent server perf dump writes across ranks
author: mickqian
body:
## Motivation

In server mode, every rank in a diffusion replica can write the same `perf_dump_path` with `open(..., "w")`. Concurrent writes can leave malformed JSON or replace the output rank's metrics with another rank's report. The September 19 nightly comparison artifact contains seven malformed perf reports out of 36 (`JSONDecodeError: Extra data`).

Evidence: [nightly comparison job](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/35447786547/job/105909616906).

## Modifications

- Write the server perf report only on the replica's existing `is_output_rank`.
- Keep replica peak-memory collection outside that guard so all participating ranks still enter the reduction.
- Add a regression test covering output/non-output ranks and warmup/non-warmup requests, using the real JSON writer. Non-writing ranks must leave an existing report untouched.

This fixes report ownership rather than tolerating corrupted JSON or changing performance thresholds.

## Accuracy Tests

No model-compute changes. The regression test exercises `GPUWorker._execute_forward_common`, JSON serialization, and the call boundary for replica memory collection; it does not substitute for a real multi-GPU collective test.

At head `0f090c53c24`, an isolated B200 development environment passed all 48 tests in `test_performance_metrics.py`, `test_logging_utils.py`, and `test_diffusion_nightly_comparison.py` (PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130, Diffusers 0.37.0).

## Speed Tests and Profiling

No inference speedup claim. This change improves the integrity of server-side performance evidence without changing benchmark configuration or ground truth.

title: [Doc] Add kernel benchmark rule on L2 cache reuse
author: DarkSharpness
body:
> (auto generated by Claude)

Kernel benchmarks that time the same kernel on the same inputs (e.g. `triton.testing.do_bench_cudagraph` with fixed args, or a bare `for` loop) measure an L2-hot kernel and can be very misleading.

- Add `.claude/rules/kernel-benchmark.md` (path-scoped to benchmark files): benchmarks must measure cold L2 unless the working set far exceeds L2 or hot L2 is the real serving pattern, with the reason stated. Host-memory loads bypass device L2; peer-GPU reads still see reuse. `marker.do_bench` is recommended but not mandatory — any tool is fine as long as the numbers are valid.
- `add-sgl-kernel`: replace the fixed-input `do_bench_cudagraph` benchmark template with `marker.do_bench`.
- `add-jit-kernel`: link the rule; fix the contradictory `graph_clone_args` guidance (keep read, in-place and output tensors).

Docs only.

title: [Refactor] Select reduction fusion at the consumer
author: ch-wan
body:
This PR is part of a stack (oldest at bottom):

* #41557
* #41556
* #41555
* #41554
* #41553
* #41552
* __->__ #41551
* #41550
* #41549
* #41548
* #41547

## Motivation

Producers currently inspect consumer fusion details to decide whether to skip reduction. The output contract should describe owed work while the consuming boundary selects a compatible completion.

## Modifications

- Carry static and runtime reduction work with the output and select compatible fused completion at the consumer, with an unfused fallback.
- Keep mixer reduction in the producer under attention DP, restoring the existing exclusion from cross-layer deferral. The producer completes over attention TP, rather than deferring a partial that could later be summed over the full TP group.
- Preserve statically declared partial sums across PP when the receiver reconstructs that contract; complete dynamic handoffs before transport.
- Preserve eligible LoRA/shared-expert fused completion, including explicitly selected CuTeDSL with an installed, compatible workspace. The consumer still completes the sum with an ordinary all-reduce if its fused kernel declines.
- Outside attention DP, a movable mixer output can complete at the next input even without a fused consumer; that path still runs the same all-reduce.
- Remove DeepSeek's finalize-consumer hint. A PP stage's last layer may now hand off finalize work to stack completion; the unfused finalize and post-expert reduction still execute there.
- Retarget AMD fusion-gate coverage to the consumer and producer checks.

- Declare the all-reduce deferral capability on the fusion provider protocol.

title: [DeepSeek V4.1] Use DeepSelect for Hopper full top-k decode.
author: yuyu5333
body:
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->

## Motivation

PR #41364 adds `topk_page_transform`, which combines DeepSelect Top-K selection with the page-table transform in its epilogue.

DeepSeek V4.1 on Hopper still uses:

```text
torch.topk
  -> sort raw indices
  -> gather physical KV slots
```

This PR connects the new DeepSelect operator to that runtime path.

<!-- Describe the purpose and goals of this pull request. -->

## Modifications

- Use `topk_page_transform` for the SM90 full-topk decode path.
- Write transformed int32 KV slots directly into the existing output buffer.
- Preserve raw-index ordering with `sorted_index=True`.
- Keep the existing Torch path when raw indices are also required.
- Keep SM100 and newer architectures on the existing DeepGEMM path.
- Add CPU dispatch/fallback tests and an H20 runtime integration test.

<!-- Detail the changes made in this pull request. -->

## Accuracy Tests

Validated on NVIDIA H20:

| Test | Result |
|---|---:|
| DeepSelect kernel tests | 10/10 passed |
| Related indexer unit tests | 28/28 passed |
| New runtime integration tests | 5/5 passed |
| `_torch_decode` statement coverage | 90% |

Coverage includes short contexts where `width < topk`, variable row lengths, page-table mapping, sorted output, and the raw-index fallback.


<!-- If this pull request affects model outputs (e.g., changes to the kernel or model forward code), provide accuracy test results. -->

## Speed Tests and Profiling


The replaced region was benchmarked on NVIDIA H20 with CUDA 13.0 and PyTorch 2.13. Each complete run used 20 warmup iterations followed by 5 groups of 100 measurements. The table reports the mean of the medians from two complete runs.

The measured regions were:

```text
Before:
torch.topk -> raw-index sort -> slot gather -> output copy

After:
DeepSelect top-k -> sorted-index epilogue -> page-table transform
```

| Rows | Width | Top-K | Before | After | Speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 32K | 512 | 163.264 us | 31.744 us | 5.14x |
| 8 | 32K | 512 | 163.992 us | 31.592 us | 5.19x |

| 1 | 128K | 1024 | 162.864 us | 31.760 us | 5.13x |

This is a microbenchmark of the replaced Top-K and transform region, not an end-to-end serving throughput claim.

title: [KDA] Fix ptx_kda prefill NaN without a gate lower bound and workspace growth
author: yuan-luo
body:
## Motivation

Validating `--linear-attn-prefill-backend ptx_kda` end to end on B200 turned up two problems in the PTX prefill path. Neither depends on the arch: both exist on SM103, where ptx_kda runs today.

1. **Models without a gate lower bound get NaN.** On Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B-Instruct, ptx_kda scored GSM8K 0.000 against 0.902 for Triton, every prompt logprob of a 6K-token prefill was NaN, and nothing was logged. The kernel only handles the safe gate (`lower_bound` set, as in Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3-Flash).
2. **The workspace cache grows with every batch shape until the process runs out of memory.** A GLM-5.3-Flash TP4 server on ptx_kda hit CUDA OOM about 20 s into GSM8K, while Triton on the same args ran the full eval.

## Modifications

- `srt/layers/attention/linear/kernels/kda_ptx.py`: batches from a model without a gate lower bound take the wrapper's existing Triton fallback, the same path as spec draft-extend, track-state snapshots and unsupported shapes. It logs one warning.
- `kernels/jit/csrc/attention/kda_prefill.cu`: `get_workspace` clears its cache once it holds 4 entries. The device code is unchanged.
- `test/registered/kernels/ops/attention/test_kda_prefill.py`, one regression case per fix. Like the existing ptx cases they run on SM103 (GB300 CI).
  - `test_ptx_without_lower_bound_matches_triton`: with no lower bound and `exp(A_log)` near 200, the output must be finite and match Triton.
  - `test_ptx_workspace_memory_is_bounded`: 16 new batch shapes must not keep one workspace each.

## Accuracy Tests

Unit tests on B200, with the companion PR's SM100 enablement applied so the ptx cases run there (on this branch alone they run on SM103 only):

```
test_kda_prefill.py::TestKdaPrefill::test_nvidia_prefill PASSED
test_kda_prefill.py::TestKdaPrefill::test_ptx_padded_raw_beta PASSED
test_kda_prefill.py::TestKdaPrefill::test_ptx_prefill PASSED
test_kda_prefill.py::TestKdaPrefill::test_ptx_without_lower_bound_matches_triton PASSED
test_kda_prefill.py::TestKdaPrefill::test_ptx_workspace_memory_is_bounded PASSED
5 passed in 152.71s
```

Both new cases fail on the code before this change: the output has NaN, and 16 shapes keep 107.6 MB against a 37.9 MB bound.

End-to-end on B200, same setup:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| Kimi-Linear-48B, TP2, ptx_kda: GSM8K | 0.000 (Triton 0.902; 500 questions, 5-shot) | 0.93 (200 questions, 5-shot) |
| GLM-5.3-Flash, TP4, ptx_kda: GSM8K, 500 questions, 20-shot | CUDA OOM during the eval | 0.932 (Triton 0.924) |

- Kimi-Linear now runs its prefill on Triton, and the server logs the fallback once per rank.
- GLM-5.3-Flash uses the cookbook Blackwell recipe plus `--disable-radix-cache`, which keeps its tracked batches off the Triton fallback. Its prompt logprobs on a 2040-token prefill are bit-identical with and without the cache bound.

## Benchmarking and Profiling

The bound can make a cache hit into a miss, so this measures what a miss costs: the latency of the first call of a batch shape against a repeat of it. B200, 16 heads, safe gate, 16K tokens, CUDA events:

| batch | new shape (miss) | repeated shape (hit) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 sequence (fused route) | 895–939 µs | 764–798 µs |
| 2–9 sequences (builder + chain) | 573 µs | 532 µs |

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the pre-commit hooks (isort 7.0.0, ruff 0.15.1 check and format are clean on the changed Python files).
- [x] Add unit tests (a regression case for each fix).
- [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results.

title: [DSV4.1] Add opt-in TRT-LLM sparse attention support
author: Oasis-Git
body:
## Motivation

Extend the existing opt-in TRT-LLM sparse MLA backend to DeepSeek-V4.1. The default attention backend is unchanged. Enable with `--dsv4-attn-backend trtllm --cuda-graph-backend-prefill disabled`.

## Modifications

- Add uniform FP8 compressed-cache writes for V4.1's ratio-1/2 layers.
- Support indexed ratio-1/2 metadata, empty compressed histories, and DSpark's noncausal SWA draft blocks.
- Use native query-head counts, fuse RoPE with FP8 Q conversion, and combine sparse-index copying and length preparation into one kernel.
- Reject V4.1 TRT-LLM prefill CUDA graphs and SWA bounded replay for now. Existing context-parallelism/online-compression restrictions remain.

## Accuracy Tests

Local tests before the cluster outage, using real DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash weights on 4×GB300, TP4/EP4, and FlashInfer 0.6.18.post1:

- 24 fused Q/metadata checks matched their unfused references exactly.
- Attention reference checks covered prefill, decode, verification, short contexts, and DSpark. Relative RMSE against FP32 attention was below 2.6%; tested decode/verify CUDA-graph outputs matched eager outputs exactly.
- 30/30 arithmetic/retrieval checks passed, including approximately 128K contexts.
- GSM8K subset: 124/128 for this integration and 124/128 for FlashMLA. This does not establish bitwise output equivalence.
- Two C64 serving repeats completed all 256 requests with the expected input/output token counts; speculative acceptance was real, not simulated.

These GPU results used base `6fa3fe69e2e5e19b75cadd9fc285b72634551992`. This draft is rebased onto `79cafec`; GPU reruns on the rebased tree remain pending because the cluster is unavailable.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Tested DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on 4×GB300, TP4/EP4, with FlashInfer 0.7.0.post1.
- Sparse attention: at C64 × 6 verification rows and 128K context, FlashMLA took 73.5–73.8 μs, versus 44.6–45.1 μs for TRT-LLM, or 46.2 μs including the wrapper and sparse-table packing. These measurements exclude Q/KV preparation and the rest of the model.
- Fused preparation: at 384 rows, Q preparation decreased from 23.65 to 13.41 μs, and KV normalization/RoPE/cast/cache-store decreased from 15.49 to 7.34 μs, compared with their unfused implementations.
- End-to-end serving: at C64, 32K input/1K output, temperature 0, DSPARK with five draft tokens, and Engram offload, average output throughput across two repeats increased from 564.6 to 575.4 tok/s total (+1.9%). Each backend completed all 256 benchmark requests.

- [x] Report local correctness and performance measurements.
- [ ] Add upstream regression coverage; existing local harnesses are not included in this draft.

title: [Feat] [AMD] moe: Add native GLM MXFP4 Triton Gluon backend
author: jiejingzhangamd
body:
## Motivation GLM-5.2/5.3 decode on MI355X spends a material part of each step in the MoE layer. The existing runner boundary receives already-materialized top-k IDs and weights, so a model-specific kernel cannot optimize across router projection, top-k, route sorting, expert scheduling, activation quantization, routed experts, and the shared expert. This PR adds an **explicit, strict, whole-layer Triton Gluon MoE backend** for the audited GLM Quark MXFP4 contract. Its main optimization is not a standalone faster top-k operation: the selected routes directly become the expert schedule, removing the generic `topk_ids -> moe_sorting -> expert GEMM` handoff. The backend is opt-in and fail-closed. `auto` never selects it, unsupported contracts raise before execution, and a requested Gluon path never silently falls back to AITER or another MoE runner. ## Modifications ### 1. What this adds - `gluon` as a `MoeRunnerBackend` choice. - A reusable whole-layer `GluonMoeBackend` interface with model-specific binding, eager weight preparation, execution, and output ABI validation. - A GLM-5.2/5.3 implementation for serialized Quark W4A4 MXFP4 target experts and the audited BF16 NextN expert layout on gfx950. - Shape-family kernels for decode, speculative verification, and prefill, including continuous TP4/EP1 and TP8/EP1 coverage through a 32K prefill chunk. - TP/EP-aware shared-expert handling and reuse of SGLang's existing post-expert collective/finalization path. Enable the target and speculative paths explicitly: ```bash --moe-runner-backend gluon \ --speculative-moe-runner-backend gluon ``` ### 2. Kernel design The optimized layer owns this model-specific sequence: ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph A["Current SGLang + AITER boundary"] A0["BF16 hidden states"] --> A1["router GEMM"] A1 --> A2["M x 256 logits"] A2 --> A3["biased sigmoid top-8"] A3 --> A4["dense IDs + weights"] A4 --> A5["generic moe_sorting
count, bucket, pad, publish metadata"] A5 --> A6["quantize + GEMM1 + activation + GEMM2"] A6 --> A7["shared expert + add"] end subgraph G["GLM Triton Gluon whole-layer path"] G0["BF16 hidden states"] --> G1["router projection + input quant work
co-scheduled in one launch grid"] G1 --> G2["fixed 256-expert sigmoid top-8"] G2 --> G3{"active-token family"} G3 -->|"tiny M"| G4["selection/expert CTAs share a launch;
expert CTAs recompute the needed route rank"] G3 -->|"medium M"| G5["selection directly emits expert tickets,
sorted routes, and job descriptors"] G3 -->|"large M"| G6["chunk histogram + prefix/scatter
and bucketed grouped projections"] G4 --> G7["MXFP4 experts + shared expert"] G5 --> G7 G6 --> G7 end ``` Important details: - **Tiny M:** the router uses split-K CDNA4 MFMA work to expose enough CTAs on MI355X. Selection is compile-time specialized for 256 experts/top-8. The up-projection launch consumes the selected route directly instead of waiting for a generic sort. - **Medium M:** top-k appends routes directly to expert buckets and publishes the descriptors consumed by the expert projection. - **Large M:** chunked counting, prefix/scatter, and bucketed projections cover prefill shapes. The 32K family splits large routed-partial/code buffers so every gfx950 buffer address remains below the 4-GiB window. - **Quantization:** router projection and activation quantization are independent CTAs in the same launch grid; this removes a host launch and lets both work classes occupy the device together. They are not incorrectly described as a single CTA reading the input once. - **Shared expert:** TP/EP1 target execution consumes SGLang's normal appended shared-expert representation (257 experts). EP and NextN keep the native shared expert and add it before SGLang's existing collective. The isolated measurements below show that standalone top-k is approximately tied with AITER. The useful difference is the producer/consumer boundary: ```text AITER: router -> top-k metadata -> generic MoE sort -> expert work Gluon: router/quant -> top-k becomes the expert schedule -> expert work ``` ### rocprofiler-sdk kernel decomposition To separate GPU work from Python/dispatcher/launch overhead, the full TP8/EP1 MoE call was profiled at PR HEAD `317b7156d` with rocprofiler-sdk 1.1.0 (`--kernel-trace --marker-trace --stats`). Each AITER and Gluon arm was enclosed in its own ROCTx range and repeated 100 times on MI355X. `GPU active` below is the sum of device kernel durations per call. `GPU span` is from the first kernel start to the final kernel end under tracing; its parenthesized component is time between kernels and is profiler-sensitive. The `full MoE` column retains the low-overhead HIP-event result from the table above rather than treating traced wall time as application latency. | M | Path | Kernels / layer | GPU active | Traced GPU span (inter-kernel gaps) | Full MoE, low-overhead | |---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | AITER | 15 | 60.82 us | 649.17 us (587.41 us) | 574.97 us | | 1 | Gluon | 4 | 13.47 us | 70.76 us (57.44 us) | 99.42 us | | 16 | AITER | 14 | 95.57 us | 611.47 us (516.93 us) | 543.89 us | | 16 | Gluon | 3 | 39.05 us | 63.12 us (24.06 us) | 94.34 us | | 32 | AITER | 15 | 119.22 us | 657.49 us (537.73 us) | 706.99 us | | 32 | Gluon | 5 | 64.30 us | 104.74 us (40.52 us) | 159.48 us | The exact AITER device-time decomposition is: | AITER stage | M=1 | M=16 | M=32 | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Router matmul, including BF16-to-FP32 cast where present | 2.69 us | 6.39 us | 7.78 us | | Biased grouped top-k | 4.06 us | 4.96 us | 4.89 us | | Generic route metadata sort/pad | 6.25 us | 9.72 us | 14.06 us | | Routed input quantization + scatter | 2.76 us | 4.25 us | 4.68 us | | Routed gate/up GEMM + SiLU/multiply | 18.11 us | 27.87 us | 36.77 us | | Routed activation quantization + scatter | 2.67 us | 3.02 us | 3.81 us | | Routed down GEMM | 3.82 us | 14.42 us | 19.68 us | | Shared input quantization | 2.15 us | 2.88 us | 3.34 us | | Shared gate/up GEMM, including split-K reduce | 7.90 us | 6.26 us | 7.04 us | | Shared SiLU + multiply | 3.75 us | 8.15 us | 9.15 us | | Shared activation quantization | 1.51 us | 1.96 us | 2.18 us | | Shared down GEMM | 3.43 us | 3.40 us | 3.47 us | | Routed + shared final add | 1.73 us | 2.27 us | 2.37 us | | **Total GPU active** | **60.82 us** | **95.57 us** | **119.22 us** | Gluon performs the same logical work with fused shape-specific stages: | Gluon kernel/stage | M=1 | M=16 | M=32 | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Router GEMM + routed/shared input quantization | 2.48 us | 3.25 us | 3.60 us | | Top-k scheduling + routed/shared gate/up GEMM | 5.18 us | - | - | | Top-k scheduling + routed/shared gate/up + activation quantization | - | 23.91 us | - | | Top-k to expert-job schedule | - | - | 4.61 us | | Routed/shared gate/up GEMM + activation quantization | - | - | 33.80 us | | Activation + quantization | 2.52 us | - | - | | Routed/shared down GEMM + weighted reduction | 3.30 us | 11.89 us | - | | Routed/shared down GEMM | - | - | 18.10 us | | Weighted route reduction + shared add | - | - | 4.19 us | | **Total GPU active** | **13.47 us** | **39.05 us** | **64.30 us** | This changes the interpretation of the earlier isolated timings. At `M=1`, the Gluon `_router_linear` device body is **not** slower: it takes `2.48 us` while also quantizing routed and shared inputs, versus `2.69 us` for AITER's router-only GEMM. The earlier `17-18 us` versus `8-9 us` result measured the complete launch boundary, so it exposed launcher/dispatcher latency rather than slower router arithmetic. The current small-M optimization target should therefore not be the `2.48 us` router body in isolation. ### 3. SGLang integration, isolation, and support matrix The integration sits above `MoeRunnerCore`, because that interface starts after routing has already been computed. The runtime flow is: ```text explicit Gluon selection -> validate quant/model/runtime contract -> bind GLM backend -> prepare packed weights after checkpoint load and before CUDA graph capture -> dispatch by TP/EP, target/NextN, and active M -> validate rank-local output tensor ABI -> existing SGLang _finalize_normal_output / post_experts_all_reduce ``` Isolation from other paths: - `auto` never selects Gluon; AITER, Triton, FlashInfer, MegaMoE, DeepEP, CPU, and other models retain their existing behavior. - GLM modules and Gluon kernels are imported lazily only after explicit selection. - Binding validates `model_type`, hidden/intermediate dimensions, 256 routed experts, sigmoid normalized top-8, quant ABI, gfx950, TP/EP-local shapes, shared-expert state, stream mode, A2A, EPLB, MoE DP, and routed scaling. - Quark layout preparation is owned by the selected backend; Gluon does not construct a dummy AITER runner. - Unsupported M/topology/model/quant combinations raise an actionable error. There is no native/AITER fallback from the Gluon backend. Current audited matrix: | Total TP | EP | Rank-local routed experts | Rank-local intermediate | Target/NextN M coverage | |---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 4 | 1 | 256 | 512 | 1..32768 | | 4 | 4 | 64 | 2048 | 1..16768 | | 8 | 1 | 256 | 256 | 1..32768 | | 8 | 2 | 128 | 512 | 1..16768 | | 8 | 4 | 64 | 1024 | 1..16768 | | 8 | 8 | 32 | 2048 | 1..16768 | Current model scope: - GLM-5.2/5.3 `glm_moe_dsa` target with serialized Quark W4A4 MXFP4 experts. - GLM NextN/EAGLE draft with the exact audited BF16 expert ABI. This is intentionally not a generic Gluon MoE claim. Future fixed-topology MoEs can reuse the backend boundary, but each model still needs its own strict validator, weight-layout adapter, routing semantics, kernel family, correctness comparison, and performance evidence. The most direct next extension is another GLM-family Quark MXFP4 shape; unrelated models should not be enabled by relaxing the current checks. ## Accuracy Tests ### 4. Kernel correctness - Low-M old/new Gluon schedule comparison at M=1..8: exact bitwise match. - Router/top-k isolation at M=1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128: - identical dense logits: top-8 ID match fraction `1.0`; - maximum top-k weight difference `<= 5.96e-8`; - production split-logit selector vs. dense selector: IDs match `1.0`, weights exactly equal. - EP2/EP4/EP8 compact kernels vs. rank-masked AITER at M=65,96,192,255: - all outputs finite; - relative L2 ranges: `0.004556-0.004568` (EP2), `0.004146-0.004172` (EP4), `0.003849-0.003886` (EP8); - maximum absolute error `<= 9.77e-4`. - Large-M TP8/EP1 Gluon vs. AITER at M=128..32768: relative L2 `1.81%-2.33%`, consistent with different MXFP4 quantization/accumulation order. ### 5. End-to-end correctness Current integration was exercised on GLM-5.2-MXFP4 with EAGLE/NextN, FP8 KV cache, DSA Triton attention, and CUDA graphs: | Topology / arm | Result | |---|---| | TP4/EP4, AITER vs. Gluon | 8/8 exact response texts and 8/8 exact output-token ID sequences | | TP4/EP1, AITER vs. Gluon default shared fusion | 8/8 exact texts and token IDs | | TP4/EP1, AITER vs. Gluon with `--disable-shared-experts-fusion` | 8/8 exact texts and token IDs | Logs confirm the intended shared policy on every rank (EP target/NextN native; EP1 target fused and NextN native) and contain no fallback, skipped Gluon dispatch, assertion, runtime exception, memory access fault, or GPU fault. Strict AgentX functional canaries using the InferenceX workload configuration also completed for TP8/EP2, EP4, and EP8 with target and draft Gluon enabled: 16 backend reports per topology, zero skipped dispatches, zero request/benchmark errors, and no fallback. ### 6. GSM8K **Score: `0.9437` (94.37%, 1,240/1,314 correct).** The full run completed without request errors in 896.44 s at 146.98 output tok/s. This is above the existing 0.92 MI35x GSM8K accuracy threshold used by SGLang's GLM MXFP4 accuracy coverage. Configuration: - full 1,314-question GSM8K test set, 5-shot completion prompt; - GLM-5.2-MXFP4, TP4/EP1, target + NextN Gluon; - EAGLE `3/4/1`, FP8 KV cache, Triton DSA, CUDA graph; - `--chunked-prefill-size 32768`, 256 client threads, temperature 0, maximum 512 output tokens; - strict backend: no fallback. This run also covers the TP4/EP1 large-prefill family. An initial run exposed a real coverage boundary at `M=16802`; the implementation was extended to the full 32K chunk instead of reducing the prefill chunk or hiding the shape behind a fallback. A separate strict request with exactly 32,768 prompt tokens then completed successfully (`prompt_tokens=32768`, one generated token, 8.49 s E2E) with no runtime/GPU error or fallback. ### 7. Test inventory Latest local validation on MI355X: - `72 passed` across: - `test/registered/unit/models/test_gluon_moe_backend.py` - `test/registered/unit/spec/test_draft_construction_isolation.py` - `test/registered/unit/layers/moe/test_fused_shared_expert_scaling.py` - `test/registered/unit/models/test_glm_nextn_moe_ptpc.py` - Continuous dispatch tests enumerate every integer M in each supported range and assert strict rejection immediately outside the audited ranges. - Official Ruff error selection (`F401,F821,F823,UP037`): pass. - Ruff format check over all 25 changed Python files: pass. - `git diff --check`: pass. - Full repository CI: pending; this PR is intentionally opened as Draft. ## Speed Tests and Profiling ### Microbenchmark method - AMD Instinct MI355X, one rank of TP8/EP1 unless stated otherwise. - AITER `acf8fdf9307431ece8ee275971c41cb3d1a7020b`. - PyTorch `2.9.1+rocm7.2.0.git7e1940d4`, Triton `3.8.0`. - 20 warmups, 200 timed repetitions, alternating arm order, HIP-event medians. - The AITER baseline includes SGLang's real small-M sorting patch and native shared-expert work. - Measurements were collected on equivalent pre-rebase kernel revisions; the rebased integration and 32K TP4 adapter were subsequently correctness-tested as described above. #### Route preparation decomposition (microseconds) | M | AITER router + top-k + sort | Gluon router + quant + select/schedule | Speedup | |---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | 62.16 | 32.94 | 1.89x | | 8 | 62.86 | 31.96 | 1.97x | | 16 | 61.48 | 31.90 | 1.93x | | 32 | 200.78 | 47.40 | 4.24x | | 64 | 190.74 | 52.58 | 3.63x | | 128 | 175.76 | 47.06 | 3.73x | At M=1..16, AITER's standalone router is about 2x faster and standalone top-k is approximately tied. The net win comes from eliminating the generic `moe_sorting`/handoff, which costs about 38-50 us by itself. At M>=32, Gluon also has the faster router schedule. #### Complete rank-local MoE layer (microseconds) | M | AITER | Gluon | Speedup | |---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | 574.97 | 99.42 | 5.78x | | 8 | 578.35 | 85.32 | 6.78x | | 16 | 543.89 | 94.34 | 5.77x | | 32 | 706.99 | 159.48 | 4.43x | | 64 | 670.25 | 172.78 | 3.88x | | 128 | 674.65 | 203.26 | 3.32x | A later M=1 fusion removed the standalone activation-quant launch and improved the Gluon arm from `100.80 us / 4 launches` to `81.94 us / 3 launches` (`-18.71%`, exact bitwise output). The shared MTP M=6 schedule improved its isolated layer from `121.44 us / 5 launches` to `85.86 us / 3 launches` (`-29.30%`). #### Large-M complete layer | M | Gluon | AITER | Speedup | Latency reduction | |---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 128 | 0.153 ms | 0.510 ms | 3.33x | 69.9% | | 1024 | 0.224 ms | 0.563 ms | 2.52x | 60.3% | | 8192 | 0.789 ms | 1.941 ms | 2.46x | 59.4% | | 16384 | 1.370 ms | 3.600 ms | 2.63x | 61.9% | | 32768 | 2.711 ms | 7.042 ms | 2.60x | 61.5% | rocprof confirms that the savings are not only CPU launch timing: | M | AITER launches / GPU-active time | Gluon launches / GPU-active time | |---:|---:|---:| | 1 | 15 / 60.82 us | 4 / 13.47 us (later optimized to 3 launches) | | 16 | 14 / 95.57 us | 3 / 39.05 us | | 32 | 15 / 119.22 us | 5 / 64.30 us | ### AgentX end-to-end performance TP8/EP1, GLM-5.2-MXFP4, MTP `3/4/1`, strict target+draft Gluon, 32K chunk, two-node forward/reverse A/B: Con / MTP | P90 ITV | vs 09/24 baseline | tput/chip | succ request -- | -- | -- | -- | -- C1 3/4/1 | 316.970 | +22.98% | 2338.423 | 258 C1 5/6/1 | 295.403 | +14.62% | 2304.512 | 256 C2 3/4/1 | 243.293 | +29.63% | 2555.224 | 434 C2 5/6/1 | 175.893 | -6.28% | 2419.022 | 409 ## Checklist - title: [XPU] publish nightly docker image with sgl-kernel-xpu built from main
author: arathi-hlab
body:
The Intel XPU nightly now publishes two `intel/sglang-dev` images:

| Image | sglang | sgl-kernel-xpu | Dated tag | Rolling tag |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (unchanged) | main | prebuilt wheel from `pyproject_xpu.toml` | `nightly-dev-xpu-bmg-<date>-<sha>` | `latest` |
| 2 (new) | main | built from source at `main` | `nightly-dev-xpu-bmg-<date>-<sha>-kernel-main-<kernel sha>` | `latest-kernel-main` |

## Changes

- `release-docker-intel-xpu-nightly.yml`: matrix `kernel: [wheel, main]` (`fail-fast: false`). For `main`, the kernel commit is resolved once via `git ls-remote`, so the tag names exactly the built commit.
- `docker/xpu.Dockerfile`: new `SG_LANG_KERNEL_SOURCE` (`wheel` | `source`, default `wheel`) and `SG_LANG_KERNEL_TARGET` (default `bmg`, set explicitly since no GPU is visible during `docker build`). `source` clones `SG_LANG_KERNEL_REPO` at `SG_LANG_KERNEL_BRANCH` (branch, tag or SHA), builds with `--no-build-isolation` against the installed torch, force-reinstalls over the wheel, and removes `build/`.

## Impact on existing images

- Image 1 tags are unchanged, and only image 1 advances `:latest`, which is the only tag CI pulls (`scripts/ci/xpu/xpu_ci_start_container.sh`).
- The Dockerfile defaults to `wheel`, so `release-docker-intel-xpu.yml` and manual builds are unaffected.
- As before, rolling tags move only for `main` builds.

## Tests

- pre-commit passes; the workflow YAML parses; the shell blocks pass `bash -n` / `sh -n`.
- Dry-ran the tag step for `main` and `release/v0.5.20` in both variants against the real kernel main.
- Full image build not run yet. To watch on the first run: kernel compile time on `intel-bmg`, and the kernel build's 4 GiB per-file memory guard.

title: [DSv4.1] Fold q_rope_store into fused_q_norm_rope
author: DarkSharpness
body:
> (auto generated by Claude)

Part of #41589 (DeepSeek-V4.1 prefill optimizations, split into smaller PRs).

## Motivation

The Q RoPE store before FlashMLA used a Triton kernel (`q_rope_store`) that only covered some shapes; the rest went through a separate copy plus in-place RoPE. The JIT Q norm+RoPE kernel already does the same work and can skip the norm.

## Modifications

- `main_norm_rope.cuh`: the Q kernel gains a `kApplyNorm` switch; `fused_q_norm_rope(q, q_out, eps=None, ...)` applies RoPE only while copying Q into the (padded) output.
- `MQALayer._compute_q_b` calls `fused_q_norm_rope` for every CUDA call with a `q_out` buffer, replacing the shape-gated `q_rope_store` path.
- `q_rope_store.py` is removed.
- Under ROCm the kernel rounds the sine product before the cosine fma, the gfx950 batched-RoPE order that the Triton kernel reproduced, so `test_dsv4_q_rope_store.py` keeps its AMD CI registration and now tests `fused_q_norm_rope` (bitwise against `fused_rope_inplace`, on CUDA and on gfx950).

title: [DSv4.1] Faster fp4 index-K gather and combine_topk_swa_indices
author: DarkSharpness
body:
> (auto generated by Claude)

Part of #41589 (DeepSeek-V4.1 prefill optimizations, split into smaller PRs).

## Motivation

Two DSv4.1 prefill helper kernels were dominated by launch count or poor parallelism rather than bandwidth.

## Modifications

- **Triton gather for packed fp4 index-K rows**: `get_index_k_fp4` built int64 byte-index tensors and ran a chain of small kernels per call. `gather_fp4_index_k` (`fp4_indexer.py`) reads the paged layout as int32 words (16 payload words plus 1 scale word per slot) in one launch; `deepseek_v4_memory_pool.get_index_k_fp4` uses it on CUDA.
- **Token-blocked `combine_topk_swa_indices`**: the kernel ran one program per (request, worker) with 128 workers, so a single long prefill request had 128 programs walking its tokens serially, and the wrapper filled the whole output with `-1` first. The grid now covers tokens (two per program); each token finds its request by a binary search over `query_start_loc` and writes its whole `-1` padded row, so the output needs no fill pass and preallocated buffers are overwritten entirely. Rows past the last request are `-1` with length 0, as before. Output is unchanged.
