title: [DSv4.1] Fused c1/c2 compress for eager extend, faster c2 decode
author: DarkSharpness
body:
> (auto generated by Claude)

Part of #41589 (DeepSeek-V4.1 prefill optimizations, split into smaller PRs).

## Motivation

Eager extend batches ran the ratio-1 and ratio-2 compressors as a chain of torch ops, while decode already had fused kernels.

## Modifications

- **Fused c1/c2 compress for eager extend**:
  - Ratio 1 reuses the per-token c1 kernel.
  - Ratio 2 gets a Prefill mode of the c2 kernel: an odd position pairs with the previous row when that row is the same request's previous position, else with its ring slot; pending rows are skipped.
  - `c2_prefill_store_kernel` then parks each request's last `ring_size` rows in the ring, `ring_size` CTAs per request from `extend_start_loc` / `extend_seq_lens`. It cannot run inside the pooling kernel because a chunk whose first row is odd and last row is even reads and writes the same ring slot.
  - The backend takes this path for extend-without-speculative batches when the compressor has `use_fused_compress`; the prefill CUDA graph and CP paths keep the torch compressor. Decode and prefill share one c2 JIT module.
- **c2 decode**: decode / target-verify rows issue their input and partner loads before a CUDA graph padding row returns, and the ring offset uses a precomputed multiply-shift divisor. `fast_mod_div_u32_t` moves to `sgl_kernel/math.cuh` from `nvlink_comm.cuh`, which now uses the shared one.
- Adds `bench_dsv4_c2_decode.py`.

title: [diffusion] Fuse Flux3 rowwise FP8 quantization with Triton
author: trebladev
body:
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->

## Motivation

FLUX.3 FP8 linear layers currently use separate PyTorch operations for row padding, FP32 conversion, rowwise absmax reduction, scaling, clamping, and FP8 conversion. This introduces intermediate allocations and multiple kernel launches for each activation quantization.

This PR fuses these operations and row padding into a single Triton kernel, reducing quantization kernel launches from `8` to `1` and eliminating intermediate activation buffers while preserving the existing quantization semantics.

## Modifications

- Add a Triton rowwise E4M3 quantization kernel with fused zero-row padding.
- Preserve the existing scale calculation and minimum scale of `1e-12`.
- Use IEEE-rounded division and direct FP32-to-E4M3 PTX conversion to avoid intermediate FP16 double rounding on SM89.
- Register and export the kernel through the diffusion kernel facade.
- Integrate it into `Flux3Fp8RowwiseLinear`, retaining the existing eager implementation for unsupported inputs or devices.
- Add correctness tests and a quantization microbenchmark.

The fused path supports contiguous 2D FP32, FP16, and BF16 inputs on NVIDIA SM89+, with feature dimensions from 1 to 16384.

## Accuracy Tests

Compared the fused implementation against the existing SGLang eager quantization path on a single RTX 4090 D.

Kernel tests cover all three input dtypes, irregular shapes, zero and small values, row padding, FP8 rounding boundaries, linear-layer output, and CUDA graph replay.

For end-to-end validation, used a real Cosmos3-DROID observation from episode 0, frame 232, with seed 0 and the instruction “Pour the contents of the yellow cup into the pink bowl”. Each variant was checked with two repeated requests.

| Variant | Maximum absolute action difference | Bit-identical actions | Audited quantization calls | FP8 payload / scale mismatches |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|
| fp8r | 0\.0 | Yes | 1828 | 0 / 0 |
| gd-fp8r | 0\.0 | Yes | 1119 | 0 / 0 |
| sd-fp8r | 0\.0 | Yes | 357 | 0 / 0 |


## Speed Tests and Profiling

Hardware: single NVIDIA RTX 4090 D.

Used the repository's `sglang.multimodal_gen.benchmarks.bench_flux3_action` benchmark with:

- Identical fixed synthetic three-camera inputs and seed 0.
- 10 warmup requests followed by 50 serial measured requests per configuration.
- Warm text cache and NATTEN VAE attention.
- No compilation, offloading, profiling, or quantization audit hooks during timing.
- Identical service and sampling settings between baseline and fused runs.

The baseline uses the original SGLang eager quantization path; the fused run uses this PR's Triton kernel.

| Variant | Baseline median latency (ms) | Fused median latency (ms) | Speedup | Latency reduction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| fp8r | 1563\.37 | 1155\.90 | 1\.35× | 26\.1% |
| gd-fp8r | 878\.71 | 662\.63 | 1\.33× | 24\.6% |
| sd-fp8r | 278\.31 | 223\.30 | 1\.25× | 19\.8% |

| Variant | Baseline P90 latency (ms) | Fused P90 latency (ms) |
|---|---:|---:|
| fp8r | 1582\.92 | 1172\.45 |
| gd-fp8r | 898\.47 | 678\.21 |
| sd-fp8r | 292\.21 | 238\.00 |

Latency measures the complete server-side inference request, excluding model loading and cold startup. Measurements were collected on a shared host, with one measurement group per configuration; they do not measure concurrent throughput.

Added microbenchmark:
`test/registered/kernels/benchmark/diffusion/bench_fp8_rowwise.py`

title: [CI] [NPU] tests: Reduce HiCache sizes and enable expandable pinned memory in focused tests
author: cl-vv-h
body:
## Motivation

Several Ascend NPU CI tests have intermittently failed while allocating pinned host memory. Large HiCache host pools increase the allocation pressure, and the Indexer/GSM8K tests also allocate pinned host buffers.

This change reduces HiCache capacity where appropriate and enables the expandable pinned allocator in nine focused NPU tests. It is a mitigation for these allocation failures, not a claim that their underlying cause is fully resolved.

## Modifications

- Follow the existing MLA sizing policy from #43308: change the MHA test from 30 GB per rank to `1 if _is_pr_pipeline else 10`, and set both Prefill HiCache and Decode KV offload in the PD test to `2 if _is_pr_pipeline else 10`. MLA already has this sizing policy in the base branch.
- Set `PYTORCH_NPU_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True,pin_memory_expandable_segments:True` in the server subprocess environments for:
  - HiCache MHA and MLA.
  - PD disaggregation, on both Prefill and Decode.
  - DeepSeek-V4 and GLM-5.2 Indexer replay.
  - GLM-5 top64-pruned BF16 GSM8K.
  - Qwen3.6-35B-A3B AIME26 with 64K input and prefix reuse.
  - Expert distribution recorder modes.
  - EPLB minimum rebalancing utilization thresholds, in both server launch environments.
- Keep the changes in these nine NPU test files. There are no shared runtime/helper, workflow, or diagnostic logging changes.

The size selection follows `GITHUB_EVENT_NAME == "pull_request"`: PR-triggered runs use 1 GB per rank for MHA/MLA and 2 GB per rank for PD Prefill/Decode; other invocations use 10 GB per rank. This is a logical HiCache pool size, not a cap on all pinned allocations.

## Accuracy Tests

The existing assertions and accuracy thresholds are unchanged.

Local validation passed: Python syntax checks, Ruff lint/format checks, and `git diff --check`. The PR/non-PR size expressions were checked to resolve to 1/10 GB for MHA/MLA and 2/10 GB for both PD endpoints. No NPU model execution was performed locally.

The following results were confirmed from individual test summaries in [Nightly run 38371635452](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/38371635452), at commit `66d96bfd4f`:

| Focused test | Result |
| --- | --- |
| HiCache MHA | [Passed](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/38371635452/job/115211804440) |
| HiCache MLA | [Passed](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/38371635452/job/115211804521) |
| DeepSeek-V4 Indexer replay | [Passed](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/38371635452/job/115211804585) |
| GLM-5.2 Indexer replay | [Passed](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/38371635452/job/115211804585) |
| GLM-5 top64-pruned BF16 GSM8K | [Passed](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/38371635452/job/115211805039) |

No pinned host OOM was found in the completed job logs reviewed for that run. That commit contains the same six test-file contents as this PR, but also contained other changes that have since been removed. These results are supporting evidence, not a complete validation of the current head commit `3607a8df7f`.

Additional validation: individual summaries in [Nightly run 38490526535](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/38490526535) confirmed all six original focused tests and the three additional allocator-configured tests passed; no OOM was found in the completed job logs reviewed. The run was replaced at the user's request before its final accuracy job completed, so it does not establish a complete clean run or two consecutive clean runs. A later run observed a default pinned OOM in the unmodified LLaDA2 Mini FDFO test; this PR does not change that test.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

No controlled throughput/latency comparison or profiling was performed for this change. The CI results above do not establish the performance impact of enabling the expandable pinned allocator.

title: [ROCm] Select DSA indexer top-k wave size by arch (wave32 on gfx1250)
author: jiaryang
body:
## Motivation

This extends the ROCm cooperative DSA indexer top-k (`dsa_topk_coop.cuh`) to MI455 (gfx1250).
gfx942 and gfx950 keep the same wave size and compile to the same device code (see below).

The kernel's wave-level steps are sized with `kWaveSize = 64`, which matches the wave64 CDNA
targets:
- the wave prefix sum (`__shfl_up(v, o, kWaveSize)`);
- the per-wave scratch (`BlockSize / kWaveSize` slots);
- the lane and wave indexing used by the block scans and histograms.

gfx1250 runs 32-lane waves (`warpSize == 32`; ROCm clang 23 (MI455 toolchain) rejects `-mwavefrontsize64` for
gfx1250: `option '+wavefrontsize64' cannot be specified on this target`). Measured on MI455 with GLM-5.2-MXFP4 (`index_topk` = 2048):
- rows no longer than `topk` select every element and are correct;
- rows longer than `topk` get wrong or out-of-range indices, which show up as memory faults in
  `coop_topk_kernel` on an 8K-token prefill, and in the sparse MLA decode kernel that reads the
  indices on GSM8K once contexts pass 2048.

Builds on the cooperative top-k kernel from #37591.

## Modifications

- Select `kWaveSize` by arch family, the same way as `deepseek_v4_topk.cu` (#41020):
  `__GFX10__` / `__GFX11__` / `__GFX12__` → 32, otherwise 64. gfx942 and gfx950 still get 64;
  the host pass also keeps 64.
- Add `check_wave_size()` at the top of all five kernels. It traps when
  `__builtin_amdgcn_wavefrontsize() != kWaveSize`. The builtin is a constant after target lowering,
  so the check compiles away when the sizes match. RDNA targets built wave64 predefine the same
  macros as wave32; on those builds the check compiles to a trap (see the gfx1100
  `-mwavefrontsize64` row below), so they fail loudly instead of returning wrong indices.

This only changes the AOT kernel; no op or signature changes, so no `sglang-kernel` pin bump.
It takes effect for users with the next `sglang-kernel` release.

## Accuracy Tests

`python/sglang/kernels/aot/tests/test_topk.py`:

| GPU | without this change | with this change |
|---|---|---|
| MI455 (gfx1250) | 5 passed, then `test_topk_kernel[True-4096-2048-132]` and `[True-4096-2048-256]` return wrong indices and `[True-4096-2048-4096]` aborts | 160 passed, 1 skipped |
| MI355X (gfx950) | 162 passed, 1 skipped | 162 passed, 1 skipped (same per-test list) |

On MI355X both dispatch paths run: bs=1 takes the row-split path (`coop_mb_hist0/hist1/scatter/refine`)
and bs ≥ 132 takes `coop_topk_kernel`. The one skip is
`test_topk_uses_score_device_and_rejects_mixed_devices`, skipped in both builds.
The MI455 run used a slightly older `test_topk.py` that does not yet have
`test_deepseek_v4_topk_transform_sorted_output` (2 cases, not this kernel), hence 161 vs 163 cases.

End to end on MI455 (GLM-5.2-MXFP4, TP2, eager, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3`, on a gfx1250
development branch that carries this change plus other local gfx1250 changes): the 8192:1024
serving benchmark at conc 16 completes 80/80 requests (up to 133,101 tokens in flight); before
this change, the same setup hit a memory fault in `coop_topk_kernel` on an 8K-token prefill.

GSM8K on MI455, same server setup as above (5-shot, 3 runs): 0.938 / 0.949 / 0.944, mean 0.944.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Device assembly of `csrc/elementwise/topk.hip` with the `setup_rocm.py` flags (`-O3`), before and
after this change (MI355X toolchain: ROCm 7.2.4, AMD clang 22):

- gfx950: the five `coop_*` kernel bodies are identical, and so are LDS, VGPR, SGPR and scratch.
  The whole `.s` differs only in the `__hip_cuid_*` symbol, which hashes the source path. The gfx950
  code object extracted from the built `topk_hip.o` has byte-identical `.text` and `.rodata`.
- gfx942 (compile only): the five kernel bodies and their LDS, VGPR, SGPR and scratch are identical.

| kernel (gfx950, `<2048, 12, 4096, 1024>`) | LDS (bytes) | VGPR | SGPR | scratch |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `coop_topk_kernel` | 49248 | 42 | 92 | 0 |
| `coop_mb_hist0` | 16388 | 16 | 28 | 0 |
| `coop_mb_hist1` | 140 | 32 | 32 | 0 |
| `coop_mb_scatter` | 144 | 38 | 55 | 12 |
| `coop_mb_refine` | 49248 | 34 | 86 | 0 |

Guard check, `s_trap` count in the device assembly of `csrc/elementwise/topk.hip`:

| build | `s_trap` |
|---|---|
| this change, gfx1100 `-mwavefrontsize64` | 5 (one per `coop_*` kernel) |
| this change, gfx1100 (wave32) | 0 |
| without this change, gfx1100 `-mwavefrontsize64` | 0 |
| this change, gfx950 / gfx942 | 0 |

Since the gfx950 and gfx942 code is unchanged, no speed run was done there. On gfx1250 this is a
correctness change; there is no working baseline to compare speed against.

- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests). (covered by the existing `kernels/aot/tests/test_topk.py`)

title: [Fix] [AMD] mamba: Keep a chunked prefill cut on the mamba chunk grid so DCP can donate checkpoints
author: chien-an-chen
body:
## Motivation

Under DCP, #39115 donates a mamba checkpoint only when
`prefix_len % mamba_cache_chunk_size() == 0`. `PrefillAdder` cuts a chunk
wherever the prefill budget runs out, and every later chunk inherits that
offset, so a request donates every checkpoint or none. With nothing donated,
`effective_cache_len` is 0 and the KV segment never enters the radix tree.
#40907 restored the old rule only on the non-DCP branch. This PR keeps the
DCP mask and makes the cut land on the grid.

Kimi-K3 MXFP4, 8×MI355X, TP=8 DCP=8, fp8 KV, `page_size=32`,
`chunked_prefill_size=8192`, `max_running_requests=96`,
`mamba_radix_cache_strategy=extra_buffer`, HiCache on, agentic workload at
concurrency 48. Each row is the same 240 s window after warmup. The last two
rows share a host, so the recovery is a within-host measurement. The first two
identify the commit that introduced the regression.

| tree | `kv_evictable_tokens` | `mamba_evictable_tokens` | device cache hit | prompt tokens / 240 s |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `fa8d22e665` (#39115's parent) | 11,382,528 | 473/480 | **91.5%** | 59.8 M |
| `6460082c05` (#39115) | 620,800 | 123/480 | 50.3% | 4.8 M |
| `main` (`8d1643b21e`) | 392,448 | 88/480 | **30.4%** | 3.3 M |
| `main` + this PR | 11,614,464 | 464/480 | **90.7%** | 59.5 M |

## Modifications

No-op unless `enable_mamba_extra_buffer` is set.

- `Scheduler.init_mamba_truncation_align()` folds `mamba_cache_chunk_size()`
  into `truncation_align_size` with an LCM, the same way DSA kpool alignment
  does. This covers `exact_chunk_fill`.
- `PrefillAdder.floor_chunked_tokens()` rounds a truncated chunk down to that
  grid in `add_chunked_req` and `add_one_req_ignore_eos`.

A chunk that finishes a request may stop anywhere. A cut shorter than one
chunk is not rounded to zero. The unit test walks a 100k prompt through six
chunks cut to arbitrary leftover budgets and checks that each one still donates.

Once donation works, the mamba pool's working set grows. A 60-slot pool that
was sized while donation was failing can assert in `_alloc_ping_pong_buffer`
at concurrency 4 and long context. Raise `--max-mamba-cache-size`.
Concurrencies 8, 16 and 48 were unaffected.

## Accuracy Tests

Tested at head `a5f74268` on 8×MI355X with Kimi-K3, TP8 + DCP8,
`mamba_radix_cache_strategy=extra_buffer`, `page_size=32`, and
`chunked_prefill_size=8192`.
For eight concurrent 17k–31k prompts followed by identical repeats, the
repeated requests reported:
| main (`4e0609ea27`) | this PR |
|---|---|
| 121,856 / 201,718 cached tokens (60.4%) | 200,704 / 201,718 cached tokens (99.5%) |
GSM8K was also run with the same DCP8/extra-buffer configuration:
- 1,319 questions, 5-shot
- Accuracy: **95.3%**
- Invalid: **0.1%**
- Exit status: 0
No accuracy regression was observed.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

kimi-k3 AgentX 3600 s, concurrency 48, non-speculative. 2026-09-01 (pre-#39115) was
7272 tok/s/GPU; 2026-09-28 plus this PR is 7492 (103%), GPU hit 84.6%.
The rows span weekly images, so the eviction-pool table above is the
controlled measurement.

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).
- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).

- [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed).
- [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance).

title: [DSv4.1] Trim prefill model-entry overhead
author: DarkSharpness
body:
> (auto generated by Claude)

Part of #41589 (DeepSeek-V4.1 prefill optimizations, split into smaller PRs).

## Motivation

Before the first decoder layer and after each Engram layer, DSv4.1 prefill ran full-residual elementwise work that is either redundant or can be done in one pass.

## Modifications

- **`hc_broadcast`** (`kernels/ops/layernorm/mhc.py`): builds the initial mHC residual `[T, hc_mult, H]` from the embedding with one Triton kernel instead of `unsqueeze(1).repeat(...)`. Output is identical; non-CUDA tensors and a non-unit last stride fall back to `repeat`.
- **Strided first-sublayer norm** (`DeepseekV4DecoderLayer._hc_combine`): with no previous pre-mix, the copies are all equal, so the CUDA RMSNorm now reads the row-strided copy 0 directly instead of making it contiguous first. Other platforms keep the contiguous copy.
- **Skip the image-token `torch.where` for text-only batches** (`_forward_layers_hc_pre_from_prev`): the full-residual `where` after each Engram layer now runs only when `forward_batch.contains_mm_inputs()`. Behavior change at the edge: a text-only prompt that literally contains the image token id used to skip Engram for that token and now gets it.
- Type annotations for the `EngramHasher` buffers.

title: [diffusion] kernels: stop specializing on per-request sequence lengths
author: mickqian
body:
## Motivation

Triton compiles one variant of a kernel per class of each integer argument it specializes: divisible by 16, equal to 1, or neither. Sequence lengths and row counts change with the resolution, the prompt and the input image, so a request whose sizes fall into a class the server's warmup did not hit compiles kernels on the spot.

Qwen-Image-Edit shows it on the nightly's first request. The server warmup conditions on a square image, giving 8192 tokens; the nightly's 1024×704 input gives a count not divisible by 16. With a cold Triton cache (a fresh machine or container), that first request spent 1.95 s in its first denoising step against 0.34 s for later steps. The Triton cache shows what compiled during that request: the select-0/1 LayerNorm modulation kernel, its residual variant and the LayerNorm-modulate kernel, each a second variant whose TTIR signature differs from the warmup's only in `seq_len` and `stride_i_b` losing `tt.divisibility = 16`.

## Modifications

The per-request sizes of these kernels go into `do_not_specialize`:

| Kernel | Arguments |
| --- | --- |
| `_fused_layernorm_scale_shift_gate_select01_kernel`, `_fused_residual_layernorm_scale_shift_gate_select01_kernel` | `seq_len`, `stride_i_b` |
| `_fused_scale_shift_4d_kernel` | `seq_len`, `num_frames`, `frame_seqlen` |
| `fuse_scale_shift_kernel_blc_opt` | `B`, `L` |
| `_layernorm_modulate_kernel` | `seq_len`, `n_rows` |
| `_qk_ln_head_kernel` | `n_rows` |
| `_temb_table_slices_kernel` | `rows` |
| `_pack_qkv_destination_major_kernel` | `rows` |
| `_cat_pad_cl3d_kernel` (Wan VAE) | `T`, `H`, `W`, `out_t`, `out_h`, `out_w` |
| `_dup_up3d_add_kernel` (Wan VAE) | `out_t`, `out_h`, `t_offset` |

Each of these arguments only feeds a row index or a row mask, while the loads and stores vectorize along the hidden dimension (the channels, for the VAE kernels), whose size and strides stay specialized. The arithmetic is unchanged and outputs are bit-identical. `mrope.py` and `vision_rope.py` already do the same for their sequence lengths.

The Wan VAE kernels keep more of their arguments specialized: the channel count, the element total and the strides, which the channel vectorization relies on, and the per-layer padding and cache length, whose constant folding is worth 1.5% of the cat/pad kernel's time. In the channels-first traversal of the DupUp3D kernel the output width is the contiguous dimension, so it stays specialized too. With channels a multiple of 16, those arguments stay in one class at every resolution.

## Accuracy Tests

- New `test/registered/kernels/ops/diffusion/test_shape_specialization.py`: each launch runs at a length divisible by 16, then at 57 and at 1 (frames only, for the VAE kernels), and a `triton.knobs.runtime.jit_post_compile_hook` asserts that the last two compile nothing. All 11 cases fail on main and pass with this change.
- The existing tests of these kernels pass unchanged (`test_modulate.py`, `test_layernorm_modulate.py`, `test_layout.py`, `test_wan_temb_table_slices.py`), including the bitwise cat/pad, DupUp3D and chunked causal-conv tests.
- Specialized and unspecialized variants give `torch.equal` outputs on the same inputs.

## Speed Tests

H200, `triton.testing.do_bench`, production-like shapes at one length divisible by 16 and one not:

| Launch | Shape (the two lengths) | main | This PR |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| select-0/1 LN modulation | 8192 / 8152 tokens × 3072 | 51.2 / 51.0 µs | 51.3 / 50.8 µs |
| residual select-0/1 | 8192 / 8152 tokens × 3072 | 80.6 / 80.4 µs | 80.6 / 80.7 µs |
| `fuse_scale_shift_kernel` (3D) | 8192 / 8152 tokens × 3072 | 43.9 / 43.6 µs | 43.6 / 43.3 µs |
| `fuse_scale_shift_kernel` (4D) | 21 frames × 1568 / 1561 tokens × 5120 | 255.8 / 254.8 µs | 256.0 / 254.7 µs |
| LayerNorm-modulate | 4096 / 4081 tokens × 4096 | 37.9 / 38.0 µs | 38.0 / 37.8 µs |
| per-head q/k LayerNorm | 4096 / 4081 tokens × 32 heads × 128 | 61.2 / 61.3 µs | 53.9 / 53.9 µs |
| Wan temb table slices | 1568 / 1561 tokens × 5120 | 79.7 / 79.3 µs | 79.7 / 79.3 µs |
| Ulysses QKV pack | 16384 / 16377 rows × 24 heads × 128 | 148.8 / 149.1 µs | 148.8 / 148.9 µs |
| Wan cat/pad | 256 ch × 4 × 180 × 320 / 256 ch × 1 × 181 × 321 | 131.5 / 68.7 µs | 131.5 / 68.7 µs |
| Wan DupUp3D add | 512→256 ch, 2 × 90 × 160 / 1 × 91 × 161 | 133.2 / 70.7 µs | 133.1 / 71.0 µs |

The LayerNorm-modulate, q/k and Wan VAE rows come from both variants interleaved in one process: separate runs of the LayerNorm-modulate kernel drifted by up to 3.5% between processes, which the interleaved run does not show. The per-head q/k LayerNorm runs 12% faster unspecialized; every other kernel is within ±1%.

End to end, nightly harness with an empty Triton cache:

| Case | main: first / measured / extra | This PR: first / measured / extra |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `qwen_image_edit_2511` | 16.38 / 14.35 / **+2.03 s** | 14.76 / 14.39 / **+0.38 s** |
| `flux1_dev_t2i_1024` | 4.37 / 4.19 / +0.18 s | 4.40 / 4.20 / +0.20 s |
| `zimage_turbo_t2i_1024` | 0.90 / 0.69 / +0.20 s | 0.94 / 0.70 / +0.25 s |
| `wan22_ti2v_5b_720p` | 53.83 / 53.15 / **+0.68 s** | 53.32 / 53.19 / **+0.14 s** |

On main, 1.63 s of Qwen-Image-Edit's extra is its first denoising step and 0.64 s of Wan's is its first VAE decode, which recompiles 11 layout-kernel variants at 1280×720. With this PR the first denoising step is as fast as the rest, and Wan's first decode is 0.17 s slower than later ones instead of 0.64 s; Wan compiles 22 Triton variants instead of 45. FLUX.1 and Z-Image have nothing to recompile; their first-request extra sits in the output path, and most of it is the perf dump the harness requests (#41711). Measured requests are unchanged. (The Wan row comes from a second run of the harness with the final VAE change.)

title: [diffusion] perf dump: one writer per replica, no first-request NCCL setup
author: mickqian
body:
## Motivation

Two problems with server perf dumps (`perf_dump_path` on a request), both seen from the nightly comparison harness, which asks for a dump on every request it measures.

1. **The file.** Every rank of the replica that holds the request's metrics writes the report to the same path, each opening it with mode `"w"`. The ranks truncate and overwrite each other, and a client polling for the file can read it mid-write: the harness hit a CFG-parallel dump that did not parse. Only the output rank records memory snapshots, so a report that another rank wrote last also lacked the memory checkpoints.
2. **The first dumped request's latency.** The replica-wide memory peaks were reduced with an NCCL `all_reduce` on the replica's device group. Nothing else uses that group at runtime, so the first dumped request paid for NCCL's lazy connection setup: 171 ms on Z-Image-Turbo TP2 (H200) against 0.7 ms afterwards. The nightly records every case's first request with a dump, so this read as a 0.2 s cold start outside the pipeline, which no user without perf dumps sees.

## Modifications

- `GPUWorker`: only the output rank dumps the report, as it already does for the other per-request outputs.
- `PerformanceLogger.dump_benchmark_report`: writes `{path}.{pid}.tmp` next to the target and `os.replace()`s it into place, so a reader sees either the previous complete report or the new one.
- `GPUWorker._record_replica_peak_memory`: the five counters are host values, so they reduce over the replica's gloo group, which connects when the group is created. This also removes the host-to-device copy and the sync on the result.

## Accuracy Tests

- `test_perf_dump_write.py` reads the target path from inside `json.dump` while a second report is being written. On main that read returns an empty, truncated file; with this change it returns the previous complete report, and no temporary file is left behind.
- `test_worker_records_replica_load_and_runtime_peaks` now checks that the reduction takes the host tensor, `MAX` and the gloo group, and still produces the same replica-wide peaks.
- `test_only_the_output_rank_writes_the_report` runs the dump (now `GPUWorker._dump_perf_report`) as the output rank and as another rank; without the output-rank check the other rank writes the file too and the test fails.

## Speed Tests

Z-Image-Turbo, TP2 on 2× H200, 1024² JPEG, sequential requests from curl with distinct prompts:

| | First request | Later requests |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| no `perf_dump_path` | 0.728 s | 0.684–0.692 s |
| with `perf_dump_path`, main | 0.917 s | 0.690–0.697 s |
| with `perf_dump_path`, this PR | 0.744 s | 0.687–0.698 s |

title: [ROCm] GLM-5.2 decode path: decode-shaped MoE/MLA tiles, split speculative softmax, and bf16 GEMM routing
author: jiejingzhangamd
body:
> Resubmission of #40358 under @jiejingzhangamd. The original commit authorship and patch series are preserved; commit SHAs were rewritten by the requested rebase onto `05817a40c98a09021945f894b8200911df8e1ec6`.

## Motivation

Four changes on the GLM-5.2 decode path on gfx950, found by profiling a
GLM-5.2-MXFP4 TP8/EP1 server at 104k context. They are all the same shape: at
decode batch sizes these kernels leave a 256-CU part mostly idle, and none of
them is made faster by doing less arithmetic.

- two of them launch a handful of workgroups because the tile or the reduction
  was sized for a regime decode never enters;
- one spends more time in launch overhead than in work;
- one lands on torch because a tuned table keyed on `(N, K)` has no entry for
  the shape and does not fall back to a neighbour.

Together they are **+5.7%** end to end on that configuration.

## Modifications

**`moe`: fold the padded-row fill into the shared-expert append kernel.**
`_post_process_topk_ids` bracketed the aiter shared-expert append with two
separate fills over the padded region -- one for the routed ids, one for the
weights -- three launches for a shape whose total work is a couple of
microseconds, once per MoE layer per step. The append kernel already writes
every one of those elements, so it fills the padded region itself. The id fold
requires EPLB remap off, since it relies on `pad_fill_id = 0` commuting with
`remap(0) = 0`; the weight fold additionally excludes the per-rank shared-slot
kernel, which has no shared-slot weights to zero. Where either precondition
does not hold, the separate fills run exactly as before.

**`mla`: size the absorb BMM tiles for decode.** aiter's config table has no
entry for the MLA absorb shapes, so decode falls into a bucket tuned for square
GEMMs (`BLOCK_SIZE_M=64, BLOCK_SIZE_N=256`). The grid is
`(heads, cdiv(M, BM) * cdiv(N, BN))`, so at 16 heads per rank and `N <= 512`
that launches 16-32 workgroups on a 256-CU part: starved of workgroups, not of
bandwidth or flops. This sizes the tile so the grid covers the machine and then
stops -- it does not keep splitting, because the kernel quantizes its own A tile
per token group, so every extra workgroup repeats that work (at M=200/N=512 an
unbounded split is 3.7x slower than the starved table entry).

**`spec`: split the vocab-wide speculative softmax across CTAs.** Speculative
sampling reduces across the vocabulary at every draft step and at verify. torch
reduces each row with one block, so at the row counts speculation actually runs
(1 to 32) a 154880-wide row occupies a handful of blocks, and it is read three
times. `temperature_softmax()` splits each row across CTAs -- partial
max+sumexp, an online-softmax merge, then normalize -- and folds the temperature
divide into the first pass, which drops the separate pass that materialized
`logits / temperatures`. It hands the call back to torch above the row count
where one block per row already fills the GPU, so callers use it
unconditionally.

`fast_sample`'s argmax gets the same treatment by routing it to the existing
`row_argmax()`, which already lands this optimization for the dspark accept
path. No second implementation is added: a split argmax written for this path
is 4.7-42% faster below 32 rows but 3x *slower* above it, where it fell back to
torch, and those are the verify row counts at higher concurrency.

**`linear`: route the bf16 decode shapes aiter's tuned table misses.** The aiter
tuned GEMM keys its table on `(N, K)` and does not fall back to a neighbour, so
a shape the table never saw lands on torch. A decode step hits one of those 79
times -- the MLA q up-projection, `(2048, 2048)` -- where torch runs at 8.4 us
against a 1.05 us weight-bandwidth roofline while aiter's own Triton a16w16
kernel does it in 5.0 us. What is missing is the routing, not a kernel.

The gate is `K` rather than a list of shapes: a list keyed on `(N, K)` is what
makes the aiter table miss these shapes to begin with, and a different tensor
parallel split moves every `N`. It is also bounded in the row count, because
what torch is slow at is the weight-bandwidth-bound regime decode lives in and a
prefill chunk is its opposite -- a 32768-token chunk is 1.25-1.44x *slower* on
the Triton kernel, so prefill must not be routed. `lm_head`, `(19360, 6144)`, is
1.33x slower there and stays where it was.

## Accuracy Tests

Every change is either bit-identical by construction or checked against a
reference before any timing.

| change | property | how it is checked |
|---|---|---|
| moe padded fill | bit-identical | the append kernel already writes those elements; folded only where the preconditions above hold |
| mla absorb tiles | bit-identical | same kernel, different tile; compared at every admitted M |
| `temperature_softmax` | fp32-accurate | vs a float64 reference, not vs torch, which is not ground truth at this width |
| `row_argmax` routing | bit-identical | vs `torch.argmax`, including the sampled index and the `gather` that consumes it |
| linear routing | bit-identical at M=1 | max rel diff 1.7e-4 at M=6, with the error against a float64 reference *equal* to torch's -- not accuracy traded for speed |

`temperature_softmax` against float64, MI355X, vocab 154880:

```
rows      this PR       torch       row sum deviation
   1     3.42e-11    3.42e-11                7.44e-08
   2     2.67e-11    3.27e-11                6.07e-08
   6     2.42e-09    2.89e-09                3.62e-08
  12     3.47e-10    3.47e-10                8.26e-08
  32     3.34e-09    3.34e-09                1.44e-07
  48     1.30e-09    1.30e-09                9.04e-08
  84     2.89e-09    2.89e-09                1.29e-07
```

`row_argmax` matches `torch.argmax` exactly at all seven row counts, and returns
the lowest index on an all-tied row, which ROCm's argmax does not guarantee
(#26358).

A GLM-5.2-MXFP4 TP8 server on an fp8 KV cache comes up and serves correctly with
`--dsa-decode-backend triton`, checked against prompts with verifiable answers
on both arms of every end-to-end run below.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

### Kernel level

`benchmark/kernels/bench_bf16_linear_routing.py` ships with this PR and needs no
server or model weights. It runs both arms in one process and interleaves them
ABBA, so the clock drift that moves kernels this small by ~10% lands on both;
the figure reported is the ratio's spread, not either arm's.

The speculative reductions, MI355X, vocab 154880, fp32, under CUDA graph replay
(the path decode runs on), us/call:

```
rows |  softmax: torch     PR    speedup  spread |  argmax: torch     PR    speedup  spread
   1 |           52.37   6.03      8.7x   23.36% |          12.00   4.61      2.6x    2.34%
   2 |           53.62   6.45      8.3x    0.79% |          34.48   4.71      7.3x    7.93%
   6 |           55.92   7.88      7.1x    0.45% |          34.65   5.24      6.6x    1.15%
  12 |           58.31   9.75      6.0x    1.51% |          34.04   5.75      5.9x    0.95%
  32 |           65.09  20.78      3.1x    0.75% |          33.98   8.70      3.9x    0.90%
  48 |           76.94  76.75      1.0x    0.29% |          36.97  11.19      3.3x    0.67%
  84 |           94.13  94.13      1.0x    0.22% |          45.80  12.28      3.7x    0.65%
```

Rows 48 and 84 in the softmax column are it handing the call back to torch above
its row limit: the harness measuring one implementation against itself, which is
the control for the rest of the column. The 23% spread at one row is the ratio's
own spread over six interleaved rounds on a 6 us kernel; every other point is
under 2%.

In eager the launch cost is not amortized and the softmax win shrinks to
1.1-1.4x; this is a graph-replay optimization and the docstrings say so.

The other two, from their own commits: the MoE append fold is 4.74 -> 1.61 us at
one row and flat in the row count, because what it removes is two launches
rather than work; the MLA `w_vc` absorb (N=256, K=512) goes from 18.1 to 3.6 us
at M=48, and `w_kc` from 12.9 to 3.1.

### End to end

Steady-state decode throughput per user, median over a 150 s window at
concurrency 1 and 2, geometric mean of the two. Base and patched arms were
interleaved across the session rather than run back to back, so linear drift
lands on both:

```
GLM-5.2-MXFP4 · TP8/EP1 · concurrency 1 and 2 · fp8 KV · 104k context
EAGLE 5/6 · --dsa-decode-backend triton · hierarchical cache off

                    vs base     read-to-read spread
base                      =     0.59%  (three reads)
three kernels        +3.94%     0.14%  (two reads)
+ linear routing     +5.67%     0.05%  (two reads)

geometric mean is over the two concurrencies; separately, at +linear routing
  concurrency 1     +4.95%
  concurrency 2     +6.39%
```

The effect is about ten times the baseline's own read-to-read spread. Within it,
the absorb tile accounts for +0.85% and the linear routing for +1.66%; the
softmax and the MoE fold make up the rest.

A trace replay of the same model (aiperf, 1800 s), one read per arm, covering
the three kernel changes only -- it was taken before the linear routing existed:

```
GLM-5.2-MXFP4 · TP8/EP1 · concurrency 1 · fp8 KV · 104k context
EAGLE 5/6 · --dsa-decode-backend triton · hierarchical cache off

per-user throughput, p90     +3.55%
per-GPU total throughput     +1.62%
```

Both arms completed the same number of profiled requests with no dropped
errors, so neither figure comes from a shortened or partly failed run.

Two harnesses with different workloads and different statistics -- a median over
a fixed-shape load and a p90 over a trace replay -- agree on the magnitude for
the part they both cover.

### What this does not claim

Neither figure is a position on a published curve. Both are paired A/B deltas on
one configuration, taken with hierarchical cache off, so they are not comparable
to a leaderboard point.

The end-to-end numbers were taken with the local split argmax described above
rather than with `row_argmax`; the difference between the two is ~1.5 us of a
12.6 ms decode step at these batch sizes, so the tables were not re-taken. The
trace-replay arms are one read each, so drift is not bracketed there; only the
first harness has repeat reads (0.59% on the base side) to bound its own noise.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).
- [ ] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).
- [ ] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations).
- [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed).
- [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance).

title: [QSA] Enable breakable prefill CUDA graphs for text-only Qwen3.8 Flash-Next (capture-safe metadata, MTP side-channel padding)
author: YAMY1234
body:
## Motivation

Qwen4Exp breakable prefill is blocked by the multimodal compatibility rules, including for text-only batches. Once the indexer runs in an eager break, live lengths and the prepared slot table avoid one D2H synchronization per QSA layer on replay. MTP replay also needs current HC state and matching target/draft token buckets. PLE request layouts must follow the live batch rather than the capture batch.

## Modifications

- Run QSA indexing in an eager break with live lengths and the prepared slot table.
- Include `contains_mm_inputs` in `dp_attn`'s unified vote and share eligibility between scheduling and execution, rejecting multimodal target and draft batches.
- Move PLE metadata, prefetch, convolution and history updates into eager breaks, correcting capture 1×8 → replay 2×4 request mapping.
- Add Qwen4Exp to `multimodal_breakable_cuda_graph_supported_model_archs` and remove the special-case hook.
- Evaluate `is_qwen4_exp` once in runner initialization and read cached target/draft policy during forward.
- Preserve HC replay state, align present draft embeddings to token buckets, and retain the text-only `None` fallback.
- Share QSA bridge storage: for buckets 128…16K, topk 512 and 12 layers, `Σbucket_tokens × 512 × 4B × 12` drops from 765 MiB to 384 MiB (381 MiB saved; the `buckets × max_tokens` upper bound is 3 GiB).
- Keep DP voting, live-length bridge, HC padding and PLE layout regressions in existing suites; host the manual comparison tool with the [accuracy evidence](https://github.com/YAMY1234/task-status/blob/main/qwen38-flash-next-rubin-agentx/subtasks/qsa-prefill-cudagraph-20260929/docs/REVIEW_166_CORRECTNESS.md).

## Accuracy Tests

Bit-identical outputs between graph replay and eager are not expected: breakable capture pads prefill to token buckets, which changes kernel shapes and reduction order.

GSM8K task accuracy is unchanged: 200 questions, 5-shot, strict scoring gives 197/200 with prefill graphs enabled, the same as disabled and base (measured on the pre-rebase branch).

| Configuration | em_strict |
|---|---|
| Base, prefill graph disabled | 197/200 |
| Patched branch, prefill graph disabled | 197/200 |
| Patched breakable vs base, MTP off | 198/200 vs 198/200 |
| Patched breakable, MTP on | 197/200 |

For greedy, MTP-off generation over 16 prompts × 64 tokens (measured before this rebase), shared-prefix absolute logprob differences for the same reference-eager token are:

| Comparison (positions) | p50 | p90 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Graph C1 vs eager C1 (443) | 0.000107 | 0.065216 | 0.445882 |
| Eager C8 vs eager C1 (640) | 0.00000650 | 0.041485 | 0.437805 |
| Graph C8 vs eager C8 (941) | 0 | 0.007811 | 0.234025 |

Serial graph/eager has a higher p90 but a similar p99 to the batching baseline; on the 337 positions shared by all comparisons, their p90 values are 0.094516 and 0.093125, while concurrent graph/eager has smaller tails.
Only 2/12, 0/8 and 0/3 flips respectively have a top-1/top-2 gap below 0.05 on either side (none on both), so the flips are not uniformly near-ties; [distribution details and CDF](https://github.com/YAMY1234/task-status/blob/main/qwen38-flash-next-rubin-agentx/subtasks/qsa-prefill-cudagraph-20260929/docs/REVIEW_166_CORRECTNESS.md#172cpu同前缀分布复核) retain the measured tails and limits of this comparison.

title: [DFlash2] Keep the greedy selector walk in range for all-NaN score rows
author: rodamani
body:
## Motivation
 
The greedy branch of `_selector_walk_kernel` (`kernels/ops/speculative/dflash.py`) takes `best = tl.max(scores)` and then the first offset where `scores == best`. If a whole score row is NaN, `best` is NaN, no element compares equal, and `index` falls through to `top_k`: one past the row, so the walk resolves to a neighbouring row's candidates.
 
## Modifications
 
- Greedy branch of `_selector_walk_kernel` now makes the same pick as `torch.argmax` (and `_selector_walk_torch`): the first NaN if the row has one, else the first maximum. `index < top_k` for every row, including all-NaN rows, and mixed-NaN rows match the reference.
- `test/registered/kernels/ops/speculative/test_lilicorr_cuda.py`: `test_greedy_path_matches_the_reference_on_nan_scores` (all-NaN and mixed-NaN rows), comparing tokens and q rows from `lilicorr_sample_path` against `_selector_walk_torch`.
 
## DSpark
 
DFlash-only: `DSparkWorkerV2` does not use `candidate_selector` / `selector_walk_triton`, so DSpark is unaffected.
 
## Accuracy Tests
 
CUDA test (`test_lilicorr_cuda.py`, registered on `1-gpu-large`); results from CI. The kernel was also checked against `_selector_walk_torch` under `TRITON_INTERPRET=1` for all-NaN, mixed-NaN, finite, tied and `-inf` rows (all match).
 
## Speed Tests and Profiling
 
No hot-path change beyond the fix itself; not separately benchmarked.

title: [Refactor] nvfp4_online: Use explicit FlashInfer 4over6 config
author: zianglih
body:
## Motivation

@humansand

Use FlashInfer's explicit 4over6 API for online NVFP4 weight conversion, preserving the recipe pinned by #33621 while moving quantization settings into the online quantizer.

## Modifications

- **Recipe:** pass `NVFP44Over6Config(e4m3_max=448, err_mode="MSE", err_use_fast_math=True)` to `nvfp4_quantize(..., nvfp4_4over6=...)`; remove the four load-time 4over6 environment overrides.
- **Scale contract:** derive the E4M3 maximum from that same config. Preserve the existing per-tensor decode-scale arithmetic, zero-amax handling, and shared w1/w3 scale.
- **Ownership:** keep the exact-FP4-math environment scope in the online quantizer. A small reference-counted context reuses `temp_set_env`: the first caller sets the override, and the last caller restores the original value, including on exceptions. The lock covers only entry/exit bookkeeping; quantizer calls run concurrently.
- **Scope:** the shared helper covers `nvfp4_online` and nonserialized `modelopt_fp4` MoE weights. Keep the new FlashInfer import lazy. The generic loader retains its post-load CUDA synchronization/cache cleanup; activation recipe selection is unchanged. The monokernel weight observer still runs before `model.load_weights`; upstream FlashRL reload guards and ModelOpt layout/padding handling are preserved.

- **Required API:** [flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#5152](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5152), merged as [`7bcf91831e4640cf7b8983e8b7954e94a03746b3`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/commit/7bcf91831e4640cf7b8983e8b7954e94a03746b3).

title: [MoE] Keep the moe_align_block_size pad fill inside sorted_token_ids
author: metamergebot
body:
## Motivation

`moe_align_block_size` sizes `sorted_token_ids` as `numel + (num_experts + 1) * (block_size - 1)` int32s. The CUDA align kernels pad that buffer with 16-byte `int4` stores and round the store count *up* to a whole number of vectors, so whenever the length is not a multiple of 4 the last store writes 1 to 3 int32s past the end of the buffer. For top-8 routing over 128 experts (129 buckets with the sentinel) the length is 3 mod 4, so every call overruns by one int32.

The allocator's block rounding usually absorbs the stray write, which is why nothing faults. It shows up under a memory sanitizer, and it corrupts whatever follows when `sorted_token_ids` is a view of a larger allocation; `virtual_experts.py` and `moe_lora_merged_align.py` already pad their own allocations to a multiple of 4 for exactly this reason, but the kernels themselves and the generic wrapper did not.

## Modifications

- The pad fill in every copy of the kernel (`moe_align_block_size_kernel`, `moe_align_block_size_kernel_v2`, in both the AOT and JIT sources, and the two fills in the merged LoRA align kernel) stores whole vectors only and finishes the last 0-3 elements with scalar stores, so it never writes past `max_num_tokens_padded` however the caller sized the buffer.
- `moe_align_block_size` (the Triton-runner wrapper), the AOT test and benchmark, and the registered test round the `sorted_token_ids` allocation up to a multiple of 4. This keeps the fill fully vectorized and also covers a prebuilt AOT kernel until it is rebuilt.
- New regression test `test_moe_align_block_size_pad_fill_stays_in_bounds`: passes `sorted_token_ids` as a prefix view of a longer buffer, with lengths 1, 2 and 3 mod 4, through the small-batch, generic and v2 dispatch paths, and asserts the guard words behind the view are untouched and the tail is fully filled.

`expert_ids` sizing and the fused MoE grids are unchanged for every block size that is a multiple of 4 (all tuned configs): `cdiv` of the rounded length is the same, and the fused kernels mask by `num_tokens_post_padded` anyway, so outputs do not change.

## Accuracy Tests

Kernel-level; outputs within `[0, num_tokens_post_padded)` are byte-identical to before.

- `test/registered/kernels/ops/moe/test_moe_align_block_size.py`: full sweep passes with the fix (5129 cases, including the 9 new ones). On the unfixed JIT kernel the new test fails on the generic and v2 paths (the guard words after the view are overwritten with the fill value) and passes on the small-batch path, whose fill was already scalar.
- `python/sglang/kernels/aot/tests/test_moe_align.py`: 4440 cases pass against the prebuilt AOT kernel with the rounded buffers.
- The merged LoRA align JIT module compiles with the changed fills and pads the tail correctly on both the fused and the two-kernel path.
- Not run here: a rebuild of the AOT kernel from source (left to the sgl-kernel CI stage).

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Not applicable: the fill is the same vector loop plus at most three scalar stores per call.

title: [PD][Spec] Give a PD decode's first EAGLE draft step a proposal distribution
author: salexspb
body:
## PD stack

1. [PD] Wait for prefill completion before Mooncake early KV transfer — [#41395](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41395).
2. **[PD][Spec] Give a PD decode's first EAGLE draft step a proposal distribution — this PR.**

## Problem

With PD and EAGLE, whenever rejection sampling is enabled, the verifier is handed each draft step's proposal distribution. ROCm enables rejection sampling by default for EAGLE top-k 1 (#37134, `_should_auto_enable_hip_rejection_sampling`), which is why this crashes there out of the box. `EagleWorkerV2.draft_forward` starts that list with `spec_info.draft_probs`. PD prefill sends decode the first draft token, its probability and its hidden state, but not the distribution, so `build_eagle_disagg_draft_input` leaves `draft_probs` unset. The PD decode then fails on its first forward:

```
eagle_worker_v2.py, in draft_forward
    torch.stack(draft_probs_list, dim=1)
TypeError: expected Tensor as element 0 in argument 0, but got NoneType
```

Under a draft CUDA graph, replay skips the proposal copy, and the verify would read a stale buffer instead. This happens with PD + EAGLE (including native MTP) whenever rejection sampling is enabled. Aggregated serving is unaffected.

## Fix

`build_eagle_disagg_draft_input` sets `draft_probs` to a one-hot FP32 proposal at each received draft token (`pd_first_draft_proposal`) whenever rejection sampling is on. Single-layer EAGLE gets one (batch, vocab) row. Multi-layer EAGLE gets the (batch, num_steps, vocab) chain, because its verify reads the received chain directly and otherwise fails with "draft_probs missing".

The verify stays exact. It accepts the token X with probability p(X) and otherwise resamples from the target with X removed, so the committed token is distributed as p, the verifier's target distribution. A greedy request's target is one-hot, so it accepts X exactly when X is the target argmax, with or without the true proposal, and its acceptance is unchanged. Sampled requests accept X with probability p(X) rather than Σ min(p, q), and only at their first decode step. Nothing is added to the PD wire.

#40953 instead transfers the full FP32 distribution through PD metadata, which needs a bootstrap wire change and costs vocab × 4 bytes per request. This PR is the minimal fix that restores correctness; the two could be combined.

## Tests

`test/registered/unit/speculative/test_pd_eagle_draft_proposal.py` (CPU, 5 tests):
- the built draft input carries a one-hot FP32 proposal at each request's drafted token;
- the proposal's width matches the target vocab, as `eagle_sample` requires;
- there is no proposal without rejection sampling;
- multi-layer EAGLE gets a one-hot FP32 proposal at each received chain step;
- enumerating a single-token chain verify over a drafting q, the committed-token distribution equals p.

On this head: 5 passed. `python -m compileall` and `import sglang` are clean.

## End-to-end validation (on a HiSparse fork build)

Before this change, a PD 4:4 decode (native MTP, EAGLE 3 steps, top-k 1, rejection sampling on) died at its first request with the `torch.stack` TypeError above. After it, in every configuration tested (aggregated TP8, PD 4:4 resident decode, PD 4:4 HiSparse decode), draft CUDA-graph capture completed, every service stayed up with no traceback, and 8/8 greedy chat prompts (including two needle prompts) were answered correctly, with mean accept length in the 2.6–2.65 range across configurations, matching the aggregated baseline.

These runs used single-layer EAGLE (native MTP). Multi-layer EAGLE PD is covered by the unit test only.

body:
> Part of the SM90 Q8KV8 FP8 sparse-attention roadmap #25746. > Throughout, **q8** = `--dsa-prefill-backend flashmla_sparse_q8` and **base** = `--dsa-prefill-backend tilelang`. Both configurations run the same bf16 KV cache and the same `--dsa-decode-backend tilelang`; only the prefill backend differs. **One-line summary:** `flashmla_sparse_q8` now serves GLM-5.3-Flash on Hopper (SM90): per DSA layer the sparse prefill is 1.53-1.72x faster than tilelang, which on a prefill-dominated workload is +11.16% to +12.44% total token throughput at 3.5k-120k input and 8.37% to 10.97% lower single-request TTFT at 8k-120k at TP4/EP4 (+5.82% to +12.06% and 6.06% to 11.28% lower at TP8/EP8), with no gsm8k few-shot count (1319 questions each) where q8 scores lower than base. ## TL;DR - **Before this PR, GLM-5.3-Flash could not use `flashmla_sparse_q8` at all.** Launching with it on H200 failed at backend construction (fp8-KV-only guard); relaxing that alone still fails on the KPool tail guard, the 2051-wide KPool top-k (kernel needs a multiple of 128), and zero-length RoPE in the Triton q-prep kernel. - **Per DSA layer (single H200, real backend code paths; 11 of this model's 45 layers are DSA):** at TP4's 16 local heads, q8 sparse prefill is **1.53-1.72x faster** than tilelang across 8k-131k context (1.53-1.72x at TP8's 8 local heads; 1.79-1.98x at 64 local heads). - **End to end** on a **prefill-dominated** workload (random dataset, 3.5k-120k input, **1-token outputs**), with the same server flags at both sizes: at **TP4/EP4**, total token throughput is **+11.16% to +12.44%** and single-request **TTFT is 8.37% to 10.97% lower at 8k-120k**; at **TP8/EP8** the same rows give **+5.82% to +12.06%** and **6.06% to 11.28% lower**. At 3.5k the TTFT difference is small and varies between runs, so it is not claimed. - **Accuracy:** gsm8k at four few-shot counts (5-120 shots, all 1319 questions at every count): **no shot count where q8 scores lower than base** after subtracting the server-to-server offset measured at 5 shots, where both run the identical dense path. LongBench-v2 (336 questions, every request on the sparse prefill path): **−0.003**, against a single-run noise of about ±0.027. - **Cost:** this PR adds one int32 buffer per attention backend (one per GPU here) to pad the 2051-wide top-k to the 2176 the kernel needs, at most `--chunked-prefill-size` rows (71.3 MB at 8192); no new flags or environment variables. ## Motivation On Hopper, GLM-5.3-Flash (`Glm5NextForConditionalGeneration`) runs with a bf16 KV cache (`--kv-cache-dtype auto` resolves to bfloat16 on SM90), so its DSA prefill computes in BF16. On SM90, FP8 doubles the peak tensor-core throughput of BF16 and halves the bytes moved per operand; that is why this series added an FP8 sparse prefill, `--dsa-prefill-backend flashmla_sparse_q8`, for DeepSeek-V3.2 (#30514) and extended it to GLM-5.2 (#31888). That backend could not run on GLM-5.3-Flash at all, because three properties of the model each block it: 1. **bf16 KV cache.** The q8 backend accepted only an `fp8_e4m3` KV cache, but this model is served from a bf16 cache on Hopper. 2. **NoPE MLA** (`qk_rope_head_dim=0`). The fused fp8 q-prep Triton kernel builds `tl.arange(0, ROPE)` and fails to compile at ROPE=0, as does the KV concat-cast kernel behind the opt-in `SGLANG_ENABLE_DSA_Q8KV8_KV_CAT_FUSION`. 3. **KPool top-k** (`index_kpool=4`). The KPool indexer appends up to `index_kpool - 1` tail tokens to every top-k row, so rows are `index_topk + index_kpool - 1 = 2051` wide, but the kernel walks top-k in pairs of 64-wide blocks and needs `topk % 128 == 0`, and the KPool tail guard did not admit q8. ## Modifications None of the three needs a change to the SM90 attention kernel: `d_qk=512` is already one of its two supported widths (512 and 576), `d_v=512` and `h_kv=1` match, and padding the local heads to 64 (from 16 at TP4 or 8 at TP8) already satisfies its contract. The fixes sit around the kernel: 1. **bf16 KV cache** (`dsa_backend.py`, `dequant_k_cache.py`). The q8 kernel only needs q and KV in fp8 at call time, so the validator now accepts a bf16 pool, q8 extend batches take the RAGGED top-k transform whatever the pool dtype, and prefix rows are gathered by slot and cast to fp8 per call (`gather_cast_kv_fp8_pad_paged`: on NoPE rows one vectorized Triton kernel that also zeroes the pad band, otherwise the existing MLA gather; bit-identical to the non-prefix cast). This mirrors an existing path in the opposite direction: `flashmla_sparse` already dequantizes an fp8 cache to bf16 on a prefix hit (`dequantize_k_cache_paged`). 2. **NoPE MLA** (`cache_ops.py`, `dequant_k_cache.py`). Both Triton kernels skip the rope segment behind a static `if ROPE > 0:`, so output with ROPE>0 is byte-identical to before. 3. **KPool top-k** (`dsa_backend.py`, `dsa_backend_kpool.py`). Top-k is padded with -1 to 2176 (output-invariant), and the KPool tail guard admits q8 prefill over a bf16 pool; an fp8 pool keeps the guard, since gathering packed fp8 rows through KPool tail columns is untested. Also included: - **Guards** (`dsa_backend.py`). At launch, q8 prefill rejects `--enable-mixed-chunk`, HiSparse, an fp8 dtype whose pool is not stored packed, and (not supported yet) an fp8 pool on a NoPE model; these previously failed mid-forward. At run time, a non-RAGGED q8 batch that carries top-k indices raises instead of silently running the bf16 kernel. - **Memory.** The q8 kernel needs a top-k width that is a multiple of 128, so the 2051-wide KPool top-k is padded with -1 to 2176 (fix 3 above). tilelang pads the same rows to 2112 (a multiple of its 64-column blocks) with a new tensor on every DSA layer call; this PR instead keeps the padded ids in one `(rows, 2176)` int32 buffer per attention backend that runs q8 prefill (one per GPU here), at most `--chunked-prefill-size` rows (71.3 MB at 8192). It is filled with -1 once and reused across DSA layers and forward passes; each call copies in only the 2051 real columns. - **Docs** (separate commits). The GLM-5.3-Flash docs page (`GLM-5.3-Flash.mdx` and its config) gains a Hopper `BF16 + Q8 sparse prefill` option, listed after `BF16 + TileLang` so the Hopper default does not change, with its own empty benchmark entries so it does not show the BF16 + TileLang numbers; `attention_backend.mdx` drops the stale `requires --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3`. - **Unchanged.** The SM90 kernel and its wrapper; fp8-KV behaviour for DeepSeek-V3.2 / GLM-5.2 apart from the launch-time checks above; DeepSeek-V4; every other DSA prefill and decode backend. ## Usage ```bash sglang serve --model-path zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash --tp-size 8 --ep-size 8 \ --moe-a2a-backend megamoe --moe-runner-backend deep_gemm --kv-cache-dtype bfloat16 \ --dsa-prefill-backend flashmla_sparse_q8 --dsa-decode-backend tilelang \ --mem-fraction-static 0.70 --disable-overlap-schedule --disable-shared-experts-fusion \ --max-running-requests 32 --max-prefill-tokens 8192 --chunked-prefill-size 8192 \ --context-length 131072 --cuda-graph-backend-prefill disabled ``` Opt-in only: without `--dsa-prefill-backend flashmla_sparse_q8`, no default and no other backend changes. **Hardware scope.** SM90 only (the kernel is SM90-gated). **Short prefills.** Batches whose longest KV length is at most `SGLANG_DSA_PREFILL_DENSE_ATTN_KV_LEN_THRESHOLD` (2048 by default) can take the dense MHA path instead, where both backends are identical. The decision is made per batch and has further conditions (for example, the batch's total KV length must fit the MHA chunk capacity), so under concurrency short requests can still reach the sparse path. ## Experimental Results **Setup.** All numbers are from H200 GPUs. Both sizes run the server flags in Usage, so the two sizes compare directly (`--context-length 131072` covers the 120k-input rows), and base differs only in `--dsa-prefill-backend tilelang`: - **TP4/EP4** on 4 GPUs: `--tp-size 4 --ep-size 4`. - **TP8/EP8** on 8 GPUs: `--tp-size 8 --ep-size 8`. Software: torch 2.13.0 (CUDA 13.0), FlashInfer 0.7.0.post1, sglang-kernel 0.4.8, Triton 3.7.1. The workload uses **1-token outputs**, so the throughput rows are prefill-dominated. Each version runs first in half of the repetitions, both servers restart every time, and the improvement averages the two orders. The accuracy runs used different server flags, the same for base and q8 (TP4 without expert parallelism, the default MoE backends, `--mem-fraction-static 0.80`, the default `--max-prefill-tokens`, overlap scheduling and shared-experts fusion on; LongBench-v2 also `--context-length 180224` and `--reasoning-parser glm45`), an earlier software image and an earlier revision of this PR's code.
Benchmark commands ```bash python3 -m sglang.benchmark.serving --backend sglang-oai-chat --dataset-name random \ --random-range-ratio 1.0 --seed 5 --flush-cache \ --random-input-len --random-output-len 1 --num-prompts

--max-concurrency # throughput: c = 64/64/64/32/16/8 for N = 3.5k/8k/16k/32k/64k/120k, P = 4c # TTFT: c = 1, P = 8 for 3.5k-16k and 4 for 32k-120k # N is in tokens (3.5k = 3,500). With 1-token outputs no request stays running after # its prefill, so --max-running-requests 32 does not limit these runs. ```

### Performance Benchmark **Per DSA layer** (single H200; times only the sparse prefill attention call, through the real backend code paths with synthetic indices and values; `do_bench` median per call; q8 time includes top-k padding, fp8 q-prep and the bf16 prefix gather-cast; speedup = tilelang / q8, higher = this PR better; ms columns at 16 heads; the 32k and 64k kv_len rows are omitted and fall in between): | s_q | kv_len | tilelang (ms) | q8 (ms) | speedup, 16 heads (TP4) | 8 heads (TP8) | 64 heads | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | 4096 | 8192 | 3.07 | 1.79 | 1.72x | 1.72x | 1.98x | | 4096 | 131072 | 3.06 | 2.00 | 1.53x | 1.53x | 1.79x | | 8192 | 8192 | 5.99 | 3.48 | 1.72x | 1.72x | 1.98x | | 8192 | 131072 | 6.01 | 3.87 | 1.55x | 1.55x | 1.79x | All columns come from one run on this PR's final code with the software listed in Setup. q8 pads the local heads to 64 and tilelang pads them to 16, so 8 and 16 heads cost the same in each backend; at 64 heads (all of the model's heads on one GPU) tilelang's work grows while q8's does not. Only 11 of the model's 45 layers are DSA (the other 34 are KDA linear-attention layers, which this PR does not touch), so the end-to-end gain is much smaller than the per-layer gain. **End to end** (improvement of q8 over tilelang, + = this PR better; for TTFT, the percentage by which it is lower): | input | throughput, TP4/EP4 | throughput, TP8/EP8 | TTFT, TP4/EP4 | TTFT, TP8/EP8 | |---|---|---|---|---| | 3.5k | +11.70% | +5.82% | +0.86% | +1.91% | | 8k | +12.07% | +8.33% | +9.31% | +6.06% | | 16k | +12.18% | +10.88% | +9.60% | +7.63% | | 32k | +12.44% | +11.21% | +10.17% | +8.94% | | 64k | +11.16% | +12.06% | +10.97% | +11.28% | | 120k | +11.24% | +11.65% | +8.37% | +10.92% | Spread across repetitions (1σ): throughput ±0.07-1.18 percentage points at TP4/EP4, and at TP8/EP8 ±0.32-1.42 from 8k up and ±3.15 at 3.5k; TTFT at 8k-120k ±0.23-0.49 at TP4/EP4 up to 64k, ±3.40 at 120k, and ±0.26-2.78 at TP8/EP8. Three entries (TP8/EP8 throughput at 3.5k, TP4/EP4 throughput at 32k and TTFT at 120k) include one repetition well away from the other three; with the median of the repetitions instead of the mean, the ranges are +11.12% to +12.21% (TP4/EP4) and +4.60% to +12.03% (TP8/EP8) for throughput, and 9.34% to 10.90% and 6.64% to 11.10% lower TTFT at 8k-120k. At 3.5k the TTFT difference is small (+0.86% ±3.27 at TP4/EP4, +1.91% ±1.47 at TP8/EP8) and varies between runs, so the TTFT claim covers 8k-120k only. **Absolute numbers by configuration** (medians, base → q8; the improvement above averages the two run orders, so it is not the ratio of these medians): | input | throughput, TP4/EP4 (tok/s) | throughput, TP8/EP8 (tok/s) | TTFT, TP4/EP4 (ms) | TTFT, TP8/EP8 (ms) | |---|---|---|---|---| | 3.5k | 32,118 → 35,885 | 40,914 → 42,795 | 193 → 192 | 196 → 192.5 | | 8k | 31,531 → 35,355 | 39,888 → 43,172 | 274.5 → 248.5 | 226 → 211 | | 16k | 31,044 → 34,835 | 39,191 → 43,364 | 560 → 506 | 452.5 → 415.5 | | 32k | 30,722 → 34,450 | 38,528 → 42,953 | 1,120 → 1,006 | 906.5 → 824 | | 64k | 30,200 → 33,588 | 37,524 → 42,065 | 2,142.5 → 1,907 | 1,718.5 → 1,526 | | 120k | 29,344 → 32,611 | 35,986 → 40,167 | 4,109 → 3,699 | 3,334.5 → 2,967 | Divided by GPU count, TP4/EP4's q8 throughput is 1.60-1.68x TP8/EP8's, while TP8/EP8's q8 single-request TTFT is 15-20% lower from 8k up. Two TP4/EP4 servers were not run side by side on 8 GPUs, and TP8/EP8's larger KV capacity matters more with longer outputs. **Where the time goes** (TP8/EP8, torch profiler, kernel time per GPU, averaged over the 8 GPUs and taking the median over server sessions, on a short separate test with 16,000-token requests rather than the benchmark rows): the sparse MLA prefill is 30.7% of tilelang's total kernel time, and this PR's kernel runs it 1.72x faster (256.1 → 149.0 ms), which alone cuts the total by 12.8%. The q8 preparation it adds (top-k padding, fp8 q-prep and the bf16 prefix gather-cast, 3.6 ms) costs 0.4%, the tensor concatenation that only the tilelang path runs (8.6 ms) saves 1.0%, and the fused MoE kernel (`deep_gemm` mega-MoE, which also carries the expert-parallel exchange) grows by 2.8% (190.1 → 213.5 ms). The total kernel time falls 10.6% (834.4 → 745.8 ms). ### Correctness and Accuracy Tests The accuracy runs used TP4 without expert parallelism (flags under Setup) and an earlier revision of this PR's code. This PR's later changes (where the padded top-k ids are stored, message text, launch-time checks, a pad-buffer width check that is a no-op at this model's top-k width, and the vectorized gather with bit-identical output) do not touch the numerics. **gsm8k** (all 1319 test questions at every shot count, few-shot examples from the train split, temperature 0, completion API, 2 repetitions; σ is the spread across them): | K (shots) | ~context | base mean (sigma) | q8 mean (sigma) | raw delta | delta vs control | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 5 | 0.8k | 0.9223 (0.0016) | 0.9166 (0.0011) | -0.0057 | *control* | | 20 | 3.3k | 0.8537 (0.0096) | 0.8575 (0.0032) | +0.0038 | +0.0095 | | 60 | 10k | 0.6740 (0.0161) | 0.6820 (0.0038) | +0.0080 | +0.0136 | | 120 | 20k | 0.3082 (0.0059) | 0.3048 (0.0086) | -0.0034 | +0.0023 | K=5 stays below the 2048-token dense threshold, where both configurations take the identical MHA path, so its −0.0057 is a pure server-to-server offset; the last column subtracts it. No shot count shows q8 scoring lower than base. The largest difference, q8 0.0136 higher at K=60, varies widely between the two repetitions (+0.0224 and +0.0049), so no gain is claimed. Both configurations score lower at longer contexts (0.92 at K=5, 0.31 at K=120), partly because of the completion API (on a separate base server with the same flags, K=120 scores 0.566 with the chat API and 0.324 with the completion API), so only the differences are claimed. **Kernel engagement and numerics.** A profiler capture on the LongBench-v2 q8 server shows 132 q8 kernel calls. For gsm8k, a separate profiled run at 4k and 16k context on an earlier commit shows 44 in q8 and none in base; the sweep itself was not profiled. q and KV are cast to fp8_e4m3 with scalar-1.0 scales; the largest magnitude seen in real GLM-5.3-Flash prefills is 13.9 (q; KV at most 5.2), 32x below the ±448 limit, so no rescaling is needed. **LongBench-v2**, where every prompt is longer than 2,048 tokens, so every request takes the sparse prefill path (thinking on, temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max-tokens 16,384, the 2,300-147,000-token subset selected with GLM-5.3-Flash's tokenizer, 336 questions, exact letter match; 2 repetitions): | statistic | base | q8 | delta | |---|---|---|---| | score (max-tokens 16,384) | 0.601 (σ 0.004) | 0.598 (σ 0.025) | **−0.003** | | answered by both, same repetition | 0.714 | 0.714 | **+0.000** | | truncated (no answer emitted) | 15.0% | 14.7% | — | No way of scoring shows a difference beyond about ±0.027, the binomial standard error of one run's score at 336 questions (−0.002 on the 255 questions answered in all four runs). About 15% of responses reach the 16,384-token cap while still reasoning and count as wrong in both configurations, so the claim is the difference, not the absolute score. ## Tests - `test/registered/unit/layers/attention/test_dsa_q8kv8_bf16_prefill_routing.py` (CPU, 24 cases): which top-k layout each prefill backend, KV dtype and batch type gets; which configurations q8 accepts and which it rejects at launch; the top-k padding and its buffer reuse; and the KPool tail guard for bf16 and fp8 pools. - `test/registered/kernels/ops/attention/test_q8kv8_dsa_nope_bf16_prefill.py` (1 GPU, 16 cases): the fp8 q-prep, KV cast and bf16 prefix gather kernels, with and without a rope part, match a plain torch cast byte for byte; and the q8 path on this model's shape (NoPE, bf16 pool, 2051-wide top-k) gives the same output with and without a cached prefix, is unaffected by the padding, and matches a torch reference. - The existing `test_sparse_mla_q8kv8_prefill_sm90.py` and `test_q8kv8_sparse_prefill_backend.py` are unchanged and pass. ## Future work - **FP8 KV cache.** Our next step is to connect q8 prefill to an fp8 KV cache for this model, so the prefill reads fp8 KV rows directly instead of casting bf16 rows (about half the bytes per row); we expect this to improve end-to-end performance further. ## Checklist - [x] Format your code according to [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit) - [x] Add unit tests according to [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests) - [x] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations) - [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed) - [x] Follow the SGLang [code style guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance) --- ### CI States Latest PR Test (Base): :white_check_mark: [Run #38215276474](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/38215276474) Latest PR Test (Extra): :x: [Run #38215275710](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/38215275710) Latest PR Test (AMD ROCm 10): :x: [Run #38215275905](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/38215275905)

title: [Feature] Add --attn-dp-size and deprecate --enable-dp-attention
author: ch-wan
body:
## Motivation

`--dp-size` means two different things. With `--enable-dp-attention` it counts attention data-parallel groups inside the TP group; without it, it counts model replicas. Every reader has to look at both flags to know which meaning it has. This PR gives each meaning its own argument, and the runtime reads the meaning it needs.

## Modifications

**Arguments.**
- `--attn-dp-size N` (alias `--attention-data-parallel-size`, default 1) runs N attention data-parallel groups inside the TP group, one scheduler each, while the FFN stays tensor / expert parallel.
- `--dp-size` counts replicas only. Replicas combined with attention DP (`--dp-size` > 1 with `--attn-dp-size` > 1) were never supported and are now rejected at resolution.
- `--enable-dp-attention` is registered with `DeprecatedStoreTrueAction`: it warns and names `--attn-dp-size` as the replacement. Resolution turns `--dp-size N --enable-dp-attention` into `--attn-dp-size N --dp-size 1` before any handler reads the layout. With `--dp-size 1` the old spelling still means attention DP off. Passing it together with `--attn-dp-size` is rejected.
- Handlers that turned attention DP on declare the width directly: DWDP, the DeepSeek DSA / MLA context-parallel overrides, and DeepSeek-V4. The three DeepSeek CP handlers still run `--dp-size N` as attention DP N, as before, and reject replicas combined with `--attn-dp-size`.

**Runtime.** Outside argument handling nothing reads `enable_dp_attention`. The published parallel config gains two derived fields:
- `attn_dp_enabled`: `attn_dp_size > 1`, or an elastic EP scale joiner. A joiner's own group can be one rank wide, but it joins an attention-DP deployment and runs its DP-attention paths.
- `num_dp_ranks`: `dp_size * attn_dp_size`, the number of DP ranks (schedulers). It equals the old `dp_size` under either meaning.

Readers migrate by meaning:
- The old `dp_size` → `num_dp_ranks` (DP controllers, MLP sync, CUDA graph buffers, load snapshots, prefill delayer, startup weight load, and so on).
- The old `enable_dp_attention` → `attn_dp_enabled`.
- Replica-only readers read `dp_size`: tokenizer control, the PD bootstrap world size, `compute_world_size`.

Other runtime changes:
- Elastic EP scale-up stamps the grown `num_dp_ranks`; `attn_dp_size` keeps the local layout.
- Wire formats keep their `dp_size` keys, which still carry the DP rank count: KV-event descriptors, PD prefill server info, and load snapshots.
- The weight-cache fingerprint records `attn_dp_size` instead of the flag.
- `/server_info` reports `attn_dp_size`. The model gateway counts DP ranks as `dp_size * attn_dp_size`, and falls back to `dp_size` for a server that does not report it.

**Docs, scripts, tests.**
- Every launch command, cookbook config and playground snippet uses `--attn-dp-size N`.
- Commands that passed `--dp 1 --enable-dp-attention` ran without attention DP; they drop the flag. The DeepSeek-OCR, DeepSeek-OCR-2 and GLM-4.7-Flash generators drop the DP option that only emitted it, and the Kimi-K3 950PR/DT recipe picks DP-Attention off.
- The server-arguments table marks `--enable-dp-attention` deprecated.
- The DP / DPA guide explains the two arguments, that an elastic EP scale joiner runs attention DP at width one, and that wire formats keep the `dp_size` key for the DP rank count.
- Tests and fixtures declare `attn_dp_size`.

**Tests.** The new `test_attn_dp_size.py` covers:
- the deprecated spelling resolving exactly like `--attn-dp-size`;
- width one without attention DP;
- the rejected layouts;
- both CLI spellings, and the deprecation warning;
- the published `attn_dp_size` / `num_dp_ranks` / `attn_dp_enabled`, including a scale joiner and overrides.

Gateway unit tests cover the DP rank count.

## Accuracy Tests

H200, this PR vs its base. GSM8K uses 300 questions; greedy text is 4 prompts × 48 tokens. The DeepSeek-V2-Lite (base model) row is the mean of 6 interleaved runs per side:

| model | launch (this PR / base) | GSM8K this PR / base | `server_info` this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek-V2-Lite | `--tp 4 --attn-dp-size 4 --ep-size 4` / `--tp 4 --dp 4 --enable-dp-attention --ep-size 4` | 0.386 / 0.386 | `dp_size=1, attn_dp_size=4` |
| Qwen3-8B + EAGLE3 | `--tp 2 --attn-dp-size 2` / `--tp 2 --dp 2 --enable-dp-attention` | 0.950 / 0.950 | `dp_size=1, attn_dp_size=2` |
| Qwen3-8B | `--tp 2 --dp 2` (replicas) on both | 0.950 / 0.953 | `dp_size=2, attn_dp_size=1` |

- On this PR, `--tp 4 --dp 4 --enable-dp-attention` resolves to the same layout as `--attn-dp-size 4`, produces identical greedy text, and prints one deprecation warning. The new spelling prints none.
- Greedy text is identical to the base for Qwen3-8B, in both the EAGLE3 and the replica runs. With DeepSeek-V2-Lite, attention DP and EP, greedy text is not deterministic on the base itself (two variants across six runs), and this PR's runs produce the same variants.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

DeepSeek-V2-Lite, `--tp 4 --attn-dp-size 4 --ep-size 4` vs the old spelling on the base, 6 interleaved runs each, GSM8K output throughput: base 6069 tok/s (range 5626–6367), this PR 5883 tok/s (range 5676–6456). The difference is within the run-to-run spread; `attn_dp_enabled` and `num_dp_ranks` are computed once at publication, not per read.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).
- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).
- [x] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations).
- [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed).
- [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance).

## Review and Merge Process
