title: [diffusion] Encode the MP4 while the VAE decodes (MiniMax-H3, Wan)
author: mickqian
body:
Stacked on #41797 (the encoder takes the per-request `x264_preset` from it). It also carries #41834, which applies the same streaming to Wan.

## Motivation

The MiniMax-H3 video VAE decodes a clip in temporal chunks — seven for a 5 s clip — and writes each chunk's finished frames into the output buffer in order. The MP4 was only encoded afterwards, in the worker's save step, so x264 spent about 0.5 s on the CPU after the GPU had finished, with the GPU idle. Benchmarks that time a request to the last byte of the MP4 at batch size 1 count all of it.

The Wan VAE is a better fit for the same idea. Its feature-cache decode runs the decoder on one latent frame at a time, and the causal cache only carries context forward, so each step's frames (one, then four per latent frame) are final as soon as they come out. Wan requests also encoded the whole clip only after the decode.

## Modifications

**Encoder and MiniMax-H3**

- `CudaVideoEncoder` (`entrypoints/utils.py`) takes `[3, t, H, W]` CUDA frames in pieces. `write()` queues the uint8 conversion on the current stream and returns; a writer thread copies each chunk into registered host memory and pipes it to ffmpeg. The one-shot direct save is now a single `write()` through the same encoder, so both paths run the same ffmpeg command on the same bytes and produce the same file.
- Frames now go into the pipe with `write()` instead of `sendfile()`. `sendfile()` from a memfd into a pipe lends the pipe the staging buffer's pages rather than copying them, so reusing the buffer before ffmpeg has read them changes frames that were already sent. Written one frame at a time, frames 0-2 came out carrying frame 3's pixels. The old one-shot loop got away with it because the next chunk's GPU conversion ran before the buffer was reused, which gave ffmpeg time to drain the at most 64 KB left in the pipe. At H3 size its output matched a file-input reference encode in 3 of 3 runs, but only because of that timing.
- `decode_base` / `decode_temporal` in the H3 VAE take an `on_frames` callback. It receives every output frame once, in order, as soon as the frame is final. Temporal chunks are the unit, whether or not the decoder tiles spatially.
- `MiniMaxH3DecodingStage` decodes the audio first, because ffmpeg needs the soundtrack when it starts, and declares its component uses in that order. The streaming path runs only for requests returned as a file path, on the replica's output rank, with no frame interpolation, no upscaling and no torch.compile'd VAE. On that path the stage applies the unchanged per-frame post-processing to each run of frames, feeds it to the encoder, and returns `output_file_paths` without the frames, so the worker has nothing left to save. If encoding fails at any point, the partial file is removed and the stage returns the frames for the worker to save as before.

**Shared**

- `stages/encode_while_decoding.py`: the encoder feed (`EncodeWhileDecoding`) and the eligibility rules (`streamed_video_output_path`) that the H3 stage started with, moved unchanged. The H3 stage and the generic `DecodingStage` both import them, so both stream under exactly the same rules and fall back the same way.

**Wan**

- `AutoencoderKLWan.decode(on_frames=...)` hands the callback a finished copy of each latent step's frames: unpatchify, float, then clamp, as `decode` applies to the whole clip. It still concatenates the raw chunks and finishes them at the end, so the returned frames are unchanged.
  - The tiled and whole-clip paths, used when `use_feature_cache=False`, only finish frames at the end, so the callback then receives the whole clip once. No registered Wan config takes those paths.
  - Under spatial-parallel decode, each step all-gathers to full height before the callback. That follows from the code, but it has not been run on more than one GPU.
- `ParallelTiledVAE` declares `supports_decode_on_frames = False` and `AutoencoderKLWan` sets it to True.
- The generic `DecodingStage` streams only when the request meets the same rules as H3, the stage's own `decode` and `forward` are not overridden, the VAE is a `ParallelTiledVAE` that declares `supports_decode_on_frames`, and no trajectory is decoded.
- Stages that override `decode`, such as the SANA-WM refiner, keep their signature: the generic `forward` passes `on_frames` only when it streams.

## Accuracy Tests

MiniMax-H3:

- New `test/registered/unit/diffusion/test_minimax_h3_streamed_encode.py`:
  - The callback sees the decoded video exactly once, in order, and the frames are final when handed out, with the streaming temporal concat both on and off.
  - Trimmed decodes reject the callback.
  - Writing a clip in uneven pieces produces the same MP4 bytes as the one-shot save, with and without audio, including a size that needs the macroblock scale filter.
  - Two encoders can run concurrently.
  - A failed encode leaves no file behind.
- `test_output_saving.py` and `test_video_encode_preset.py` pass unchanged.
- End to end, every request in the runs below produced the same MP4 (same md5) with and without streaming.

Wan:

- `test_wan_vae_on_frames.py` (CPU, tiny Wan2.1 and Wan2.2 configs): the pieces concatenate to exactly what `decode` returns, and passing the callback does not change the output.
- `test_wan_streamed_encode.py` (CUDA): runs the real `DecodingStage.decode` and encoder feed, and checks that the streamed MP4 is byte-identical to the one-shot save, for Wan2.1 under bf16 autocast at a size that is not a multiple of 16 and for Wan2.2 in fp32 with 2x2 patches. It also checks the eligibility rules. Changing the streamed frames by 1% makes the byte comparison fail.
- `sana_wm/test_pipeline_config.py`: the SANA-WM refiner, which overrides `decode`, still decodes through its own override.
- On 1x H200 at the branch head: both streamed-encode tests, `test_wan_vae_on_frames.py`, `test_output_saving.py`, `test_video_encode_preset.py`, `test_webui.py` and `sana_wm/test_pipeline_config.py`, 125 passed.

## Speed Tests

MiniMax-H3:

MiniMax-H3, `--model-variant fl2va --performance-mode speed --enable-torch-compile false`, t2va, 1344x768, 5 s (124 frames). One server per setup, with the two modes interleaved on the same server by a toggle that exists only in the test tree. Time is measured from `POST /v1/videos` to the last byte of `GET /v1/videos/{id}/content`.

| Setup | Steps | Encode while decoding | Encode after decoding | Saved |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1x H200 | 4 | 21.616 s | 21.958 s | 0.342 s |
| 2x H200, TP 2 | 4 | 11.450 s | 11.808 s | 0.358 s |
| 2x H200, TP 2 | 20 | 58.334 s | 58.690 s | 0.356 s |

Medians of 3 for 4 steps, means of 2 for 20 steps; spread within a mode was at most 0.09 s.

- The decoding stage now includes the encoder's tail: 5.006 s against 4.861 s on one GPU, and 2.604 s against 2.460 s on two. Most of that tail is x264's lookahead draining after the last frames arrive. The roughly 0.5 s save step that followed the decode is gone.
- Peak memory per request on 2x H200 went from 72,130 MB to 70,664 MB, because the stage no longer materializes the whole video in float32 when it streams.

Wan, 2 denoising steps, fixed seed, time from `POST /v1/videos` to the last byte of the content:

| Workload | GPU | Encode after decoding | Encode while decoding | Saved |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Wan2.1 T2V 1.3B, 832x480, 81 frames | 1x B200 | 1.955 s | 1.757 s | 0.198 s |
| Wan2.2 TI2V 5B, 1280x704, 121 frames | 1x B200 | 6.266 s | 5.827 s | 0.439 s |
| Wan2.1 T2V 1.3B, 832x480, 81 frames | 1x H200 | 3.382 s | 3.202 s | 0.180 s |

- B200: the two modes interleaved on one server (off, on, on, off, four times), medians. H200: main (`cae69be`) against this branch, A B A with five requests each after a warmup, medians; all 18 MP4s had the same md5.
- `DecodingStage` now includes the encoder's tail (H200: 1.50 s to 1.77 s) and the worker's save step disappears, so CI perf baselines will see `DecodingStage` rise while end-to-end latency drops.
- Peak reserved memory on B200: 11,936 to 11,716 MB for Wan2.1, 33,420 to 30,756 MB for Wan2.2.
- A 25-frame Wan2.2 clip goes from 1.380 s to 1.302 s: x264 holds back its look-ahead, so short clips gain less.

title: [diffusion] kernels: take the Wan VAE decoder's remaining first-decode work off the request path
author: mickqian
body:
Stacked on #41710.

## Motivation

With #41710 and an empty Triton cache, Wan2.2-TI2V-5B's first 720p request still decoded 0.17 s slower than later requests. Two costs remained in the VAE decode, and server warmup cannot absorb either of them:

- **Two DupUp3D-add variants compile during the decode.** #41710 unspecialized the sizes but kept every stride of `_dup_up3d_add_kernel`. In the channels-first arms those strides are products of the resolution (`C*H*W`, `W`, ...), so their divisibility class changes with the shape. Two launches landed in a class warmup had not compiled.
- **The lossless norm+SiLU fusion re-verifies itself at every new resolution.** `FusedWanRMSNormSiLU` keyed its first-sight exactness check on the activation's shape and strides. A new resolution therefore re-ran the eager reference chain plus a `torch.equal` host sync 46 times: 46 `cudaStreamSynchronize` calls in the first decode, none in the second.

Warmup cannot cover either: for TI2V, `InputValidationStage` derives the output size from the condition image's aspect ratio. The 64x64 warmup image gives 928x960, while the nightly's 1024x704 photo gives 1152x768, and no fixed warmup image covers every aspect ratio.

## Modifications

- **`_dup_up3d_add_kernel`.** Plain `do_not_specialize` on these strides would make the kernel up to 98% slower: their divisibility is what lets the compiler emit one 128-bit access per four outputs. The wrapper instead derives a vector width `VEC` from the layout. It passes the non-unit strides of `main` and `out`, and `out_w` when W is innermost, divided by `VEC`; the kernel multiplies them back by the constexpr, which restates the same contiguity without depending on their values. Unit strides stay specialized, but not on alignment.
- **`_cat_pad_cl3d_kernel`.** A second instance with the input strides unspecialized serves channels-first inputs, whose loads gather along the channel stride whatever its value. Channels-last inputs keep the fully specialized kernel; unspecializing it there costs 10-12%. The per-layer `pad`/`cache_t` specialization from #41710 stays.
- **`FusedWanRMSNormSiLU`.** The exactness check is keyed on `(device, dtype, x.is_contiguous(), gamma.dtype)`, which is exactly what selects the kernel template. The per-element ops do not depend on the sizes.

## Accuracy Tests

- `test_shape_specialization.py` adds four launches: `wan_cat_pad_channels_first`, and `wan_dup_up3d` in the cf/cf, cf/cl and cl/cf layouts. All four fail on #41710 and pass with this change.
- New `test_first_sight_check_runs_once_per_layout` in `test_wan_norm_silu_post.py`: #41710 verifies 6 signatures (`6 != 2`), this change verifies 2.
- The bitwise cat/pad and DupUp3D tests in `test_layout.py` now sweep channels-last and channels-first arms (four layout pairs for DupUp3D), plus two widths that exercise vector widths 2 and 1.
- `test_layout.py`, `test_shape_specialization.py`, `test_wan_norm_silu_post.py` and `test_model_fast_paths.py`: 286 passed, 1 skipped.

## Speed Tests

H200, Wan2.2-TI2V-5B at 1280x720, empty `TRITON_CACHE_DIR`:

| | #41710 | This PR |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Decode, first / second / third request (nightly harness) | 5.244 / 5.069 / 5.078 s | 5.061 / 5.067 / 5.062 s |
| First-decode extra | +0.17 s | -0.005 s |
| `DecodingStage` from perf dumps | 5693.7 / 5518.5 / 5532.8 ms | 5514.6 / 5520.7 / 5516.1 ms |
| Compiles during the first request's decode | 2 | 0 |
| Triton layout-kernel variants in the process | 22 (12 cat/pad, 6 DupUp3D) | 15 (7 cat/pad, 4 DupUp3D) |
| Warmup's own decode | 7.30 s | 6.96 s |

- Kernel time was summed over every distinct layout-kernel call site, layout and shape that a real decode passes, with both versions interleaved (ABBA) in one process: lossless fp32 -0.05%, `quality=high` fp32 +0.27%, `quality=high` bf16 +0.11%.
- Every output is identical to #41710's, in both values and strides.
- End-to-end latency of measured requests is unchanged.

title: [Fix] MiniMax-M3: default to the breakable prefill CUDA graph
author: thanhhao98
body:
## Motivation

MiniMax-M3 defaults to the `tc_piecewise` prefill CUDA graph, and on main that launch dies at boot (reproduced on `nightly-dev-cu13-20261005-f70e8c68`, GB300 TP4):

```
Capture prefill CUDA graph failed: Unsupported object.__new__ user-defined class construction
  ... object.__new__(DeclaredSum) is not safe
```

`tc_piecewise` is being removed (#41634), so this PR moves M3 to `breakable`. That needed one fix: under `breakable`, `RadixAttention` ran M3's sparse attention inline instead of as an eager break, so the graph replayed the capture batch's metadata and the server died on its first requests with `CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered`.

## Modifications

- Run sparse attention as an eager break under `breakable`, like dense attention and like DSA's indexer and QSA (#41729).
- Add both M3 archs to the breakable allowlist, so M3 defaults to `breakable`.
- A routing test fails without the fix.

## Accuracy Tests

End to end on GB300, MiniMax-M3-NVFP4: this PR at its default (`breakable`) vs main with the prefill graph disabled, each pair on one node.

| config | GSM8K 1319 q, this PR | GSM8K 1319 q, main without prefill graph |
|---|---|---|
| TP4 | 0.870 | 0.864 |
| TP4, EP4, DP attention 4 | 0.864 | 0.877 |

Across our other runs (two nightlies, with and without DP attention), both settings stay within 0.864-0.877. Image requests replay the graph too: a colored-shape probe (nine images, sent one at a time and all at once) answers 18/18 in every arm. Every arm also passes a bs=1 GSM8K canary and an EOS-termination check.

## Speed Tests

Same pairs, ISL 8192 / OSL 1024, median TTFT and output throughput:

| config | concurrency | TTFT (ms), this PR / main | tok/s, this PR / main |
|---|---|---|---|
| TP4 | 1 | **181** / 232 | 205 / 203 |
| TP4 | 16 | 1502 / 1505 | 1441 / 1429 |
| TP4 | 64 | **4868** / 4946 | 2838 / 2812 |
| TP4, EP4, DP attention 4 | 1 | 505 / **438** | 112 / 112 |
| TP4, EP4, DP attention 4 | 64 | **4313** / 4670 | **2854** / 2699 |

With DP attention the graph makes every DP rank replay a shared MAX_LEN bucket, so at concurrency 1 the idle ranks run the busy rank's length. TPOT is unchanged except DP attention at concurrency 64 (19.13 to 18.15 ms).

## Reproduce

Container `lmsysorg/sglang:nightly-dev-cu13-20261005-f70e8c68` with `python/sglang` at this PR's head (baseline: main `efb62ce269`), checkpoint `nvidia/MiniMax-M3-NVFP4`, one 4-GPU GB300 node.

```bash
# This PR (breakable is the default). Baseline: the same command on main plus --cuda-graph-backend-prefill disabled.
# DP-attention rows add: --ep-size 4 --enable-dp-attention --dp-size 4
SGLANG_DISABLE_MSA=1 python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path nvidia/MiniMax-M3-NVFP4 --trust-remote-code \
  --tp 4 --context-length 1048576 --reasoning-parser auto --tool-call-parser auto --port 30000

# GSM8K: 5-shot, temperature 0, 128 in parallel. The bs=1 canary runs --num-questions 40 with --parallel 1 and with --parallel 40.
python3 -m sglang.test.few_shot_gsm8k --num-shots 5 --num-questions 1319 --port 30000

# Speed: --num-prompts 12 / 64 / 256 for --max-concurrency 1 / 16 / 64.
python3 -m sglang.bench_serving --backend sglang --base-url http://127.0.0.1:30000 \
  --dataset-name random --random-input-len 8192 --random-output-len 1024 --random-range-ratio 1.0 \
  --flush-cache --max-concurrency 1 --num-prompts 12
```

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).
- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).

title: [XPU] split Intel nightly into kernel-main and kernel-wheel jobs
author: arathi-hlab
body:
The Intel XPU nightly now runs two setups:

| Job | Image | sglang | sgl-kernel-xpu | Suites |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `nightly-xpu-kernel-main-{1,2,4,8}-gpu` (renamed from `nightly-xpu-*`) | `intel/sglang-dev:latest-kernel-main` | main | main (built from source) | `nightly-xpu-kernel-main-{1,2,4,8}-gpu` (renamed from `nightly-xpu-{1,2,4,8}-gpu`) |
| `nightly-xpu-kernel-wheel-1-gpu` (new) | `intel/sglang-dev:latest` | main | prebuilt wheel from `pyproject_xpu.toml` | `stage-a-test-1-gpu-xpu` + `stage-b-test-1-gpu-xpu` (PR CI, 39 files), then `nightly-xpu-kernel-wheel-1-gpu` (9 files) |

Both images are published by `release-docker-intel-xpu-nightly.yml` (#41650).

Schedule (single `intel-bmg-nightly` runner, so jobs run one after another):

- `nightly-xpu-kernel-wheel-1-gpu`: 22:30 IST (`0 17 * * *` UTC)
- `nightly-xpu-kernel-main-*`: 01:00 IST (`30 19 * * *` UTC)

Each cron runs only its own jobs; `workflow_dispatch`, push and `workflow_call` runs still run all of them. The concurrency group includes the cron, so one scheduled run doesn't cancel the other.

## Changes

- `nightly-test-intel.yml`:
  - Rename the four existing jobs and pass `--image-tag latest-kernel-main` to `xpu_ci_start_container.sh`.
  - Add `nightly-xpu-kernel-wheel-1-gpu`. It installs the PR CI test deps and the diffusion extra's deps (read from `pyproject_xpu.toml`) under a constraints file that pins the image's torch/sglang/kernel builds, so the image itself is tested. It runs the PR CI suites with the same 180-min budget and `--enable-retry`, then runs `nightly-xpu-kernel-wheel-1-gpu --nightly`. The second step runs even if the first fails. The job timeout is 600 min because the two suites together (~5h est.) exceed the 360-min default.
  - Split the schedule into two crons (above) and key the concurrency group on the cron.
  - Add the new job to `check-all-jobs`.
- `nightly-xpu-kernel-wheel-1-gpu`'s PR CI step: pass `--timeout-per-file 600 --retry-timeout-increase 0` to the stage-a + stage-b run. The slowest passing file in recent runs took 487s; hung files (e.g. `test_xpu_basic`, `kv_canary/test_self_unit_req_to_expected_token_ids_manager`) ran the full 30 min before retrying. The same cap for `pr-test-xpu.yml`, plus fail-fast per-file overrides, is in #42048.
- Rename the `nightly-xpu-{1,2,4,8}-gpu` suites to `nightly-xpu-kernel-main-{1,2,4,8}-gpu` (test registrations, `run_suite.py`, `--suite` args, metrics artifact names). This includes `test_fused_inplace_qknorm_rope_xpu` (added on main by #40190), which goes to `kernel-main` only because it imports the new `sgl_kernel.fused_inplace_qknorm_rope` op, which the released wheel may not have.
- `xpu-ci-job-monitor.yml`: point the per-model report at the renamed `nightly-xpu-kernel-main-*-metrics` artifacts.
- `run_suite.py`: add `nightly-xpu-kernel-wheel-1-gpu` to the XPU nightly suites.
- Register these tests to `nightly-xpu-kernel-wheel-1-gpu`. They keep their `nightly-xpu-kernel-main-1-gpu` registration and existing `est_time`:
  `test_deepseek_ocr_triton`, `test_gemma_4_e2b`, `test_spec_eagle_parity`, `test_xpu_classification`, `test_xpu_embedding`, `test_xpu_rerank`, `test_xpu_reward`, `test_xpu_zimage_turbo`, `test_deepseek_ocr_2_olmbench`.

The workflow file name is unchanged, so `release-branch-cut.yml` and `ci_failures_analysis.py`, which refer to it by file name, are unaffected.

## Tests

- pre-commit passes on the changed files, including the registry validator and the duplicate job-name check.
- actionlint reports no new issues (only the existing `intel-bmg-nightly` label and `cancel-in-progress` warnings).
- Suite selection via `run_suite.py`'s collector: `validate_all_suites` passes. `stage-a` + `stage-b` select 39 files (6737s est.), `nightly-xpu-kernel-wheel-1-gpu` selects the 9 files above (10500s est.), and `nightly-xpu-kernel-main-1-gpu` (renamed from `nightly-xpu-1-gpu`) was unchanged at 13 before the latest main merge; it now also selects `test_fused_inplace_qknorm_rope_xpu`.
- After the latest main merge, the registry validator passes across all files (`pre-commit run --all-files`).
- Not yet run on the runners. A `workflow_dispatch` run will be the first real check.

title: [Perf] [AMD] Qwen3.8: AITER FlyDSL hc_mix for Qwen3.8 hyper-connections on gfx950
author: amd-nprotaso
body:
**Depends on [ROCm/aiter](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/5993)**. Without that AITER build this PR changes nothing: the path is gated on `aiter.ops.flydsl.hc_mix` being importable.

## Motivation

`GatedResidual`'s input mix is a low-rank gate over the `[M, 4·2560]` hyper-state. It runs in every Qwen3.8 decode step, and at decode sizes (M ≤ 16) it is bound by reading the weights.

On gfx950, AITER's FlyDSL `hc_mix` is 1.7–2.4x faster than the persistent Triton `fused_hc_mix` SGLang uses today.

## Modifications

**`python/sglang/srt/layers/hc_mix_flydsl.py`** (new)

`flydsl_hc_mix_supported(...)` accepts a call only when all of these hold:
- HIP, gfx950, BF16, contiguous inputs;
- 1 ≤ M ≤ 16, hc = 4;
- the shape constraints of the AITER kernel;
- AITER and FlyDSL are importable.

The checks are ordered so NVIDIA and disabled paths never import FlyDSL. `weight_cache_key(...)` gives the packed-weight cache a key from the weights' data pointer and version.

**`python/sglang/srt/layers/hyperconnection.py`**

- `GatedResidual` tries FlyDSL `hc_mix` before `fused_hc_mix`.
- Weights are packed once with `pack_hc_weights`, cached on the layer, and repacked only if the weight key changes.

**Benchmark and tests**

- `benchmark/kernels/bench_hc_mix_flydsl.py` compares FlyDSL, persistent Triton and `torch.compile`. It uses CUDA-graph replay with rotating weights, so the weights are cold in L2.
- `test/registered/kernels/ops/hyperconnection/test_hc_mix_flydsl.py` is registered in the AMD `stage-b-test-1-gpu-small-amd` suite. It checks:
  - the gate rejects inputs when disabled or given unsupported shapes;
  - `GatedResidual` dispatches to FlyDSL and matches the reference (`atol=4e-3`);
  - the packed-weight cache reuses packed weights and repacks after a weight change;
  - inference-tensor weights get a key with no version.

## Accuracy Tests

The FlyDSL output matches the float64 reference within `atol=4e-3, rtol=1e-2`, in both the AITER op test and this PR's dispatch test.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Command: `python benchmark/kernels/bench_hc_mix_flydsl.py --rows 1 2 4 8 16 --weights 64`

Setup: MI355X (gfx950), torch 2.11.0+rocm7.2. Time is the per-call median of CUDA-graph replays.

| M | FlyDSL hc_mix (µs) | persistent Triton `fused_hc_mix` (µs) | torch.compile (µs) | vs Triton |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 18.1 | 36.3 | 34.3 | **2.00x** |
| 2 | 18.8 | 44.9 | 38.1 | **2.38x** |
| 4 | 20.3 | 44.9 | 38.1 | **2.21x** |
| 8 | 22.1 | 45.7 | 38.2 | **2.07x** |
| 16 | 26.3 | 45.5 | 38.6 | **1.73x** |

title: [Perf] Use FA4 by default for MiMo on SM100
author: leonardHONG
body:
## Motivation

MiMo DFlash can fall back to Triton during automatic backend selection on SM100-family GPUs. Use FA4 consistently for this model family. Backend A/B tests on 8×B300 show **1.85× DFlash decode throughput** with FA4. Ordinary decoding also improves by **9.0%**, with **34.8% lower TTFT**.

## Modifications

- Default MiMo attention to FA4 on SM100/SM103 through the existing model override.
- Preserve explicit attention, prefill, and decode backend choices.
- Extend the existing MiMo configuration test. The runtime change is five added lines.

## Accuracy Tests

- All three MiMo configuration tests pass.
- **12/12 ordinary-decoding requests produce identical output token IDs** with FA4 and Triton.
- **16 BF16 attention cases pass against an FP32 reference**, covering the TP8 per-rank shapes for hidden sizes 4096 and 6144, QK=192/V=128, full attention and SWA with sinks, decode, 8-token verify, ragged page boundaries, and CUDA Graph replay.
- Ruff, formatting, and import-order checks pass.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

`XiaomiMiMo/MiMo-V2.6-Pro-RL@73875d00b30a`, 8×B300, TP8, `--moe-runner-backend flashinfer_mxfp4`, BF16 KV, concurrency 1, 8192 input / 1024 output tokens. Three warmup requests followed by three rounds of four measured requests per backend; CUDA Graphs enabled, prefix caching and communication fusion disabled.

**Ordinary decoding, no DFlash, page size 128 and 32,768 KV slots for both backends** (benchmark revision `7faae89732`):

| Metric | Triton | FA4 | Improvement |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Decode throughput | 159.47 tok/s | **173.86 tok/s** | **+9.0%** |
| Mean TTFT | 222.52 ms | **145.17 ms** | **−34.8%** |
| Mean request latency | 6637.36 ms | **6029.08 ms** | **−9.2%** |

**DFlash8 enabled, target and draft using the same attention backend:**

| Metric | Triton / page1 | FA4 / page128 | Improvement |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Decode throughput | 504.56 tok/s | **931.40 tok/s** | **+84.6% (1.85×)** |
| Mean TTFT | 234.81 ms | **150.93 ms** | **−35.7%** |
| Mean request latency | 2262.30 ms | **1249.28 ms** | **−44.8%** |

Both configurations use 32,768 KV slots, and all 12 measured requests produce identical output token IDs.

## Checklist

- [x] Code formatting and style checks pass.
- [x] Existing unit tests updated and validated.
- [x] Correctness and speed results provided.

title: [Perf] diffusion: fused QKV norm + RoPE, cached RoPE tables for FLUX 3 video VAE
author: niehen6174
body:
## Motivation

Every attention layer of the FLUX 3 video VAE prepares Q/K/V with eager ops: unbind the packed projection, apply two affine-free RMSNorms, then rebuild the 3-D RoPE tables and apply rotate-half. Encoding one 544x736 frame launches about 2200 kernels. On RTX 5090 that encode is launch-bound (17.7 ms of wall time for 9.3 ms of GPU work). Observation encoding runs on every FLUX 3 Action request, so the cost shows up on the one-step `sd` variants.

## Modifications

- **`flux3_video_qknorm_rope`** (`kernels/ops/diffusion/rope/flux3_video_qknorm_rope_triton.py`): one Triton launch reads packed BF16 QKV and writes RMSNorm + rotate-half Q/K plus a contiguous V. The RMSNorm follows ATen's vectorized reduction for head dim 64 and keeps the BF16 rounding boundary before the RoPE products.
- **`Natten3D`**: uses that kernel when QK norm, head dim 64, and batch 1 all apply. The first call is compared with eager under `BitExactFusionGate`. A mismatch or an error disables the kernel and stays on the eager path.
- **`RotaryPositionEmbedding3D`**: memoizes cos/sin per grid and time origin. The fused and eager paths share the tables.

## Accuracy

No accuracy change. The kernel is bit-exact against eager `nn.RMSNorm` (affine-free, `eps=1e-5`) plus rotate-half, not a lower-precision approximation.

- `test_flux3_video_qknorm_rope.py` checks `torch.equal` on several shapes, and checks that `Natten3D` matches its eager prep and reuses the RoPE cache.
- The VAE latent of a frame is bit-identical to main.
- Actions on 4 frames of the public Cosmos3-DROID episode 0 are identical to main for `base` and `sd-fp8r`.
- If the first call is not bit-exact, the gate keeps the eager outputs and does not use the kernel again.

## Speed

Setup: one RTX 5090, NATTEN VAE. `bench_flux3_action` is OpenPI WebSocket, 10 warmup + 50 requests, median `server_timing.infer_ms`.

Video VAE `encode_frame` (544x736):

| | main | This PR | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Eager wall time | 17.7 ms | 12.2 ms | -31.1% |
| Kernel launches | 2220 | 840 | -62.2% |
| Kernel time | 9.3 ms | 7.5 ms | -19.4% |
| With the FLUX 3 Action CUDA graph PR | 9.5 ms | 7.6 ms | -20.0% |

End to end:

| Variant | main | This PR | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| base | 1139 ms | 1137 ms | -0.2% |
| sd | 181 ms | 174 ms | -3.9% |
| sd-fp8r | 159 ms | 155 ms | -2.5% |

The observation stage drops by about 5 ms per request (`sd`: 25.5 ms to 19.4 ms). On `base` the 50-step denoise hides that. On `sd` / `sd-fp8r` it is a few percent of the request.

title: [Perf] [AMD] quark/Qwen3.8: Quantize the BF16 shared expert of Quark MXFP4 checkpoints to MXFP4 while loading for shared-expert fusion
author: amd-oshkarav
body:
## Motivation

This is a ROCm performance change. With `--enforce-shared-experts-fusion` the
BF16 shared expert of a Quark MXFP4 checkpoint is quantized to MXFP4 at load and fused into
the routed grouped GEMM (general matrix multiply), instead of running as a separate BF16
MLP (multi-layer perceptron). On `amd/Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B-Quark-MXFP4` over 8x MI355X at TP8
that is worth **+4.5% output throughput and -4.6% mean ITL (inter-token latency)**, as a
geomean across a 12-point serving sweep.

There is currently no Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B checkpoint in which the shared expert is FP4
quantized, so shared-expert fusion is unavailable for this model family on MXFP4.

`amd/Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B-Quark-MXFP4` quantizes the routed experts to MXFP4 but lists the
shared-expert body in the Quark quantization config's `exclude` list, so
`gate_proj`/`up_proj`/`down_proj` of the shared expert ship in BF16. Shared-expert fusion
works by appending the shared expert as one more routed expert at slot `num_experts`, so
that a single grouped GEMM serves top-k routed experts plus the shared one. That requires
every slot in the fused weight to have the same dtype, so today
`QuarkConfig.can_fuse_shared_expert()` sees the format mismatch and refuses, and the model
falls back to running the shared expert as a separate BF16 MLP alongside the routed grouped
GEMM. Rather than wait for a new checkpoint, this PR quantizes the BF16 shared expert at
load time so the existing checkpoint can use the fused path.

The feature is **off by default** and gated behind the existing
`--enforce-shared-experts-fusion` server argument, which already means "fuse the shared
expert even where the gate would normally refuse". In the fused path the shared expert goes
through the routed experts' W4A4 grouped GEMM, so its weights *and* its input activations
are quantized to MXFP4, where the standalone path it replaces ran BF16 x BF16. That is a
real precision trade and should be an explicit choice rather than something a checkpoint
opts into silently.

### Reproduction

Run inside `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.21-rocm10-mi35x` with this branch reinstalled in full over
the stock SGLang:

```shell
SGLANG_USE_AITER=1 \
AITER_USE_FLYDSL_MOE_SORTING=1 \
ROCM_QUICK_REDUCE_QUANTIZATION=INT4 \
SAFETENSORS_FAST_GPU=1 \
SGLANG_WARMUP_TIMEOUT=10000 \
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
 --model-path amd/Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B-Quark-MXFP4 \
 --tp-size 8 \
 --trust-remote-code \
 --reasoning-parser qwen3 \
 --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder \
 --attention-backend aiter \
 --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 \
 --mamba-ssm-dtype bfloat16 \
 --page-size 64 \
 --chunked-prefill-size 16384 \
 --max-prefill-tokens 16384 \
 --max-running-requests 256 \
 --disable-radix-cache \
 --mem-fraction-static 0.9 \
 --model-loader-extra-config '{"enable_multithread_load": true}' \
 --watchdog-timeout 12000 \
 --enforce-shared-experts-fusion
```

Dropping `--enforce-shared-experts-fusion` gives the baseline: the shared expert stays BF16
and runs unfused.

## Modifications

Nine files, and nothing else in the tree differs from upstream: four under
`python/sglang/srt`, two documentation pages, three test files. No new flag is added, so
`environ.py` and the environment-variable reference are untouched.

| File | Delta | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `python/sglang/srt/arg_groups/fields/exec_.py` | +1 -1 | extends the `--enforce-shared-experts-fusion` help text |
| `python/sglang/srt/layers/quantization/quark/quark.py` | +211 -7 | decides whether the conversion applies |
| `python/sglang/srt/layers/quantization/quark/schemes/quark_w4a4_mxfp4_moe.py` | +52 | performs the MXFP4 quantization, ROCm only |
| `python/sglang/srt/layers/moe/fused_moe_triton/layer.py` | +81 | the weight-loader hook that calls it |
| `docs/docs/advanced_features/server_arguments.mdx` | +1 -1 | documents what the flag additionally does here |
| `docs/cookbook/autoregressive/Qwen/Qwen3.5.mdx` | +1 -1 | mentions it in the Qwen3.5 AMD recipe |
| `test/registered/unit/layers/quantization/test_quark_config.py` | +546 -3 | the gating decision |
| `test/registered/unit/layers/quantization/test_quark_shared_expert_online_mxfp4_loader.py` | +474 | the loader hook (new file) |
| `test/registered/amd/accuracy/mi35x/test_qwen38_mxfp4_eval_mi35x.py` | +103 -6 | the MI35x nightly gate, extended with a fused-shared-expert phase, skiped for now  |

The decision of *whether* to convert lives with the quantization
config, the ROCm-only kernel call lives with the MXFP4 scheme, and the copy into the fused
slot lives with `FusedMoE` alongside the FP8 hook that already solves the same problem.

The change depends on #40754
(`e2f4fed`, merged 2026-09-24), which is in `main`. That PR gave the text-only
`Qwen3_5MoeForCausalLM` the shared-expert fusion weight remapping its multimodal sibling
already had, `mlp.shared_expert.* -> mlp.experts.{num_experts}.*`. Without it those weights
were silently dropped and the fused slot left uninitialized. The remap is what makes the
shared-expert tensors arrive at the fused slot at all, and the loader hook added here
intercepts them at that slot and converts them on the way in. #40754 covered checkpoints
whose shared expert already matches the routed-expert dtype (FP8), so no conversion was
needed; this PR extends the same path to the Quark MXFP4 checkpoint, where the shared expert
is BF16 and the conversion is the missing piece.

## Accuracy Tests

### gsm8k under the nightly e2e test's own parameters, greedy

**This is the headline accuracy result.** It is the only pair measured with the parameter set
`test/registered/amd/accuracy/mi35x/test_qwen38_mxfp4_eval_mi35x.py` uses, and with sampling
switched off, so it is the pair that answers "does this change what CI will report". 

| | fusion ON | fusion OFF | Δ (on − off) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| gsm8k score | **0.9764** | **0.9726** | **+0.38 pp** |
| correct, of 1314 | 1283 | 1278 | +5 questions |
| eval wall time | 215.6 s | 227.2 s | −5.1 % |
| eval output throughput | 841.4 tok/s | 806.1 tok/s | +4.4 % |



**Both arms are one image, one node, one day.** Built from `fse-online-mxfp4` at `747482984`,
this PR's HEAD as submitted, on `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.21-rocm10-mi35x`, run back to back on the
same MI355X host, and every
logged server parameter is identical except `--enforce-shared-experts-fusion`. 



### GPQA, NIAH

The branch at `abddcd87` was re-measured end to end on 2026-10-11, and two further evals ran inside each of those two serving sweeps, against the same server instance that produced the speed numbers below:

| Eval | fusion ON | fusion OFF |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| GPQA via sglang `run_eval`, temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, thinking enabled | 0.9242 | 0.9192 |
| RULER `niah_single_2` at 65536 via `lm_eval` | 1.0 | 1.0 |
| RULER `niah_single_2` at 131072 via `lm_eval` | 1.0 | 1.0 |



## Benchmarking

Measured with `sglang.bench_serve` through a 12-point sweep, twice, changing only
`--enforce-shared-experts-fusion`.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Model | `amd/Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B-Quark-MXFP4` |
| Hardware | 8x MI355X (gfx950), single node, TP8 |
| Base image | `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.21-rocm10-mi35x` |
| Branch commit | `abddcd8701376e29ad460b80a68c1589a9835174`, rebased onto `main` at `11bfd868` |
| aiter | the base image's, ROCm/aiter `acf8fdf93` of 2026-09-12 |
| Server | `--attention-backend aiter --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --mamba-ssm-dtype bfloat16 --page-size 64 --chunked-prefill-size 16384 --max-prefill-tokens 16384 --max-running-requests 256 --mem-fraction-static 0.9 --disable-radix-cache` |
| Env | `SGLANG_USE_AITER=1`, `AITER_USE_FLYDSL_MOE_SORTING=1`, `ROCM_QUICK_REDUCE_QUANTIZATION=INT4`, `SAFETENSORS_FAST_GPU=1` |
| Sweep | ISL 8192 / OSL 1024 at concurrency 4 to 256; ISL 60000 / OSL 600 at 4/16/64; ISL 128000 / OSL 1024 at 4/16. `random_range_ratio` 0.8 and an unbounded request rate throughout |
| Baseline | fusion OFF: no `--enforce-shared-experts-fusion`, shared expert stays BF16 and unfused |
| Candidate | fusion ON: `--enforce-shared-experts-fusion`, shared expert quantized to MXFP4 at load and fused |

Every one of the 12 points improved on throughput, ITL, TPOT (time per output token), end-to-end
latency and median TTFT (time to first token). Across all logged server parameters the two sweeps
differ only in `--enforce-shared-experts-fusion`, verified programmatically.

### Geomean per metric over the 12-point sweep

| Metric | Unit | fusion OFF | fusion ON | Δ | Direction | Improved at |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | --- |
| Output throughput | tok/s | 409.8 | 428.3 | +4.51% | better | 12 of 12 |
| Request throughput | req/s | 0.5089 | 0.5319 | +4.51% | better | 12 of 12 |
| Mean ITL | ms | 46.2 | 44.1 | −4.57% | better | 12 of 12 |

No metric regresses on geomean.

title: [Perf] [AMD] dsv4: reuse the q_lora fp8 quant for the C4 indexer wq_b (4/8)
author: AMD-yanfeiwang
body:
## Motivation

On the fused qk-norm/rope path (gfx95/gfx1250), `MQALayer._forward_prepare` already quantizes the normed `q_lora` to fp8 group-128 (`_fused_rmsnorm_fp8_quant`) for the attention `wq_b`. The C4 indexer's `wq_b` takes the same `q_lora` and quantizes it again with a standalone `dynamic_per_group_scaled_quant`. For DeepSeek-V4-Pro that adds 30 extra launches per decode/verify step.

## Modifications

- `_forward_prepare` passes the existing quant (`q_lora_quant`) through `C4Indexer.forward` -> `forward_c4_indexer` -> `compute_q`, and the indexer `wq_b` consumes it directly.
- It is dropped (set to `None`) when the indexer trims `q_lora` to fewer queries. The non-fused path, the multi-stream path, NPU and the low-ratio arms are unchanged. `forward_c4_indexer` only receives the kwarg when it is set.

## Accuracy Tests

- The quantized input is the same tensor the attention `wq_b` already uses, so the indexer `wq_b` input is identical to its own quant of `q_lora`.
- DeepSeek-V4-Pro TP8, stock image `lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:v0.5.20-rocm724-mi35x-20260927` + this PR only: gsm8k 200q **0.965**. A capture-time print confirmed that the reuse path runs on all 8 ranks.
- On the stack below, DSpark b6 gsm8k 1319q over 2 boots: before 0.945 / 0.939, after 0.945 / 0.948. Accept length 4.36 -> 4.37.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Kernel: each removed `dynamic_per_group_scaled_quant` launch shows as 4.3 us in the graph-mode trace (about 3.8 us after subtracting profiler overhead). With 30 launches per step, the trace estimate was about 0.11-0.13 ms per step. The measured E2E saving is 0.06-0.09 ms per step, which is about 2-3 us per launch.

E2E, DeepSeek-V4-Pro fp8, TP8 MI355X, image `lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:v0.5.20-rocm724-mi35x-20260927`, 8k in / 1k out. Measured on our DSv4 decode stack: sgl-project/sglang#41383 (FlyDSL fused decode, with ROCm/aiter#5882 and the aiter fp32-out HGEMM fix), the DSpark verify ring write, sgl-project/sglang#38919 + sgl-project/sglang#38920 (env on), the MoE small-batch sort and the fp32 GEMM aiter route. Before = that stack; after = stack + this PR. It was developed there; the diff on main is the same minus the sgl-project/sglang#38920 `kv_score_input` plumbing. 2 boots x 3 reps, paired:

| cell | step time before -> after (ms) | delta mean [min, max] (ms) | steady decode tok/s |
|---|---|---|---|
| plain c8 | 11.87 -> 11.79 | **-0.65%** -0.077 [-0.100, -0.043] | 674 -> 678 |
| plain c32 | 15.60 -> 15.54 | **-0.39%** -0.061 [-0.087, -0.035] | 2053 -> 2062 |
| DSpark b6 c2 | 14.85 -> 14.76 | **-0.60%** -0.089 [-0.113, -0.078] | 859 -> 864 |
| DSpark b6 c4 | 17.36 -> 17.30 | **-0.33%** -0.058 [-0.135, -0.021] | 1407 -> 1417 |
| DSpark b6 c16 (1 boot) | 26.26 -> 26.27 | +0.06% (noise) | - |
| DSpark b6 c64 (1 boot) | 45.13 -> 45.05 | -0.18% (noise) | - |

All 24 two-boot pairs are faster.

title: [Diffusion] MiniMax-H3 fuse the video VAE decoder's RMSNorm and QK RoPE
author: niehen6174
body:
## Motivation

Each block of the H3 video VAE decoder runs eager RMSNorm, a scaled residual add, and per-head Q/K RMSNorm plus partial NeoX RoPE. The decoder is a 36-block ViT and runs on every H3 request. Decode is still one tile per call.

## Modifications

- **`h3_vae_rmsnorm`**, **`h3_vae_scale_add_rmsnorm`**, **`h3_vae_qk_rmsnorm_rope`** (`kernels/ops/diffusion/norm/h3_vae_fused_norm.py`): FP32 RMSNorm, the scaled residual add fused into the next RMSNorm, and affine-free Q/K RMSNorm plus partial NeoX RoPE (head 64 / rotary 48). A contract mismatch stays on the eager path. `MINIMAX_H3_VAE_DECODER_FUSED_NORM=1` by default.
- The decoder broadcasts one rotary table across the tiles in a batch, so the Q/K kernel also runs for `B > 1`.

## Accuracy

Fused matches eager to a max absolute error of about 5e-5 on a 28-tile output. `test_h3_vae_fused_norm.py` checks each kernel. `test_fused_decoder_matches_unfused_forward` checks the decoder and that the fused kernels actually ran.

## Speed

One H200, fp16 autocast, released decoder shape, one tile per call. A 1344×768, 10 s, 24 fps clip is 14 temporal units, 28 tiles each. The unit row is measured. The 10 s row is that unit times 14: same decoder, no extra run.

| | main | This PR | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| One temporal unit | 656.3 ms | 589.5 ms | -66.8 ms (-10.2%) |
| 10 s VAE decode, 1×H200 | 9.19 s | 8.25 s | -0.94 s (-10.2%) |

title: [Fix] sampling: Make top-k/top-p filtering consistent across sampling paths
author: alvion427
body:
Supersedes #36173 and addresses its final review findings.

## Motivation

SGLang normally computes the top-p cutoff from the original probability distribution and intersects that support with top-k. Some sampling paths instead applied top-k, renormalized the remaining probabilities, and then applied top-p. That applies top-p to whatever probability mass happens to remain after top-k, making its effect unpredictable and inconsistent with other sampling paths using the same parameters.

The affected paths are the FlashInfer min-p path, the shared EAGLE-family/standalone/n-gram verifier, and the target-distribution builder shared by DFlash, DSpark, and UNO. UNO's separate compact top-k path also needed the same fix; its behavior could otherwise depend on other requests in the batch.

## Modifications

- Apply top-p before top-k in the FlashInfer min-p path.
- Apply the same ordering in the shared EAGLE-family, standalone, and n-gram verifier.
- Correct dense/sparse target distributions shared by DFlash, DSpark, and UNO.
- Preserve the sparse top-k path by translating the top-p cutoff into the renormalized top-k distribution using the top-k support's original probability mass.
- Apply the same correction to UNO's separate compact top-k path.
- Fuse CUDA unseeded top-p rescaling by reusing the retained top-k maximum, avoiding a full-vocabulary maximum reduction and exponential intermediate.
- Preserve logsumexp for seeded/non-CUDA callers; UNO rejects deterministic inference.
- Document that fused FP32 rounding can change cutoff membership, without promising bitwise identity or trainer alignment.
- Reject `min_p > 0` for built-in speculative decoding, where it is not currently applied.
- Add focused CUDA regression tests for each corrected implementation.

## Accuracy Tests

The regressions use probabilities `[0.35, 0.25, 0.20, 0.05, 0.03, ...]`, `top_k=4`, and `top_p=0.82`. The FlashInfer min-p case also uses `min_p=0.1`.

The original top-p nucleus includes token 3 because the probability mass before it is `0.80`. Applying and renormalizing top-k first changes that mass to `0.80 / 0.85`, causing token 3 to be incorrectly removed.

Validated rebased commit `50e6ca6b73cc49214b5e9e28068b187ac3d7de2f` on an NVIDIA H200 with Python 3.12.3, CUDA 13.0, PyTorch 2.13.0, FlashInfer 0.6.18, and Triton 3.7.1.

`TestSamplingMaskCapture` and `test_speculative_sampling.py`: **18 passed, 6 subtests passed**, no failures/errors/skips.

Each regression passed with the fix and failed with pre-fix filtering:

| Path | With fix | Before fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FlashInfer min-p | Pass | Support length 3 instead of 4 |
| EAGLE, using the production FlashInfer kernels | Pass | Token-3 probability mismatch |
| Shared target builder, dense | Pass | Token-3 probability mismatch |
| Shared target builder, sparse | Pass | Token-3 probability mismatch |
| UNO compact | Pass | Compact support probability mismatch |

The same tests exercised pre-fix filtering from public base `d2a436446cca3d955358e7b4a5bf6881ea8591cd`; EAGLE retained the extracted helper signature for testability.

Ruff 0.15.1, isort 7.0.0, syntax, whitespace, and registry checks passed. The H200 results above apply to `50e6ca6b73cc49214b5e9e28068b187ac3d7de2f`, not current-head CI.

[Base CI](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/39500026515) passed at `f0c0a64ad1b70d9a72f9d741b9eaa2b51d088c03`; Extra/AMD had failures. CI States below tracks newer runs.

<!-- lint: profile=evidence-heavy -->

### Historical HTTP validation at `f0c0a64`

All 10 HTTP checks passed at `f0c0a64ad1b70d9a72f9d741b9eaa2b51d088c03` on H200 using `Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct` revision `7ae557604adf67be50417f59c2c2f167def9a775`, Transformers 5.19.0, and the runtime below.

NGRAM accepted `min_p=0`. With `min_p=0.1`, non-streaming requests returned HTTP 400; streaming requests emitted `abort`, embedded status 400, and `[DONE]`. Each rejection mode ran twice; all four following valid requests succeeded. Ordinary sampling accepted `min_p=0.1`. Both servers remained healthy before teardown. Other speculative modes and PD deployment were not exercised. Source Rust extensions used `SGLANG_RUST_BUILD_MODE=auto`.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

These measurements predate fusion in `b94a95d5e805e0ee214c6d355a3a6cc79dd5e073`; see the [fused-helper validation summary](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41916#issuecomment-6328764169) for results and limitations.

Historical head `f0c0a64ad1b70d9a72f9d741b9eaa2b51d088c03` versus base `f0b65907227480afc376a66db62931b7e9c46c38`:

| Setup | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Hardware/runtime | H200; driver 595.71.05; Python 3.12.15; PyTorch 2.14.1+cu130; FlashInfer 0.7.2; Triton 3.8.0 |
| Functions | Production head functions and exact base definitions with unchanged dependencies; UNO retains `torch.compile(dynamic=True)` |
| Inputs | Seed 41916; FP32 normal logits, std=2; temperature=0.8; top-k=50; top-p=0.9; draft width=6 |
| Timing | Median microseconds/call; five alternating base/head samples; 200 CUDA Graph replays/sample; compilation and warmup excluded |
| Shape order | Vocabulary 32,768 then 128,256; batch 1, 16, 64 for each |

Outputs were finite and normalized; base/head sampling semantics intentionally differ.

| Path | Batch | Vocabulary | Base (us) | Head (us) | Added (us) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| DFlash sparse | 1 | 32,768 | 79.85 | 99.50 | 19.65 |
| UNO compact | 1 | 32,768 | 28.75 | 38.01 | 9.26 |
| DFlash sparse | 16 | 32,768 | 130.29 | 158.38 | 28.09 |
| UNO compact | 16 | 32,768 | 30.45 | 48.85 | 18.40 |
| DFlash sparse | 64 | 32,768 | 373.87 | 437.04 | 63.17 |
| UNO compact | 64 | 32,768 | 61.63 | 119.92 | 58.30 |
| DFlash sparse | 1 | 128,256 | 101.42 | 139.81 | 38.40 |
| UNO compact | 1 | 128,256 | 49.55 | 70.68 | 21.13 |
| DFlash sparse | 16 | 128,256 | 320.54 | 442.95 | 122.41 |
| UNO compact | 16 | 128,256 | 59.51 | 116.82 | 57.31 |
| DFlash sparse | 64 | 128,256 | 896.05 | 1211.86 | 315.81 |
| UNO compact | 64 | 128,256 | 163.58 | 369.16 | 205.58 |

With top-p disabled at batch=16, vocabulary=128,256, DFlash measured 300.17 -> 300.31 us; UNO measured 57.71 -> 56.90 us. Costs increased 17-38% for DFlash and 32-126% for UNO in this sweep. End-to-end serving throughput and latency remain unmeasured.

`torch.profiler` CPU/CUDA traces used ten graph replays and three ordinary calls, after warmup. At batch=64, vocabulary=128,256:

| Path | Additional full-vocabulary work | Profile attribution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DFlash sparse | Eager `logsumexp`: max, subtract, exp, sum, final normalization | 9 kernels, ~350 us; ~188 MiB temporary tensor. Total kernel count: 30 -> 52. Unprofiled rerun: 886 -> 1199 us. |
| UNO compact | Compiled full-vocabulary max and exp-sum reductions | 4 kernels, ~206 us; two scans dominate. Total kernel count: 6 -> 10. Unprofiled rerun: 163 -> 369 us. |

DFlash's top-p kernel fell from ~53 to 5 us; kernel durations attribute costs but do not replace unprofiled timings.

UNO depends on shape warmup order. Starting with vocabulary=128,256 and batch 1 then 64 generated a single full-vocabulary reduction kernel (~113 us), with unprofiled timings 161 -> 275 us. Repeating the sweep restored 163 -> 369 us; the percentage is not universal.

import ast
import gc
import hashlib
import importlib.metadata
import json
import os
from pathlib import Path
import statistics
import subprocess
import time
from types import SimpleNamespace

import torch

from sglang.srt.speculative import dflash_utils as dflash
from sglang.srt.speculative import uno_utils as uno

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
OUT = ROOT / 'benchmark-results.json'


def source_node(path, name):
    source = Path(path).read_text()
    node = next(n for n in ast.parse(source).body if isinstance(n, ast.FunctionDef) and n.name == name)
    return source, node


def load_base(path, names, module):
    namespace = dict(vars(module))
    source = Path(path).read_text()
    nodes = [n for n in ast.parse(source).body if isinstance(n, ast.FunctionDef) and n.name in names]
    assert len(nodes) == len(names)
    exec(compile(ast.Module(body=nodes, type_ignores=[]), str(path), 'exec'), namespace)
    return namespace


def capture(fn):
    # Compilation and allocator warmup are outside the measured region.
    for _ in range(4):
        fn()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    graph = torch.cuda.CUDAGraph()
    with torch.cuda.graph(graph):
        output = fn()
    for _ in range(10):
        graph.replay()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    tensors = output if isinstance(output, tuple) else (output,)
    assert all(torch.isfinite(t).all().item() for t in tensors)
    probs = tensors[-1]
    assert torch.allclose(probs.sum(-1), torch.ones_like(probs.sum(-1)), atol=2e-5, rtol=2e-5)
    return graph, output


def measure(graph, repetitions=200):
    start, end = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True), torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
    start.record()
    for _ in range(repetitions):
        graph.replay()
    end.record()
    end.synchronize()
    return start.elapsed_time(end) * 1000 / repetitions


def main():
    base_dflash = load_base(ROOT / 'base_dflash_utils.py', {'build_speculative_verify_target_probs'}, dflash)
    base_uno = load_base(ROOT / 'base_uno_utils.py', {'_normalize_sparse_topk_probs', '_build_sparse_target_support_tensors'}, uno)
    for helper in ('_dflash_top_p_renorm_prob', '_dflash_top_k_renorm_prob'):
        _, before = source_node(ROOT / 'base_dflash_utils.py', helper)
        _, after = source_node(dflash.__file__, helper)
        assert ast.dump(before) == ast.dump(after), f'Dependency changed: {helper}'
    metadata = {
        'head': 'f0c0a64ad1b70d9a72f9d741b9eaa2b51d088c03',
        'base': 'f0b65907227480afc376a66db62931b7e9c46c38',
        'torch': torch.__version__, 'cuda': torch.version.cuda,
        'gpu': torch.cuda.get_device_name(),
        'driver': subprocess.check_output(['nvidia-smi', '--query-gpu=driver_version', '--format=csv,noheader'], text=True).strip(),
        'packages': {p: importlib.metadata.version(p) for p in ('flashinfer-python', 'triton', 'transformers')},
        'method': 'Production head functions, exact base function ASTs with unchanged production dependencies; UNO torch.compile(dynamic=True) retained. CUDA Graph replay, warmup and compilation excluded, 5 paired samples alternating order, 200 replays/sample. Synthetic fixed-seed float32 logits, std=2; temperature=.8; top_k=50; draft_width=6.',
        'scope': 'Sampling function microbenchmark only. No model inference or end-to-end latency claim. Base/head intentionally implement different distributions.',
        'source_sha256': {str(p.name): hashlib.sha256(p.read_bytes()).hexdigest() for p in (ROOT/'base_dflash_utils.py', ROOT/'base_uno_utils.py', Path(dflash.__file__), Path(uno.__file__), Path(__file__))},
    }
    results = []
    cases = [(b, v, True) for v in (32768, 128256) for b in (1, 16, 64)] + [(16, 128256, False)]
    for bs, vocab, enabled in cases:
        torch.manual_seed(41916)
        width, k = 6, 50
        logits = torch.randn(bs * width, vocab, device='cuda', dtype=torch.float32) * 2
        temperatures = torch.full((bs, 1), .8, device='cuda')
        top_ks = torch.full((bs,), k, device='cuda', dtype=torch.int32)
        top_ps = torch.full((bs,), .9 if enabled else 1.0, device='cuda')
        info = SimpleNamespace(temperatures=temperatures, top_ks=top_ks, top_ps=top_ps, need_top_k_sampling=True, need_top_p_sampling=enabled)
        for path in ('dflash_sparse', 'uno_compact'):
            print(json.dumps({'starting': path, 'batch': bs, 'vocab': vocab, 'top_p_enabled': enabled}), flush=True)
            if path == 'dflash_sparse':
                args = dict(next_token_logits=logits, sampling_info=info, draft_token_num=width, bs=bs, max_top_k=k, uniform_top_k_value=k, use_sparse_topk=True)
                before = lambda: base_dflash['build_speculative_verify_target_probs'](**args)
                after = lambda: dflash.build_speculative_verify_target_probs(**args)
            else:
                args = (logits, temperatures, top_ks, top_ps, bs, width, k)
                before = lambda: base_uno['_build_sparse_target_support_tensors'](*args)
                after = lambda: uno._build_sparse_target_support_tensors(logits, temperatures, top_ks, top_ps if enabled else None, bs, width, k)
            bg, bo = capture(before)
            hg, ho = capture(after)
            samples = {'base': [], 'head': []}
            for round_id in range(5):
                pairs = [('base', bg), ('head', hg)] if round_id % 2 == 0 else [('head', hg), ('base', bg)]
                for label, graph in pairs:
                    samples[label].append(measure(graph))
            bm, hm = statistics.median(samples['base']), statistics.median(samples['head'])
            row = dict(path=path, batch=bs, vocab=vocab, top_p_enabled=enabled, base_us=bm, head_us=hm, delta_us=hm-bm, ratio=hm/bm, samples_us=samples)
            results.append(row)
            OUT.write_text(json.dumps({'metadata': metadata, 'results': results}, indent=2)+'\n')
            print(json.dumps(row), flush=True)
            del bg, bo, hg, ho, before, after
            gc.collect()
            torch.cuda.empty_cache()
    print('BENCHMARK_COMPLETE', flush=True)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

import json
import os
from pathlib import Path
import signal
import subprocess
import sys
import time

import psutil
import requests

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
BASE_URL = 'http://127.0.0.1:31916'
RESULT = {'head': 'f0c0a64ad1b70d9a72f9d741b9eaa2b51d088c03', 'model': json.loads((ROOT/'model.json').read_text()), 'checks': [], 'launches': []}


def save():
    (ROOT/'http-results.json').write_text(json.dumps(RESULT, indent=2)+'\n')


def request(min_p, stream, expected_rejection, label):
    payload = {'text': 'The capital of France is', 'sampling_params': {'temperature': .7, 'top_k': 50, 'top_p': .9, 'min_p': min_p, 'max_new_tokens': 8}, 'stream': stream}
    start = time.monotonic()
    response = requests.post(BASE_URL+'/generate', json=payload, timeout=(10, 60))
    duration = time.monotonic()-start
    body = response.text
    if expected_rejection:
        assert 'min_p is not supported with NGRAM speculative decoding' in body, (response.status_code, body)
        assert response.status_code in (200, 400, 422), response.status_code
        if stream:
            assert 'data:' in body or response.status_code != 200, body
    else:
        assert response.status_code == 200, (response.status_code, body)
        parsed = response.json()
        assert isinstance(parsed.get('text'), str), parsed
        assert parsed['meta_info']['completion_tokens'] > 0, parsed
        assert parsed['meta_info']['finish_reason']['type'] != 'abort', parsed
    RESULT['checks'].append({'label': label, 'request': payload, 'status_code': response.status_code, 'elapsed_seconds': duration, 'response': body, 'passed': True})
    save()
    print(json.dumps({'label':label, 'status':response.status_code, 'seconds':duration, 'passed':True}), flush=True)


def stop_server(process):
    try:
        children = psutil.Process(process.pid).children(recursive=True)
    except psutil.NoSuchProcess:
        children = []
    try:
        os.killpg(process.pid, signal.SIGTERM)
    except ProcessLookupError:
        pass
    try:
        process.wait(timeout=45)
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
        os.killpg(process.pid, signal.SIGKILL)
        process.wait(timeout=15)
    for child in children:
        try:
            if child.is_running(): child.terminate()
        except psutil.NoSuchProcess:
            pass
    _, alive = psutil.wait_procs(children, timeout=15)
    for child in alive:
        try: child.kill()
        except psutil.NoSuchProcess: pass
    _, alive = psutil.wait_procs(alive, timeout=15)
    assert not [p.pid for p in alive if p.status() != psutil.STATUS_ZOMBIE], 'server children survived'


def run_server(speculative):
    label = 'ngram' if speculative else 'ordinary'
    cmd = [sys.executable, '-m', 'sglang.launch_server', '--model-path', str(ROOT/'model'), '--host', '127.0.0.1', '--port', '31916', '--attention-backend', 'flashinfer', '--dtype', 'bfloat16', '--mem-fraction-static', '.5', '--max-running-requests', '8', '--cuda-graph-max-bs-decode', '8', '--context-length', '2048']
    if speculative:
        cmd += ['--speculative-algorithm', 'NGRAM', '--speculative-num-draft-tokens', '16']
    env = dict(os.environ, PYTHONPATH=str(ROOT/'source/python'), HF_HOME=str(ROOT/'hf'), HF_HUB_CACHE=str(ROOT/'hf/hub'), TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR=str(ROOT/'inductor'), TRITON_CACHE_DIR=str(ROOT/'triton'), SGLANG_JIT_DEEPGEMM_PRECOMPILE='0', SGLANG_RUST_BUILD_MODE='auto', SGLANG_CACHE_DIR=str(ROOT/'sglang-cache'))
    with open(ROOT/f'server-{label}.log', 'w') as log:
        process = subprocess.Popen(cmd, env=env, cwd=ROOT/'source', stdout=log, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT, stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL, start_new_session=True)
        RESULT['launches'].append({'mode':label, 'command':cmd, 'pid':process.pid})
        save()
        try:
            deadline = time.monotonic()+600
            while time.monotonic()<deadline:
                if process.poll() is not None:
                    raise RuntimeError(f'{label} server exited: {process.returncode}; see server-{label}.log')
                try:
                    if requests.get(BASE_URL+'/health',timeout=2).status_code == 200:
                        break
                except requests.RequestException:
                    pass
                time.sleep(2)
            else:
                raise TimeoutError(f'{label} server startup exceeded 600 seconds')
            print(f'SERVER_READY {label}',flush=True)
            if speculative:
                request(0, False, False, 'ngram valid initial control')
                for iteration in range(2):
                    for stream in (False, True):
                        request(.1, stream, True, f'ngram reject min_p=.1 stream={stream} repeat={iteration}')
                        request(0, False, False, f'ngram valid after rejection stream={stream} repeat={iteration}')
            else:
                request(.1, False, False, 'ordinary accepts min_p=.1')
            assert requests.get(BASE_URL+'/health',timeout=10).status_code == 200
            assert process.poll() is None
        finally:
            stop_server(process)
            RESULT['launches'][-1]['stopped'] = True
            save()


try:
    run_server(True)
    run_server(False)
    RESULT['complete'] = True
    print('HTTP_CHECK_COMPLETE',flush=True)
except Exception as exc:
    RESULT['error'] = repr(exc)
    raise
finally:
    save()

title: [PD] Fix crash for allocation when mamba + pd + decode radix cache
author: ByronHsu
body:
## Why?

With Mamba/KDA, PD decode, and decode radix cache, [PD admission on `main`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/a9c97c9f6973c03e778d1fe1e63a6b9f58a55012/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/decode.py#L1373-L1387) checks whether **zero** Mamba slots are free. It does not evict cached states when one slot is free, even though a fresh request needs **three** slots with overlap scheduling: one live state and [two tracking buffers](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/a9c97c9f6973c03e778d1fe1e63a6b9f58a55012/python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/memory_pool.py#L1450-L1471). The [buffer allocation](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/a9c97c9f6973c03e778d1fe1e63a6b9f58a55012/python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/memory_pool.py#L1599-L1613) then asserts and exits the decode worker.

```text
Fresh request: 1 free slot, cached states are evictable
  -> PD admission sees free > 0 and skips eviction
  -> request row and live Mamba state allocate (1 -> 0 free)
  -> two tracking buffers cannot allocate
  -> AssertionError: Not enough space for mamba ping pong idx
```

## What?

- Extract `ensure_mamba_capacity` from the [combined-engine allocation logic on `main`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/a9c97c9f6973c03e778d1fe1e63a6b9f58a55012/python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/allocation.py#L300-L323). It counts the live state and tracking slots each request still needs, evicts enough cached states to cover any shortfall, then rechecks capacity.
- Use that check before PD decode preallocation and before resuming a retracted request. If capacity is still short, leave the request queued rather than partially allocating it.
- Keep combined serving's existing behavior: attempt eviction, then let its allocator run. Only PD uses the capacity check to defer a request.

## Verification?

On one H200 node, two GPUs ran the tiny Kimi Linear model with real weights, NIXL PD, decode radix cache, overlap scheduling, and 16 sequential distinct requests (257 input / 256 output tokens each):

```text
Unpatched, 5 Mamba slots: 3 requests complete; request 4 crashes
                         at 2 free + 3 evictable slots
Patched,   5 Mamba slots: all 16 complete
Unpatched, 128 slots:     all 16 complete (capacity control)
Patched, repeated prompt: request completes with 256 cached tokens
```

Relevant traceback, with framework wrappers omitted:

```text
DecodePreallocQueue.pop_preallocated
  -> DecodePreallocQueue._pre_alloc          (decode.py:2075)
  -> HybridReqToTokenPool.alloc              (memory_pool.py:1471)
  -> HybridReqToTokenPool._alloc_ping_pong_buffer
  -> AssertionError: Not enough space for mamba ping pong idx
```

## Test?

- On the current source tree, pinned isort `7.0.0`, Ruff `0.15.1` selected checks and formatter, Python syntax checks, and `git diff --check` pass.
- On the original pinned source (`7b079c9c26`), the Mamba-capacity and decode-queue tests passed: **13 passed, 3 subtests passed** on H200. The end-to-end H200 comparison above also used that source, before the per-request sizing refinement.

title: [diffusion][xpu] FLUX.2: enable the bit-exact Triton SwiGLU on XPU
author: AgainstEntropy
body:
## Motivation

FLUX.2's packed SwiGLU fast path (`fused_packed_silu_mul_bitexact`) is a Triton
kernel, so there is no reason it cannot run on Intel XPU. Both the kernel's own
guard and the FLUX.2 call site required `x.is_cuda`, and the kernel entered
`torch.cuda.device`, so XPU always fell back to the two-kernel eager chain
(`F.silu(x[..., :half]) * x[..., half:]`).

## Modifications

- `kernels/ops/diffusion/activation/silu_mul_bitexact.py`: accept XPU tensors in
  `fused_packed_silu_mul_bitexact`, and enter the device through
  `torch.get_device_module(x.device).device(...)` instead of `torch.cuda.device`.
- `multimodal_gen/runtime/models/dits/flux_2.py` (`_flux2_swiglu`): accept XPU in
  the `can_fuse` predicate, and use the device-generic
  `torch.get_device_module(x.device).is_current_stream_capturing()` for the
  graph-capture check.

No CUDA behaviour changes: the predicate gains an `or x.is_xpu`, and both
`torch.get_device_module` calls resolve to `torch.cuda` on a CUDA tensor.

## Accuracy Tests

The existing `BitExactFusionGate` already verifies this path: on the first call
per signature the kernel output is compared with `torch.equal` against the live
eager chain, and the fast path is disabled permanently on mismatch. On Arc Pro
B70 (torch 2.13.0+xpu) it verifies and stays enabled — no
"not bit-exact ... falling back to eager" warning in any end-to-end run.

Existing CUDA coverage (`test_activation.py::test_packed_silu_mul_is_bit_exact`,
`test_model_fast_paths.py::TestFlux2EagerFusions`) is unchanged and still applies.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

FLUX.2-dev, 1024x1024, 8 denoise steps, guidance 4.0, seed 42, bf16, eager (no
`torch.compile`), warm request, TP4 on 4x Arc Pro B70:

| | denoise (8 steps) |
|---|---|
| before | 6.64 s |
| after | 6.569 / 6.572 s |

About 1%. The fused kernel replaces two eager elementwise passes over a
per-rank `[4608, 4608]` bf16 buffer; at this size it is a small win, and 1% is
close to run-to-run noise on this machine — the main value is that the
already-existing fast path stops being silently skipped on XPU.

title: [Perf] [XPU] flux2: Fuse bit-exact LayerNorm and gated residual norm
author: AgainstEntropy
body:
## Motivation

FLUX.2 has two eager fast paths that only exist for CUDA:

- `LN(x) * (1 + scale) + shift` → `fused_layernorm_modulate_raw`, a Triton
  kernel that reproduces **CUDA aten's** `vectorized_layer_norm_kernel` bit for
  bit, using inline PTX (`_rcp4`, `shfl.down` fold order, `div.rn` + `MUFU.RSQ`).
- gated residual + LN + modulate → `flux2_gated_resnorm_raw`, a Blackwell-only
  PTX JIT kernel, which also gates the cross-block residual deferral.

Neither can run on XPU: the PTX does not compile, and — more fundamentally —
the eager reference on XPU is torch-xpu-ops' own LayerNorm, whose reduction
order differs from CUDA aten's. FLUX.2's `BitExactFusionGate` compares against
the live eager chain with `torch.equal` and disables any kernel that does not
match, so a "close enough" kernel is not an option. On XPU both chains
therefore ran as 3-5 eager kernels per site.

## Modifications

New `kernels/ops/diffusion/norm/layernorm_modulate_xpu_triton.py` replicating
torch-xpu-ops `VectorizedLayerNormKernelFunctor` for bf16 rows with `N/4 > 1024`
(`src/ATen/native/xpu/sycl/LayerNormKernels.cpp`, `compute_stats`):

- work-group of 1024 (32 sub-groups x SIMD 32), vec_size 4;
- work-item `t` Welford-pushes vectors `t, t + 1024, ...`, each scalar as
  `mean' = fma(delta, recip(count), mean)`, `m2' = fma(delta, val - mean', m2)`;
- lane fold with `shift_group_left` offsets 16..1 (self = lower lane), then the
  sub-group fold with the same pairing;
- `var = div_rn(m2, N)`, `rstd = rsqrt(var + eps)`,
  `y = bf16(rstd * (x - mean))`, then the modulate chain rounding to bf16 after
  each op.

Two entry points share one kernel (a `GATED` constexpr selects whether the
residual add runs first), because the whole replicated reduction — Welford
accumulation, two-level fold, reciprocal table — is common to both.

**The reciprocal is the subtle part.** torch-xpu uses `sycl::native::recip` on
the running count, which differs from correctly-rounded `1/i` for 992 of the
first 8191 integers. Triton's `fast_dividef(1, x)` reproduces it in some
layouts but not others (at `num_warps=8` the statistics dropped to 96-98%
exact), so the kernel reads reciprocals from a small per-device table built once
by a kernel in the one configuration that was verified against a SYCL dump of
`native::recip`. Results are then independent of `num_warps`.

Wiring in `flux_2.py`:

- `_flux2_norm_modulate` dispatches to the XPU kernel under the existing
  `_FLUX2_LN_MOD` gate;
- `_flux2_gated_resnorm` gets an XPU path verified once per signature by a new
  `_FLUX2_XPU_GATED_RESNORM` gate;
- `_defer_gated_residual` also defers on XPU, so the block-end residual add
  fuses into the next block's norm.

Guards: bf16, contiguous 8-byte-aligned rows, `N % 4 == 0`, `1024 < N/4 < 8192`,
per-channel scale/shift/gate rows. Anything else keeps the eager path.

## Accuracy Tests

New `test/registered/kernels/ops/diffusion/test_flux2_xpu_norm_fusions.py`
(registered `register_xpu_ci(est_time=30, suite="stage-b-test-1-gpu-xpu")`),
4 cases at this point in the stack: bit-exactness of each kernel, the FLUX.2
dispatch actually taking the XPU path and the gate staying enabled, and
unsupported inputs (fp16, batch > 1, narrow rows) staying eager. All pass on
Arc Pro B70. (Later PRs in the stack add 2 more cases to the same file.)

Standalone sweep before wiring — **0 mismatching elements** vs the eager chain:

| rows | mismatches (LN+mod / gated out / residual) |
|---|---|
| 4608 | 0 / 0 / 0 |
| 4096 | 0 / 0 / 0 |
| 512 | 0 / 0 / 0 |

for 4 seeds x value scales {0.05, 1, 8, 30} x `num_warps` {4, 8, 16}
(28.3M elements per case at 4608 rows).

End to end, FLUX.2-dev 1024x1024: no
"not bit-exact ... falling back to eager" warning. Output images vs the
previous commit are 43.0 / 46.5 dB PSNR — the same level as two runs of
*identical* code (44.2 dB), because at TP>1 oneCCL's all-reduce reduction order
already makes runs non-deterministic on this stack. Image hashes are therefore
not a usable bit-exactness check here; the `torch.equal` gate and the unit tests
are.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Kernel micro-benchmark, one card, bf16, `num_warps=4`:

| kernel | rows | eager | fused | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| LN + modulate | 4608 | 0.707 ms | 0.231 ms | 3.06x |
| LN + modulate | 4096 | 0.628 ms | 0.209 ms | 3.00x |
| LN + modulate | 512 | 0.046 ms | 0.030 ms | 1.52x |
| gated residual + LN + modulate | 4608 | 1.246 ms | 0.454 ms | 2.75x |
| gated residual + LN + modulate | 4096 | 1.129 ms | 0.408 ms | 2.77x |
| gated residual + LN + modulate | 512 | 0.087 ms | 0.037 ms | 2.37x |

At 4608 rows the memory-traffic floor is ~0.21 ms, so LN+modulate is at the
bandwidth limit.

End to end (FLUX.2-dev, 1024x1024, 8 steps, bf16, eager, warm, TP4 on 4x
Arc Pro B70), 2 runs per side:

| | denoise (8 steps) | per DiT forward |
|---|---|---|
| parent commit | 6.569 / 6.572 s | 821.3 ms |
| this commit | 6.227 / 6.234 s | **778.8 ms (-5.2%)** |

torch.profiler: `_xpu_ln_modulate_kernel` runs 91 times per forward for 34.6 ms,
replacing ~117 ms of eager LayerNorm + elementwise work (norm 29.7 → 7.1 ms,
elementwise 87.8 → 1.8 ms); device-busy time per profiled forward 919.5 → 901.7 ms.

Under `torch.compile` the kernels step aside (`torch.compiler.is_compiling()`)
and Inductor fuses the same chains, as before.


## Checklist

- [ ] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).
- [ ] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).
- [ ] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations).
- [ ] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed).
- [ ] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance).

title: [Perf] flux2: Build the single-block output projection without a cat
author: AgainstEntropy
body:
## Motivation

Each of FLUX.2's 48 single-stream blocks built the input to its row-parallel
`to_out` projection with

```python
hidden_states = torch.cat([hidden_states, mlp_hidden_states], dim=-1)
hidden_states, _ = self.to_out(hidden_states)
```

That is a full read and write of the `[tokens, attn + mlp]` buffer immediately
before the GEMM consumes it — pure data movement, 48 times per forward. The FP8
and NVFP4 paths already avoid it (`try_flux2_token_cat_fp8` /
`try_flux2_token_cat_nvfp4` write a packed GEMM input directly); only bf16 still
materialised the cat.

## Modifications

On the bf16 path, preallocate the `[tokens, attn + mlp]` GEMM input, let the
fused SwiGLU write its columns straight into it, and copy only the narrower
attention output:

```python
gemm_input = hidden_states.new_empty((*hidden_states.shape[:-1], attn_dim + mlp_out))
self.mlp_act_fn(mlp_hidden_states, out=gemm_input[..., attn_dim:])
gemm_input[..., :attn_dim].copy_(hidden_states)
hidden_states, _ = self.to_out(gemm_input)
```

- `fused_packed_silu_mul_bitexact(x, out=None)` now accepts a row-strided `out`
  (a column slice of a wider buffer), via a new `out_row_stride` kernel
  argument; an `out` that is not a dense-row column slice raises.
- `_flux2_swiglu` / `Flux2SwiGLU` pass `out` through and copy into it on the
  eager fallback, so the caller always gets its buffer filled.
- FP8 / NVFP4 token-cat paths untouched.

Splitting the GEMM instead (`attn @ W1 + mlp @ W2`) would also remove the cat,
but it changes accumulation order and rounding; this keeps the GEMM input
byte-identical.

## Accuracy Tests

The GEMM input is byte-identical to the old `torch.cat` result, so model output
is unchanged by construction.

- `test_flux2_xpu_norm_fusions.py::test_swiglu_into_out_projection_input_matches_cat`
  (added here): asserts the in-place buffer equals `cat([attn, swiglu(mlp)])`,
  that `out` is written in place (same `data_ptr`), and that the untouched
  columns stay untouched.
- End to end on XPU: no bit-exact fallback warnings; images differ from the
  parent commit only at the level of oneCCL run-to-run noise (see PR 2).

**CUDA accuracy is not yet measured** — see below.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Micro-benchmark, one card, per-TP4-rank shapes
(`[4608, 1536]` attn + `[4608, 9216]` packed SwiGLU input):

| | time per block |
|---|---|
| `swiglu(mlp)` + `cat` | 0.699 ms |
| in-place build | 0.344 ms |

−0.355 ms per block × 48 blocks ≈ −17 ms per forward expected.

torch.profiler: `CatArrayBatchedCopy_contig` (21.3 ms per forward) disappears;
device-busy time per profiled forward 919.5 → 901.7 ms (−17.8 ms).

End to end (FLUX.2-dev, 1024x1024, 8 steps, bf16, eager, warm, TP4 on 4x
Arc Pro B70), 2 runs per side:

| | denoise (8 steps) | per DiT forward |
|---|---|---|
| parent commit | 6.227 / 6.234 s | 778.8 ms |
| this commit | 6.140 / 6.129 s | **−12 ms (−1.5%)** |

End to end recovers less than the 17.8 ms the profile shows; I did not chase
the difference.

- [ ] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).

title: [Perf] [XPU] diffusion: Avoid QKV copies in flash attention
author: AgainstEntropy
body:
## Motivation

`XPUAttentionImpl.forward` called `.contiguous()` on q, k and v before every
flash-attention call:

```python
q_ = query.contiguous().reshape(bsz * seqlen_q, nheads_q, d)
k_ = key.contiguous().reshape(bsz * seqlen_k, nheads_k, d)
v_ = value.contiguous().reshape(bsz * seqlen_k, nheads_k, d)
```

In FLUX.2's single-stream blocks q/k/v are head-packed, row-strided *slices* of
one fused projection output (`[tokens, 13824]` = `q | k | v | mlp`), so each
`.contiguous()` materialised a fresh `[tokens, heads, 128]` tensor — 3 copies
per block, 144 per DiT forward, 8.8 ms of profiled device time.

The sgl-kernel-xpu flash-attention kernel reads rows through their stride, so
the copies are not needed.

## Modifications

`multimodal_gen/runtime/layers/attention/backends/xpu_backend.py`: new
`_as_fa_input` helper used for q, k and v. It passes the tensor through
untouched when the `[rows, heads, head_dim]` view is one the kernel can read
directly — unit last-dim stride, heads packed at `head_dim`, row stride a
multiple of 8, 16-byte-aligned base — and otherwise copies exactly as before.

This is XPU-only; no other backend is touched.

## Accuracy Tests

Kernel-level probe at the FLUX.2 shape (`[4608, 12, 128]`, token stride 13824):
output with strided q/k/v is `torch.equal` to output with contiguous inputs.
The same probe also confirms the kernel accepts a strided *output* buffer and
leaves neighbouring columns untouched (not used by this PR — see follow-up).

`test_flux2_xpu_norm_fusions.py::test_attention_reads_fused_projection_slices_in_place`
(added here): asserts `_as_fa_input` returns the input's own `data_ptr` for a
fused-projection slice, and that `XPUAttentionImpl.forward` gives a
`torch.equal` result for strided and contiguous inputs. The file is now 6 cases,
all passing on Arc Pro B70.

End to end: no bit-exact fallback warnings; images differ from the parent commit
only at oneCCL run-to-run noise level (see PR 2).

## Speed Tests and Profiling

End to end (FLUX.2-dev, 1024x1024, 8 steps, bf16, eager, warm, TP4 on 4x
Arc Pro B70), 2 runs per side:

| | denoise (8 steps) | per DiT forward |
|---|---|---|
| parent commit | 6.140 / 6.129 s | — |
| this commit | 6.077 / 6.095 s | **−6 ms (−0.8%)** |

torch.profiler: the 144 `aten::copy_` kernels per forward (8.8 ms) are gone.
Flash attention itself costs ~1.2 ms more per forward with strided reads, so the

title: [AMD][V4.1][*/N] Route low-ratio indexer and candidate-block top-k through top-k v2
author: RolaoDenthu
body:
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->

## Motivation

<!-- Describe the purpose and goals of this pull request. -->
On ROCm, the DSV4.1 low-ratio indexer still uses the older AOT kernels for its top-k. On MI355X, v2 is 1.4-2.6x faster at decode shapes and selects exactly the same indices.

Two AOT kernels are replaced:
- `deepseek_v4_topk_transform_512`, which picks the top 512 positions, both over the full row and inside the candidate blocks;
- `fast_topk`, which picks the top 2048 candidate blocks.

The AOT top-512 kernel also sorts each row by position. This sort is not needed, because the attention kernels that read the selection do not care about its order:
- decode attention reads the first `lengths[t]` entries and skips -1;
- prefill (`combine_topk_swa_indices`) only requires unused entries to be -1.

The CUDA path already passes the selection through unsorted, so this PR drops the sort as well.
