title: [Perf] moe: Extend FlashInfer CUTLASS MoE autotune coverage to prefill chunks
author: JackChuang
body:
## Summary

**TL;DR: This PR enables sglang's startup autotune to tune FlashInfer's CUTLASS MoE kernel for prefill sizes too, not only for decode sizes.** sglang already autotunes this kernel (`cutlass_fused_moe`, FlashInfer's MoE kernel, not its attention backend) at startup, but each call tells FlashInfer to tune only up to its own token count. The startup run is one decode-sized batch, so only decode sizes get a tuned kernel configuration (tactic), and prefill chunks above that size run FlashInfer's untuned fallback tactic (its default kernel configuration). This PR gives FlashInfer one tuning range per server instead: the largest prefill batch the MoE layer sees (chunk size × attention data-parallel size, capped at 8192, FlashInfer's own default range for this call), so the same startup autotune also covers prefill. No new flag, kernel or extra pass. It applies on every GPU this kernel runs on (SM90, SM100, SM110, SM120), where it is the default MoE kernel of DeepSeek-V4.1/V4, Ling-3.0, Nemotron-H, gpt-oss and ModelOpt NVFP4 MoE models (which GPU for which model: Design notes), and to any other MoE model that runs on it. Other MoE kernels and the decode servers of prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation are unchanged. Measured on H200 (SM90).

- **Performance** (H200): faster prefill on all seven MoE models measured (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Nemotron-3.5, Ling-3.0, gpt-oss-20b, GLM-5.3-Flash, MiniMax-M3, Gemma-4): TTFT (time to first token) for 8k-token prompts **30.3–57.8% lower** (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: 573.9 → 400.0 ms, **30.3%**), for 32k-token prompts **23.0–52.8% lower**, prefill throughput **43.4–143.4% higher**; decode ITL (inter-token latency) unchanged on the three models measured for it. It complements open PR #42736 (an extra startup tuning pass): with both, 8k-token TTFT on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is **24.7% lower** than with #42736 alone.
- **Accuracy:** unchanged by design (only the tile configuration, or tactic, of the same GEMM changes); GSM8K on all seven models and the DeepSeek-V4-Flash CI GSM8K test stays within the 95% noise range (−0.83 to +0.15 points on the seven models).
- **Cost:** a longer startup autotune when no saved results exist: 41–42 → 176–177 s on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 8×H200 (server ready 153–154 → 288–289 s), 116 → 604 s on Ling-3.0-flash, and 4–26 s more on the other five models. Saved results are reused on one GPU, but multi-GPU servers currently re-tune at every start; `--disable-flashinfer-autotune` turns the startup autotune off. Each GPU has 0.4–1.2 GiB (0.3–0.9% of an H200) less free memory while the server runs, mostly the buffer FlashInfer keeps for timing tactics at startup, now sized for the prefill chunk instead of the decode batch; the KV cache size is unchanged. PD decode servers pay nothing.

## Motivation

sglang runs FlashInfer's autotune at startup (#12306, on by default since #14357). For `cutlass_fused_moe`, FlashInfer keeps one tactic per token-count bucket (powers of two up to 256, then larger steps up to 8192: 21 buckets) and tunes every bucket up to the caller's `tune_max_num_tokens`; the same value also decides which bucket a call uses. Both sglang call sites (the `flashinfer_cutlass` runner, used for BF16, FP8 and NVFP4 experts, and the CUTLASS path of `flashinfer_mxfp4`, used for MXFP4 experts) pass `next_power_of_2(x.shape[0])`, which dates from #7327, before the startup autotune existed. This has two effects:

1. **Prefill runs an untuned tactic.** The startup batch is decode-sized, one token per request up to the request limit (256 tokens on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, 138 on Nemotron-3.5-Lightning, 4096 on gpt-oss-20b), so nothing above that size is tuned: an 8k-token chunk maps to bucket 8192 and gets FlashInfer's fallback tactic. The server log shows nothing, because sglang sets FlashInfer's logger to ERROR.
2. **The tactic depends on earlier requests.** Every `cutlass_fused_moe` call that runs Python code (the startup autotune, CUDA graph capture, and every serving forward that is not a CUDA graph replay) first calls `MoERunner.refine_tuning_config(tune_max_num_tokens)`. That method is wrapped in `functools.lru_cache` and rebuilds FlashInfer's class-wide bucket list only the first time it sees a value, so a call with a value seen before keeps the list built for the latest new value. On DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with `--cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 64`, the first decode batch of 65–128 requests while serving runs without a CUDA graph and rebuilds the list for 128 tokens (a short prompt of a new size likewise rebuilds it, for its own size); later prefill chunks of an already-seen size, such as every 8k-token chunk after the first, then run the 128-token bucket's tactic, because a list built for 128 tokens ends at bucket 128 and every larger call falls into that last bucket.

flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#5625 was filed by an sglang user who hit both effects serving DeepSeek-V4-Flash on 4×H100 with `flashinfer_mxfp4`. One value for the whole server, computed from its configuration and used by every call, as large as the largest prefill batch (up to 8192 tokens), removes both.

## Modifications

- **`python/sglang/srt/layers/moe/moe_runner/flashinfer_cutlass.py`** -- the new `_cutlass_moe_tune_max_num_tokens(num_tokens)` gives both `cutlass_fused_moe` calls their `tune_max_num_tokens`: `min(prefill chunk size × attention DP size, 8192)`, with the chunk size (`--chunked-prefill-size`, or `--max-prefill-tokens` when chunked prefill is off) read the way `flashinfer_autotune.py` already does (`max_prefill_buffer_tokens() or get_schedule().max_prefill_tokens`). PD decode servers keep `next_power_of_2(num_tokens)`.
- **`test/registered/unit/layers/moe/test_flashinfer_cutlass_swiglu_params.py`** (CPU suite) -- new `TestCutlassMoeTuneMaxNumTokens`. With the kernel stubbed, it checks at both calls that token counts 1, 257, 777, 2048, 4097, 8192 and 16384 map to a bucket the startup autotune tunes, in five server configurations, and that PD decode servers keep the per-call value. 60 of its 80 sub-cases fail on main.
- **`test/registered/unit/layers/quantization/test_mxfp4_sm{90,120}_cutlass.py`, `test/registered/unit/layers/moe/test_moe_runner_config_placement.py`** -- their fused-MoE calls now run inside `get_context().override_server_args()`, because the helper reads the server configuration.

Design notes:

- Where this kernel is the default MoE path: on SM90 and SM120, DeepSeek-V4.1/V4 and Ling-3.0 (MXFP4 experts, through `flashinfer_mxfp4`) and BF16/FP8 Nemotron-H (`flashinfer_cutlass`); on SM120 also gpt-oss and ModelOpt NVFP4 MoE models, the latter on SM110 too since #41765. On SM100 no model uses it by default (`flashinfer_mxfp4` runs a TRT-LLM kernel there). Any other MoE model reaches it with `--moe-runner-backend flashinfer_cutlass` (BF16, ModelOpt FP8/NVFP4) or `flashinfer_mxfp4` (MXFP4).
- DP attention: sglang splits `--chunked-prefill-size` across the DP ranks, and the MoE layer runs on the tokens gathered from all of them, so the largest batch the MoE layer sees is each rank's chunk × the DP size, which is the `--chunked-prefill-size` the user set.
- The 8192 cap is a choice, not a limit on chunk size: it is FlashInfer's own default range for this call, and chunks larger than 8192 tokens still run, using bucket 8192's tactic, which in a one-layer test with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash's MoE shape is as fast as a tactic tuned for each larger size (One MoE call, under Experimental Results); tuning beyond 8192 would only lengthen startup. Omitting the argument would also give one value, but PD decode servers and servers with smaller chunks would then tune sizes they never use.
- Servers whose startup decode batch is above 8192 tokens (for example attention DP 8 with the default request limit) tune fewer buckets than main and start faster, at no MoE run-time cost: main cannot use those larger buckets at run time either (item 2), and in a one-layer test bucket 8192's tactic is about as fast as each size's own tactic at 12288–32768 tokens (One MoE call, under Experimental Results).

## Experimental Results

### Performance

Setup: **in every prefill row below, every server with this PR beats every server without it** (main, or #42736 alone). Every number in this section was measured with this PR's code at head `a4c96d4080f` on main `c7f3ae1dd59` (H200, CUDA 13.0, torch 2.14.1, FlashInfer 0.7.0.post1). Every measurement starts a new server for each version, alternating which goes first; each value is the median over server starts (for TTFT, of each server's median over the 8 prompts). TTFT rows send 8 random prompts one at a time (2k, 8k and 32k mean 2,000, 8,000 and 32,000 tokens; percentages are computed from unrounded medians). Prompts are prefilled in chunks of 8192 tokens (`--chunked-prefill-size 8192`, set on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and the default on the other models here), so a 32k prompt runs as four chunks and every MoE call has at most 8192 tokens. With this chunk size this PR's tuning range is also 8192 (it follows the chunk size; the 8192 cap is FlashInfer's default range for this call, see Design notes); throughput rows send 64 prompts at 8 concurrent requests with 1 output token, so they measure prefill throughput (`bench_serving` total token throughput). Launch commands are under Commands below; settings not listed there are the defaults.

This table measures the main claim: on a newly started main server, prefill chunks larger than the startup decode batch run FlashInfer's untuned fallback tactic (Motivation, item 1), and with this PR a tuned one. Result: **on all seven models, TTFT is 30.3–57.8% lower (8k-token prompts) and 23.0–52.8% lower (32k), and prefill throughput 43.4–143.4% higher.**

**Prefill speed, all models** (each server newly started; main → this PR, improvement; +% = this PR better)

| Model (expert weights), GPUs, MoE runner | TTFT, 8k-token prompts (ms) | TTFT, 32k-token prompts (ms) | Prefill throughput, 8k-token prompts (tok/s) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (MXFP4 experts), 8×H200, `flashinfer_mxfp4` (default) | 573.9 → 400.0 (**+30.3%**) | 2,685.0 → 1,994.3 (**+25.7%**) | 14,755 → 21,154 (**+43.4%**) |
| Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B (BF16), 1×H200, `flashinfer_cutlass` (default) | 309.1 → 136.6 (**+55.8%**) | 1,227.5 → 599.9 (**+51.1%**) | 27,320 → 63,131 (**+131.1%**) |
| Ling-3.0-flash (MXFP4 experts), 1×H200, `flashinfer_mxfp4` (default) | 430.4 → 254.7 (**+40.8%**) | 1,761.0 → 1,073.3 (**+39.1%**) | 18,961 → 31,557 (**+66.4%**) |
| gpt-oss-20b (MXFP4 experts), 1×H200, `flashinfer_mxfp4` ¹ | 422.0 → 177.9 (**+57.8%**) | 1,790.9 → 846.2 (**+52.8%**) | 20,301 → 49,408 (**+143.4%**) |
| GLM-5.3-Flash (BF16), 8×H200, `flashinfer_cutlass` | 495.1 → 250.3 (**+49.5%**) | 1,896.4 → 1,019.3 (**+46.3%**) | 17,160 → 34,122 (**+98.8%**) |
| MiniMax-M3 (BF16), 8×H200, `flashinfer_cutlass` ² | 631.2 → 294.4 (**+53.4%**) | 2,547.0 → 1,224.8 (**+51.9%**) | 13,657 → 30,302 (**+121.9%**) |
| Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it (BF16), 1×H200, `flashinfer_cutlass` | 408.3 → 244.3 (**+40.2%**) | 2,798.8 → 2,156.1 (**+23.0%**) | 19,978 → 34,302 (**+71.7%**) |

Runners not marked "(default)" are set with `--moe-runner-backend`. ¹ With gpt-oss's default request limit of 4096, main already tunes buckets up to 4096; this PR adds bucket 8192. ² Both versions also run `--disable-prefill-cuda-graph`: capturing MiniMax-M3's prefill CUDA graph fails at startup on main too.

**DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on a server that has already served traffic** (+% = this PR better)

On main, the tactic a prefill chunk gets depends on what the server has served before (Motivation, item 2). On a newly started server (the table above), an 8k chunk gets FlashInfer's untuned fallback tactic. After one decode batch larger than the CUDA graph limit (here 65–128 requests, above `--cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 64`), later 8k chunks get the tactic tuned for 128 tokens instead: faster than the fallback, but not tuned for 8k. This PR uses the tactic tuned for its 8192-token chunks in both cases. A long-running main server stays in whichever state its last new batch size left it: a busy server whose decode batches often exceed the CUDA graph limit tends to end in the second state, a lightly loaded one in the first. This test measures the second case. Both servers first get the same requests (listed under Commands), and every main server's log shows such a batch.

Result: **this PR is faster in both cases.** main's 8k-token TTFT is 573.9 ms on a new server and 496.5 ms after this traffic; this PR's is 400.0 ms and 398.2 ms:

| Benchmark | main | this PR | improvement |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| TTFT, 8k-token prompts (ms) | 496.5 | 398.2 | **+19.8%** |
| TTFT, 32k-token prompts (ms) | 2,383.5 | 1,991.9 | **+16.4%** |
| Prefill throughput, 8k-token prompts (tok/s) | 17,152 | 21,152 | **+23.3%** |

This table measures the two costs of tuning more buckets, a longer startup autotune and a larger buffer for timing tactics, and checks the KV cache size. Result: **the KV cache size is unchanged, and each GPU gives up 0.4–1.2 GiB (0.3–0.9% of an H200)**; with no saved results, the startup autotune takes 4–26 s more on five models, about 135 s more on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (8×H200, paid at every start) and 488 s more on Ling-3.0-flash (1×H200, paid once).

**Cost of this PR: startup time and GPU memory** (main → this PR, from the server logs of the servers above)

| Model | Tuned buckets per MoE GEMM | FlashInfer autotune at startup, no saved results (s) ³ | Free memory per GPU after startup, lowest GPU (GiB; in parentheses, the extra memory this PR uses as a share of the H200's 140.4 GiB, so here + is a cost) | KV cache size (tokens), unchanged |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, 8×H200 | 9 → 21 | 41–42 → 176–177 | 20.72 → 19.64 (+0.77%) | 21,542,656 |
| Nemotron-3.5-Lightning, 1×H200 | 9 → 21 | 6–7 → 21–22 | 12.46 → 11.88 (+0.41%) | 6,137,490 |
| Ling-3.0-flash, 1×H200 | 8 → 21 | 116 → 604 | 11.80 → 11.37 (+0.31%) | 4,239,637 |
| gpt-oss-20b, 1×H200 | 20 → 21 | 132 → 157–158 | 5.78 → 5.28 (+0.36%) | 2,641,507 |
| GLM-5.3-Flash, 8×H200 | 9 → 21 | 7–8 → 17 | 16.28–16.48 → 15.27 (+0.72–0.86%) | 2,118,400 |
| MiniMax-M3, 8×H200 | 16 → 21 | 16–17 → 21 | 9.88 → 9.15 (+0.52%) | 407,296 |
| Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, 1×H200 | 16 → 21 | 11 → 18–19 | 20.88 → 20.38 (+0.36%) | 382,802 |

³ This column leaves out each model's first start after download, whose autotune window also JIT-compiled other kernels (main: Ling-3.0 170 s, GLM-5.3-Flash 61 s, Gemma-4 33 s); that start's other values are included.

The extra memory is mostly the buffer FlashInfer uses at startup to time each candidate tactic. It is sized for the largest token count being tuned: the prefill chunk size with this PR (capped at 8192, so 8192 tokens in these measurements) instead of the decode batch size on main, and FlashInfer keeps it while the server runs. The KV cache is sized before the startup autotune runs, so its size is unchanged and the buffer comes out of the memory left outside it.

**Together with open PR #42736** (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, same setup; **baseline: main with #42736 applied**). This shows what this PR adds when both land: #42736 adds a startup pass that tunes the same 21 prefill-sized buckets, and this PR makes the prefill calls use them, so the two work well together, and **the improvements are what this PR adds on top of #42736's own gain** (#42736's own gain over main, from a separate set of server starts: 8k-token TTFT 574.8 → 522.7 ms, 9.1% lower): with both, 8k-token TTFT is **24.7% lower** than with #42736 alone (527.1 → 396.8 ms), and **19.8% lower** on a server that has already served the traffic above (497.0 → 398.7 ms). For this kernel's prefill, both together match this PR alone (396.8 vs 400.0 ms; 398.7 vs 398.2 ms after the traffic), as this PR already tunes the same buckets; #42736 also tunes other FlashInfer operations. This combination was measured on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash; since both PRs act on the same buckets in the same way, the other models above should also gain on top of #42736 (expected from the mechanism; not measured here).

<details>
<summary>Together with #42736: table and mechanism (baseline: main + #42736; +% = with both better)</summary>

#42736 at its head `ef17b191caf0` (2026-10-06), on the same main. Startup is the same for #42736 alone, this PR alone and both (autotune 176–179 s, 21 buckets).

| Benchmark | #42736 alone | #42736 + this PR | improvement |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| TTFT, 8k-token prompts (ms) | 527.1 | 396.8 | **+24.7%** |
| TTFT, 32k-token prompts (ms) | 2,511.8 | 1,996.8 | **+20.5%** |
| Prefill throughput, 8k-token prompts (tok/s) | 16,006 | 21,152 | **+32.2%** |
| After the traffic above: TTFT, 8k-token prompts (ms) | 497.0 | 398.7 | **+19.8%** |
| Same: TTFT, 32k-token prompts (ms) | 2,376.5 | 2,003.6 | **+15.7%** |
| Same: prefill throughput, 8k-token prompts (tok/s) | 17,157 | 21,190 | **+23.5%** |

With #42736 alone, CUDA graph capture runs after its extra pass and captures from the largest batch down to 1 (`decode_cuda_graph_runner.py`), so FlashInfer's cached bucket list ends as the 1-token list (item 2) and the prefill calls look up small buckets even though the large ones are tuned; this PR's fixed range makes them find the tuned large bucket. A profile agrees (TP rank 0, three 8k-token prefills): every MoE GEMM runs a 64×16 or 128×16 tile with #42736 alone and a 128×64 tile with both; per prefill both MoE GEMMs together take 123 → 58 ms, the all-reduce that waits for them 119 → 75 ms, and the GPU time 480 → 370 ms (22.9% less). FlashInfer does not log the bucket, so the list state is inferred from the code and the tile shapes. #42736 also tunes other FlashInfer operations; this PR does not overlap with that part.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Decode (+% = this PR better)</summary>

This PR targets prefill, but it also changes the tuning range that decode calls pass, so this checks that decode does not get slower. Result: **decode ITL is unchanged on all three models**, and TTFT and throughput improve, mostly at 8 and 32 concurrent requests, where several 2k-token prompts are prefilled together in batches of up to 8192 tokens, sizes main leaves untuned.

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, newly started servers running 1, then 8, then 32 concurrent requests; 2k-token prompts, 256 output tokens.

| Concurrent requests | median ITL (ms) | throughput (tok/s) | TTFT (ms) |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1 | 7.48 → 7.24 (+3.2%) | 1,085 → 1,121 (+3.3%) | 168.0 → 162.0 (+3.6%) |
| 8 | 9.68 → 9.67 (+0.1%) | 5,186 → 5,615 (+8.3%) | 978.9 → 725.4 (+25.9%) |
| 32 | 13.96 → 13.95 (+0.1%) | 9,779 → 11,558 (+18.2%) | 2,520.3 → 1,785.4 (+29.2%) |

GLM-5.3-Flash and MiniMax-M3 (8×H200, `flashinfer_cutlass`), the same requests:

| Model | Concurrent requests | median ITL (ms) | throughput (tok/s) | TTFT (ms) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| GLM-5.3-Flash | 1 | 6.62 → 6.63 (−0.2%) | 1,189 → 1,217 (+2.4%) | 198.4 → 153.2 (+22.8%) |
| GLM-5.3-Flash | 8 | 10.24 → 10.25 (0.0%) | 5,068 → 5,707 (+12.6%) | 781.0 → 480.7 (+38.5%) |
| GLM-5.3-Flash | 32 | 15.83 → 15.82 (0.0%) | 10,035 → 12,870 (+28.3%) | 1,909.6 → 1,007.6 (+47.2%) |
| MiniMax-M3 | 1 | 8.61 → 8.61 (0.0%) | 964.5 → 964.8 (0.0%) | 138.4 → 137.3 (+0.9%) |
| MiniMax-M3 | 8 | 15.16 → 15.17 (−0.1%) | 3,616 → 4,069 (+12.5%) | 878.2 → 501.7 (+42.9%) |
| MiniMax-M3 | 32 | 23.77 → 23.76 (0.0%) | 6,922 → 8,958 (+29.4%) | 2,589.1 → 1,212.2 (+53.2%) |

On all three models, decode batches use buckets 1–256, which main already tunes, so ITL is unchanged (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash's 1-request difference is smaller than main's own spread between restarts, 3.4%); the throughput and TTFT gains at 8 and 32 requests come from these batched prefills (MiniMax-M3's main already tunes up to 2048 tokens, so a single 2k-token prompt gains only 0.9% there).

</details>

<details>
<summary>One MoE call</summary>

The tables above time whole requests; this test times one MoE call alone to answer two questions. (1) Does the gain come from the tactic, that is, from replacing FlashInfer's fallback tactic with a tuned one? (2) This PR tunes up to 8192 tokens, so a chunk larger than 8192 tokens reuses bucket 8192's tactic: is that slower than a tactic tuned for the chunk's own size? Result: **(1) yes: at 8192 tokens the tuned tactic is 2.6× faster than the fallback; (2) no: above 8192 tokens, bucket 8192's tactic is never slower than each size's own tactic.** It even measured 1.5–3.4% faster, but that is within the measurement spread: at 8192 tokens, where the last two columns run the very same tactic, the last column also measured 2.3% slower (1.549 vs 1.514 ms). `cutlass_fused_moe` on one H200, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash's per-GPU shape under EP8 (48 of 384 experts, hidden size 5120, intermediate size 2304, top-6, uniform random routing; median time per call), tuned once up to 8192 tokens (this PR's range with 8192-token chunks) and once up to 32768 tokens. Time per call (ms):

| Tokens | fallback tactic | bucket 8192's tactic (this PR) | tactic tuned for the call's own bucket |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 8192 | 3.990 | 1.514 | 1.549 (the same tactic) |
| 12288 | 5.900 | 2.138 | 2.194 |
| 16384 | 7.744 | 2.733 | 2.825 |
| 24576 | 11.482 | 3.976 | 4.035 |
| 32768 | 14.998 | 5.137 | 5.222 |

Tuning this layer's two GEMMs up to 8192 tokens takes 185 s, about as long as the server's whole startup autotune (176–177 s), because FlashInfer tunes each input shape once and every MoE layer has this shape; up to 32768 tokens it takes 232 s. The three tactics give bit-identical output at every size in the table.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Commands</summary>

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash \
  --trust-remote-code --tp-size 8 --ep-size 8 --mem-fraction-static 0.8 --chunked-prefill-size 8192 \
  --attention-backend dsv4 --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_mxfp4 \
  --max-running-requests 256 --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 64 --watchdog-timeout 7200
python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-BF16 --trust-remote-code \
  --moe-runner-backend auto --watchdog-timeout 7200   # request limit 138 (set by the Mamba state cache)
python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path inclusionAI/Ling-3.0-flash-fp4 --trust-remote-code --moe-runner-backend auto --watchdog-timeout 7200
python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path openai/gpt-oss-20b --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_mxfp4 --watchdog-timeout 7200
python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash-BF16 --trust-remote-code --tp-size 8 --ep-size 8 \
  --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_cutlass --watchdog-timeout 7200
python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3 --trust-remote-code --tp-size 8 --ep-size 8 \
  --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_cutlass --disable-prefill-cuda-graph --watchdog-timeout 7200
python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it --trust-remote-code \
  --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_cutlass --watchdog-timeout 7200
# --watchdog-timeout is not needed: the scheduler's watchdog starts after the startup autotune
B="python3 -m sglang.bench_serving --backend sglang --dataset-name random --random-range-ratio 1.0 --seed 5 --flush-cache"
$B --random-input-len 8000  --random-output-len 1 --num-prompts 8  --max-concurrency 1
$B --random-input-len 32000 --random-output-len 1 --num-prompts 8  --max-concurrency 1
$B --random-input-len 8000  --random-output-len 1 --num-prompts 64 --max-concurrency 8
for nc in "8 1" "64 8" "128 32"; do set -- $nc   # decode rows
  $B --random-input-len 2000 --random-output-len 256 --num-prompts $1 --max-concurrency $2; done
# requests before the "already served traffic" rows (--seed 7): --random-input-len 400/800/1600/3000/6000 --random-output-len 1
#   --num-prompts 2 --max-concurrency 1, then --random-input-len 2000 --random-output-len 64 --num-prompts 384 --max-concurrency 96
```

</details>

### Accuracy

**By design this PR does not affect accuracy: it only changes which tile configuration (tactic) of the same MoE GEMM runs**, so the GEMM computes the same values, at most with a different summation order (with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash's MoE shape, one call at 8192–32768 tokens is bit-identical to the fallback tactic). **Measured: GSM8K stays within sampling noise on all seven models (−0.83 to +0.15 points) and in the DeepSeek-V4-Flash CI test (+1.5).**

| Test | main | this PR | difference, percentage points (95% noise range) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| GSM8K, all 1,319 test questions, 20-shot, temperature 0: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash | 91.43% | 90.60% | −0.83 (±2.2) |
| Same: Nemotron-3.5-Lightning | 87.64% | 87.79% | +0.15 (±2.5) |
| Same: Ling-3.0-flash | 86.28% | 86.05% | −0.23 (±2.6) |
| Same: gpt-oss-20b | 80.14% | 79.38% | −0.76 (±3.1) |
| Same, through the chat API (up to 4096 output tokens): GLM-5.3-Flash | 97.35% | 96.82% | −0.53 (±1.3) |
| Same, chat API: MiniMax-M3 | 97.19% | 97.27% | +0.08 (±1.3) |
| Same, chat API: Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it | 96.36% | 96.06% | −0.30 (±1.5) |
| CI `TestDSV4FlashFP4H200FlashInferCutlass.test_gsm8k` (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, TP4 + EAGLE, 200 questions; threshold 93%) | 96.0% | 97.5% | +1.5 (±3.5) |

The noise range is 1.96 standard errors of the difference between two scores over that many questions (an independent-sample approximation, conservative here because both versions answer the same questions). GPQA and long-context evals were not run.

<details>
<summary>GSM8K command</summary>

The 20 shots are the first 20 training examples, so no test question appears in the prompt.

```bash
D=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openai/grade-school-math/master/grade_school_math/data
{ curl -sL $D/train.jsonl | head -n 20; curl -sL $D/test.jsonl; } > gsm8k_k20.jsonl

  --num-threads 32 --api completion --gsm8k-data-path gsm8k_k20.jsonl
# GLM-5.3-Flash, MiniMax-M3, Gemma-4: --api chat --max-tokens 4096 instead of --api completion
```

</details>

## CI

**No file fails only with this PR, and the new CPU test passes all 80 sub-cases (60 fail on main).** Local CI on 8×H200 with the commands CI uses: every CPU and GPU suite this machine can run (1,427 files) with this PR, and on its parent main every CPU suite in full plus every file that failed with this PR. SM100, SM110 and SM120 cannot run here; the CI tests that reach the changed call there (`test_mxfp4_sm120_cutlass.py` on the RTX 5090 runner, `test_nvfp4_moe_backends.py::test_flashinfer_cutlass` on B200) are in upstream CI; this command runs them with the other changed test files and the DeepSeek-V4-Flash H200 test: `/rerun-test -c registered/unit/layers/quantization/test_nvfp4_moe_backends.py registered/e2e/models/test_deepseek_v4_flash_fp4_h200.py::TestDSV4FlashFP4H200FlashInferCutlass`.

title: [diffusion] perf: pipeline MiniMax-H3's Ulysses exchange against cuDNN SDPA on Blackwell
author: mickqian
body:
Stacked on #43361 (#43164 is merged). Merge #43361 first; this PR's own change is the cuDNN gate in `minimax_h3.py` and one cookbook line.

## Motivation

On Blackwell, MiniMax-H3's dense attention runs on cuDNN SDPA through `DynamicCudnnSDPAImpl`. The pipelined Ulysses exchange from #43164 only accepted the FlashAttention backend, so B200/B300 kept the sequential exchange and got none of it.

## Modifications

- The pipeline also accepts `AttentionBackendEnum.DYNAMIC_CUDNN_SDPA`. Attention still runs through the backend's `forward_varlen`, one head group at a time.
- The skip-softmax check only exists on the FlashAttention impl, so it is now optional.
- Cookbook: the configuration note says the pipeline runs against FlashAttention on Hopper and cuDNN SDPA on Blackwell.

## Accuracy Tests

- **Per head group, cuDNN SDPA gives the same bytes as those heads inside the full call.** Checked with `torch.equal` on 4×B300 at H3's per-rank attention shapes:
  - 49652 tokens × 28 heads in groups of 4 (Ref2VA, Ulysses 2);
  - 37742 tokens × 28 heads in groups of 4 (T2VA, Ulysses 2);
  - 37744 tokens × 14 heads in groups of 2 (T2VA, Ulysses 4).

  It holds on both torch 2.14.1 with cuDNN 9.24 and torch 2.13 with cuDNN 9.20.
- End to end on 4×B300, the MP4 md5 is the same for the sequential exchange and for 7, 4 and 2 groups, in every cell.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Client end-to-end latency, 4×B300, 50 steps, default quality, one run per arm. The base is this stack (#43164 + #43361) with #43327 and #43337, and `SGLANG_DIFFUSION_ULYSSES_PIPELINE_GROUPS` selects the sequential exchange (0) or a group count:

| Case | sequential | 7 groups (default) | 4 groups | 2 groups |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| T2VA 5 s, Ulysses 2 | 65.83 s | 63.24 s (−3.9%) | 63.40 s (−3.7%) | 63.48 s (−3.6%) |
| T2VA 5 s, Ulysses 4 | 34.20 s | 32.75 s (−4.3%) | — | 32.90 s (−3.8%) |
| Ref2VA 5 s, Ulysses 2 | 102.68 s | 99.24 s (−3.4%) | 98.70 s (−3.9%) | 98.89 s (−3.7%) |

- Blackwell gains more than Hopper (2–3%) because its exchange is a larger share of a faster step.
- Splitting heads costs cuDNN some efficiency, which FlashAttention 3 does not pay. On B300, 7 group calls over the Ref2VA shape take 3.5% longer than one call over all heads, and over the Ulysses 4 shape (2 heads per call) 5.4% longer. That is why 4 groups edge out 7 for Ref2VA in this single-run pass.
- A paired ABBA of 7 against 4 groups on B300 puts 4 ahead by only 0.1–0.2%, within run-to-run noise: Ref2VA 98.70 → 98.51 s, T2VA 63.74 → 63.68 s. So the automatic count stays at 7 for both backends.

title: [Fix] unified_cache: Prevent misaligned Mamba checkpoints after speculative truncation
author: alphabetc1
body:
## Motivation

With Mamba `no_buffer` + speculative decoding, verify advances the live state before CPU grammar/finish truncation. Donating that state under a shorter cache key corrupts subsequent prefix reuse.

## Changes

Require the live state length to match `owned_kv_len()` before donation, accounting for grammar-retained tokens and each algorithm's non-draft count. Otherwise skip the finished request's insertion, preserving existing prefixes and normal resource cleanup. The decision survives deferred release and adds no GPU synchronization.

Extend `test/registered/radix_cache/test_mamba_cache_kl.py` with `TestMambaSpecTruncationKL`. NEXTN count/story requests end at short length limits; the test compares full-vocabulary next-token distributions for identical probe token IDs using warm cache versus a cold recompute. It also checks that speculative verify accepted drafts and that cache reuse actually occurred. Shared HTTP/distribution helpers retain the existing lazy checkpoint test.

This branch includes #43567's shared test file and should merge after #43567. The no_buffer fix itself is independent of the lazy extra-buffer fix.

## Validation

GB300, TP1, Qwen3.5-0.8B pinned at `2fc06364715b967f1860aea9cf38778875588b17`, NEXTN (3 steps, topk 1, 4 draft tokens), no_buffer, page size 1, overlap/CUDA graphs disabled. The negative control retains #43567 and removes only #43387's finished-state guard.

| Scenario | KL without guard | KL with guard | Warm cache length without / with guard |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Count, max_new_tokens=9 | 0.876971 | 0.000235300 | 51 / 42 |
| Story, max_new_tokens=5 | 4.107031 | 0.000941570 | 27 / 22 |

KL is `D_KL(cold || warm)` over all 248,320 vocabulary entries at the same next-token position. The threshold is 0.005: valid prompt-prefix reuse versus cold prefill has numerical differences, while the corrupted-state cases are much larger. Unsafe finished suffixes now fall back to the cached prompt; this can reduce cache hits for truncated requests.

- Registered in `extra-a`, `1-gpu-large`; the new GPU test covers NEXTN length truncation. Grammar, EOS/stop, zero-commit, deferred release, and dedicated-slot controls remain covered by CPU tests.
- GPU: each NEXTN case repeated three times with identical KL values; all six negative controls failed and all six fixed cases passed. The existing lazy in-place KL test also passed with KL=0.
- CPU: 8 tests and 11 subtests passed after integrating #43567.
- Pre-commit passed. GPU validation is limited to GB300; no throughput benchmark.

```bash
python test/registered/radix_cache/test_mamba_cache_kl.py TestMambaSpecTruncationKL
python -m pytest -q test/registered/unit/managers/test_batch_result_processor_spec_grammar.py
```

title: [Perf] [NVIDIA] fp8_fa_sm120: Use the block-scaled MMA encoding
author: emre570
body:
## Motivation

`fp8_fa_sm120` computes QK and PV with the plain FP8 `mma.sync` (E4M3 x E4M3, FP32
accumulate). On GeForce SM120 this instruction runs at half rate. I measured the raw MMA
peak on an RTX 5080 with back-to-back chains and no memory traffic:

| instruction | SASS | TFLOP/s |
|---|---|---:|
| plain FP8, FP32 accumulate | `QMMA.16832.F32.E4M3.E4M3` | 246 |
| block-scaled FP8, FP32 accumulate | `QMMA.SF.16832.F32.E4M3.E4M3.E8` | 488 |

The block-scaled encoding (`kind::mxf8f6f4.block_scale`) multiplies each operand by a
UE8M0 scale, one byte per 32 k elements. With every scale byte set to 0x7F (2^0) the math
is the same product. On random finite E4M3 inputs, 0 of 704 M accumulator registers differ
between the two instructions.

So the kernel was limited by the instruction encoding, not by its design.

## Modifications

- `kernels/ops/attention/fp8_fa_sm120/kernel.py`
  - The MMA atom is `warp.MmaMXF8Op` when the compile target has it (sm_120a/f,
    sm_121a/f), `warp.MmaFP8Op` otherwise.
  - Four scale fragments (for Q, K, P, V) hold the constant byte 0x7F. They live in
    registers: no shared memory, no extra loads.
  - The two `cute.gemm` calls pass `[operand, scale]` pairs.
- `kernels/ops/attention/fp8_fa_sm120/plan.py`: the public `fp8_attention()` signature is
  unchanged. An internal compile-time parameter selects the encoding. It is not a user
  option, because the output is bit-equal and there is no speed against accuracy choice.
- One unit test runs both encodings on the same inputs and requires equal bits.

Operand layouts, shared memory, the softmax, the P pack and the prep do not change.
Register count goes from 244 to 250, no stack.

## Accuracy Tests

The output is bit-identical to `main`. Same inputs (seed 42), SHA-256 over the O and LSE
bytes, `main` against this branch:

| H | S | equal |
|---:|---:|---|
| 8 | 1052 (key mask path) | yes |
| 56 | 20440 | yes |
| 56 | 30272 | yes |

Unit tests: 10/10, including the new bit-equality test.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

RTX 5080, H=56, D=128, median of 5 runs, same process and inputs.

| S | prep (ms) | kernel `main` (ms) | kernel this PR (ms) | full call `main` (ms) | full call this PR (ms) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 20440 | 2.60 | 56.34 | 37.66 | 58.91 | 40.27 |
| 30272 | 3.84 | 123.60 | 83.28 | 127.26 | 86.29 |

The full call is 1.47x faster at both lengths. Against cuDNN SDPA BF16 on the same card
(226 ms at S=30272) the backend is now 2.6x faster, was 1.8x.

title: [Fix] attn_residual: int64 program ids in the score/combine kernels (int32 overflow at 37,451 tokens)
author: jiuqiant
body:
## Motivation

`_score_kernel` and `_combine_kernel` in `srt/layers/attn_residual.py` read the attention-residual bank `[T, NB, H]` at `bank_ptr + pid_t * stride_bm`. `pid_t = tl.program_id(0)` is int32 and so is the product. With Kimi-K3's `NB = 8`, `H = 7168`, `stride_bm = 57,344`, so the offset passes 2^31 − 1 at `pid_t = 37,450`: any call with **≥ 37,451 tokens** reads at a negative offset and dies with `an illegal memory access was encountered`. The error is reported asynchronously, usually at a later, unrelated launch.

Where this path runs:
- **SM100+ (Blackwell):** the main aggregation uses the int64-safe TMA kernel, but `_mix_fused` still runs for the DSpark aux-hidden capture (`aggregate_stream`). So a DSpark prefill pass with more than 37,450 tokens (e.g. `--chunked-prefill-size` ≥ 40k) crashes.
- **GPUs without the TMA path:** `_mix_fused` is the main aggregation of every layer.
- `attn_res_hip.py`'s `_agg_kernel` has the same `t * stride_bm` pattern.

## Modifications

- Cast the token program id to int64 in `_score_kernel`, `_combine_kernel` (`attn_residual.py`) and `_agg_kernel` (`attn_res_hip.py`). Only addressing changes.

title: [Scheduler] Fix the deterministic-inference hang when a prefill chunk is shorter than its alignment
author: hnyls2002
body:
- Deterministic inference truncates each prefill chunk to a multiple of an alignment (4096 by default). A per-rank chunk below it, from `--chunked-prefill-size` < 4096 or from DP attention splitting the chunk across ranks, truncated every chunk to zero tokens, so a prompt longer than the chunk waited in the queue forever
- Triton: drop the alignment; `align_window_kv_to_tiles` pads each sliding-window KV list to an absolute multiple of 128, so a chunked prefill sums keys in the same tiles as an unchunked one (built once per forward, deterministic inference only; the attention kernel is unchanged)
- Flashinfer and the DSA kpool alignment: a per-rank chunk shorter than the alignment fails at startup instead of hanging; decode servers are exempt
- Deprecate `SGLANG_TRITON_PREFILL_TRUNCATION_ALIGN_SIZE`
- Add `test_deterministic_chunk_align.py` and a chunked-vs-unchunked sliding-window case in `test_triton_attention_kernels.py`

No behavior change without deterministic inference. With it, triton prefill chunks are no longer aligned (chunked and unchunked outputs stay bitwise equal), and flashinfer configurations that used to hang now fail at startup.

title: Disable DualGemm fusion for Inkling dense MLP
author: alisonshao
body:
#41887 routed `LlamaMLP.forward` through a fused gate/up + SwiGLU kernel for unquantized MLPs at ≤16 tokens. `InklingDenseMLP` inherits that forward but uses interleaved gate/up weights and its own FP32 `InklingSwiglu`, which the fused path bypasses. title: [Fix] deepseek_v4: Fix mHC prewarm when chunked prefill is disabled
author: maocheng23
body:
## Motivation

`prewarm_mhc_pre` sizes its token buckets from `chunked_prefill_size`. With `--chunked-prefill-size -1` (chunked prefill disabled) that produces a single bucket of `-1` tokens, so `residual.new_zeros(-1, ...)` raises while weights load. DeepSeek V4 cannot start with chunked prefill disabled.

Servers that capture prefill hidden states turn chunked prefill off, so a request's states arrive in one forward. They hit this on DeepSeek V4.

## Modifications

When chunked prefill is disabled or unset, size the prewarm buckets from `max_prefill_tokens`, which bounds a prefill batch in that case. This is the same rule `pre_capture_activation_reserve_mb` uses.

## Accuracy Tests

Not applicable: startup-only change. No kernel or forward code changed.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Not applicable: startup-only change.

## Tests

No unit test: removed per review. The fallback cases (`-1` / `0` / `None` chunked prefill) were exercised by a since-removed CPU test that failed without the fix and passed with it.

title: [Feat] spec: Capture aux hidden states on the target without a speculative draft
author: maocheng23
body:
## Motivation

Auxiliary hidden-state capture is the per-layer concatenation that EAGLE3, DFLASH and DSPARK drafts consume. Today it is only reachable by loading a speculative draft; `ModelRunner` carries a `TODO: expose this to server args?` for it.

Data-generation and draft-training pipelines need these hidden states from a plain target server. Without this change they either patch SGLang or re-run the target in a separate process.

## Modifications

- **New server arguments** (`exec.features`, defaulting to `False` and `None`):
  - `--enable-return-aux-hidden-states` wires the target model's existing capture hook without a draft. `--speculative-algorithm` then only names the capture convention: `set_eagle3_layers_to_capture`, `set_dflash_layers_to_capture`, or the native `set_dspark_layers_to_capture` when the model has one. The resolution hook resets `speculative_algorithm` to `None`, so no draft is loaded, nothing is reserved for one, and the speculative stack stays off. The resolved convention lives in a non-CLI `aux_hidden_state_capture` field; it stays an enum because the models' capture hooks still differ by draft family (layer-id conventions, mHC contraction), with a TODO to unify those hooks and collapse it to the bool. It sets `--return-hidden-states-mode` to `full` when unset.
  - `--return-aux-hidden-state-layer-ids` selects layers in the target model's capture convention. It is required for DFLASH and DSPARK; EAGLE3 falls back to the model's default EAGLE3 layers. Draft-checkpoint IDs can differ: DFLASH uses zero-based layer-output IDs for Llama and Qwen3, but layer-input IDs for Muse Glimmer. A Muse `DFlash2DraftModel` or `MuseGlimmerAssistantModel` output-layer ID of 4 therefore becomes capture ID 5; capture-only mode does not perform that conversion automatically.
- **Resolver.** `resolve_spec_aux_hidden_state_config` handles the capture-only case. It resolves no draft layer counts, so the KV pool reserves nothing for a draft.
- **DSPARK hook routing.** It moves from `spec_algorithm.is_dspark()` to the resolved config (`SpecAuxHiddenStateConfig.is_dspark`), so capture-only DSPARK picks the native hook. Behavior is unchanged for speculative runs.
- **Hidden-state capture output.** Requests use the existing `return_hidden_states` and `--return-hidden-states-mode` paths to receive the auxiliary concatenation. Under full capture, `LogitsProcessorOutput.last_hidden_states` separately retains the post-norm final-layer states for in-process consumers (#43450 and the SpecForge capture plugin, sgl-project/SpecForge#945); it is not added to HTTP responses. CUDA, CPU and NPU graph output slicing, DP/MLP padding removal, and encoder-SWA folded-row removal keep these rows aligned with the auxiliary output. Inkling preserves the final-layer states before μP logit scaling while retaining its existing scaled logit computation.
- **Validation.** `handle_aux_hidden_state_capture` runs before any reader of `speculative_algorithm`. It rejects layer ids without the flag, the flag without `--speculative-algorithm` EAGLE3/DFLASH/DSPARK, the flag together with `--speculative-draft-model-path`, DFLASH/DSPARK without layer ids, an empty, negative or repeated layer id, and `pp_size > 1` (the capture hooks only see the last pipeline rank's layers). The resolver rejects a layer id beyond the target's layer count before weights load. At the first forward, `LogitsProcessor` fails if the model captured fewer layers than requested, since most models cannot capture their last layer; a model without the requested hook is reported as a `ValueError`.
- **Docs.** Rows added to `server_arguments.mdx`.

Example (no draft loaded):

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \
  --speculative-algorithm DFLASH --enable-return-aux-hidden-states \
  --return-aux-hidden-state-layer-ids 1 9 17 25 33 \
  --return-hidden-states-mode full
```

A request with `"return_hidden_states": true` then receives the concatenated hidden states of the five layers.

## Accuracy Tests

The following GB300 results are historical validation of an earlier revision, run with the earlier `--aux-hidden-state-capture <method>` spelling. The examples below use the current flags. These GPU accuracy tests have not been rerun after the latest cleanup, rebase, and output-alignment fixes.

One GB300 (CUDA 13), image `lmsysorg/sglang:nightly-dev-cu13-20261006-f3fe7534` with SGLang main `8c273d6813` + #43448, this PR and #43450 (maocheng23/sglang `spec-capture/integration`) overlaid. The SpecForge capture plugin (sgl-project/SpecForge#945) is the consumer.

- **Against an independent forward.** Tiny Llama target (8 layers, hidden 64), `--speculative-algorithm EAGLE3 --enable-return-aux-hidden-states --return-aux-hidden-state-layer-ids 1 3 4 --return-hidden-states-mode full`:
  - across the three gate tests (EAGLE3 and DFlash feature layouts), the aux states match a separate HF forward of the same layers within bf16 tolerance (2e-2);
  - `lm_head(last_hidden_states)` reproduces HF's logits within that tolerance;
  - one EAGLE3 training step on the captured features gives a finite loss.
- **Real model.** Qwen3.8-27B (hybrid GDN, 64 layers), TP1, `--speculative-algorithm DFLASH --enable-return-aux-hidden-states --return-aux-hidden-state-layer-ids 5 19 33 47 61 --return-hidden-states-mode full`:
  - shapes are `[L, 25600]` (aux) and `[L, 5120]` (last hidden) for L = 7 to 4096;
  - the captured aux rows equal what this PR returns through `return_hidden_states` (max abs diff 0.0);
  - `lm_head` of the last kept hidden state picks the token the server samples greedily.
- On the GPU image, this PR's tests pass together with the #43448 and #43450 suites and `test_auxiliary_output.py` (75 passed).

## Speed Tests and Profiling

With auxiliary capture disabled, `last_hidden_states` stays `None`; existing hidden-state outputs retain their behavior. Enabled full capture retains the final-layer tensor alongside the auxiliary output for in-process consumers. The latest revision has not received a new GPU performance or memory benchmark.

Historical measurement together with #43450 (see the `bench_serving` A/B there) found parity with main on Qwen3.8-27B for both decode and prefill. That result predates the latest cleanup, rebase, and output-alignment fixes.

## Tests

Current CPU validation: **265 passed, 230 subtests passed, 1 existing skip; scoped pre-commit checks passed**.

- `test/registered/unit/model_executor/model_runner_components/test_aux_hidden_state_capture.py`: CLI parsing, rejected argument combinations, capture defaults, EAGLE3/DFLASH/DSPARK resolution, draft-free KV sizing, model-hook routing, and full/last/null output behavior.
- `test/registered/unit/model_executor/test_aux_hidden_state_row_alignment.py`: DP/MLP padding removal and encoder-SWA folded-row removal preserve final-layer and auxiliary row correspondence, including stock-mode controls and token-index remapping.
- Existing MLP pad/unpad, encoder-SWA replay, server-argument registry/namespace/CLI, and focused Inkling capture-contract tests cover the surrounding behavior. The Inkling checks verify unscaled post-norm capture and unchanged scaled logits.

The CPU checks do not run distributed inference or CUDA/NPU graph capture. GPU accuracy and benchmark results above are historical; new CI results belong to the final pushed head.

title: [srt] Allow mixed chunk prefill on the Full prefill CUDA graph backend
author: metamergebot
body:
## Motivation

Starting a server with `--enable-mixed-chunk` and the Full prefill CUDA graph backend fails in `PrefillCudaGraphRunner.__init__`, which asserts that mixed chunk prefill is served by the Breakable backend only. That guard was written when Breakable was the only padded prefill topology. Full now captures a padded EXTEND topology on both the token and request axes and refreshes the live attention metadata before every replay, and `MIXED` forwards already replay the EXTEND-captured graphs on both backends (the runner maps `MIXED` to `EXTEND` before the replay lookup). Nothing on the mixed path is Breakable-specific any more, so the guard only blocks a working configuration.

Mixing prefill chunks with running decode rows under Full prefill graphs lets a serving deployment that prefers Full's static request-axis shape keep decode rows moving while prefills arrive, instead of choosing between the two.

## Modifications

- `python/sglang/srt/model_executor/runner/prefill_cuda_graph_runner.py`: the startup guard accepts `Backend.FULL` as well as `Backend.BREAKABLE`. Defaults are unchanged: mixing stays opt-in and every other backend is still rejected with the same assertion. Shapes the Full backend cannot replay (more requests than captured slots, uncapturable prefix chunks, and so on) fall back to eager execution exactly as before; this change touches only the constructor check.
- `test/registered/unit/model_executor/test_prefill_cuda_graph_runner.py`: a CPU case constructs the runner with mixed chunk enabled on the Full backend, with base initialization patched to raise a sentinel, and checks that the sentinel is reached. It fails on the previous guard with `Mixed chunk prefill requires the breakable prefill CUDA graph backend; got 'full'`.

## Accuracy Tests

Not applicable to default configurations: the change is a constructor check and is a no-op unless `--enable-mixed-chunk` is set with the Full backend. On that configuration the forward path is the existing Full EXTEND replay with refreshed attention metadata, which is already exercised by non-mixed Full prefill; decode rows in a mixed batch take the same padded slots they would in a Breakable mixed batch.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Not applicable: no kernel or runtime path changes. Mixed chunk prefill interleaves prefill and decode for better decode concurrency in mixed workloads, trades prefill completion latency for it, and remains opt-in.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit): formatting, import sorting and spelling checks pass on both changed files.
- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests): the whole of `test_prefill_cuda_graph_runner.py` passes with the change; the new case fails against the unmodified runner.
- [x] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations): none needed.

title: [QSA] Bound the decode indexer's work by the context length
author: yuan-luo
body:
## Motivation

For Qwen3.8-Flash-Next B200 BF16 (TP4, NEXTN MTP 3/1/4) the QSA decode indexer takes about 3 ms of a 28.75 ms bs64 decode step. It costs that much even at short contexts, where QSA selects every block anyway. Three pieces of it scale with the max context instead of the live one:

- `tilelang_qsa_mqa_decode` launches a `(rows, max_pages / 4)` grid. The CUDA-graph page table is sized for the max context: 262144 tokens are 65536 compressed tokens, which is 4096 pages of 16, or 1024 CTAs per row. At bs64 verify (256 rows) this launches 262K CTAs per layer, almost all of which exit immediately. Each call takes 137 us, 1.78 ms per step.
- For a row whose compressed length fits the k = 512 top-k, `fast_topk` writes `0..len-1` without reading its scores. So the scoring work on that row is thrown away, and so is the `-inf` pre-fill of the whole `rows x max_model_len` logits matrix, since `fast_topk` never reads past a row's length.
- `_qsa_fused_kv_prepare` writes every row's full packed width: 2112 tokens of K and V at 256 dims, zero-filling the part past the valid count. `trtllm_decode` reads each row only up to `valid_counts`. At 256 rows this writes 537 MB per call, 76 us per call and 1.06 ms per step.

## Modifications

- `qsa/mqa.py`:
  - The decode kernel now takes `ctas_per_row`, chosen as 1, 16 or 256 by row count so the grid covers about four waves; the three levels bound the number of TileLang specializations. Each row's CTAs stride over its 64-token groups up to `context_len` in a dynamic loop.
  - `min_scored_len` skips rows at or below that length.
  - `tilelang_qsa_mqa_decode(..., min_scored_len=)` leaves those rows, and the columns past each row's length, unset (`torch.empty`). The default of 0 keeps the previous fully `-inf`-filled output.
- `qsa/qsa_indexer.py`: `select_decode_tokens` passes `min_scored_len=block_topk` only on the `fast_topk` (k = 512) path. That path writes `0..len-1` for rows that fit k without reading their scores, and never reads past a length. Every other top-k path keeps the full `-inf` fill.
- `qsa/fused_kv.py`: `fused_kv_prepare(..., visible_page_size=)` applies on the block-index path (`compress_ratio > 1`). A packed tile at or past the row's valid count, rounded up to the page, returns before loading or storing. The count uses the same formula as the `COUNTS` tile.
- `qwen_sparse_attn_backend.py`:
  - The trtllm sparse decode passes `visible_page_size=64`, the trtllm page.
  - The packed scratch is allocated with `torch.zeros`, so bytes that are never written cannot be NaN. The allocation happens once, at full graph capacity during the eager warmup before capture.
- Tests:
  - `test_qsa_indexer.py`: the decode grid scores every group at 256, 16 and 1 CTAs per row, checked against the torch reference. With `min_scored_len`, `fast_topk` returns the same selection; the unset logits are NaN-poisoned through the caching allocator.
  - `test_qsa_fused_kv_prepare.py`: with `visible_page_size`, the visible pages are bitwise equal to the full write and nothing past them is written (NaN sentinel), for counts at and around page edges and widths 1 and 4.

## Accuracy Tests

- `test_qsa_indexer.py` and `test_qsa_fused_kv_prepare.py`: 187 passed. `test_qsa.py`: 49 passed, 1 skipped. All run on B200.
- GSM8K through `sglang.test.run_eval` (chat, 5-shot, 200 questions, greedy, max 4096 tokens), Qwen3.8-Flash-Next BF16, TP4, MTP: 0.985 with this PR, 0.98 on main.
- Needle in a haystack: a 4-digit code planted at 10/50/90% depth in natural text of 1.1K, 4K, 16.6K, 35K and 70K tokens, chat API, greedy. 15/15 pass. Above 2048 tokens QSA's sparse selection is active, so these runs exercise the restructured scoring path.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Setup:
- 8x B200, two servers built from the same commit: main `5cbf949839` on GPUs 4-7 and this PR on GPUs 0-3.
- Both use the cookbook B200 BF16 low-latency flags.
- Load: closed bursts of chat requests with `ignore_eos`, 1536 output tokens each.
- Step time = running × accept_len / gen_throughput, taken as the median over the steady-state `Decode batch` log lines.

| Concurrency | main | this PR |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | 6.29 ms | 6.22 ms |
| 16 | 16.55 ms | 15.77 ms (-4.7%) |
| 64 | 28.75 ms | 26.54 ms (-7.7%) |

Torch profile, bs64 decode, TP0, 10 steps. The main-side profile is from `fba3ad4b1f`, whose QSA files are identical to `5cbf949839`.

| Kernel, per step | main | this PR |
|---|---:|---:|
| TileLang decode scoring | 1.778 ms (137 us/call) | 0.041 ms (3.2 us/call) |
| `_qsa_fused_kv_prepare` | 1.060 ms (76 us/call) | 0.317 ms (22.6 us/call) |
| logits fill | 0.165 ms | 0.036 ms |
| Total | 3.03 ms | 0.42 ms |

Long contexts do not regress. Scoring plus `fast_topk` for 256 rows over a 64K-token context takes 365 us on main and 333 us with this PR. This is an eager measurement including launch overhead, and its 287 MB compressed cache is larger than L2.

Trade-off: up to three TileLang decode-scoring specializations are compiled per head configuration, where main compiled one.

title: [Perf] [NPU] glm5.2: Support dynamic INT8 MLAProlog for attention
author: xiedeyantu
body:
## Motivation

Enable fused MLA preprocessing for **GLM-5.2-w4a8c8 decode on Ascend NPU** when `SGLANG_NPU_USE_MLAPO=1` is set. This checkpoint uses `W8A8_DYNAMIC` for the attention projections `q_a_proj`, `q_b_proj`, and `kv_a_proj_with_mqa`.

Previously, these projections entered the legacy static ModelSlim MLAPO path, which expects `input_offset`. Dynamic INT8 layers do not have that attribute, so enabling MLAPO fails with:

```text
AttributeError: 'ReplicatedLinear' object has no attribute 'input_offset'
```

This PR routes eligible decode layers through **MLAProlog V3 dynamic INT8 mode**, fusing attention projections, normalization, Q absorption, RoPE, and KV cache writes. It also lets dynamic INT8 indexers reuse the quantized low-rank query returned by the fused operator.

The supported configuration is `weight_quant_mode=2`, `kv_cache_quant_mode=0`, and `query_quant_mode=0`: projection weights and intermediate activations use INT8, while the final query and both KV latent and RoPE key caches use BF16. The checkpoint's `w4a8c8` name describes a mixed quantization configuration; this attention path requires BF16 caches.

## Modifications

- **Fix dispatch for dynamic INT8 attention.** Detect the loaded QKV-A and Q-B quantization methods together, and use `uses_mlaprolog()` consistently for backend selection and output unpacking. Other ModelSlim projections retain their existing backend selection.
- **Add mode 2 weight and activation preparation.** Use ModelSlim's existing `[K, N]` INT8 weight layout, split the merged QKV-A weights and per-channel scales into Q-A and KV-A, and convert projection weights to FRACTAL_NZ. Dynamically quantize BF16 input activations per token and pass the activation and weight scales to `npu_mla_prolog_v3`.
- **Reuse the fused query output in the indexer.** Pass the returned INT8 `q_lora` and FP32 scale directly to dynamic INT8 indexers, eliminating repeated quantization. Recompute BF16 `q_lora` for other indexer implementations, and skip this handling when `indexer=None` on layers that reuse top-k indices.
- **Validate compatibility and preserve required weights.** Require interleaved RoPE, BF16 inputs/caches/`w_kc`, and BF16 final query output; reject unsupported weight layouts, scales, and nonzero RMSNorm bias. Keep the original projections and `w_kc` available for subsequent computation.

The runtime changes are in `mla_preprocess.py` and `deepseek_v2_attention_mla_npu.py`.

## Accuracy Tests

Validation previously reported for this PR:

- Manual smoke test: GLM-5.2-w4a8c8 runs successfully with `SGLANG_NPU_USE_MLAPO=1` in the tested configuration.
- All six CPU regression tests passed. The dispatch test reproduces the original `input_offset` error against the pre-change implementation.
- Formatting, lint, and CI registration checks passed.

```bash
python test/registered/unit/attention/test_npu_mlaprolog.py -v
```

The CPU tests mock NPU operators and verify the Python adaptation logic. Full model accuracy evaluation and numerical comparison against real NPU operators remain pending.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

The supplied GLM-5.2-w4a8c8 profile compares MLAPO disabled (`ori`) with dynamic INT8 MLAProlog enabled (`new`) on the same machine:

| Metric | MLAPO disabled | MLAPO enabled | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Steady-state decode latency (ms/token) | 31.583 | 28.943 | -8.36% |
| Equivalent BS=1 generation rate (token/s) | 31.66 | 34.55 | +9.12% |
| Compute kernels per rank per decode step | 3041 | 2707 | -10.98% |

Configuration: BS=1, 3-token prefill, decode KV lengths 4-23, 78 layers per rank, 20 decode steps, and 8 ranks; CANN 9.1.0 and torch_npu 2.10.0.post6. Latency is measured between consecutive `ArgMaxV2` completion points: 19 intervals per rank, averaged across ranks. The equivalent generation rate is calculated as `1000 / latency`.

The enabled path executes 1,560 `MlaPrologV3` calls per rank across 20 steps. Standalone `DynamicQuant` calls drop from 8,220 to 6,240: 1,560 Q-B input quantizations move inside MLAProlog, and 420 redundant indexer quantizations are eliminated across 21 indexer layers.

Prefill does not use MLAProlog V3. In the 3-token sample, enabling MLAPO adds 467 compute kernels and approximately 1.23 ms of cumulative kernel time for RoPE layout compatibility; this is not a measured TTFT increase.

These results are device-profile measurements from a single A/B capture. The exact capture commit, full launch arguments, and checkpoint revision were not retained; end-to-end throughput and TTFT benchmarks remain pending.

title: [diffusion] Run head_dim-128 QK-norm + RoPE two rows per warp for every RoPE layout
author: mickqian
body:
## Motivation

#43337 runs the head_dim-128 QK-norm + RoPE kernel two rows per warp: 16 lanes per row, 16-byte loads. That removed a fifth of the kernel's time, but only for MiniMax-H3's configuration, NeoX RoPE with the norm rounded before it and a half-width cache.

Every other head_dim-128 caller kept the one-row-per-warp kernel:

| Callers | RoPE | Norm rounded before RoPE | Cache |
|---|---|---|---|
| FLUX.1/2, Qwen-Image, Z-Image, FLUX 3, Krea2, Joy | interleaved | no (FP32 path) | FP32, half width |
| LongCat | interleaved | yes | full width |
| Ernie-style | NeoX | yes | full width |

## Modifications

- `fused_qknorm_rope_half_warp` now takes the RoPE layout, the rounding mode and the cache width as template parameters. It covers:
  - interleaved RoPE in both rounding modes;
  - NeoX RoPE with the norm rounded;
  - full- and half-width caches;
  - BF16, FP16 and FP32 caches;
  - every rope width that ends on a lane boundary (multiple of 8; of 16 for NeoX).
- Each lane still covers two lanes of the one-row kernel and repeats their arithmetic step for step:
  - the same partial sums and xor butterfly;
  - on the FP32 path, the one-row kernel's pairwise square sums and `x * (norm * w)`;
  - on the rounded path, its per-element sums and `(x * norm) * w`;
  - the same rotary expressions.
- **NeoX on the FP32 path keeps the one-row kernel.** There, nvcc's choice of which product of `e * cos + swapped * sin` to fuse into the FMA depends on the cache dtype. The one-row kernel compiles to `fma(cos, e, sin * swapped)` with an FP32 cache and to `fma(swapped, sin, cos * e)` with a BF16 one. A second kernel cannot be guaranteed to make the same choice, and the first version of this PR did not: about 1 element in 10⁵ differed. No interleaved or rounded path has this ambiguity in either kernel.

## Accuracy Tests

- `test_two_rows_per_warp_match_one_row_per_warp` now covers every layout that runs two rows per warp, against the one-row kernel with `torch.equal`:
  - NeoX and interleaved RoPE;
  - both rounding modes;
  - full- and half-width caches;
  - BF16, FP16 and FP32 caches;
  - rope widths 32 to 128 (including 120);
  - in place and out of place.

  13 passed on B300.
- A wider sweep on B300 compared the two kernels over every combination of rope width (64, 96, 128), layout, rounding mode, cache width and cache dtype, with 6 seeds of 4099 tokens × 8 heads each. Every layout this PR routes to the two-rows kernel matched in all 8.4M elements of every seed. The FP32 NeoX path was the only one that differed, which is why it stays on the one-row kernel.
- These checks ran on sm_103 (B300). The registered test compares the two kernels' bytes the same way on the B200 and H100 CI runners, and a contraction mismatch shows up in the large row count as above.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

In-place kernel time on B300 (triton `do_bench`, median), at each model's 1024² token count, FP32 cache unless noted:

| Config (callers) | one row per warp | two rows per warp |
|---|---:|---:|
| interleaved, FP32 path: FLUX.1/2, FLUX 3, Krea2 (4608 × 24 heads) | 42.0 µs | 33.8 µs (−19.5%) |
| interleaved, FP32 path: Qwen-Image (4352 × 24) | 39.9 µs | 31.7 µs (−20.5%) |
| interleaved, FP32 path: Z-Image (4352 × 30) | 48.0 µs | 37.8 µs (−21.2%) |
| interleaved, FP32 path, rope 64 (4096 × 32) | 48.0 µs | 35.8 µs (−25.5%) |
| interleaved, rounded, full width: LongCat (4608 × 24) | 48.1 µs | 40.1 µs (−16.6%) |
| NeoX, rounded, full width, BF16 cache (4096 × 32) | 50.3 µs | 39.8 µs (−20.9%) |
| NeoX, FP32 path (stays one row per warp) | 93.1 µs | 93.2 µs |
| MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA, Ulysses 2 (already two rows per warp, control) | 504.4 µs | 405.7 µs (−19.6%) |

title: [Perf] Cache msgspec struct fields in the batch splitter
author: ToLiveAndLove
body:
Follow-up to #44288, which landed the grouping half of #43096.

`_handle_output_by_indices` called `msgspec.structs.fields(output)` on every split. That call takes about 300 us, nearly the whole cost of a split. Since #44288, both IPC hops split each output batch once per destination, so the cost grows with the number of TokenizerWorkers (return hop) and detokenizers (router hop). This caches the field list per output type.

Split plus pickle of a 256-request `BatchStrOutput`, CPU only:

| destinations | main (ms) | this PR (ms) |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 0.64 | 0.28 |
| 4 | 1.58 | 0.35 |
| 8 | 3.17 | 0.48 |
| 32 | 11.49 | 1.12 |

For reference, the per-request path before #44288 took 4.52 ms for the same batch.

title: [Fix] [SM120] quantization: Requantize block-FP8 MoE weights to UE8M0 for DeepGEMM
author: lucifer1004
body:
## Motivation

On SM120, `should_deepgemm_weight_requant_ue8m0` returns False for every caller, so block-FP8 MoE experts served by the DeepGEMM runner keep their FP32 checkpoint scales. SM120's grouped GEMM converts FP32 scales to UE8M0 itself, and it faults (CUDA error 719) on scales that are not powers of two.

With `nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` and `--speculative-moe-runner-backend deep_gemm`, the block-FP8 MTP draft experts crash at the first prefill graph capture, at every token count. The same weights with power-of-two scales run.

#39065 (open, fixing #39063) makes the same guard change by inferring a grouped layer from `weight.ndim == 3`, without tests. This PR differs in two ways:
- `Fp8MoEMethod` passes `grouped_moe=True` explicitly.
- It adds a regression test.

Split out of #42566 at a maintainer's request. #42566 now carries only the TP block-scale refinement, which depends on this change for its DeepGEMM path on SM120.

Fixes #39063

## Modifications

- Keep the SM120 exemption for dense block-FP8 GEMMs, which run on CUTLASS or Triton with FP32 scales there.
- Requantize grouped MoE weights to UE8M0 as on SM90 and SM100.
- `should_deepgemm_weight_requant_ue8m0` and `requant_block_scale_ue8m0_for_deepgemm` take a keyword-only `grouped_moe` flag, which `Fp8MoEMethod` sets for its expert weights.

## Accuracy Tests

`test/registered/unit/layers/quantization/test_deepgemm_ue8m0_requant.py` adds a case for the SM120 grouped-MoE requant.

Two existing tests in that file fail on SM120 hosts both with and without this PR:
- `test_helper_requants_supported_deepgemm_bf16_once`
- `test_compressed_tensors_block_processing_preserves_ue8m0_marker`

They patch DeepGEMM's UE8M0 flags on but not the device, and SM120 deliberately skips the dense requant they exercise. The file passes on the CPU runner it is registered for.

End to end, together with the TP refinement in #42566:
- `nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` at TP2 with its own MTP head (NEXTN 3/1/4, draft experts on DeepGEMM) scores 0.976 on GSM8K through the chat template (lm-eval `gsm8k`, 1,319 questions, flexible-extract) on 2x RTX PRO 6000.
- Without this change, the same draft experts on DeepGEMM fault on SM120 at TP1 already.

title: [Fix] Account for captured inputs in DeepGEMM masked workspace budget
author: BBuf
body:
## Motivation

DeepGEMM's automatic standard-layout policy can select a masked workspace that OOMs during prefill CUDA Graph capture. The estimate assumes the runner input is released after the gate/up GEMM, but capture makes `dispose_tensor` a no-op: the input and its scales remain live during activation and the down GEMM.

Reproduced on H200 with the default memory fraction, prefill chunk size, and graph settings:

| Model | TP | Failing prefill shape | Masked budget | Failing `down_output` allocation |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 | 1 | 4608 | 3.15 GiB | 2.38 GiB, with 1.20 GiB free |
| Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-FP8 | 2 | 3072 | 5.37 GiB | 4.88 GiB, with 1.89 GiB free |

The 30B failure reproduces with a warm compilation cache. Minimal 30B reproduction: `python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 --tp-size 1 --moe-runner-backend deep_gemm`.

## Modifications

Include the retained input and scales in the activation/down-GEMM peak estimate. Use the same conservative bound during warmup and capture so layout selection stays consistent. Extend the existing layout-policy test with the two failing geometries and packed/unpacked scales; no new test files.

Explicit layout overrides and the budget fraction are unchanged. Automatic selection can switch to compact earlier on other models too: the existing 397B-shaped fixture now selects compact at 8K under its 42.5 GiB budget, while 4K remains masked. That can change performance near the selection boundary.

## Accuracy Tests

- Existing `test/registered/kernels/ops/moe/test_minimax_quant_scatter.py`: **53 passed** on GB300. The six parameterized policy cases fail against the original estimator.
- Both affected models complete startup, graph capture, serving benchmarks, and GSM8K with the fix on H200. Validation base: `e35f60b9`.
- GSM8K: 1,314 held-out cases, greedy, 2,048-token cap, identical case IDs/prompt hashes. Qwen3-30B fixed-auto scored **1215 / 1217** across two runs; forced-compact controls scored **1223 / 1221**. All requests stopped normally, with no errors. The reverse pair loses 13 and gains 9 cases; these results do not establish numerical equivalence.
- Qwen3.5-122B fixed-auto scored **1275**, versus **1277** with the default Triton MoE runner. Both have the same two length-capped cases, retained in scoring, and no request errors. Original DeepGEMM auto cannot supply an accuracy baseline because startup fails.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Qwen3-30B, one H200, 320 requests, nominal 8K input / 1K output, concurrency 64. Saved prompts and actual token counts match across all four runs. Repeated in reverse order:

| Configuration | Output token/s, runs 1 / 2 | Median TPOT ms, runs 1 / 2 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Forced compact | 1852.52 / 1853.72 | 30.608 / 30.596 |
| Fixed auto | 2083.69 / 2083.45 | 26.780 / 26.779 |

Fixed auto retains masked decode while using compact for large prefills: about **12.4%** faster than the forced-compact workaround, with median TTFT around 4.04 seconds in both configurations. The default Triton runner remains faster at 2140.95 token/s; this fixes capture reliability rather than establishing a generally faster backend. Qwen3.5-122B also remains slower with DeepGEMM than with its default Triton runner.

## Checklist

title: [Perf] Compact GDN causal-conv grids for skewed prefill batches
author: BBuf
body:
## Motivation

GDN's prefill convolution launches a rectangular grid sized by the longest sequence. With an 8K prefill chunk and 127 decode rows, this schedules about 3.1 million CTAs, most of which immediately return. The same overhead is repeated across 36 GDN layers in Qwen3.5-122B-A10B.

## Modifications

Build a compact `(sequence, chunk)` table once per forward and reuse the existing causal-conv kernel's `block_table` path across layers. This reduces the example above to 27,264 CTAs without changing convolution arithmetic or state updates.

Enable this for CUDA EXTEND/MIXED batches only when the rectangular grid has more than four times as many sequence/chunk blocks as the compact grid. Uniform and mildly ragged batches keep the existing launch to avoid table-construction overhead. MIS, TBO, speculative modes, non-CUDA paths, and unavailable or mismatched host lengths retain the existing behavior.

This is narrower than the prefill/decode split in #36065: it only compacts the convolution grid and does not change GDN attention dispatch.

## Accuracy Tests

- Extended three existing test files; no new test files. On both H200 and GB300, all 29 tests and 55 subtests pass:
  ```bash
  python -m pytest -q \
    test/registered/unit/layers/attention/test_gdn_prefill_backend_policy.py \
    test/registered/unit/layers/attention/test_mamba_track_state_dtype.py \
    test/registered/attention/test_gdn_prefill_layout.py
  ```
- CUDA tests compare convolution output and the entire state cache bitwise, including strided QKV, ragged/empty rows, initial state, permuted cache indices, and a padded cache slot. A separate microbenchmark also checks bitwise output/state at the model's actual convolution dimension of 6,144.
- Full held-out GSM8K validation uses 1,314 cases, five separate few-shot examples, temperature 0, seed 42, concurrency 64, and a 2,048-token limit. Case IDs and prompt hashes match; all runs have zero request errors. The first and reverse-order pairs give:

  | Run | Correct / 1314 | Token-limit case IDs |
  | --- | ---: | --- |
  | Baseline A | 1270 | 119, 423, 641, 1176, 1183 |
  | Compact A | 1273 | 119, 711 |
  | Compact B | 1273 | 119, 304, 423 |
  | Baseline B | 1276 | 119, 423, 1176 |

  The first pair has three losses/six gains; the reverse pair has five losses/two gains. Case 711 is correct on the candidate repeat; case 304 is newly capped there. No case is correct in both baseline runs and incorrect in both candidate runs. Baseline answers also vary across repeats. These measurements do not establish identical full-model outputs or statistical non-inferiority.

- Default cached-path regression check (mixed chunk disabled): C128 throughput 2693.96 -> 2699.97 output tok/s, median TTFT 12.886 -> 12.913 s, TPOT 34.90 -> 34.86 ms, and p99 E2E 48.87 -> 48.72 s. Exact requests/token counts match. GSM8K is 1277/1314 in both runs, with three losses and three gains and zero errors; token-limit finishes increase from two to four (new cases 87 and 157). This is a completed regression check with the per-case differences disclosed, not a claim of identical model outputs.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Same 2x H200, TP2, Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-FP8 revision `a099dee70ccfcd8d5dda56aaa0b60cb8ecadabc9`; baseline `e35f60b9`, candidate adds only this patch. Nominal 8192-token inputs and fixed 1024-token outputs, seed 42, 320/640 requests at C64/C128. Exact request records and actual token counts match. Timings exclude profiling and follow warmup/cache flush.

Both versions use FlashInfer full attention, Triton GDN prefill, BF16 Mamba state, `--enable-mixed-chunk`, and `--disable-radix-cache`. These numbers isolate the convolution change; they do not validate enabling mixed chunk with the default prefix-cache path.

| Concurrency | Version | Output tok/s | Median TTFT (s) | Median TPOT (ms) | p99 E2E (s) |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 64 | Baseline | 2126.54 | 1.120 | 28.94 | 42.68 |
| 64 | Compact grid | 2204.10 | 1.024 | 27.85 | 40.95 |
| 128 | Baseline | 2470.12 | 1.205 | 50.92 | 79.48 |
| 128 | Compact grid | 2686.89 | 1.073 | 46.36 | 72.63 |
| 128 | Compact grid, repeat | 2698.68 | 1.068 | 46.09 | 72.21 |
| 128 | Baseline, reverse repeat | 2475.35 | 1.273 | 50.62 | 78.95 |

C64 output throughput improves by 3.6%. C128 improves by 8.8% in the first pair and 9.0% in the reverse-order pair (A-B-B-A), with matching request records and actual token counts. Median TPOT and p99 E2E also improve in both C128 pairs.

A second full pair using `--prefill-attention-backend fa3` also improves C64 from 2193.74 to 2275.06 output tok/s and C128 from 2564.33 to 2797.15 (+9.1%). At C128, median TTFT changes from 1.205 to 1.000 s, TPOT from 48.94 to 44.55 ms, and p99 E2E from 75.45 to 68.98 s. Inputs and actual token counts match. GSM8K is 1272/1314 in both versions, with three losses and three gains, zero request errors, and three token-limit finishes each (candidate case 425 is newly capped). This separately checks the FA3 prefill backend; the repeated same-configuration results above isolate the convolution patch.

For `[8065] + [1] * 127`, dimension 6144 and width 4, isolated convolution time changes from 1873.5 to 104.0 us on H200 and 1568.4 to 86.7 us on GB300. Host table construction plus transfer takes about 280 us once per forward, amortized across layers. The approximately 18x kernel speedup is not an end-to-end model speedup.

A separate TP2 trace with 127 active decode requests confirms the actual dispatch: across eight mixed steps and 288 convolution launches, per-rank convolution GPU time drops from 525.87 to 29.26 ms on rank 0 and 525.88 to 29.79 ms on rank 1. Decode progress differs between those profiling probes, so their total wall times are not treated as matched end-to-end measurements.

## Checklist

- [x] Existing CPU/CUDA tests extended and run on H200 and GB300.
- [x] First full-model timing and accuracy pair completed.
- [x] Default cached-path C128 timing and full GSM8K regression check (results and per-case differences above).
- [x] Reverse-order C128 timing and full GSM8K confirmation, including per-case and token-limit comparisons.
