Local validation on MLU hardware:

- `pr-test-1-mlu`: all 7 RMSNorm tests passed, covering native-reference comparisons, residual fusion, empty and non-contiguous inputs, mixed-dtype fallback, and shape preservation for 1D, higher-rank, and transposed inputs across FP32, FP16, and BF16.

## Motivation

NPU decode and target-verify graph replay require host-side sequence lengths
to update graph inputs. Reading these lengths through
`forward_batch.seq_lens.cpu()` introduces a blocking device-to-host copy,
even when the batch already provides a CPU mirror.

Reuse the existing CPU mirror to avoid this redundant synchronization and
reduce host-side stalls during graph replay preparation.

## Modifications

- Prefer `forward_batch.seq_lens_cpu` when preparing sequence lengths for
  NPU decode and target-verify graph replay.
- Slice the CPU mirror to the active batch size before adding graph padding.
- Preserve the captured verify-width adjustment for target verification.
- Preserve the existing DFlash metadata path.
- Retain the device-to-host fallback when `seq_lens_cpu` is unavailable.

## Accuracy Tests

Accuracy evaluation of the final graph-runner-only patch is pending.

Previous accuracy runs included an additional FutureMap change that has
since been reverted, so those results do not validate the final patch.

Completed static checks:

- Python syntax validation.
- `git diff --check`.
- AST comparison confirming that the subsequent comment cleanup did not
  change executable code.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Benchmarking and profiling of the final graph-runner-only patch are pending.

The previous combined-patch performance results are excluded because they
do not isolate the benefit of the retained change.

Planned validation:

- Compare the parent commit against this patch under identical model,
  workload, and server settings.
- Measure TPOT and output token throughput.
- Inspect NPU traces for host-side D2H synchronization and device idle gaps
  around graph replay preparation.

## Checklist

- [ ] Run repository formatting and pre-commit checks.
- [ ] Add or run relevant regression tests.
- [ ] Confirm whether documentation updates are required.
- [ ] Provide accuracy results for the final patch.
- [ ] Provide speed benchmark and profiling results for the final patch.
- [ ] Verify compliance with the SGLang code style guidance.

title: [Fix] Minimax-M3: Deterministic tie-breaking in the CUDA radix decode top-k
author: Godmook
body:
>pr description is generated by AI tool

## Motivation

`minimax_decode_topk` has three selection regimes. Two of them already break exact score ties by block id (the lower id wins):

- the small path (`num_blocks <= 128`): `is_greater(...)`, "lower block id wins"
- the ROCm path: a packed `(score, ~id)` total order

The CUDA radix paths (`num_blocks > 128`, i.e. contexts above 16k tokens at block size 128) place the final-round ties in `atomicAdd` order instead. When tied blocks straddle the top-k boundary, the selected set changes from run to run. ROCm indexer CP already depends on a fixed tie order ("requires ... the ROCm radix top-k tie ordering"); the CUDA paths gave no such guarantee.

Exact ties are common for indexers whose keys carry no RoPE: the block score is the max over units, so repeated text produces equal scores. On such a model, serving the same prompts twice from a cold cache with the radix cache on gave 43/45 identical greedy outputs; with this change, 45/45.

## Modifications

- Final radix round: rank the tied candidates by block id (warp ballot + prefix sum) and keep the lowest ids, matching the small and ROCm paths. Applied to both the single-element path and the multi-element (register bucket) path.
- Fast path: when every tie is selected (`equal_count <= topk_remain`), the order does not matter (the output is sorted ascending), so the ties are written with a plain atomic as before and the ranking is skipped.
- Removes the now unused `counter_final`.
- Adds `test_decode_topk_ties_pick_lowest_ids`, which checks the selected set against `(score desc, id asc)` for 300 to 9,000 blocks with heavy ties.

ROCm is unchanged.

## Accuracy Tests

MiniMax-M3 (bf16, TP8, H200, radix cache on), main vs this PR:

- Greedy outputs on 40 MMLU-Pro prompts plus needle-in-text prompts up to 60k tokens (radix path): 45/45 identical.
- GPQA-Diamond (n=1, max_tokens 32k): 89.4 (main) vs 90.4 (this PR). (range in noise)

## Speed Tests and Profiling

MiniMax-M3, TP8, H200, one request at a time, radix cache flushed before each request:

| input tokens | prefill TTFT, main / PR | decode TPOT, main / PR |
|---|---|---|
| 4k | 0.395 / 0.396 s | 13.42 / 13.11 ms |
| 16k | 1.496 / 1.499 s | 13.62 / 13.26 ms |
| 32k | 3.042 / 3.051 s | 13.68 / 13.46 ms |
| 48k | 4.639 / 4.643 s | 13.76 / 13.54 ms |
| 60k | 5.936 / 5.951 s | 13.81 / 13.59 ms |

Kernel microbenchmark (2 heads, 8 to 64 rows, 2k to 8k blocks): within ±0.2 us of main for distinct scores; equal or faster with ties.

title: [Perf] diffusion/minimax-h3: Batch the video VAE decoder tiles and fuse the output chain
author: triple-mu
body:
## Motivation

MiniMax-H3's video VAE decodes a request as overlapping spatial tiles over temporal windows and blends them back together. On `main`, base H3 runs one tile per ViT decoder forward at every quality level (only FastH3 stacked its tiles, through `stack_tiling`), and the output chain after the decoder (tile blend + crop + place, temporal window blend into the destination frames, RGB de-normalization + clamp) is a sequence of FP32 aten ops, each a full pass over the frames. On 4x RTX PRO 5000 the decode stage is 3.26 s of a 30 s five-step 768p t2va request.

This PR:

- decodes up to 64 equal-shaped tiles per decoder forward under `quality="lossless"` (the default) and `"high"` on CUDA. Batching changes the GEMM shapes and therefore the output at rounding level, so it belongs to the lossless tier like the existing fused QK RMSNorm+RoPE;
- replaces the temporal blend write and the de-normalization with JIT kernels that reproduce the eager arithmetic bit-exactly and verify that on first use, so they are not tied to a quality level and run at every level, `exact` included. The tile blend + crop + place stays eager: a kernel for it needs the tiles as one tensor, which neither the one-tile-per-forward decode nor the parallel-tiled decode (whose all-gather hands back rank-interleaved views) provides without a copy, and it is worth under 1 ms per request where it would apply.

## Modifications

Decoder batching (`minimax_h3_video_vae/klvae.py`, `batching.py`, `configs/models/vaes/minimax_h3_video.py`, `configs/pipeline_configs/minimax_h3.py`):

- `MiniMaxH3VideoVAEConfig.decoder_tile_batch` (tiles per decoder forward, default 64, 0 = all of a rank's tiles) and `window_batch` (temporal windows per forward, default 1) replace `stack_tiling`. `_run_tile_tasks` has one path through `batching.forward_many`; width 1 is the released recipe, so `exact` decodes exactly as before. The caps apply only while the VAE's `VaeFastPathGate` is enabled, through the decode stage's existing `use_vae_fast_path(vae, quality_allows(quality, "lossless"))`. No new flag or environment variable.
- `MiniMaxH3VideoVAE` creates the gate; the CUDA installer `maybe_optimize_minimax_h3_vae` registers it, hangs the fused QK RMSNorm+RoPE / cuDNN SDPA attention on it and logs the caps once. Other platforms keep one tile per forward, as on `main`.
- FastH3 sets `decoder_tile_batch = 0`, its previous all-tiles recipe, under `lossless`; its `exact` level now decodes tile by tile like base H3. `--performance-mode memory` resets both caps to 1 at every level. `window_batch` stays at 1: pooling every window into one forward measured 8% slower with a 70.2 GB peak (+10 GB) on the PCIe SM120 box (previous revision of this branch).

Output kernels (`kernels/jit/csrc/diffusion/minimax_h3_vae_output.cuh`, `kernels/ops/diffusion/layout/minimax_h3_vae_output_jit.py`, SM100+):

- `minimax_h3_vae_temporal_blend_write` (temporal ramp blend written straight into the destination frames) and `minimax_h3_vae_denorm_clamp` (RGB de-normalization + clamp, with an in-place mode `out=value` for the frames the decode stage owns, so no second copy of the video is kept). Every step spells the aten arithmetic with explicit round-to-nearest intrinsics (one rounding per op, ramp weights as `k * rcp(n)`), so `torch.equal` holds against the eager chain on both the strided and the 128-bit path.
- Each site sits behind a module-level `BitExactFusionGate`: on first use it compares against the eager result, and a mismatch drops the kernel for the process. The blend site verifies per signature (with and without a previous window, so a plain copy cannot vouch for the blend arithmetic); the de-normalization verifies one probe frame. `is_cuda_sm_at_least` in `kernels/ops/diffusion/common/platform.py` keeps ROCm's gfx-derived capability out of the SM check.

Docs: cookbook quality-level descriptions, FastH3 paragraph and deployment-details bullet; `fused_kernels.mdx`; kernels README; `existing-fast-paths.md`; performance skill.

Tests:

- `multimodal_gen/test/unit/test_minimax_h3_vae_fast_path.py` (CPU, 25 cases): batch partitioning and window iteration, the caps reach the VAE only while the gate is on, the real installer shares one gate between attention and batching, batched decode matches tile-by-tile decode with the expected batch widths, first-use verification and fallback of each output site, in-place de-normalization only on owned frames. `test_server_args.py`: memory mode keeps one tile per forward for H3 and FastH3.
- `test/registered/kernels/ops/diffusion/test_minimax_h3_vae_output.py`: `torch.equal` against the eager chain over blend extents (ramp, strided, zero-count), the in-place mode, alias and input rejections; the temporal blend site bit-exact and verified per signature; batched decode within 1e-3 of tile-by-tile with the expected batch widths on any CUDA GPU; `revert_tensor` bit-exact, in place only on owned frames. The tiny H3 VAE fixture is shared with the CPU unit tests through `sglang.test.kernels.minimax_h3_vae`.

## Accuracy Tests

4x RTX PRO 5000 72 GB (SM120), cookbook TP2 + Ulysses2 recipe, t2va 768p 16:9 5 s, 5 steps, seed 1101. The reference is `main` (62cee1b15c, the rebase base) at the same quality level, so the DiT trajectory is identical and only the VAE differs. At 1344x768 the decoder splits each frame into a 4x7 = 28-tile grid over the 4 decode ranks, so under `lossless` each rank decodes its 7 tiles in one forward per temporal window. Frame PSNR / SSIM by ffmpeg on the decoded frames; audio compared as a hash of the decoded stream.

| Request | vs `main` at the same level | Audio |
|---|---|---|
| `exact` | bit-identical frames, 3 runs (both output kernels in the loop) | identical |
| `lossless`, 7 tiles per forward per rank | worst frame 52.1 dB, mean 52.6 dB, SSIM min 0.995 | identical |

The lossless difference is the batching alone: on the previous revision of this branch (whose lossless decode is bit-identical to this head on t2va), one tile per forward with the output kernels kept gave frames and audio bit-identical to `main`'s lossless. No run on this head logged a first-use fallback. The branch was first measured against 57db5089c2 and re-measured after the rebase: `main`'s `lossless` decode and this PR's `lossless` output are bit-identical across the two bases, while `main`'s `exact` decode changed in #44690 (it dropped the Triton QK RMSNorm+RoPE the ViT attention ran at every level), and this PR's `exact` follows it bit for bit on both. On fl2va (first-frame conditioning) the previous revision measured a worst frame of 44.2 dB, mean 45.2 dB, SSIM min 0.986 and identical audio against `main` lossless; that clip differs more for the VAE on its own.

Tests on SM120: `test_minimax_h3_vae_output.py` + `test_model_fast_paths.py -k "minimax_h3 or h3_vae"`, 21 passed. The MiniMax-H3 and VAE unit files pass on CPU (379 cases; the four `test_fasth3_selects_vsa_h3_for_the_transformer` subtests fail on `main` as well on this host).

Tests on B200 (SM100, torch 2.14.1+cu130) after the rebase onto `main` 2da6c0c237: `test_minimax_h3_vae_output.py` + `test_model_fast_paths.py`, 112 passed, 21 skipped, 1 failed. The failure, `test_model_fast_paths.py::test_ernie_qknorm_rope_is_bit_exact`, fails the same way on `main` 2da6c0c237 and on the PR base 62cee1b15c in that environment (the ERNIE gate logs a mismatch against the platform's reference dispatch and falls back); `main` never runs this file on B200, and this PR no longer registers it there. CPU: `test_minimax_h3_vae_fast_path.py`, `test_minimax_h3_admission.py`, `test_minimax_h3_vdn.py` and `test_server_args.py`, 298 passed; the one failure is a `main` MOVA case that needs Hub access.

CI exposure: the H100 cases that keep goldens pin `quality="exact"` in memory mode, where the decode is unchanged; the 4-GPU H100 cases run at the default level without a golden. `minimax_h3_t2va_consumer_budget_1gpu_5090` (SM120, memory mode, pinned `exact`) is the one golden case that exercises the temporal blend and de-normalization kernels; their first-use check adds a one-window reference and a one-frame probe inside its 12 GiB cap. The kernel tests live in `test_minimax_h3_vae_output.py`, registered on the `4-gpu-b200` kernel-unit lane (the batching test also runs on the `1-gpu-large` lane, and the file is in the AMD nightly kernel suite for the ROCm fallback); `test_model_fast_paths.py` keeps its H100 registration only. This PR's CI is the kernels' first run on SM100; a first-use mismatch there would drop a kernel for the process rather than change output.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

4x RTX PRO 5000 72 GB (SM120, PCIe), torch 2.14.1+cu130, CUDA 13.0, sgl-kernel 0.4.9, flashinfer 0.7.1, driver 580.178.04; base `main` 62cee1b15c. `sglang generate` with `--tp-size 2 --ulysses-degree 2 --encoder-parallel auto --performance-mode speed`, t2va 768p 16:9 5 s, 5 steps (the VAE time does not depend on the step count), one timed request per fresh process after two warmup steps, configurations interleaved in blocks, `SGLANG_DIFFUSION_SYNC_STAGE_PROFILING=1`. Decode = `MiniMaxH3DecodingStage` duration from `perf_dump.json`; peak = runtime peak reserved.

| | decode ms, median (min–max) | vs `main` same level | peak reserved |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `main`, `exact` | 3404 (3402–3406), n=3 | | 58120 MB |
| this PR, `exact` | 3400 (3391–3409), n=3 | within noise | 58120 MB |
| `main`, `lossless` | 3258 (3252–3264), n=2 | | 58120 MB |
| this PR, `lossless` | 3158 (3147–3162), n=3 | −3.1% | 58120 MB |

On the previous revision of this branch (on 57db5089c2, where `main`'s `lossless` decode measured 3262 (3258–3264), n=7), the output kernels alone (one tile per forward; that revision still fused the tile assembly as well) saved 11 ms (0.3%; 3251 vs 3262 ms, n=2); the rest is the tile batching. The fl2va request showed a similar −3.4% there. End to end, the five-step request stays at 30.2 s; the decode is a tenth of it.

Kernel microbenchmarks (one SM120 GPU, 448x448 frames; measured with a local script that is not part of this PR):

| op | frames | eager µs | JIT µs |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| temporal_blend_write | 17 | 129.8 | 81.2 |
| temporal_blend_write | 33 | 293.4 | 150.9 |
| denorm_clamp | 17 | 80.5 | 37.1 |
| denorm_clamp | 33 | 299.1 | 140.8 |

Not measured on H100/H200 (where only the batching applies) or on SM100/SM103. No benchmark script ships with this PR.

- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).

title: [Perf] [AMD] Kimi-K3: prepare the attention interface for mono fusion
author: billishyahao
body: This PR co-work with mono patch: https://github.com/sgl-project/sgl-amd-mono/pull/13 ## Motivation The AMD monokernel backend runs a Kimi-K3 decode or DSpark verify step as two persistent launches a layer. They run in this order. - **K1, the KDA front launch**, covers the attention side of a KDA layer: the attention-side residual seam, `input_layernorm`, the in-projection, `f_b`, the conv, the recurrence and the gated output norm. It covers the 69 KDA layers. The 24 full-attention layers keep stock SGLang's attention instead. - **K2, the layer launch**, takes the TP-local attention output from there and runs o_proj, the attention-TP all-reduce, the MLP attention-residual seam and the MoE. It covers all 92 MoE layers, whichever attention produced its input. That backend is sgl-project/sgl-amd-mono. It loads through the `sglang.srt.plugins` entry point and is selected with `--monokernel-backend amd`. SGLang needs nothing else for it: `install_monokernel_forward` swaps the whole model forward (`srt/monokernels/runtime.py`), so the kernels, the spec and its registration all live in the plugin. This method is the one thing the plugin cannot reach from outside, which is why it is the only change here. In short, this change follows the sgl mono kernel RFC https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/43949 ## Modifications **1. The KDA in-projection gate**, which K1 reads. Take the merge when `do_fuse_qkvbfg` allows it, as before, or when a monokernel backend is selected: ```python if not self.use_full_rank_gate: return False if not (self.do_fuse_qkvbfg or get_exec().kernel.monokernel_backend): return False ``` With no backend selected this reduces to `use_full_rank_gate and do_fuse_qkvbfg`, which is what the predicate tested before. That identity is deliberate. The fused GEMM is a different kernel from the split pair. A wider gate on its own would move decode output by one bf16 rounding step for every ROCm Kimi-K3 user. The file's own docstring records that the two paths agree to bf16 rounding and not bitwise. The weight checks below the gate do not change, and they still decide. The backend changes the policy. It does not remove the safety checks. `_is_unquantized_mergeable` requires the three weights to share one dtype, and that dtype to be bf16 or fp16. A per-channel FP8 weight or a packed MXFP4 weight still refuses, because `_merge_weights_as_views` concatenates `.weight` alone. Nothing else changes. `do_fuse_qkvbfg` also gates a weight-loader branch and the low-rank gate's projection layout. This commit touches neither. **2. `forward_pre_o_proj()` on `KimiK3DeltaAttention` and `KimiK3MLAAttention`**, where K2 starts. It returns the TP-local attention output after the output gate and before o_proj. The caller owns o_proj and the attention-TP reduction that o_proj carries, so `o_proj(forward_pre_o_proj(x)) == forward(x)`. - `KimiK3DeltaAttention`: a plain extract. `forward()` now calls the new method and keeps the o_proj tail. The moved body does not change. - `KimiK3MLAAttention`: the MLA cores reach o_proj from several places. The split therefore uses the instance-level wrapper that already applies the output gate. `forward_pre_o_proj()` sets `_return_pre_o_proj`, runs `forward()`, and takes the tensor that the wrapper puts in `_pre_o_proj_out` instead of running o_proj. Four guards hold the MLA path together. It has no in-tree caller to exercise it, and a fault on it gives wrong numbers rather than an error. - `use_output_gate` must be on. Without it the wrapper does not exist. - The method is not re-entrant. A second entry while the flag is set raises. - `_pre_o_proj_out` holds one tensor. If o_proj is reached twice in one attention forward, the second call raises instead of overwriting the first. The message names the layer. - A quantized o_proj input raises. On ROCm the MLA core quantizes what it hands to o_proj when o_proj's weights are MXFP4 or block-scale fp8 (`forward_mla_rocm.py:325,351`). The output gate is skipped with it, so there is no gated bf16 tensor to hand back. Every rank quantizes alike, so this raises on all of them. It does not split the TP group. The standard path remains no change. `forward()` produces what it produced before if no mono kernel server args are specified. ## Accuracy Tests 8 x MI355X, TP8 / DCP1, FP8 KV cache, DSpark block size 7. `/data-models/Kimi-K3`, GSM8K 200 questions, `--parallel 2`: | | Accuracy | |---|---:| | This branch, no monokernel backend | 0.990 | | This branch, `--monokernel-backend amd` | 0.985 | ## Speed Tests and Profiling `--monokernel-backend amd` against the standard path, both launches on. Two server instances an arm, four probe runs each, the first run of each server dropped. Decode steps/s rather than tok/s, because the speculative accept length swamps tok/s on this recipe. | | decode steps/s | sd | range | |---|---:|---:|---| | Monokernels off | 41.63 | 0.62 | 40.28 - 42.10 | | Monokernels on | **55.26 (+32.8%)** | 0.38 | 54.72 - 55.94 | The ranges do not overlap. The win is on 8-row verify steps; wider steps and all prefill take the standard path. #### Fixed-length decode latency at long context The table above is short prompts at the draft's real acceptance. This one is the interactive shape the backend is for: a cached long prefix, a small new turn, and a short answer. It also reports the inter-token latency the backend moves, rather than a step rate that a reader has to convert. | ISL | ITL P50 off | ITL P50 on | Δ | ITL P90 off | ITL P90 on | Δ | steps/s off | steps/s on | Δ | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 64k | 6.17 ms | **4.62 ms** | **−25.2%** | 8.11 ms | **6.17 ms** | **−24.0%** | 40.4 | **52.7** | +30.5% | | 128k | 6.67 ms | **5.29 ms** | **−20.6%** | 8.56 ms | **6.88 ms** | **−19.7%** | 37.3 | **47.1** | +26.3% | | 256k | 7.70 ms | **6.19 ms** | **−19.6%** | 9.86 ms | **8.10 ms** | **−17.9%** | 32.2 | **40.3** | +24.9% | `off` / `on` is `--monokernel-backend amd`. Lower ITL is better, so Δ is the reduction; as a speedup the same numbers are +33.7% / +25.9% / +24.3% at P50. **P90 moves with P50** (−24.0% against −25.2% at 64k) and the P90/P50 ratio is unchanged (1.31 off, 1.33 on). The launch shifts the whole distribution rather than clipping a tail. The three columns agree because acceptance is pinned: `ITL ~= 1000 / (steps/s * accept)`. **The gain falls as ISL grows** (−25.2% to −19.6%). Attention over a longer KV takes a larger share of the step, and that part is outside the launch. **TTFT is unchanged** -- 0.24/0.25 s, 0.30/0.29 s and 0.41/0.41 s at 64k/128k/256k. The launch covers decode only. #### End-to-end agentic replay The two tables above are synthetic prompts at a pinned acceptance. This one is a full AgentX agentic-coding replay, one hour per arm. It therefore carries real session content, real prefix-cache behaviour and the batching of the scheduler itself. | conc 1, 8 rows a step | off | `--monokernel-backend amd` | Δ | |---|---:|---:|---:| | **TPOT mean** | 6.28 ms | **4.94 ms** | **−21.3%** | | TPOT P50 | 6.23 ms | **4.91 ms** | −21.2% | | TPOT P75 | 6.60 ms | **5.26 ms** | −20.3% | | **TPOT P90** | 6.74 ms | **5.37 ms** | **−20.3%** | | TPOT P95 | 6.77 ms | **5.43 ms** | −19.8% | | interactivity P50 | 160.4 tok/s | **203.7 tok/s** | +27.0% | | interactivity P90 | 148.5 tok/s | **186.1 tok/s** | +25.3% | | TTFT mean | 2.70 s | **2.10 s** | −22.4% | | e2e P90 | 37.3 s | **30.0 s** | −19.5% | | output | 97.5 tok/s | **112.0 tok/s** | +14.9% | | requests completed | 205 | **222** | +8.3% | **Every percentile moves by the same amount**, −19.8% to −21.3%, as in the fixed-length table. Throughput rises less than latency falls, +14.9% against −21.3%. AgentX replays a closed loop, so a faster answer shortens only the part of each session's cycle that the engine owns. **The number of steps the backend can take bounds the gain.** An earlier pair of the same runs admitted two requests instead of one. That pair held the SSM state in bf16, so read its percentages against its own baseline and not against the table above. There 6 to 7% of decode windows held two running requests. That is 2 x 8 = 16 rows, which is outside the spec, and the result split: P50 −16.5%, but **P90 −2.6%** and P95 −2.1%, with the mean diluted to −9.4%. The server log shows it directly when read by `#running-req`: the one-request steps ran 9.8% faster and the two-request steps 2.2%. Admitting one request removes the steps that are not covered, and the whole distribution then moves together. title: [Fix] mamba: Skip zero-width conv pools in the MTP verify scatter
author: mmangkad
body:
## Summary

Fixes the nightly `test_ling_2_6_flash.py` crash on the first MTP verify step:

```
ValueError: fused_conv_window_scatter_with_mask: dst entry dims (dims 2..3) must be contiguous; got shape=(28, 257, 0, 0) strides=(257, 1, 1, 1)
```

Lightning linear-attention layers (Ling-2.5/2.6, MiniCPM lightning hybrids) have no conv state, so their conv pool is zero-width. `dst.is_contiguous()` accepted it, but #44971's explicit stride check rejects it. The pool then falls back to the per-pair scatter, which raises.

- `scatter_mamba_states_after_mtp_verify` skips empty conv pairs, like the existing SSM guard, so mixed sets keep the single-launch path.
- `fused_conv_window_scatter_with_mask` returns early on an empty `dst`, as a safety net.

New `TestScatterAfterVerifyZeroWidthConv` and `test_ling_2_6_flash.py` both fail before the fix and pass after.

title: [Perf] mamba: Copy tracked decode states at HBM bandwidth in one persistent launch
author: metamergebot
body:
## Motivation

`track_mamba_state_if_needed_kernel` copies a request's conv and ssm state rows from `cache_indices[i]` to `mamba_track_indices[i]` whenever `mamba_track_mask[i]` is set, so the state can be reused across turns. It launched one program per batch row, so a single SM copied one whole state row for one layer: the copy's parallelism was bounded by the number of tracked rows rather than by the amount of data, and a backend that calls the copy once per layer serialized that work once per layer. The copy is pure bandwidth, so it should run on every SM.

## Modifications

- `track_mamba_state_if_needed_kernel` is now persistent. Every program reads the whole track mask, the tracked rows are compacted in-kernel (`cumsum` over the mask), and their (row, layer, 32 KB chunk) work items are strided over a grid of four programs per SM. A step with no tracked row reads one mask vector per program and exits; one tracked row runs at HBM bandwidth on every SM. `batch_size` and `num_layers` are `do_not_specialize`, so the graph-captured launch does not recompile per batch size.
- `track_mamba_states_if_needed` and `track_mamba_states_all_layers` keep their signatures and share one launcher, `_launch_track_mamba_states`; the separate `track_mamba_states_all_layers_kernel` is removed. The per-layer wrapper passes a zero layer stride and `num_layers=1`.
- The copy is bitwise identical to the old kernel, including the freed-slot (`-1`) skip for the unified pool and the int64 index promotion before the row-stride multiply. It stays CUDA-graph safe: the grid depends only on the padded batch size, the layer count and the pool shapes, and the mask is read on the device at replay.
- New `test/registered/unit/layers/test_mamba_track_states_triton.py` (base-b, 1-gpu-small, ~20 s) checks both wrappers against a torch reference over padded batches 1..40, mixed conv/ssm dtypes, freed slots, partial chunks with the persistent loop forced onto one SM, every row tracked, and CUDA-graph replay with a changing mask.

Tests:
- `python -m pytest test/registered/unit/layers/test_mamba_track_states_triton.py`: 6 passed on one B300-class GPU against this branch.
- `pre-commit` on the two changed files is clean (isort, ruff, ruff-format, codespell, registered-test checks).

## Accuracy Tests

Not applicable: the copy is bitwise identical to the old kernel. The new unit test asserts `torch.equal` against a torch reference for both wrappers, and a direct old-vs-new comparison on the benchmark shape below was bitwise equal.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Measured for this PR with the script below, which runs the kernel file from `main` (saved as `old_mamba_state_scatter_triton.py` next to the script) against this branch under CUDA-graph replay on one B300-class GPU. Shapes: 36 linear-attention layers, padded batch 40, conv state `(8192, 3)` and ssm state `(32, 128, 128)` in bf16 (about 1 MB per row per layer). "per-layer x36" is `track_mamba_states_if_needed` called once per layer; "all-layers" is one `track_mamba_states_all_layers` launch.

| tracked rows | old per-layer x36 | old all-layers | new per-layer x36 | new all-layers |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 43 us | 4.2 us | 55 us | 4.2 us |
| 1 | 6621 us | 239 us | 129 us | 12.8 us |
| 4 | 8587 us | 269 us | 158 us | 55 us |
| 40 | 8910 us | 527 us | 592 us | 493 us |

With no tracked row the persistent kernel reads one mask vector per program, so a per-layer call site pays about 0.3 us more per launch than before; every case with a tracked row is faster, most of all the one-row benchmark case, where the old kernel's single program per row left the rest of the GPU idle.

<details>
<summary>Benchmark script</summary>

```python
import sys, torch
sys.path.insert(0, ".")
import old_mamba_state_scatter_triton as old  # python/sglang/kernels/ops/mamba/mamba_state_scatter_triton.py from main
from sglang.kernels.ops.mamba import mamba_state_scatter_triton as new

NUM_LAYERS, POOL, BS = 36, 128, 40
CONV_SHAPE, SSM_SHAPE = (8192, 3), (32, 128, 128)
dev = "cuda"
conv = torch.randn((NUM_LAYERS, POOL) + CONV_SHAPE, device=dev).to(torch.bfloat16)
ssm = torch.randn((NUM_LAYERS, POOL) + SSM_SHAPE, device=dev).to(torch.bfloat16)
cache_indices = torch.arange(BS, device=dev)
track_indices = torch.arange(BS, 2 * BS, device=dev)
mask = torch.zeros(BS, dtype=torch.bool, device=dev)

def per_layer(mod):
    for l in range(NUM_LAYERS):
        mod.track_mamba_states_if_needed(conv[l], ssm[l], cache_indices, mask, track_indices, BS)

def all_layers(mod):
    mod.track_mamba_states_all_layers(conv, ssm, cache_indices, mask, track_indices, BS)

def graph_time(fn, iters=50):
    s = torch.cuda.Stream(); s.wait_stream(torch.cuda.current_stream())
    with torch.cuda.stream(s):
        fn(); fn()
    torch.cuda.current_stream().wait_stream(s)
    g = torch.cuda.CUDAGraph()
    with torch.cuda.graph(g):
        fn()
    g.replay(); torch.cuda.synchronize()
    st, en = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True), torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
    st.record()
    for _ in range(iters):
        g.replay()
    en.record(); torch.cuda.synchronize()
    return st.elapsed_time(en) / iters * 1000  # us

mask.copy_(torch.rand(BS, device=dev) < 0.5)
conv_a, ssm_a = conv.clone(), ssm.clone()
old.track_mamba_states_all_layers(conv_a, ssm_a, cache_indices, mask, track_indices, BS)
conv_b, ssm_b = conv.clone(), ssm.clone()
new.track_mamba_states_all_layers(conv_b, ssm_b, cache_indices, mask, track_indices, BS)
assert torch.equal(conv_a, conv_b) and torch.equal(ssm_a, ssm_b)
del conv_a, ssm_a, conv_b, ssm_b
print("bitwise equal old vs new: ok")
for n in (0, 1, 4, 40):
    mask.zero_(); mask[:n] = True
    print(n, [round(graph_time(f), 1) for f in (
        lambda: per_layer(old), lambda: all_layers(old),
        lambda: per_layer(new), lambda: all_layers(new))])
```

</details>

- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).
- [ ] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations).

title: [Perf] qknorm: run head_dim-128 rows two per warp with 16B lanes, bit-identical
author: Monishver11
body:
## Motivation

In short: `fused_qknorm_warp` is the default QK-norm for Qwen3 dense and Qwen3-MoE on CUDA. At head_dim 128 it gives each warp one (token, head) row, so a lane moves only 8 B per row. This PR runs two rows per warp with 16 B lanes, the same scheme mickqian merged for the diffusion QK-norm + RoPE kernel. The output is bit-identical. On an H100 NVL the kernel is 1.09-1.45x faster from 32 tokens up, and 1.29x inside a Qwen3-8B prefill trace; serving throughput is flat because the kernel is under 1% of GPU time.

Details:

`fused_qknorm_warp` (`python/sglang/kernels/jit/csrc/elementwise/qknorm.cuh`) runs through `apply_qk_norm` in `python/sglang/srt/models/utils.py`. Per row it does a load, a 5-step xor reduce, an rsqrt and a store, then moves to the next row. With 8 B per lane that is at most 64 warps x 32 lanes x 8 B = 16 KB in flight per SM, and out of L2 the kernel reaches 2.8-2.9 TB/s on an H100 NVL.

## Modifications

In short: a new `fused_qknorm_half_warp` kernel for head_dim 128, picked at compile time. Each row gets 16 lanes and each lane moves 16 B. Every other head_dim, the CTA path and ROCm keep their current kernels.

How it stays bit-identical: each lane covers two lanes of the warp kernel. It keeps their two partial sums, accumulated in the same order, and replays that kernel's xor butterfly with `warp::reduce_sum<16>` (the same `Trait::reduce` as before). Offsets 16..2 become 8..1 on each partial, and the final xor-1 step becomes `part0 + part1`. The rsqrt and the per-element output are the same expressions.

Changes:

- `fused_qknorm_half_warp`: two rows per warp; a missing second row recomputes the last one and skips its store.
- The new kernel needs 16 B alignment where the warp kernel needed 8 B. If a q/k or weight pointer, or a q/k row stride, is not 16 B aligned, the launcher keeps the one-row-per-warp kernel, so every input that ran before still runs.
- `_jit_qknorm_module(half_warp=False)` builds the one-row-per-warp kernel, for the new test.
- New test `test_two_rows_per_warp_match_one_row_per_warp`: byte-compares the two kernels with q and k sliced from one qkv row as Qwen3 passes them, BF16 and FP16, 5 q heads so a q/k boundary falls inside a row pair, an odd row count, 4099 tokens so the persistent grid loops, and rows padded by 8 B so odd-token rows are only 8 B aligned and the launcher falls back.

Same scheme as [#43337](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/43337) and [#43508](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/43508), which changed only the diffusion `qknorm_rope.cuh`.

Not a duplicate: no PR runs `fused_qknorm_warp` two rows per warp. The open [#43425](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/43425) refactors `fused_qknorm_warp` into a per-row helper with an epilogue hook for Qwen3-VL MRoPE fusion on Blackwell; it keeps the 8 B lane layout, but the two PRs will conflict in `qknorm.cuh`, so whichever lands second needs a rebase. [#39071](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39071) and [#40585](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40585) touch this file only for ROCm `#include` lines.

## Accuracy Tests

The output is bit-identical to main, so model accuracy can't change. I checked it at the kernel level:

- Bitwise vs main 97d3150a6a, CPU-seeded inputs, whole qkv buffer compared: 384 cases, each run with both branch kernels, **768 of 768 identical**. The two-rows kernel runs in 192 of them (head_dim 128: Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, TP2 and ragged head counts, 1 to 16384 tokens, qkv-slice and contiguous layouts, BF16 and FP16, with and without PDL). The rest cover the 8 B-aligned fallback and head_dim 64 and 256, which are unchanged.
- `test_qknorm.py` and `test_rope.py`: 1827 passed. `test_rope.py` uses `fused_inplace_qknorm` as its `torch.equal` reference.
- Registers: 28 -> 40 per thread, 0 spills.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

H100 NVL (PCIe, 400 W), driver 595.91, CUDA 13.0, torch 2.14.1+cu130. Validated on main 97d3150a6a; the branch is rebased onto 5ed306bd69, and upstream only removed unused helpers from `norm.py` and `test_qknorm.py` in between. `triton.testing.do_bench_cudagraph`, median of 5 rounds that interleave the two kernels in one process. q and k are slices of one qkv row (Qwen3 layout), BF16, in place.

| tokens | Qwen3-8B (32 + 8 heads) | Qwen3-30B-A3B (32 + 4 heads) |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | 1.03 -> 1.06 us (0.97x) | 1.16 -> 1.22 us (0.95x) |
| 8 | 1.39 -> 1.32 us (1.05x) | 1.45 -> 1.53 us (0.95x) |
| 32 | 1.65 -> 1.48 us (1.12x) | 1.76 -> 1.69 us (1.04x) |
| 128 | 3.11 -> 2.26 us (1.38x) | 3.04 -> 2.38 us (1.28x) |
| 256 | 4.31 -> 3.19 us (1.35x) | 4.38 -> 3.02 us (1.45x) |
| 1024 | 6.31 -> 5.32 us (1.19x) | 6.11 -> 4.98 us (1.23x) |
| 2048 | 11.13 -> 8.39 us (1.33x) | 10.33 -> 7.84 us (1.32x) |
| 4096 | 25.96 -> 22.18 us (1.17x) | 22.13 -> 17.86 us (1.24x) |
| 8192 | 58.65 -> 53.83 us (1.09x) | 53.20 -> 48.59 us (1.09x) |
| 16384 | 116.16 -> 105.23 us (1.10x) | 104.23 -> 94.73 us (1.10x) |
| 65536 | 459.86 -> 414.60 us (1.11x) | 417.29 -> 374.92 us (1.11x) |

Over BF16 and FP16, both models and 1-65536 tokens: geomean 1.14x up to 256 tokens (0.95-1.45x) and 1.17x from 512 tokens (1.09-1.36x). From 8192 tokens q and k no longer fit in L2, and the kernel goes from 2.8-2.9 TB/s to 3.1-3.3 TB/s. At 1-8 tokens the difference is 0.03-0.08 us, the same spread as two runs of the same kernel.

In a model: torch profiler, Qwen3-8B TP1, 32 requests of 4096 input tokens. The QK-norm kernel goes from 43.82 to 34.09 ms over 720 launches (1.29x), from 0.94% to 0.73% of GPU time. `sglang.benchmark.serving` on the same model, 3 interleaved rounds, is flat: random 4096/1 input throughput 26597 -> 26567 tok/s (-0.11%) and random 1024/128 19.94 -> 19.93 req/s (-0.07%), while main alone moves 0.6-0.7% between rounds.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).
- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).

- [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed). (bitwise, microbench, profile and serving)
- [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance).

title: [Perf] mlp: Fuse dense SwiGLU with block-FP8 quantization on decode
author: JiaFengYu
body:
## Motivation

Dense block-FP8 MLPs normally launch SwiGLU to materialize a BF16 activation, then launch activation quantization before the down-projection GEMM. This PR fuses those two operations for eligible decode calls, removing one launch and the intermediate BF16 write/read per MLP.

The latest controlled comparison measured **1.92% lower single-request decode TPOT** on Qwen3-8B-FP8 on a B200. This is activation/MLP fusion, independent of KV-cache dtype. Concurrent decode and the full-patch prefill non-regression claim have the limitations documented below; this is not an unconditional performance clearance.

## Modifications

- Extend the existing JIT `per_token_group_quant` kernel with an explicit dense SwiGLU mode. Match the dense CUDA activation's compiler math and round the product to source precision before quantization, without materializing it in HBM. Reuse the existing quantizer and UE8M0 packing machinery; the default/legacy mode is unchanged.
- Allow the DeepGEMM block-FP8 wrapper to consume validated prequantized FP8 activations and column-major packed UE8M0 scales. Reject incompatible packed layouts instead of passing them to a fallback that cannot consume them.
- Add a shared `DenseSiluAndMulQuant` helper and small Llama/Qwen2 MLP integrations; Qwen3 uses the Qwen2 implementation. The runtime fast path is limited to SM100-family CUDA, TP1, ordinary decode, BF16 activations, and dynamic block-128 FP8 with DeepGEMM/UE8M0.
- Call the helper only for decode. Prefill/extend, speculative verification, other non-decode modes, and calls without a forward batch invoke the original activation directly. Keep the helper's own eligibility checks and preserve fallbacks for unsupported layouts/dtypes/backends, LoRA, deterministic execution, compilation, and overrides. Preserve DualGemm unchanged. The model-level phase check remains; this is not a claim of literally zero host overhead.
- Use the current fused-op `_resolve_forward_method()` API when the activation's cached method is unset. This resolves the callable without launching activation; it preserves the check that the dense CUDA activation implementation is selected.
- Keep operator tests with the quantizer and real-MLP dispatch/graph tests under `test/registered/unit/layers/quantization/`, registered for the B200 runtime-test stage. Cover cold dispatch and require every non-decode mode to bypass the helper. Include the kernel benchmark extension and standalone numerical-sweep/MLP microbenchmark; keep server A/B automation local and outside this PR.


Checks on B200 with PyTorch 2.14.1+cu130 and CUDA toolkit 13.0:

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Full per-token-group quantizer suite | 167 passed |
| Kernel namespace and fused-op dispatch suites | 119 passed, 1 skipped |
| Real Llama/Qwen MLP integration, fallback gates, CUDA graph replay | 3 passed, 13 subtests passed |
| Packed DeepGEMM input regression | 1 passed, 3 subtests passed |
| Existing DualGemm regressions | 6 passed, 2 subtests passed |
| Llama parallel regressions | 2 passed, 32 subtests passed |
| Total unique registered tests | 298 passed, 1 skipped, plus 50 subtests |
| Extended numerical sweep | 240 cases; 184,023,040 FP8 bytes checked; exact FP8/scales parity |
| Compute Sanitizer memcheck | 46 repeated subset cases; zero memory errors |
| Full pinned pre-commit suite and diff whitespace checks | Passed |

The dense quantizer tests compare FP8 bytes and scale bits against the real CUDA SwiGLU followed by the existing quantizer, including BF16/FP16 sources, multiple shapes and scale layouts, special values, non-mutation, and graph replay. Runtime integration is narrower than the standalone operator: BF16 only. Real-MLP and packed-DeepGEMM comparisons use zero tolerance. The non-decode bypass regression failed before the dispatch changes and passed afterward. Repeated test runs and the memcheck subset are not added to the unique-test total.

In the latest full A/B, all 174,720 measured client requests completed without reported request errors. All 81,920 paired prefill texts and 320/320 concurrency-1 decode responses matched. Concurrency-32 decode matched 5,084/5,120 paired responses: those differences are disclosed, and their cause was not isolated. A separate 192-output-token probe had identical token IDs and zero corresponding logprob difference. Both variants scored 19/20 on the GSM8K sanity sample. These focused checks are not a comprehensive model-quality evaluation or a claim of bit-identical concurrent generation.


## Speed tests and profiling

### Full fusion versus direct unfused activation

Ten paired fresh-server comparisons on one B200, TP1, `Qwen/Qwen3-8B-FP8`, DeepGEMM, BF16 activations, TRTLLM MHA, KV dtype `auto` resolving to BF16, full decode CUDA graphs, breakable prefill CUDA graphs, and torch.compile disabled. Runtime dependencies included Python 3.12.15, PyTorch 2.14.1+cu130, CUDA toolkit 13.0, sgl-deep-gemm 0.2.3, sglang-kernel 0.4.10, and FlashInfer 0.7.2.

Five pairs were baseline-first and five fused-first, with matched requests and alternating phase/concurrency order. There were no result-dependent retries, exclusions, or added pairs. All 80 timed windows were unprofiled and excluded server startup:

- Prefill: exact 1,024 input token IDs and one output token; 1,024 warmups and 4,096 measured requests per window. Every response reported zero cached tokens. TTFT uses the first token-bearing SSE event, including blank rendered output.
- Decode: nominal 1,024 inputs and 512 outputs using the stock serving benchmark, random-ids, seed 42, temperature zero. Concurrency 1 used 16 warmups and 32 measured requests; concurrency 32 used 128 warmups and 512 measured requests. Actual input lengths after text round-trip were 992-1,325 and 867-1,360 respectively, with identical vectors across variants. These are client concurrency limits, not fixed GPU batch sizes.

Changes are geometric means of ten paired per-window median ratios. Negative means lower latency. Intervals are paired log-ratio Student-t **97.5% two-sided confidence intervals**, df=9. The absolute columns are medians of ten run medians; their ratio is not the paired estimator.

| Workload | Metric | Baseline | Fused | Paired change | 97.5% interval | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Decode, concurrency 1 | Median TPOT | 3.02064 ms | 2.96433 ms | -1.921% | [-2.082, -1.759]% | Faster in 10/10 pairs |
| Decode, concurrency 32 | Stock median TPOT | 4.35948 ms | 4.30988 ms | -0.919% | [-1.643, -0.188]% | Provisional: client timing defect |
| Prefill, concurrency 1 | Median TTFT | 13.199 ms | 13.363 ms | +0.662% | [-0.464, +1.800]% | Inconclusive against the +1% non-regression bound |
| Prefill, concurrency 32 | Median TTFT | 314.701 ms | 314.469 ms | +0.062% | [-0.132, +0.256]% | Passes the +1% bound; not a speedup claim |

Secondary whole-request latency decreased 1.901% at concurrency 1 (interval [-2.077, -1.724]%) and 0.837% at concurrency 32 ([-1.083, -0.590]%), with 10/10 paired wins each. These are secondary metrics, not substitutes for an invalid primary endpoint.

**Limitations:** the stock decode client records timing only when rendered text is nonempty. One response per concurrency-32 window had empty text, TTFT zero, no inter-token timings, and a defaulted completion length. All 20 affected responses were retained; no statistics were silently corrected. That TPOT result remains provisional. Prefill concurrency 1 also remains inconclusive against the +1% bound and showed execution-order sensitivity. The full experiment therefore does not establish unconditional prefill neutrality or an all-workload performance clearance.

### Incremental prefill effect of bypassing the helper

A separate, predeclared ten-pair experiment compared the **previous fused implementation** (always enters the helper; helper falls back on prefill) against **the new decode-only call sites**. Both retain decode fusion and the callable-resolution fix; only the two MLP dispatch sites differ. It used the same model/runtime, exact 1,024-input/one-output uncached requests, and concurrency 1/32, with 1,024 warmups and 4,096 measured requests per window.

All 163,840 measured requests and 40,960 warmups succeeded, and all 81,920 paired texts matched. No pairs were retried, excluded, or added. The paired estimator and 97.5% Student-t intervals are reported separately from the full-fusion experiment.

| Client concurrency | Previous fused TTFT | New bypass TTFT | Paired change | 97.5% interval | +1% non-regression bound |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| 1 | 13.353 ms | 13.326 ms | -0.155% | [-0.979, +0.676]% | Pass |
| 32 | 315.272 ms | 314.586 ms | -0.158% | [-0.470, +0.156]% | Pass |

This supports keeping the bypass for explicit non-decode isolation. Neither a prefill speedup nor a slowdown is statistically established. It bounds the incremental change relative to the previous fused implementation.
### Engagement and scope

Post-timing first-pair profiles from the full A/B recorded 5,667 GPU kernels in the baseline and 5,343 with fusion, including 324 dense-fused launches only in the fused variant. Separate activation launches decreased from 360 to 36. This is 324 net launches removed in a mixed ten-step capture (one prefill plus nine decode steps), not a per-token count. Profiler durations were not used for end-to-end latency claims.

Both experiments retained frozen source manifests, plans, raw measurements, and ownership/telemetry checks. No foreign compute process was observed on the selected GPU in sampled checks; its 750 W power cap was unchanged and no thermal-slowdown samples were recorded. Clocks were not locked and the host was shared. Results apply to this model/configuration, not all workloads. H100, TP greater than one, and MoE are outside the runtime fast path.

### Reproduction and retained evidence

With this checkout and matching dependencies installed on a B200:

```bash
python test/manual/kernels/bench_dense_swiglu_quant.py --check-only
```

Representative server command used in the full A/B and direct bypass comparison:

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-8B-FP8 \
  --revision 220b46e3b2180893580a4454f21f22d3ebb187d3 \
  --dtype bfloat16 --tp-size 1 --fp8-gemm-backend deep_gemm \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.6 --random-seed 42 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 30000
```

Variant selection used frozen Python source snapshots; all other server settings were identical. The local-only `full_run.py`/`runner.py` and direct-comparison `run.py` retain the orchestration, preregistered plans, and raw results. Evidence identifiers are `sglang-swiglu-prefill-bypass.dCzr2o` (focused checks), `sglang-swiglu-prefill-bypass-run.4j38zT` (full A/B), and `sglang-swiglu-direct-bypass.9mmC3I` (incremental bypass comparison). These artifacts are retained locally and are not publicly attached. Independent reproduction of the exact server tables requires supplying those harnesses/manifests; the included microbenchmark and server command alone do not reproduce them.

## Checklist

- [x] Run local correctness, graph-replay, fallback, and memory-safety checks.
- [x] Provide controlled live A/B measurements and disclose their limitations.

title: [Perf] unified-memory: Allocate free pages from each sub-pool's own end first
author: metamergebot
body:
## Motivation

The unified memory pool shares one buffer between sub-pools that grow toward each other from its two ends (for example SWA from the low end and FULL from the high end). When a sub-pool reused freed pages, `MultiEndedAllocator.take_physical` drained `_free_phys_pages[:n]` in list order for both grow directions. Compaction sorts that list ascending and frees append to it unsorted, so a grow-down pool handed out its lowest free pages first: the ones nearest the boundary it shares with its neighbour rather than the ones nearest its own end. Pages in use near the boundary hold it in place until compaction moves them, because a flush retreats the watermark only over free pages already contiguous with it.

## Modifications

- End pools (`grow_direction` "up" or "down"): `take_physical` now drains the free pages nearest the pool's own end, the lowest ids for a grow-up pool and the highest for a grow-down pool.
- `_take_free_pages_from_end` sorts the free list on the device and takes a prefix or a suffix, so the remainder stays ascending. The sort runs only when the list was rebound since it was last known sorted, tracked by tensor identity (`_free_phys_sorted`); there is no host sync because the length comes from tensor metadata. A request that takes every free page needs no sort.
- Float middle pools (`FloatMultiEndedAllocator`): a middle pool has no end of its own, so each request takes its holes from one end of the ascending hole list and the next request takes them from the other end. Only a request that drains holes and succeeds flips the turn.
- Only the order in which already-free pages are handed out changes. Free-list membership, accounting, binding, compaction, the growth path, pending-reuse protection, move gates and rollback are unchanged.

## Test

- `test/registered/unit/mem_cache/test_unified_hicache_transfer_lifecycle.py::TestPhysicalReservation::test_pending_reservation_blocks_moves_until_its_load_is_queued` now frees its interior hole after the reservation instead of before. It used to rely on the reservation landing on the end-of-band rows that list order handed out first; with own-end-first order the reservation would fill the interior hole and leave nothing to relocate. The test checks the same property and passes before and after this change.
- The unified-pool unit tests under `test/registered/unit/mem_cache/` were run on this branch and on its base commit with the same outcomes.

title: [Perf] deepseek-v4.1: Check request-window SWA history without per-layer host syncs
author: hnyls2002
body:
- With encoder SWA bounded replay on, `RequestWindow.buffer` checked each SWA layer's history before use with boolean-mask indexing and `torch.equal`: three host syncs per SWA layer per extend step, so the scheduler could not run ahead of the GPU.
- The check now goes through the sync-free invariants API (`utils/invariants.py`): `expect` on a `dsv41.swa_history_present` invariant (`FATAL_CONTAINABLE`), so `SGLANG_INVARIANT_CHECK` decides it: off in production (no detection), a throttled count and log at WARN, a device-side assert at STRICT.
- Behavior change: with `SGLANG_INVARIANT_CHECK` off (the default), servers no longer check SWA history; CI runs at STRICT and still fails on a missing history.
- Verification: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on GB300, DP2 attention + MegaMoE (EP2), encoder and decoder replay on, a multi-turn agentic prefill trace at concurrency 512, 900 s per run, same-node pairs.
  - Before: py-spy put 75% of the scheduler main thread's samples in `RequestWindow.buffer`.
  - Removing the per-layer check: +4.5% to +6.7% tok/s/GPU on three nodes; the step interval went from ~405 to ~375 ms at the same step shape.
  - The deferred-flag version of this check (an earlier revision of this PR) ran within -1.3% to +0.7% of removing the check on three nodes, with no false raise; the invariants version adds only the comparison kernels.
  - `test_dsv41_request_window_copy.py` passes. A one-off GPU script confirmed: matching history passes at STRICT; missing history passes at OFF and trips `invariant-check FAILED [dsv41.swa_history_present]` at STRICT.

title: [Perf] dspark: Make the prefill SWA valid-from update sync-free
author: hnyls2002
body:
- After a target prefill with encoder SWA replay, `DSparkWorkerV2._forward_prefill` marks each newly placed request's draft SWA ring valid from its cached prefix. It built the slots by indexing a CUDA tensor with a Python list and the prefix lengths with `torch.tensor(..., device=...)`. Both are pageable host-to-device copies that block the host. They run after the target forward is enqueued, so each prefill step stalled the scheduler until the whole target forward finished.
- Both copies now go through `async_h2d` (pinned, non-blocking), and the slots come from an `index_select` on the device. No behavior change: same slots, same values.
- Verification: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on GB300, DP2 attention + MegaMoE (EP2), DSpark, encoder and decoder replay on, a multi-turn agentic prefill trace at concurrency 512, 900 s per run, same-node pairs.
  - Before: py-spy put 50% of the scheduler main thread's samples on the list index line.
  - After: that line is gone from the profile. The step interval went from ~375 to ~312 ms, and throughput rose from 1,459,199 to 1,581,184 tok/s/GPU (+8.4%) on one node and from 1,453,741 to 1,598,164 (+9.9%) on another, with no errors.

title: [Perf] deepseek-v4.1: Reset request-window tags without a host sync
author: hnyls2002
body:
- `RequestWindow.reset` cleared a slot's tags with a scalar index_put (`tags[:, loc] = -1`), which blocks the host until the stream drains. It runs once per newly placed request with encoder SWA replay, so each such prefill step stalled the scheduler behind the GPU.
- It now uses `index_fill_`, which stays on the device. No behavior change: same rows, same value.
- Verification: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on GB300, DP2 attention + MegaMoE (EP2), DSpark, encoder and decoder replay on, a multi-turn agentic prefill trace at concurrency 512. py-spy put 44% of the scheduler main thread's samples on that line. In isolation, with GPU work queued, the old line held the host for 371 ms and `index_fill_` for 0.14 ms.

title: [Refactor] kda: Import recurrent_kda from the canonical flashinfer namespace
author: kahyunnam
body:
### Motivation

`flashinfer.kda_decode.recurrent_kda` ships in flashinfer-python 0.7.2 as a deprecated shim (added in 0.7.1 by flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#5248, marked `.. deprecated:: 0.8`): it forwards to the same decode dispatcher as `flashinfer.recurrent_kda`, calls `warnings.warn(DeprecationWarning)` with a frame walk on every call (the cost is paid even when Python's default filters hide the message), and is scheduled for removal. SGLang already pins `flashinfer_python[cu13]==0.7.2`, which ships the canonical entry point with the same decode contract, so the FlashInfer KDA wrapper can move off the shim before it disappears.

### Modifications

- `python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/linear/kernels/kda_flashinfer.py`: import `recurrent_kda` from `flashinfer` instead of `flashinfer.kda_decode`; update the module docstring.
- `benchmark/bench_linear_attention/bench_kda_flashinfer_mtp.py`: update the docstring that named the deprecated facade.

No call-site change. The shim resolved an omitted `backend` to `"cute-dsl"`; the canonical function defaults to `backend="auto"`. Both SGLang call sites (`decode` and `target_verify`) pass `cu_seqlens`, and in flashinfer 0.7.2 `backend="auto"` keeps explicit-`cu_seqlens` decode on the CuTe DSL kernel without consulting the Cake selector, so the kernel that runs is the same as before.

### Accuracy Tests

The wrapper calls the same kernel with the same arguments. `bench_kda_flashinfer_mtp.py` compares the FlashInfer output against the Triton KDA reference on every row; the max abs diff is reported in the last column of the table below and is identical before and after on every row.

### Speed Tests and Profiling

B200 (SM100), bf16, H=HV=16, K=V=128, pool 512, `benchmark/bench_linear_attention/bench_kda_flashinfer_mtp.py` per-call time from CUDA events around 100 back-to-back calls after 20 warmup calls; two independent process runs per arm, reported as run1 / run2. Decode and verify at B<=32 are host-bound, so those rows are per-call host issue time; verify at B>=64 is kernel-bound and the host path is not visible there. Before = `flashinfer.kda_decode.recurrent_kda`, After = `flashinfer.recurrent_kda`.

| task | B | before (us) | after (us) | out_max_diff vs Triton |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| decode | 1 | 69.3 / 69.7 | 65.4 / 71.3 | 3.05e-05 |
| decode | 4 | 70.1 / 70.2 | 67.6 / 68.6 | 6.10e-05 |
| decode | 16 | 52.8 / 56.7 | 50.6 / 54.3 | 6.10e-05 |
| decode | 32 | 53.2 / 53.6 | 50.8 / 55.4 | 1.22e-04 |
| decode | 64 | 53.1 / 53.3 | 50.7 / 55.0 | 1.22e-04 |
| decode | 128 | 54.1 / 54.1 | 52.0 / 54.5 | 1.22e-04 |
| verify (T=8) | 1 | 137.2 / 131.1 | 124.7 / 133.5 | 6.10e-05 |
| verify (T=8) | 4 | 139.8 / 126.3 | 120.0 / 129.1 | 1.22e-04 |
| verify (T=8) | 16 | 133.1 / 127.2 | 120.3 / 128.8 | 2.44e-04 |
| verify (T=8) | 32 | 145.8 / 133.2 | 123.9 / 121.7 | 2.44e-04 |
| verify (T=8) | 64 | 149.2 / 149.2 | 149.0 / 149.1 | 2.44e-04 |
| verify (T=8) | 128 | 296.5 / 296.5 | 296.5 / 296.4 | 1.22e-04 |

No regression: on every row the after arm is equal to or faster than the before arm in at least one run, and every before/after difference is inside the run-to-run spread of the same arm (up to about 10% on the host-bound rows). The kernel-bound verify rows at B>=64 agree to within 0.1 us. `out_max_diff` vs Triton is identical before and after on every row. The Cake selector (`_select_flash_kda_decode_variant_cached`, `_select_flash_kda_decode_variant`) and the Cake launcher (`_run_flash_kda_decode`) were called zero times in every run, so `backend="auto"` keeps these `cu_seqlens` call sites on the CuTe DSL kernel. An earlier set of eight runs on 2026-10-16 against the pre-rebase commit gave the same picture.

### How this was measured

One NVIDIA B200 (SM100, CC 10.0) on `cudnn-dev-keel-26-04`, container `lmsysorg/sglang:dev` with torch 2.14.1+cu130 and the flashinfer-python 0.7.2 wheel (SGLang's current pin), SGLang imported from this branch at `67b3dd32`. Each arm ran in its own process with the arm's function forced into the wrapper's lazy-import slot and asserted active (`active=flashinfer.kda_decode.recurrent_kda` vs `active=flashinfer.kda.recurrent_kda` in the log headers); default warning filters were left in place so the deprecated arm paid the shim's `warnings.warn` as SGLang does in production. Each process ended with `counts={'dispatch': 726, 'select_cached': 0, 'select_inner': 0, 'cake_launch': 0}` and `EXIT_OK`. An idle `VLLM::EngineCore` belonging to another user (55 GB, 0% utilization) was resident on the GPU throughout and was not touched. Script and logs under `/home/scratch.knam/flashinfer-work/general/.projects/recurrent-kda-unification/sglang-migration/rework_2026-10-16/`: `ab_sglang_migration.py` and `logs_{deprecated,canonical}_{decode,verify}_2026-10-19_run{1,2}.log` (eight files); the 2026-10-16 runs are the `logs_{deprecated,canonical}_{decode,verify}.log` and `_run2.log` files beside them. Correctness is against SGLang's Triton KDA kernel only, bf16, H=HV=16, K=V=128, T=1 and T=8; no other head counts, dtypes or fused-accept paths were measured, and only SM100 was exercised (the wrapper is SM100-gated).

Not applicable: an import-path swap with no behaviour change. `test/registered/attention/test_kda_decode_flashinfer.py` exercises the wrapper on SM100 but is registered disabled in public CI ("recurrent_kda (SM100 KDA decode) not guaranteed in public CI FlashInfer build"), so it does not run there; the bench's per-row max abs diff against the Triton KDA reference is the correctness evidence here.
- [ ] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations). Not applicable: no user-facing docs name the import path.

title: [Perf] deepseek-v4.1: Score a request's verify rows as one request in the full-scan indexer
author: kpham-sgl
body:
## Motivation

Under DSpark target verify the ratio-1 and ratio-2 DeepSeek-V4.1 indexers call DeepGEMM's paged logits kernel with every draft row as its own request, so each row streams its request's whole index-K cache: six times per request with block 5. On a DEP16 decode at 64 requests per rank and 128K contexts the four full scans take 1.27 ms of a 22.6 ms DSpark cycle.

## Modifications

- `PagedIndexerMetadata.rows_per_request`: the draft block for static verify, 1 for ragged verify and everywhere else. The DeepGEMM schedule is planned over the lengths viewed `[requests, block]` (the JIT planner flattens them, so grouped rows use DeepGEMM's).
- `DeepGEMMDecodeData.paged_logits_args` views `q` as `[requests, block, heads, 64]`, the lengths as `[requests, block]`, and takes one page-table row per request. Both full-scan callers use it: `FullTopK._deep_gemm_decode` and the candidate-source `publish_decode`.
- No kernel change: `fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits` already schedules `next_n` rows per request in blocks of `128 / heads`, so six rows read the cache twice instead of six times.
- The logits tensor, the per-row lengths and page table handed to top-k are unchanged, so the bf16 DeepSelect top-k, top-k v2 and the paged top-k all see the same input as before.

## Validation

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, one DEP16 worker on 4x4 GB300 (DP attention 16, EP16, MegaMoE, `flashmla_mega`, DSpark block 5, static ragged verify, bf16 index logits, decode graphs at batch 64), 1,024 random-id prompts of 128K tokens held at 64 per rank, golden acceptance 3.51, main `49766a74f9` against this branch, one run each. Step time from the scheduler's `Decode batch` lines over the steady window; kernel times from a torch trace of 20 steps.

| 64 per rank, 128K contexts | main | this PR |
|---|---:|---:|
| Full scans, layers 2 / 8 / 14 (ratio 2) / 20 (ratio 1), us | 249 / 259 / 246 / 516 | 96 / 96 / 97 / 183 |
| Four scans per verify step, ms | 1.27 | 0.47 |
| DSpark cycle (draft + verify), ms | 22.57 | 21.57 |

Other kernels unchanged within 1%. GSM8K at native acceptance on one DEP2 node (5 shots, 1,314 examples, temperature 0): 97.56% main, 97.11% this branch, inside the run-to-run spread, as the check below shows.

Kernel-level check on one GB300 (DeepGEMM v0.2.2, bf16 logits): the same `fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits` call on identical random inputs, per row (`next_n` 1) and grouped six per request (`next_n` 6), on three batches: 64 x 6 rows at 128K slots with two seeds, and 16 x 6 at 64K. Every logit a row scores inside its own length is bit-equal (78M values, max abs diff 0), so the per-row top-k is identical on all three. The fp32-logits output type was not run.

title: [Feat] kernels: Beam model support
author: Jiminator
body:
## Motivation

Split #44747 into reviewable parts. This is the kernels part, position 3 of 7 in the merge order below.

## Modifications

- **Beam fused ops**, listed by class method as in Muse Spark's kernels part:
  - `elementwise.beam_attention_gate`: the per-head gate, with Beam's activation-dtype bias and sigmoid rounding.
  - `layernorm.beam_sandwich_residual_rmsnorm`: the post-norm, depth-scaled residual and next RMSNorm in one launch.
- **`communication.beam_all_reduce_norm`**: Beam's BF16 TP all-reduce fused with that norm and residual, on CustomAllReduceV2's push plane. Each row runs on one CTA, or on a 5-CTA cluster at TP8 for up to 16 rows. It needs a new `CustomAllReduceV2.supports_push` capacity check.
- **FP32 router gates:**
  - FP32 weights in main's `tiny_gemm` (N variant) and `router_gemv` (CUDA, up to 8 rows);
  - `gemm.router_gemm_bf16x3_cublas` for larger batches, with the weight split per call by `quantization.split_fp32_to_bf16x3`.

Main's existing callers are unchanged:
- BF16 tiny GEMM builds the same kernel with the same split as on main (its JIT build key gains the weight type, so it recompiles once on first use);
- the gfx950 BF16 router GEMV path is unchanged.

`gemm.router_gemv` is registered for Triton CUDA/HIP; its existing predicate retains CUDA FP32 and gfx950 BF16 gating. `split_fp32_to_bf16x3` lives in `ops.quantization.bf16x3_split`, which #45361 now imports directly. The cuBLAS wrapper keeps its internal import.

Committed coverage adds 18 representative numerical cases, reusing the existing tiny GEMM and fused-op parity suites plus a focused CUDA router test. The collective test covers both native unicast and multicast, changing-input graph replay, interleaved regular all-reduce, and both TP8 launch shapes. These checks complement the model E2E test from #45257.

The optional SM103 single-token BF16 MoE GEMV and shared SiLU helper moved to draft #46401, with their own correctness test and performance benchmark. They are outside Day-0 kernel support; performance measurements for that follow-up remain pending.

This part changes 21 files (+1,364 / -34).

## Validation

The following focused results belong to the tested review changes preserved in `851658f9b8`. The branch subsequently merged main at `d360915f64`; verification has not been rerun after that merge.

On GB300/SM103, with torch 2.14.1+cu130 and Triton 3.8.0:

- Numerical tests: **196 tiny GEMM, 5 router and 13 fused-op parity cases passed**. The added cases check FP32 router results against FP64, exact gate rounding, BF16 norm output within one ULP, and fixed FP16 cancellation bounds. FP16 has no universal one-ULP guarantee.
- The registered collective test passed at TP2, TP4 and cross-node TP8 over MNNVL, in native unicast and multicast modes. It covers rows 1/8/16/32/64/128, top-k 1/8, optional next norm, changing payloads during graph replay, and interleaved regular all-reduce. TP8 covers one-CTA and five-CTA launches. Native pointer inspection confirmed the selected modes.
- The existing 42-tensor-per-rank probes found zero byte differences between unicast and multicast, and between multicast and the saved original baseline. Those probes cover rows through 64.
- Beam-kernel memcheck passed at TP2/TP4 through 64 rows; TP8 racecheck and synccheck passed the full registered matrix in both modes. These runs used `--report-api-errors no` after a setup-only control reproduced 41 `cuGetProcAddress_v2` API errors per rank without calling either all-reduce. Device-memory/race/sync checks remained enabled. The setup/API issue remains unresolved; this is not clean CUDA API validation. No TP8 or row-128 memcheck claim.
- Namespace tests passed 101 cases. Existing MoE suites passed. The generic custom-all-reduce TP4 suite retained **309 passes and one failure**, `test_custom_all_reduce_eager_plan_follows_config`, reproduced on the unchanged baseline.
- No physically multicast-incapable hardware, H200, ROCm or SM120 rerun was added for these review changes.

An earlier NVFP4 integration with the model/parser stack passed the original Beam verifier at `dfa85fe771`: **133/133 required chat cases and 5/5 optional raw-completion cases**. Temperature 0 applied only to recall; `no_stop_trim` applied only to raw completions. That integration included a separate parser compatibility fix and predates the final unicast restoration; it is not a fresh model run on this head or a matched reference comparison.

<details>
<summary>Historical validation and performance from earlier revisions</summary>

The original results below are retained as historical evidence. They were not rerun for the latest review commits or main merge; references to pending work describe the state at those earlier runs.

On GB300 (SM103), with torch 2.14.1+cu130 and Triton 3.8.0:

- **Main's tests for the touched code pass:**
  - tiny GEMM;
  - fused MoE (SwiGLU epilogue, padding, TMA cache, `test_fused_moe`);
  - collectives;
  - the kernel registry and fused-op CPU tests.

  `test_custom_all_reduce.py` has one failure, `test_custom_all_reduce_eager_plan_follows_config`, which main also fails on the same machine.
- **Each new op checked against an independent reference:**
  - The attention gate is bitwise equal to eager over every finite FP16 and BF16 gate value (two bias and two attention settings), including through the `torch_compile` backend.
  - The sandwich norm matches eager in BF16 within one ULP. In FP16, 3 of 327,680 elements at a residual-cancellation point differ by 2^-11. As its docstring states, cancellation can amplify reduction-order differences, so there is no one-ULP guarantee.
  - The all-reduce boundary matches an all-gather reference at TP2, TP4 and TP8 within BF16 tolerance, and its CUDA-graph replays are bitwise reproducible across payload changes. TP8 ran across two 4×GB300 nodes over MNNVL, where the outputs are bitwise equal between the one-CTA and cluster launches.
  - The FP32 router tiny GEMM and GEMV show errors comparable to SGEMM against FP64 references over the tested shapes.
  - The BF16x3 split is exact for 2^-110 <= |w| < 2^128 - 2^119.
  - The decode GEMV matches an FP64 reference with BF16 rounding points to within 7.6e-6 across 20 graph replays.
- **End to end:** this part with #45256, #45257 and #43216, on 4×GB300, with the cookbook GB300 NVFP4 low-latency recipe and the public `reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-NVFP4` checkpoint:
  - GSM8K 96.59% (sgl-eval, 1,319 questions, temperature 0, 0 errors);
  - the [Beam Verifier](https://github.com/reflection-oss/beam-verifier) at `dfa85fe771` passes its required suites 133/133: 131 cases at its defaults and the 2 recall cases at temperature 0. The optional suites did not run;
  - chat reasoning, streaming, chat tool calls, Responses text, function and shell, and `/tokenize` all pass.
- Merges into main without conflicts. pre-commit passes.

On 8×H200 (SM90), with the same torch and Triton and FlashInfer 0.7.2:

- **Main's tests pass:** tiny GEMM, fused MoE (SwiGLU epilogue, padding, TMA cache, `test_fused_moe`), and the kernel registry and fused-op CPU tests.
- **Numerical checks:**
  - The attention gate is bitwise equal to eager over every finite FP16 and BF16 gate value.
  - The all-reduce boundary matches an all-gather reference at TP2, TP4 and TP8 within BF16 tolerance, and its outputs are bitwise equal between the one-CTA and cluster launches.
  - compute-sanitizer racecheck and synccheck are clean on the all-reduce boundary at TP8, covering both launch shapes.
- **FP32 router:** the boundary norm followed by the FP32 tiny GEMM is 0.02–1.26 µs per layer faster than with this PR's earlier PDL ordering and split selection, at 1–16 tokens, with bitwise-identical outputs.
- **End to end:** with the same parts as above, at FP8 TP8 (`fa3`, DFlash), with the public `reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-FP8` checkpoint:
  - GSM8K 96.21% (sgl-eval, 1,319 questions, temperature 0, 0 errors);
  - the Beam Verifier required suites pass 133/133, with the recall cases at temperature 0;
  - chat reasoning, streaming, chat tool calls, Responses text and function calls, and `/tokenize` pass. The Responses shell round trip fails with the current public chat template; the fix goes in #45257.

**TP8 cluster launch.** At TP8 with up to 16 rows, each row runs as a 5-CTA cluster. Per call, compared with one CTA per row:
- on 8×H200, it is 4–10% faster with top-k 1 and 8–16% faster with top-k 8 (6.76 vs 5.68 µs at one row);
- on 8×GB300 across two nodes (MNNVL), it is 3–11% faster with top-k 8. With top-k 1 it ranges from 2.2% faster to 0.9% slower, inside run-to-run noise (median of five sweeps).

One CTA per row stays at TP2 and TP4, where it is as fast or faster on GB300 and H200. It also stays for TP8 batches above 16 rows. At 32 rows with top-k 8, a cluster would be 1.4% faster on H200 but is 3.4% slower on GB300.

Not measured here:
- end-to-end serving and compute-sanitizer at TP8 on Blackwell (TP8 there covers the all-reduce boundary only);
- ROCm (the gfx950 BF16 path is unchanged and was checked statically);
- the unicast publish path.

</details>

## Merge order

Each part is based on the one before it, so its diff shows only its own changes. Merge bottom-up; after each part merges, the next part is retargeted to `main` and `main` is merged into it. #44747 stays open, unchanged, as the full reference. Merge in this order:

1. #45253: Beam CUDA Docker image (merged)
2. #45291: OpenAI SDK 2.8.0, needed by the Responses shell tools in #45257 (merged)
3. #45254: Kernels
4. #45256: Attention, memory and DFlash DP support, and the Beam model (#45255 folded in; also after #43216)
5. #45257: Beam reasoning, tool calls, response templates and the Beam E2E test (merged into #45256)
6. #45290: `nvidia-cuda-tileiras`, needed by #45361
7. #45361: cuTile BF16x3 router GEMM (optional: without it Beam uses the cuBLAS router)

#45292 (Dynamo and `grpcio-tools` pins for the Beam image) is not in the merge order for now.
