title: [Perf] [AMD] kda: Use a HIP fused decode kernel by default for KDA (Kimi-K3) on gfx950
author: Monstertail
body:
## Motivation On MI350X / MI355X (gfx950), Kimi-K3 KDA decode runs the unfused chain by default (`f_b` tiny GEMM, causal Conv1D update, Triton recurrent decode, gated RMSNorm), or the AITER FlyDSL fused boundary with `SGLANG_ROCM_K3_KDA_FUSED_BACKEND=aiter`. This PR adds a HIP kernel for the same fused boundary and makes it the default on gfx950. It is the decode companion of #45710 (KDA prefill); the two PRs change disjoint runtime files. **Note: This kernel is generated by [KDAgent](https://nvlabs.github.io/kda/blog/2026-09-27-kda-for-kda/) in AMD ecosystems. Cost around 5k dollars in humanize2 flow to get this.** ## Modifications The kernel follows the `sglang.kernels` layout of RFC #29630: it was produced with the Kernel Design Agents workflow, so the implementation lives in `kernels/kda_kernels`, it is registered with `KernelBackend.KDA`, and runtime code reaches it only through the `sglang.kernels.ops` facade. - `kernels/kda_kernels/csrc/attention/kda_decode_gfx950.cu` and its loader `kernels/kda_kernels/kda_decode_gfx950.py`, JIT-compiled on first use. One 256-thread workgroup per (token, head), for 12 heads of 128 per rank (Kimi-K3 TP8), runs the `f_b` projection, the depthwise Conv1D update with SiLU, the q/k L2 norms and gate decay, the delta-rule update of the 128 x 128 fp32 state, and the gated RMSNorm. State and Conv1D slot strides are read from the tensors, so padded hybrid cache layouts work. Slot 0, the mamba pool's padding slot, returns zeros without touching either cache. - `kernels/kda_kernels/README.md`: provenance entry. - `kernels/ops/attention/__init__.py`: registers `attention.kda_decode_gfx950` (`KernelBackend.KDA`, HIP). - `kernels/ops/attention/kda_fused_decode_gfx950.py` (facade): the same fail-closed `available` / `covered` / `warmup` / `run` interface as `kda_fused_decode_aiter_hip`; `run` calls the kernel through `get_kernel`. - `srt/models/kimi_k3.py` (ROCm branch of `_prepare_fused_decode`): maps `SGLANG_ROCM_K3_KDA_FUSED_BACKEND` to a facade, `gfx950` (the new default) or `aiter`; any other value keeps the unfused chain. The chosen facade is stored on the layer. - `srt/layers/attention/linear/kda_backend.py` (gfx950 fused-decode branch): calls the facade stored on the layer instead of the hard-coded AITER adapter. - `test/registered/kernels/ops/attention/test_kda_fused_decode_gfx950.py` (MI35x suite): matches the Triton chain over 4 steps under the default backend, skips slots <= 0, and CUDA graph replay equals eager. Behavior change: on gfx950 the fused decode is now on by default. `SGLANG_ROCM_K3_KDA_FUSED_BACKEND=aiter` selects FlyDSL, and any other value (for example `none`) selects the unfused chain. Both edits in `srt/` are inside the existing ROCm-only branches. ## Accuracy Tests MI355X, `lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:v0.5.22-rocm10-mi35x-20261020`. - Against a per-token fp32 PyTorch reference (batch 1, 2, 8 and 37 with padded rows, and batch 16 over 64 steps): output relative RMSE at most 7.1e-6 (the Triton chain reaches 1.2e-5 and FlyDSL 2.7e-5 in the same checks). title: [Perf] dsv41: Fuse request-window layout construction
author: alphabetc1
body:
## Motivation

Eager request-window layout construction launches many small kernels to build attention indices, valid lengths, history metadata and commit masks. Fuse the pointwise work after the existing request-group scans to reduce launch overhead and temporary tensors.

## Modifications

- Add two Triton kernels for query and history metadata on CUDA; retain the existing CPU and HIP implementation.
- Preserve padding, input strides, per-request floors, contiguous-run grouping and graph refresh behavior.
- Keep row counts and history size as runtime arguments to avoid compiling a separate kernel for each batch length.
- Keep the PR focused on the implementation; standalone UT and microbenchmark files were removed following review.

## Accuracy Tests

Before the review cleanup, local validation on GB300 using `test_dsv41_window_layout.py` passed both tests: 64 shape/dtype/floor/padding combinations plus graph replay with changing request groups. Every output field is compared exactly with the CPU reference. The existing `test_dsv41_request_window_copy.py` passes all four tests. Repository pre-commit checks pass.

The standalone layout test was removed following review; the results above describe validation of the unchanged implementation at `fc63b690ea`. No full model accuracy score is claimed by this draft.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

The benchmark used only generated request IDs and positions, with no model or dataset. Its script was removed from the final diff following review and remains available at commit `fc63b690ea` as `benchmark/kernels/bench_dsv41_window_layout.py`. To reproduce, extract that historical script and run it against each checkout:

```bash
git show fc63b690ea:benchmark/kernels/bench_dsv41_window_layout.py > /tmp/bench_dsv41_window_layout.py
PYTHONPATH=<checkout>/python python /tmp/bench_dsv41_window_layout.py
```

GB300, PyTorch 2.14.1+cu130 and Triton 3.8.0, eager wall time after warmup, 100 calls per sample and five samples per checkout. Input positions start at 8192; the benchmark fixes the window to 128 and supplies a floor tensor. Baseline is `780a5b1accd`; candidate is `fc63b690ea`. Measurements are medians:

| Rows / groups | Baseline (ms/call) | Fused (ms/call) |
|---|---:|---:|
| 4096 / 1 | 0.897 | 0.407 |
| 32768 / 8 | 0.884 | 0.415 |

These are metadata-construction timings, not end-to-end serving speedups. Baseline samples ranged from 0.874–0.905 ms/call (4096 rows) and 0.873–0.905 ms/call (32768 rows); fused samples ranged from 0.397–0.444 and 0.414–0.452 ms/call, respectively.

## Checklist

- [x] Format code with repository pre-commit checks.
- [x] Validate CPU-reference parity and graph replay on GB300.
- [x] Record metadata-construction benchmark results.
- [x] Remove standalone UT and benchmark files as requested in review.
- [ ] Full model accuracy and serving benchmark qualification.

title: [Perf] diffusion/preprocess: Extend exact GPU input processing across pipelines
author: mickqian
body:
## Summary

Extend the exact RGB preprocessing introduced in #45398 beyond Cosmos3, using one shared resize/crop/normalize entry point rather than per-model kernels.

This PR includes the original commit from @xupinjie with its authorship preserved because #45398 is still open. It should land after that PR; merging main afterwards will remove the overlapping diff.

- Cover FLUX.2/Klein reference images, Qwen-Image-Edit 2509/2511 VAE inputs, Wan TI2V, Cosmos3 I2V/V2V, and RGB conversion in the shared image-VAE stage.
- Upload compact uint8 pixels, fuse Lanczos/crop/FP32 normalization, and fast-path identity resize. Preserve Pillow rounding, each model's crop geometry, and encoder input strides.
- Bound video decoding for first-frame and control-video consumers instead of decoding the full clip and slicing afterwards.
- Retain CPU processing for unsupported platforms/modes and small workloads; reuse `SGLANG_FORCE_CPU_IMAGE_PREPROCESSING=1` as an override. Include output area when deciding whether an upscale is too small for GPU processing.
- Document temporary VRAM, first-use compilation, and the distinction between input-chain and full-request speedups.

The extension beyond #45398 adds about 146 production lines and removes 30, with no additional production files.

## Accuracy And Tests

- Registered CUDA entry points: all 5 kernel tests and all 3 runtime preprocessing tests pass.
- Existing input-validation/Cosmos3 suite: **158 passed, 55 subtests passed**.
- Exact external Diffusers FLUX.2 and Qwen VAE processor comparisons, including odd/portrait/4K shapes; compare both values (`rtol=atol=0`) and strides.
- Real Wan TI2V geometry and real MP4 first/last/prefix decoding match the CPU reference exactly. Non-RGB floating-point VAE inputs retain their original normalization policy.
- Native E2E: all **12 paired output files** (warmup plus three distinct requests for each of three models) match baseline SHA-256, including saved PNG/MP4 files. No GT or consistency threshold changes.
- Pre-commit and diff whitespace checks pass.

Cosmos3 is covered by preprocessing tests, not a full checkpoint E2E run. No general cross-hardware bitwise-equivalence claim is made.

## Performance

Hardware/software: **1 NVIDIA H200, 143771 MiB reported total VRAM**, Intel Xeon Platinum 8558P host; PyTorch 2.14.1+cu130, CUDA 13.0, Triton 3.8.0, Diffusers 0.37.0, Transformers 5.19.0, Pillow 11.3.0, PyAV 16.1.0.

### Complete Native Requests

Baseline: `5f62e23d3051d09fa711f825b20abead20c3a717`; candidate: `17c917344bd639a90abae9c2644c12de96853396`. Both sides use the native SGLang pipeline, one GPU, batch 1, four steps, seed 42, `quality=exact`, manual/resident placement, no torch.compile or CUDA Graph. Input: distinct 1920x1080 PNGs/prompts to avoid conditioning-cache hits. One warmup and three measured requests per process; report medians, excluding loading but **including file decoding, preprocessing, transfer, learned encoding, denoising, decoding, output encoding/saving, and API return**.

| Model / Output | Baseline | GPU input path | Observed latency reduction |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| FLUX.2-klein-4B / 512x512 | 494.3 ms | 454.6 ms | 8.0% |
| Wan2.2-TI2V-5B / 17x704x1248 | 2240.9 ms | 2210.4 ms | 1.4% |
| Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 / 512x512 | 1530.7 ms | 1498.9 ms | 2.1% |

These are bounded low-step samples, not a statistical guarantee or a universal model speedup. Longer denoising workloads amortize input processing further.

Peak allocated VRAM (same requests): FLUX 16893.02 -> 16904.59 MiB; Wan 48772.43 -> 48772.53 MiB; Qwen 57158.03 -> 57170.23 MiB. This is **not zero-extra-VRAM**: temporary pixels and coefficient buffers live on GPU. Peak reserved VRAM was unchanged for Wan/Qwen and increased by 12 MiB for FLUX.

### Input Chain In Isolation

Synthetic RGB JPEGs, quality 92, warm filesystem cache, resize to 1024x1024, three warmups plus ten measured samples. Includes JPEG file decode, resize/crop/normalize, H2D, and CUDA synchronization; excludes learned encoder/denoiser work. CPU override vs GPU path in the same checkout; outputs match exactly.

| Source | CPU input chain | GPU input chain |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 1024x1024 | 22.94 ms | 12.55 ms |
| 1920x1080 | 60.97 ms | 25.22 ms |
| 3840x2160 | 204.44 ms | 112.20 ms |

Image/video codec decoding and tokenization remain on CPU where they were previously. Output codecs are unchanged: this does not silently substitute NVENC for libx264 or claim that all CPU work has moved to GPU.

title: [Perf] [AMD] Qwen3-Next: fused QK Gemma RMSNorm + partial RoPE on gfx950
author: karverma-amd
body:
## Summary

Route the Qwen3-Next full-attention prologue — the per-head `[Q||gate]` split, Q/K Gemma RMSNorm (`x*(1+w)`), and partial NeoX RoPE (rotary_dim 64) — through the fused aiter op `fused_attention_qk_norm_rope` on gfx950, replacing three small launches with one.

## Gating 

- Gated on `SGLANG_USE_AITER` + `is_hip()` — no bespoke per-kernel flag.
- The aiter import is lazy and only reached on HIP, so the NVIDIA common path never imports or touches the AMD-only code.
- Support is probed (`fused_attention_qk_norm_rope_supported`), not asserted, so any uncovered shape (dtype/width/arch) falls back to the native split + GemmaRMSNorm + RoPE. The attention backend still writes the KV cache.

## Dependencies

- **aiter op**: `fused_attention_qk_norm_rope` in ROCm/aiter — https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/compare/main...karverma-amd:aiter:karverma/qwen3-next-fused-prologue?expand=1
- **Stacked on #45738** (the `smallm_fp8_blockscale_gfx950` import fix), which Qwen3-Next FP8 needs to serve on gfx950. The first commit in this PR is that fix; the second commit is the wiring under review here.

## Test results

E2E on Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-FP8, MI355X 2×TP4, latest nightly (`v0.5.22-rocm724-mi35x-20261021`) with **Triton 3.8.0**:

- Median TPOT **−2.3 to −3.0%** at concurrency 1/8/32 (throughput +2.3 to +7.9%); stable through cuda-graph capture and sustained conc-8/32/64 load.
- GSM8K 1319-question 5-shot: parity (fused 0.941 / native 0.948, 0 invalid).
- Engagement confirmed on the fused arm; fail-closed to native verified on the control arm.
- The same nightly on stock Triton 3.7 and v0.5.21 + Triton 3.8 reproduce the same −2.5 to −3.0% TPOT and GSM8K parity.

title: [Perf] dsv4: Gather V4.1 index-K slots once per prefill graph replay
author: hnyls2002
body:
- Prefill graph replays take the same index-K slot snapshot as eager extend (#45577): `prepare_forward_metadata_for_breakable_cuda_graph_replay` calls `_snapshot_low_ratio_k_slots` after refreshing the full and tail metadata, so the full top-k and low-ratio source breaks read `low_ratio_k_slots` and one `PrefillIndexPlan` per ratio instead of gathering from `req_to_token` and rebuilding the plan in every layer. The snapshot's condition moves into the helper, so both callers make the same one-line call; only the capture pass still gathers per layer.
- The late-layer tail that leaves the prefill graph for its row-bucket graphs builds fresh metadata for the live rows; `_share_low_ratio_k_slots` hands it the same snapshot with its own plan cache, as `_snapshot_low_ratio_k_slots` already does for the tail metadata of an eager extend.
- The replay-context test stubs the snapshot like the other backend collaborators.

No behavior change: the snapshot holds the same slots and plans the per-layer path builds, which assertions confirmed on every layer, tail included, of 639 prefill graph replays of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (DEP4 with MegaMoE on GB300, 4,096 and 8,192 tokens per rank). At 4,096 tokens per rank the scheduler thread spends about 3.4 ms less per step (sampled), with the index-K gather down from 4.0 to 0.9 ms.

title: [Perf] QSA: Optimize the prefill indexer gather
author: Shunkangz
body: ## Motivation `get_prefill_mqa_inputs` packed each request's complete compressed keys using a Python loop. For every request, it performed a cast, a `// ratio` operation, and an `index_select`, followed by a final `torch.cat`. This required `3B + 1` launches per QSA layer. When metadata did not contain host-side lengths—which happens on every eager forward on `main`—it also called `sequence_lengths.tolist()`, introducing a host synchronization. ## Modifications - Replace the GPU packing loop with `gather_qsa_compressed_keys`, which gathers keys in one Triton launch over `(block tile, sequence)`. - Copy raw bytes so the same kernel supports both BF16 and FP8 caches. - Reuse the compressed `cu_seqlens` that `build_qsa_row_ranges` already computes for row offsets. - Record the scheduler's `seq_lens_cpu` as `prefill_sequence_lengths_cpu` for every extend, allowing output sizing without a device read. - Preserve the per-request gather for CPU tensors. ## Accuracy Tests The packed keys are **byte-equal** to the original loop's output. ## Speed Tests and Profiling For `B=32 × (128K + 1K)` on B200, measured for one QSA layer: | Metric | Before | After | | --- | --- | --- | | Execution time | 0.90 ms | 0.05 ms | | Kernel launches | 97 | 1 | Before the change After the change ## Checklist - [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit). - [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests). - [x] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations). - [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed). - [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance). ## Review and Merge Process 1. title: [Perf] gemma4: Capture single-step frozen-KV drafts
author: alexnails
body:
## Motivation

`FrozenKVMTPDraftWorker._capture_cuda_graphs` returns early when `speculative_num_steps <= 1`, so a one-step frozen-KV draft never gets a draft graph. That guard is off by one: a one-step draft still runs the assistant seed forward every decode step, and that forward is exactly what the capture covers. With the guard as written, it always runs eagerly.

### How it was found

While profiling Gemma 4 E2B frozen-KV MTP with one draft step and two verification tokens, the assistant seed forward showed up as eager work on every decode step, even with full decode graphs enabled. `/server_info` confirmed it: `startup_time.cuda_graph.draft_decode` was `0`, while the same server with three draft steps reported a nonzero capture time. The cause turned out to be the `<= 1` early return.

## Modifications

Change the early-return guard from `<= 1` to `<= 0`, so one-step drafts are captured. The zero-step and graphs-disabled cases are still excluded. Nothing else changes; multi-step drafts take the same path as before.

## Accuracy Tests

`google/gemma-4-E2B-it` + `google/gemma-4-E2B-it-assistant`, one H200, the cookbook E2B MTP command with `--speculative-num-steps 1 --speculative-num-draft-tokens 2` (the case this PR changes).

- Six greedy chat prompts: identical output on all four runs (main ×2, this PR ×2).
- GSM8K via `sgl-eval==0.1.3`, 200 examples, greedy (`temperature=0`, `max_tokens=2048`, `enable_thinking=false`): **79.5%** on main and **79.5%** on this PR, zero errors.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Same H200 and launch as above. `bench_serving` random dataset, 256 input / 256 output tokens fixed, one discarded warmup pass per concurrency, runs ordered main → PR → PR → main.

| | main (run 1 / run 2) | this PR (run 1 / run 2) | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `draft_decode` capture time | 0.00 s / 0.00 s | 1.64 s / 1.17 s | captured |
| Median TPOT, concurrency 1 | 5.30 / 5.33 ms | 3.53 / 3.54 ms | **−33%** |
| Median TPOT, concurrency 8 | 6.10 / 6.13 ms | 4.30 / 4.31 ms | **−30%** |
| Accept length | 1.95–1.96 | 1.95–1.96 | unchanged |

## Checklist

- [x] Pre-commit checks.
- [x] Draft graph captured for one-step drafts (`draft_decode` > 0), not before.
- [x] Greedy parity and 200-example GSM8K parity.
- [x] Same-device serving benchmarks, both orders.
- [x] No new configuration required.

title: [Refactor] dsv4: Keep only the two-level V4.1 indexer in the prefill graph
author: hnyls2002
body:
- The prefill CUDA graph captures the DeepSeek-V4.1 ratio-1/2 indexer only with two-level candidates (`SparseTableBackend`), the path released checkpoints take on SM100: `low_ratio_prefill_graph` now means exactly that and absorbs `_prefill_graph_two_level`. Any other config runs the ratio-1/2 sources as one eager break, as SM90 already does.
- Remove what served the other path: the captured full top-k (`FullTopKIndexer.topk_prefill_captured`, `topk_transform_paged_torch`) with its candidate-window assert, and the c1/c2 paged indexer metadata every replay built for it (full-width page tables, row chunks, DeepGEMM schedules). The captured consumer read only the index page size from that metadata, now `CapturedPrefillInputs.index_page_size`; `refresh_for_breakable_cuda_graph_replay_` drops `two_level`, and `PagedIndexerMetadata` drops `row_chunk`.
- Remove `SGLANG_DSV41_TORCH_PREFILL_INDEXER`, a development switch that forced the torch prefill indexer on SM100; SM90 keeps the torch indexer. HIP states `low_ratio_prefill_graph = False` instead of borrowing the CUDA property, which reads the CUDA backend's candidate indexer.

No behavior change for released checkpoints: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 set `candidate_topk_blocks: 2048`, so SM100 already runs the two-level path and SM90 the eager break; a replay just no longer builds metadata that nothing reads. Supersedes #45073.

title: [Feat] paged-experts: AWQ, compressed-tensors, MXFP4, NVFP4, W8A8 and block-INT8 experts
author: N3mezis
body:
# [Feature] Paged Experts: AWQ, compressed-tensors, MXFP4, NVFP4, W8A8 and block-INT8 experts

## Motivation

This PR aims at improving Paged Experts' (#42557) format compatibility. It currently only supports unquantized, block-FP8 and GPTQ experts.

These formats will be supported: 
| Experts | MoE runner | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| unquantized (bf16/fp16) | triton | already supported |
| block-quantized FP8 | triton | already supported |
| GPTQ int4/int8 | Marlin | already supported |
| AWQ int4 | Marlin | new |
| compressed-tensors W4A16/W8A16 | Marlin | new |
| compressed-tensors NVFP4 | Marlin | new; weight-only (nvfp4a16, or w4a4 before Blackwell) |
| MXFP4 (gpt-oss) | Marlin | new; `--moe-runner-backend marlin` |
| ModelOpt NVFP4 | Marlin | new; `--moe-runner-backend marlin`, runs W4A16 |
| compressed-tensors FP8, per-channel or block, dynamic activations | triton | new (e.g. `FP8-dynamic` checkpoints) |
| W8A8 FP8 (`--quantization w8a8_fp8`) | triton | new |
| W8A8 INT8 (`--quantization w8a8_int8`) | triton | new |
| block-quantized INT8 | triton | new |

## Modifications

**Derived formats** (`formats.py`, `runners.py`). #42557 declares each format by hand: which tensors are loaded and paged, whether the post-load step repacks, which runner contract applies. Adding the five Marlin formats in that style showed it fails silently:
- an unlisted tensor is not paged, so paged-in experts run with another expert's values (AWQ control with the zero points unpaged: median 1.67 nats, against 0.003 paged);
- the declared runner can differ from the one the layer builds (ModelOpt NVFP4 defaults to FlashInfer CUTLASS, which sums the top-k inside the kernel; compressed-tensors int4 defaults to Triton WNA16 on SM100);
- each repacking format needed a hook to reset its "already converted" flag (ModelOpt `_w13_deinterleaved`, compressed-tensors `is_marlin_converted`), or every chunk after the first stayed in the checkpoint layout;
- repacking K experts at a time was assumed valid, never checked.

Paged experts now derives these from the layer, as SGLang already does elsewhere (EPLB's `filter_moe_weight_param_global_expert`; the runner backend as execution contract):
- **Expert tensors:** every `w13_*`/`w2_*` parameter with one row per local expert. Tensors sized for all experts (`_sglang_require_global_experts`) stay whole on the GPU. Biases, zero points and kernel padding need no code.
- **Runner contract:** from the runner the base method builds (its own, its scheme's, or its scheme kernel's). Triton → masked waves; Marlin → compacted waves, with the post-load repack run over the host store K experts at a time. Any other runner is rejected at startup with a message naming it and `--moe-runner-backend`.
- **Repack state:** the layer's attributes are snapshotted before the first chunk and restored before each later one.
- **Independence check:** one more chunk, experts 1..K, must reproduce their bytes from the first pass; startup fails if the post-load step mixes experts.
- **Format classes:** every format, main's three included, is a `supports` check (8–19 lines), plus an `unpaged` or `freed` tuple for three of them and a runner route for compressed-tensors W4A16. `formats.py` is 340 lines for twelve formats (main: 184 for three; the declared version: 389 for eight). The four triton formats were added after the refactor as a test of it; they needed one shared fix, letting the triton contract find a runner held on the layer's scheme.

**Loading** (`method.py`):
- Stacked checkpoint tensors (all experts in one tensor, e.g. gpt-oss) go to the layer's native loader on the whole host store, as called.
- Loaders of vLLM-style parameters (read-only `weight_loader` property) are redirected through `_weight_loader`.
- The host store starts from each parameter's created values instead of uninitialized memory, so what a loader leaves unwritten matches the GPU. No format on main loads partially, but Marlin pads gpt-oss-20b's MXFP4 experts (2880 → 2944 / 3072) and its loader fills only the checkpoint's part: without this, paged gpt-oss-20b scores GSM8K 0.000 with every answer truncated; with it, 0.960 (unpaged 0.975). `test_host_store_starts_from_the_created_values` fails without it.
- compressed-tensors W4A16/W8A16 waves run through the scheme's Marlin runner: the scheme's own `apply` calls the kernel directly and sums the top-k outputs.

**Prefill capture:** the paged break skips its waves while a breakable graph captures it (a `capture_stub`), since the routing ids are not computed yet then; warmup and replay run them as before. Without it, gpt-oss-20b paged an out-of-range expert id at capture and failed to start.

**Kernel** (`paged_experts.cuh`): the gather copies rows of any even byte size (16-, 4- or 2-byte loads). NVFP4 on Marlin keeps one bf16 global scale per expert, a 2-byte row.

**Runner output:** the top-k sum is trimmed to the input's hidden size (MXFP4 Marlin pads it, 2880 → 3072 on gpt-oss-20b).

## Accuracy Tests

**Repack, byte oracle.** The real post-load step on a full layer vs K experts at a time through `_repack`: byte-identical in all 8 cases (AWQ; compressed-tensors int4 symmetric, asymmetric, act-order, and int8; compressed-tensors NVFP4 with and without w4a4 input scales; MXFP4).

**Paged vs unpaged, 4-layer test models** (E=32, top-4, K=8; prompt and greedy decode logprobs, without deterministic inference; RTX 5070 Ti):

| model | runner | prompt median / max | decode max |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-MoE bf16 | triton | identical | identical |
| Qwen2-MoE bf16 (shared expert) | triton | identical | identical |
| gpt-oss bf16 (biases) | triton | identical | identical |
| compressed-tensors FP8, per-channel | triton | identical | identical |
| compressed-tensors FP8, block 128×128 | triton | identical | identical |
| W8A8 FP8 (same checkpoint, `--quantization w8a8_fp8`) | triton | identical | identical |
| W8A8 INT8 | triton | identical | identical |
| block INT8 | triton | identical | identical |
| gpt-oss MXFP4 | Marlin | identical | identical |
| AWQ int4 | Marlin | 0.0033 / 0.012 | 0.015 |
| compressed-tensors W4A16, symmetric | Marlin | 0.029 / 0.64 | 0.12 |
| compressed-tensors W4A16, asymmetric | Marlin | 0.021 / 1.02 | 0.20 |
| compressed-tensors NVFP4 | Marlin | 0.044 / 1.20 | 0.99 |

Marlin is not batch-invariant, and on SM90+ not run-to-run reproducible, so its formats are judged against controls with one tensor deliberately not paged:

| model | paged median diff | control: tensor not paged | control median diff |
|---|---|---|---|
| AWQ | 0.0033 | zero points | 1.67 |
| compressed-tensors int4 | 0.021–0.029 | zero points | 2.06 |
| compressed-tensors NVFP4 | 0.044–0.058 (unpaged vs unpaged: 0.004–0.026) | global scales | 0.47 |

**GSM8K (200 questions), RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB:**

| model | experts resident | main | this PR, paged | unpaged |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-30B-A3B-GPTQ-Int4 | 92 of 128 | 0.935 | 0.945 | — (does not fit) |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 (block) | 40 of 128 | 0.955 | 0.950 | — (does not fit) |
| gpt-oss-20b MXFP4 | 16 of 32 | not supported | 0.960 / 0.970 / 0.960 (3 runs) | 0.975 |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B ModelOpt NVFP4 (`--moe-runner-backend marlin`) | 85 of 128 | not supported | 0.935 | — (does not fit) |

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Output tok/s, paged, RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB:

| model | | bs=1 | 4 concurrent | 2k prompt, bs=1 | weight load |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-30B-A3B-GPTQ-Int4, K=92 | main | 190.3 | 372.2 | 152.3 | 32.2 s |
| | this PR | 190.5 | 373.1 | 152.4 | 37.4 s |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8, K=40 | main | 80.3 | 84.8 | 78.8 | 54.5 s |
| | this PR | 80.5 | 82.5 | 79.0 | 49.2 s |
| gpt-oss-20b MXFP4, K=16 | this PR | 107.7 | 140.1 | 96.2 | 18.8 s |

Weight load on the Marlin runner grows by the independence check, one extra repack chunk per layer: 32.2 → 37.4 s on Qwen3-30B-A3B-GPTQ-Int4.

## CI

`test_paged_experts.py` gets a fourth case, gpt-oss-20b MXFP4 on the Marlin runner (compared like GPTQ). It covers what no other real checkpoint does: stacked checkpoint tensors, per-expert biases, and padding by the runner (host store init, output trim). `openai/gpt-oss-20b` is already used by six registered tests. `est_time` goes from 360 to 450 s; the 360 s was measured (313 s warm on an H100), the new case's ~90 s is an estimate. Other new coverage: the CPU unit test (23 tests, 15 on main) and the kernel test (2- and 6-byte rows).

- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).

title: [Perf] QSA: Optimize prefill indexer in long cached prefixes
author: Shunkangz
body: ## Motivation This PR speeds up the Qwen3.8 QSA prefill indexer when a batch contains many requests with long cached prefixes. Previously, each query row’s score buffer had space for all compressed keys in the batch. The PR stores scores in request-relative columns, reducing the buffer width to the longest request’s compressed-key count. ## Modifications The implementation: - Removes batch-wide zero-fill and masking; top-k reads only each row’s valid scores. - Fits more query rows into the same workspace budget, reducing scoring chunks and kernel launches. - Derives buffer width from CPU sequence lengths to avoid an additional GPU synchronization. - Splits key ranges across GPU blocks to improve parallelism. ## Accuracy Tests ## Speed Tests and Profiling Before this PR After this PR ## Checklist - [ ] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit). - [ ] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests). - [ ] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations). - [ ] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed). - [ ] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance). ## Review and Merge Process 1. title: [Perf] [NVIDIA] deepseek-v4.1: Align BF16 prefill indexer score width
author: BJWang-ant
body: ## Motivation The DeepSeek V4.1 Torch prefill indexer computes BF16 scores over request-local compressed keys. On H200, unaligned visible lengths such as 28,799 and 57,343 are significantly slower than nearby 64-aligned lengths. Padding the score width to a multiple of 64 improves GEMM alignment while preserving the logical scoring range. ## Modifications - Restore request-row mapping from per-request local token counts when `req_rows` is `None` under CP. - For BF16 device tensors with a visible length of at least 1,024, pad the dequantized index-key tensor to a multiple of 64 once per request and reuse it across query chunks. - Calculate query chunk sizes using the padded width to respect the existing score-tensor memory budget. - Slice scores back to the logical visible length before causal masking and top-k selection, so padded positions cannot enter selection. ## Accuracy Tests Local validation on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash: - 20 CP request-row mapping cases passed. - 12 score-shape and boundary cases using model-style FP4 inputs passed with exact agreement on valid columns. - 8 Prefill integration cases passed with exact raw-index and KV-slot writeback agreement. - 8 synthetic arithmetic/retrieval probes at approximately 32K and 64K context lengths matched the reference outputs. GSM8K, 1,319 examples per run: | Configuration | Accuracy | Request error rate | | --- | ---: | ---: | | Fresh baseline, run 1 | 96.74% | 0% | | Fresh baseline, run 2 | 96.36% | 0% | | Optimized | 96.74% | 0% | The baseline A/A runs show run-to-run variation. These results do not establish bitwise equivalence of complete generated outputs or replace representative long-context quality evaluation. ## Speed Tests and Profiling ### Setup - Model: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. - Hardware: 8 × NVIDIA H200. - Prefill: TP4 / CP4 / EP4. - Decode: TP4 / DP4 / EP4. - Prefill BCG: disabled. - Decode and router processes held fixed across comparisons. Both baseline and optimized runs include the same CP request-row mapping fix. The measured differences therefore isolate the score-width alignment change. ### End-to-end benchmark Primary workload: all input 65,536, cache hit rate 50%,70%,90%, output 512 tokens. Results are means of three runs with 512 requests each and 10 warmup requests per run. ### Scoring microbenchmark Timings include the scoring epilogue and, for the optimized implementation, padding. | Query rows | Logical score width | Baseline | Optimized | Reduction | | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 582 | 28,799 | 4.113 ms | 2.462 ms | 40.1% | | 292 | 57,343 | 4.088 ms | 2.472 ms | 39.5% | | 582 | 28,800, already aligned | 2.443 ms | 2.445 ms | Approximately unchanged | ### Trace before-cp-rank0: before-cp-rank1: before-cp-rank2: before-cp-rank3: cur-cp-rank0: cur-cp-rank1: cur-cp-rank2: cur-cp-rank3: ## Checklist - [x] Format code with pre-commit. - [ ] Add CI-registered regression tests. - [ ] Update documentation, if required. - [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results. - [x] Follow the existing code style. --- ### CI States Latest PR Test (Base): :x: [Run #39758846111](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/39758846111) Latest PR Test (Extra): :x: [Run #39758846147](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/39758846147) Latest PR Test (AMD ROCm 10): :x: [Run #39758846145](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/39758846145)

title: [Fix] GLM: Preserve NextN PTPC quantization for excluded experts
author: lunarwhite
body:
## Motivation

With `SGLANG_GLM_NEXTN_MOE_PTPC=1`, GLM NextN adds a per-channel FP8 scheme for routed experts, but also maps checkpoint per-expert excludes into runtime names. Quark treats those leaf exclusions as excluding the fused expert module, so its quantization method is never selected even though the loader converts the expert weights to FP8.

## Modifications

Skip mapped routed-expert leaf exclusions when the existing PTPC predicate is enabled. Preserve checkpoint exclusions for loading, other runtime exclusions, flag-off behavior, and the shared-expert fusion guard. Add a regression using Quark's actual ignore predicate.

## Accuracy Tests

Using the same test file on base and patched trees:

- Existing registered PTPC suite: base reproduces the new assertion; patched passes all 12 tests without skips.
- CPU component check with real QuarkConfig and FusedMoE types: base selects no quant method with PTPC enabled; patched selects QuarkFusedMoEMethod and the per-channel FP8 scheme. The real parameter loader correctly places both experts' gate/up/down weights and scales. Flag-off and shared-expert BF16 behavior are preserved.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Not measured; this fixes quantization configuration selection and makes no performance claim.

title: [Fix] [AMD] quark: Skip no-copy loads after MXFP4 quantization
author: lunarwhite
body:
## Motivation

With expert parallelism, the online Quark MXFP4 loader can receive a nonlocal expert after finishing its local weights. The underlying loader correctly copies nothing, but the wrapper compares the accumulated BF16 element count with the now-packed parameter size and raises an assertion. This affects online-quantized MoE loading, including the Qwen3.5 MTP path on ROCm.

## Modifications

Return after a zero-copy load, following weight-name validation. Local copies retain the existing completion and quantization logic. Add CPU regressions for both packed weight parameters and invalid names.

## Accuracy Tests

CPU test file: `test/registered/unit/layers/quantization/test_quark_w4a4_mxfp4_moe.py` 5 passed. The two new no-copy cases fail without the fix; the invalid-name case rejects an incorrectly placed early return.

On an MI355X with real AITER quantization, compared base `9301ca37` with the three-line fix: six loading sequences and sixteen controls per version passed the expected base-failure/head-success checks. Packed weights and scales matched direct-quantization references and corresponding EP1/EP2 expert fixtures. Invalid names and duplicate local loads retained their expected errors.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Not applicable: the change handles a no-copy call during weight loading; no inference-speed claim.

title: [Perf] fp8: Hopper small-M GEMV, fused KDA output quant, CUDA grouped top-k, partial-block tails
author: JustinTong0323
body:
## Motivation

Split out from the Ling-3.1-flash day-0 support effort.

Block-FP8 decode on Hopper spends small-M linear work in GEMM kernels that are built for large batches, the KDA output normalization and FP8 quantization run as separate kernels, the 512-expert sigmoid router goes through a generic Triton top-k, and weights whose K dimension is not a multiple of the 128-wide quantization block cannot use the native Triton/DeepGEMM paths at all. This PR adds opt-in fast paths for each, with explicit dispatch contracts and no change to default behavior.

Measured on H200 with Ling-3.1-flash (FP8, TP8+EP8+NEXTN, fp32 router as on current main): batch-size-1 decode output throughput **+7.3%** (218.6 → 234.6 tok/s), median TPOT **−8.5%**, both environment flags on vs current main; throughput at concurrency 16 is unchanged. Accuracy on full GSM8K is unchanged (see below).

## Modifications

- **Hopper small-M GEMV** (`SGLANG_ENABLE_FP8_BLOCK_GEMV`, default off): CUDA block-FP8 GEMV for M≤8 with optional fused side projection, and a BF16 tiny GEMV (N≤64, M≤4, SM90 only) under `--bf16-gemm-backend gemv`. Dispatch checks device, dtype, layout, scale grid, and shape; anything else keeps the existing path. Also a CUDA router gate matvec (fp32/bf16 weight) for the Bailing-class gate shape, gated the same way.
- **Fused KDA output quant** (`SGLANG_ENABLE_FUSED_KDA_OUTPUT_QUANT`, default off): the gated RMSNorm at the KDA output fuses with FP8 quantization, emitting the `(q, scale)` tuple the FP8 o_proj consumes; requires target-verify batches and BF16, falls back otherwise.
- **CUDA grouped top-k** for the 512-expert / 8-group / group-top-4 / topk≤8 sigmoid routing shape. Dispatch is shape-driven (no model check): any model with the matching shape uses it, everything else keeps the Triton path. Shared-slot weighting follows the same contract as `moe_fused_gate` (incl. `renormalize=False` and zero-score semantics).
- **Partial-block FP8 support** (opt-in per layer): serialized block-FP8 weights whose K crosses a quantization block boundary — partial-block quant/GEMM in the native Triton MoE, a `prequant_k_tail` dispatcher for pre-quantized inputs (DeepGEMM only when the TMA alignment contract holds: contiguous operands, base pointer and K divisible by 16), and fused SwiGLU+quant for two-group K-tails. All admission is opt-in and default-off; no in-tree model enables it yet (the Ling3 model PR follows separately).

Traces on H200 (bs=1 decode, flags on): the 510 dense FP8 GEMM calls move from DeepGEMM `sm90_fp8_gemm_1d2d` to the GEMV kernel, the 189 KDA norm+quant pairs collapse into the fused kernel, and the router matvec runs its CUDA path. On GB300 (SM103) every SM90-gated path is a no-op — OFF/ON kernel sequences are identical — while the shape-driven top-k runs normally.

## Accuracy Tests

- H200 8x, Ling-3.1-flash FP8, TP8+EP8+NEXTN, full GSM8K (1319 questions, temp 1.0, top_p 0.95, 2 rounds per mode): OFF 96.89% / stop 99.92% vs ON 97.04% / stop 99.89% (within ±0.5pp run noise). GB300 4x TP4+EP4: OFF 96.82% vs ON 96.97%, stop 99.92% both.
- Kernel numerics (H200 + GB300): new GEMV/side-projection, router matvec, fused KDA quant, grouped top-k (incl. `renormalize=False` shared-slot and zero-score cases), block quant tail, Triton K-tail (incl. aligned-K non-fusion and explicit zero clamp vs `None`) suites all pass; partial-K linear matches a dequant-fp32 reference on both the DeepGEMM route (K=160, descriptor built) and the Triton fallback (K=161). On GB300 the SM90-only suites skip cleanly and the K160 selector rejects with bitwise-generic output.
- Kimi-Linear-48B BF16 smoke (KDA fallback path): 100-question GSM8K 93.0%, stop 100%.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

H200, Ling-3.1-flash TP8+EP8+NEXTN, 3 rounds bs=1 (2048/512) + 2 rounds conc16 (8192/1024), `--flush-cache`, seed 11:

| workload | main | this PR (env off) | this PR (flags on) |
|---|---|---|---|
| bs=1 output tok/s | 218.6 | 221.6 (+1.4%) | 234.6 (+7.3%) |
| bs=1 median TPOT (ms) | 4.351 | 4.191 (−3.7%) | 3.981 (−8.5%) |
| conc16 output tok/s | 1087.6 | 1087.8 | 1094.9 (+0.7%, within run noise) |

The +1.4% with flags off comes from the shape-driven grouped top-k; the flags-on gain comes from the GEMV and fused KDA quant. The CUDA router matvec is neutral at fp32/M=4 (1.41 vs 1.30 ms in trace) and is not claimed as a speedup. Concurrency-16 gains are diluted by MoE/attention compute; low-batch decode is where these kernels pay.

Note: the K160 large-M specialization (H20-3e) is intentionally **not** in this PR — it needs qualifying-hardware evidence and will follow separately.

title: [Perf] DFLASH: route draft bf16 GEMMs through tuned dispatch on GB300
author: wookjeHan
body:
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->

<!-- PR title: [Type] scope: title, or [Type] [Hardware] scope: title.
Type: Feat, Fix, Refactor, Perf, Doc, Test, CI, or Chore.
Scope: any module or model name (no fixed list or letter-case restriction), e.g. attention, qwen3, or flash-attn.
Hardware: optional single tag without spaces. Use uppercase hardware tags (AMD, NVIDIA, NPU, MI300X), except for exactly these four spellings: Intel, Apple, Huawei, Ascend.
Title: no letter-case restriction.
Reverts: use GitHub's default title, Revert "original title".
Examples: [Fix] attention: Fix KV cache indexing; [Perf] [AMD] flash-attn: Optimize decode performance. -->

## Motivation

<!-- Describe the purpose and goals of this pull request. -->

At low concurrency the DFLASH draft model runs its bf16 linears at small M: one block of `num_draft_tokens` tokens per request. 
Two of its paths bypass SGLang's tuned bf16 GEMM dispatch and always use cuBLAS:

- `DFlashGroupedConv.kernel_projection` is a plain `nn.Linear`;
- the candidate head in `_project_candidate_logits` calls `torch.matmul` directly.

Most of the draft's other GEMM shapes have no GB300 tuned entry and fall back to cuBLAS, which is well below the memory bandwidth
limit at these M sizes. The exception is TP4 qkv at M = 8 and 16, which already used the split-K tactics of the "GB300 TP16" block.

## Modifications

<!-- Detail the changes made in this pull request. -->
- `models/dflash.py`
  - `kernel_projection` becomes `ReplicatedLinear`, so it goes through `UnquantizedLinearMethod.apply` and the tuned dispatch.
  - The candidate head calls `bf16_gemm_dispatch` when the backend is cutedsl/gemv and the weight is bf16 on CUDA; otherwise it
    keeps `torch.matmul`.
- `layers/quantization/unquant.py`: GB300 split-K / warp split-K entries at M <= 32, TP4 and TP8.
- `kernels/ops/gemm/cutedsl_bf16_gemm.py`: TGV M ranges for three shapes at M = 17..32.

Each entry was kept only if it beats the current kernel in all three timings of the micro-benchmark below.

The tables are keyed by (M, N, K) only, so the entries are not draft-specific:

- The qkv / gate_up / down shapes (hidden 8192, intermediate 28672, 64 q / 8 kv heads) are also those of Llama-3-70B-class dense
  models at TP4 and TP8. With the default `auto` backend on SM10x those models switch kernels at M <= 32 as well. Only GB300 was
  measured; GB200 was not.
- For TP4 qkv at M = 8 and 16, the new warp split-K entries replace the existing GB300 TP16 split-K tactics (warp split-K takes
  precedence). They are faster in all three timings; see the micro-benchmark.

title: [Perf] engram: Read host-table rows in address order on GPUs without host page tables
author: hnyls2002
body:
- `engram_gather` takes `sort_ids`: it sorts the ids, reads the rows in address order and stores each row at its original position. Output is bitwise identical.
- `EngramEmbedding` turns it on for host tables only when `CU_DEVICE_ATTRIBUTE_PAGEABLE_MEMORY_ACCESS_USES_HOST_PAGE_TABLES` is 0, i.e. the GPU maps pinned host memory in its own page tables (PCIe hosts). On NVLink-C2C hosts the attribute is 1, reads go through the host page tables, sorting only adds work, and the path is unchanged. Device tables and HIP are unchanged. No new flag.
- Why: random rows spread over a host table far larger than the GPU's address-translation reach miss on nearly every row; the same rows read in address order share pages, which makes the host-table lookup several times faster on PCIe hosts.

No behavior change except the order of host-table reads on GPUs without host page tables.

Verification: bitwise-equal gather output; DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash DEP4 with host Engram tables on a PCIe host is faster in prefill, and on an NVLink-C2C host the path is not taken (throughput unchanged); GSM8K unchanged.

title: [Perf] dsv4: Score the V4.1 index logits in bf16 on SM100
author: hnyls2002
body:
- On SM100, the DeepSeek-V4.1 ratio-1/2 index layers now pass bf16 head weights and request bf16 logits from DeepGEMM's `fp8_fp4_mqa_logits` / `fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits`, so the kernels reduce in bf16. This is the configuration the reference kernels use on SM100: they take bf16 head weights only and emit bf16 logits there. The sparse candidate path already used bf16 weights and logits.
- The dtype is decided once (`index_logits_dtype()` / `index_weights_dtype()` in `index_logits.py`), resolved on first use so importing the module does not touch CUDA.
- `SGLANG_OPT_DSV41_BF16_INDEX_LOGITS` now defaults to unset: unset means bf16 on SM100 and fp32 elsewhere; setting it keeps working as an explicit override (true: bf16 logits, with bf16 head weights on SM100 only; false: the fp32 path everywhere). Recipes that set it to 1 are unaffected except that SM100 now also passes bf16 head weights.

No change on other architectures (SM90 keeps the torch indexer; SM120 keeps fp32 weights and logits), or anywhere the flag is set to false.

Verification: a dispatch check over SM100 / non-SM100 with the flag unset, true and false gives the expected head-weight and logits dtypes on both the flat and paged calls; on SM100 with no env set the branch resolves to bf16 logits and bf16 head weights at runtime; the existing V4.1 indexer unit tests pass.

- Flat prefill logits tiles are now sized as fp32 logits whatever the logits dtype (`flat_index_logits_rows_per_tile`), as its docstring intended: with bf16 logits the old formula doubled the rows per tile, so the per-row selection scratch that grows with the tile pushed the scoring peak past the fp32 path's budget. fp32 tiling is unchanged. The SM100 prefill indexer tests now score their reference in the indexer's dtypes and accept block or pick differences only where bf16 scores tie at the selection floor; they pass with bf16 (the SM100 default) and with `SGLANG_OPT_DSV41_BF16_INDEX_LOGITS=0`.

title: [Fix] moe: Broadcast scalar block scales correctly with swap_ab on Triton 3.9
author: janbernloehr
body:
## Motivation

Fixes https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/45887.

On SM90, block-FP8 MoE can select `swap_ab` while the weight scale is rank 0 (`BLOCK_SIZE_N <= group_n`). Swapping the operands also swaps their scales, so the current expression slices a scalar as `a_scale[:, None]`. Triton 3.9 rejects this after [triton-lang/triton#10429](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/pull/10429), causing DeepSeek-R1 FP8 startup to fail during prefill CUDA graph capture.

## Modifications

- Add the scalar-scale `swap_ab` case: multiply the scalar weight scale by `b_scale[None, :]`, placing the per-token scales along the transposed dot product's last axis.
- Add a numerical regression test covering swapped and unswapped operands with `BLOCK_SIZE_N=64,128,256` and `group_n=128`. Nonuniform activation/weight scales, two K groups, permuted tokens, padding and routed weights check the output against independently dequantized PyTorch matmul.

## Accuracy Tests

The current kernel's six regression configurations were checked against the PyTorch reference through Triton's CPU interpreter on 3.8.0 and the 3.9 nightly build `3.9.0+gitfc8d31a5`, using FP8 inputs and FP32 outputs (`rtol=2e-4`, `atol=2e-4`). Offline compilation for SM90 with that 3.9 nightly passes all six patched cases. The unpatched upstream kernel fails exactly the two scalar-scale cases (`swap_ab=True`, `BLOCK_SIZE_N=64,128`) with `too many indices for tensor of rank 0`; the four other cases compile. This is kernel numerical and compiler validation; no full-model accuracy evaluation was run. The registered CUDA test has not been executed on a GPU in this chat.

Existing validation of the same arithmetic change on SGLang `c1c287a42` ran DeepSeek-R1 FP8 on 2×8 H100 80GB, TP16, with DP attention off and default MoE/CUDA graph settings. The unmodified server failed on Triton `3.9.0+gitaad2a60d`; the patched server started and served. That run predates this branch and does not validate every subsequent upstream change or the new test's GPU execution.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Existing paired serving measurements used the same public base-image digest, SGLang `c1c287a42`, checkpoint and launch flags. Benchmark: 8,000 input / 1,000 output tokens; one run per arm. Output throughput:

| Concurrency | Unpatched, Triton 3.8.0 | Patched, Triton 3.9.0+gitaad2a60d |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 76.24 tok/s | 75.62 tok/s |
| 64 | 734.19 tok/s | 737.21 tok/s |
| 256 | 753.10 tok/s | 755.11 tok/s |

Differences range from −0.81% to +0.41%; a single run per arm is not enough to establish a performance improvement. No profiling trace was collected. H200/H20, other models and DP attention were not run end to end.

title: [Feat] lora: Add plan-driven dense and MoE LoRA engines
author: jybsuper
body:
## Motivation

Provide a single-PR alternative for merging the complete, currently published 21-part LoRA runtime stack. This is the same implementation and history, not a separate development variant.

The existing stacked PRs remain open and unchanged. Choose one merge route; this PR does not add a 22nd feature layer.

## Modifications

- Plan-driven dense LoRA execution through `triton_v2`, shared routing/workspace management, grouped and per-row shrink/expand kernels, and shipped SM90/SM100 plans.
- LoRA-free decode graphs, absorbed-MLA corrections, and Inkling shared-sink integration.
- Per-expert and shared-outer MoE LoRA execution, with Triton/CuTeDSL BF16 and FP8 providers and the Marlin NVFP4 provider.
- The stack's existing correctness, CUDA-graph, numerical, serving-integration tests and runtime configuration tables.

This branch reuses the final stack commit directly: no squash, rebase, cherry-pick, source edit, or additional commit. Benchmark/tuning tools and the deferred Triton MoE tuning-table changes from the development branch are intentionally excluded, exactly as in the stack.

title: [Perf] dsv41: Serve token-interleaved V4.1 KV caches with sgl-flash-mla
author: DarkSharpness
body:
> (auto generated by Claude)

## Motivation

FlashMLA's 2026.09.30 V4.1 kernels read a token-interleaved KV cache and are faster at decode. They ship in the `sgl-flash-mla` wheel (release workflow #45651), which also carries every pre-release kernel sglang uses behind `use_legacy=True`. This moves all CUDA FlashMLA calls to that wheel and adds the interleaved layout as an opt-in, so existing deployments are unchanged.

Supersedes the serving side of #45635 (co-authored), keeping the block-split `v41` layout so gfx950 / aiter_sparse keeps working.

## Modifications

- New `SGLANG_DSV4_KV_LAYOUT=v41_new` (`KVLayout.V41_NEW` / `V41_FP4_NEW`): the V4.1 bytes interleaved per token, unpadded. `v41` keeps the block-split layout. Writers, dequant and the request-window copy address both through `row_addressing`; the PD layout string names the arrangement, so mismatched prefill / decode pairs are refused.
- `sglang.kernels.ops.attention.flash_mla_interface` wraps the wheel with the call signatures of the former `sgl_kernel.flash_mla` / `flash_mla_mega` ops. Old kernels default to `use_legacy=True`; only `V41_NEW` uses the current kernels. The V3/R1 dense, V3.2 DSA and DSv4 backends import from it; HIP / XPU keep their sgl-kernel ops.
- Decode skips the schedule precompute when the current kernel does not split the KV (`topk + extra_topk <= 640`).
- `KVLayout` properties are `functools.cached_property`.
- Adds `sgl-flash-mla` to the dependencies.

## Accuracy and speed

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, 4x B200, TP4 / EP4 / DSpark, sgl-eval with temperature 1.0 / top_p 0.95:

| | v41 | v41_new |
|---|---|---|
| gsm8k (1319) | 96.66 | 96.51 |
| ruler2 64K (240 x 3) | 86.31 / 87.03 (two servers) | 87.57 |
| decode TPOT, 8K in / 1K out, concurrency 16 | 2.50 / 2.46 ms | 2.41 / 2.35 ms |

Greedy ruler2 outputs agree as often across layouts (65.0%) as across two v41 servers (66.7%). On the same tokens the current and legacy V4.1 sparse decode kernels give bitwise-identical outputs.

## Checklist

- [ ] Pin `sgl-flash-mla` to the first published version (`1.0.0` is not on PyPI yet)

title: [Perf] dsv4: Drop local references that keep residual-stream tensors alive through the prefill step
author: hnyls2002
body:
- In `DeepseekV4Model`, three local names kept a full residual-stream tensor alive longer than needed during a prefill step:
  - `before_engram` in the Engram block held the pre-Engram residual until the next Engram layer; the image-row `torch.where` now reads `state.residual`, which is the same tensor at that point.
  - `aux` in the DSpark capture block kept the captured residual after its mean was appended; it is now deleted.
  - `_forward_impl` kept a reference to the layer input while `_forward_layers_hc_pre_from_prev` ran; it now hands the tensor over without a caller-frame reference, so the layer loop can free it once the first residual replaces it.
- At large prefill batches each of these is a multi-GiB tensor; holding them raises the in-step peak and, after partial steps, forces an allocator retry that can fail with fragmentation at high `--mem-fraction-static`.

No behavior change: the same values are computed; only tensor lifetimes are shorter.

Verification: the in-step memory peak of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash DEP4 prefill at large batches drops and consecutive full-size steps no longer need an allocator retry; throughput is unchanged; GSM8K is unchanged.

title: [Perf] dsv4: Write the MegaAttention output straight into the prefill graph buffer
author: hnyls2002
body:
- The breakable prefill graph's MegaAttention break computed `_mega_core` into a fresh tensor and then copied it into the graph's output buffer, one device-to-device copy of the attention output per layer per step.
- `_mega_core` takes an optional `out` and passes it to the wo_a einsum, and the break passes `output[:real_num_tokens]`, so the einsum writes the graph buffer directly.

No behavior change: the output is bit-identical; the copy is gone. Other callers of `_mega_core` pass no `out` and are unchanged.

Verification: outputs are identical with and without the change; the device-to-device copy disappears from the prefill-graph profile; prefill with the breakable graph is slightly faster at small batches.

title: [Perf] dsv4: Use the fused MXFP8 producers in eager prefill
author: hnyls2002
body:
- `fused_mxfp8_rows` in `deepseek_v4_mhc.py` decides when the mHC post and RMSNorm steps write MXFP8 activations directly for the next DeepGEMM consumer instead of writing bf16 and quantizing in a separate kernel.
- It previously returned `False` for every extend batch, so eager prefill always paid the separate quantize pass.
- Extend batches now take the fused path, except inside a breakable prefill graph, where the captured buffers stay bf16. Decode and verify keep the existing row cap, and sequence-parallel batches stay excluded.

No change to the computed values: the fused producer emits the same MXFP8 tensor the separate quantize kernel produced.

Verification: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash DEP4 eager prefill is faster at large batches; the breakable-graph prefill path is unchanged; GSM8K is unchanged.

title: [Perf] dsv4: Keep V4.1 image rows inside the Engram gate kernel
author: hnyls2002
body:
- After each Engram layer, DeepSeek-V4.1 put the pre-Engram residual back on image-token rows with a separate full-width `torch.where` over the residual stream. It ran on every forward, including text-only batches where it selected nothing, and allocated a second residual-sized output.
- The Engram gate kernel now takes the layer's input ids and the image token id, and stores the unchanged residual for image rows in the same pass. The `torch.where` and its extra output are gone.
- `Engram` now takes `image_token_id`, as `EngramHasher` already does. It is set only for V4.1 checkpoints with a vision tower, and both read it from one helper, `_engram_image_token_id`. Other models pass no ids and run the kernel unchanged.
- The ids are the model's prepared input ids (multimodal pad ids already mapped to the image token id), the same tensor the old select read. Under the breakable prefill graph, the kernel reads them from the captured buffer at replay.
- The torch fallback path applies the same select after its gate.

Output is bitwise identical to before, for text rows and image rows, in eager mode and in graph replay.

Verification:
- The fused kernel matches the old gate + `torch.where` bit for bit. This covers several batch sizes, bf16 and fp32 activations and weights, int32 and int64 ids, and no, some, or all image rows. A captured CUDA graph reads the live ids at replay.
- A micro benchmark with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash shapes on B300 and GB300 shows the fused kernel well ahead of the old gate + select at every prefill size tested, with and without image rows.

title: [Feat] openai: parse DeepSeek output through deepseek-recipe
author: zhendonghua
body:
Stage B of the deepseek-recipe integration, stacked on #45315 (Python host; its commits show in this diff until it merges). Under `--chat-encoding-backend recipe`, the output of DeepSeek-V4 / V4.1 is parsed by [deepseek-recipe](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-recipe)'s `StreamProcessor` instead of SGLang's `deepseek-v41` reasoning and `deepseekv41` tool-call detectors, so the prompt (stage A) and the output come from the one implementation of the format, the one behind the official API. The builtin backend is untouched.

## What changes

- `parser/deepseek_recipe_output.py`: `DeepSeekRecipeOutputParser` feeds the engine's token ids to recipe's `StreamProcessor` (markup is recognized by token id only) and yields `RecipeOutputDelta`s; a matched stop string is cut in the raw ids where the scheduler matched it, a matched stop token is dropped, and `no_stop_trim` keeps either, as the detokenizer does for text. `serving_deepseek_recipe.py`: the adapter implements the `ChatEncodingOutputAdapter` seam of #45300 itself, as the Inkling adapter does; it maps the deltas to SGLang's chunks, messages and Responses items. The handler keeps its role, finish and usage chunks, logprobs, `matched_stop` and `sglext`. `select_new_output_ids` moves to `chat_encoding_adapters.py`, shared with Inkling.
- All four output paths: Chat Completions streaming and non-streaming, Responses streaming and non-streaming. The two Responses protocol methods gain `request` and `require_reasoning`, which the parser needs for the thinking mode and the stop strings; both call sites had them in scope.
- SGLang's `separate_reasoning=false` (reasoning folded into `content`) and `stream_reasoning=false` (reasoning withheld until it ends) keep working.
- Startup: the recipe backend requires `--reasoning-parser deepseek-v4` / `deepseek-v41` and `--tool-call-parser deepseekv4` / `deepseekv41`, what `auto` selects, because the engine's think-end token and the tool-choice grammar still come from them.
- `server_arguments.mdx` row.

## Client-visible changes, recipe backend only

- Streamed tool-call arguments arrive incrementally, as the API streams them: the first chunk carries `id`, `function.name` and `arguments: ""`, later chunks carry pieces of the JSON. SGLang's detector emitted the whole arguments when the invoke tag closed. Clients that concatenate, as the OpenAI SDK does, are unaffected; clients that parsed each chunk's `arguments` as complete JSON must concatenate.
- Tool-call ids use the API's format (`call_00_` + 20 random characters + 4-digit checksum, an `ET_` marker on thinking turns that produced no reasoning) instead of `call_` + 24 hex characters.
- Reasoning / content boundaries follow recipe: leading newlines after `<think>` and `</think>` are dropped, a second `</think>` is dropped, text after the calls block is dropped. Matched stops are cut wherever the engine matched them, in reasoning or in content.
- `finish_reason` is recipe's (`tool_calls` once a call was named, which is what the builtin path reported too). `usage.reasoning_tokens` and `completion_tokens` stay the engine's exact counts.
- Thinking-mode requests sample at the API's temperature 1.0 and top_p even when the request asks for 0 (recipe's sampling overlay from #45315); the no-thinking path honours the request. The flag's docs row now says so.
- Requests served through sgl-router or sglang-server keep the Rust parsers until the Rust stage lands (a separate PR after #45715): whole tool-call arguments, ids in the old format.

## Tests

`test/registered/unit/parser/test_deepseek_recipe_output.py`: the outputs of `deepseek_recipe_golden.json` (sampled ids parsed by deepseek-recipe's own stream processor, whole and token by token: calls, parallel calls, cuts by `max_tokens`, `tool_choice` none, plain-token spellings of the markers, a stray `</think>`, a stop sequence, JSON output, prefix continuations), the matched-stop cut table (across tokens, inside a token, in reasoning, plain and special stop tokens, overlapping matches, `no_stop_trim`), the SGLang switches. `test/registered/unit/entrypoints/openai/test_serving_deepseek_recipe.py`: the parser pairing check, the package check, the served-tokenizer markers, the Responses handler's hooks; the chat adapter's tool-call output whole and streamed with `tool_choice` none and `separate_reasoning=False`, every token parsed once (cumulative and incremental chunks, the abort re-send, tokens appended after a chunk), matched stops in both response modes, prefix continuations. `test_serving_responses.py`: stream and non-stream Responses items from the same ids at several split points, with `tool_choice` auto and required. `deepseek_recipe_served.json` (recorded from a live V4.1-Flash server by `test/manual/parser/record_deepseek_recipe_served.py`, 14 temperature-0 requests with the prompt ids and output ids the server reported): `test_served_prompts_match` renders each request and asserts the live prompt ids; `test_served_outputs_replay` parses the live output ids whole and token by token, asserts the served message, and checks that SGLang's own DeepSeek parsers read the same reasoning, content and calls from the same ids. The e2e run on 4x B300 (both backends, chat + Responses, stream + non-stream, GSM8K) is reported in the PR comments.

## Review follow-ups

- Self-review: `RecipeStream` takes the encoder; `_accumulate` is named after recipe's own term; comments trimmed. Merged main through #45315 (field-order conflict only).
- Round 2: layout follows #45340 (`parser/deepseek_recipe_output.py` + serving glue, the adapter implements the output seam itself); the matched stop string is cut in the ids and `no_stop_trim` is honored; test coverage mirrors #45340's, with a library-generated golden fixture.

title: [Perf] dsv4: Dequantize each shared sparse-prefill KV source once per forward
author: hnyls2002
body:
- DeepSeek-V4.1's ratio-1/2 layers read the compressed KV of a few kv_source layers, and sparse prefill dequantized that cache into the shared buffer in every one of them. The layers that share a source now reuse its dequant: no later layer of the forward writes that cache, and graph replay keeps the layer order.
- `SparsePrefillWorkspace` is renamed `SparsePrefillKVBuffer` and owns the reuse. `get_with_head` returns the rows and whether the head already holds the given source (source cache, gather ids, row count). A plain `get`, a reallocation, or the start of a new forward forgets the head.

Outputs are unchanged: the skipped dequants would have written the same rows.

Verification:
- Every reused dequant in a DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash DEP4 prefill run matched a fresh dequant of the same rows.
- GPU profiles on B300 and GB300 show the sparse-prefill KV dequant running once per kv_source instead of once per layer, with no other kernel or copy added. Prefill step time drops on both at every batch size tested, with and without the prefill graph.
- No out-of-memory at the recipe memory fraction; GSM8K is unchanged.

title: [Fix] [NVIDIA] jit: Build sm_100f on CC 10.7 until the bundled CUTLASS supports SM107
author: zcnrex
body:
## Motivation

On CC 10.7 devices, SGLang JIT kernels are built for `sm_107a`, but they include FlashInfer's bundled CUTLASS (`flashinfer/data/cutlass`, 4.5.0). That CUTLASS has no SM107 support (`struct Sm107` and the `CUTLASS_ARCH_MMA_SM107A_ENABLED` gates arrive in CUTLASS 4.8). Against it, an `sm_107a` build compiles cleanly but loses features:

- `CUTE_ARCH_TMA_SM90_ENABLED` is undefined, so every cute TMA copy compiles to `CUTE_INVALID_CONTROL_PATH` and asserts at runtime.
- `CUDA_CTA_RECONFIG_ACTIVATED` is off, so `warpgroup_reg_alloc/dealloc` (`setmaxnreg`) become no-ops.

This is reachable today. DeepSeek-V4.1 with DP attention and `--dsv4-attn-backend trtllm` runs the DeepSelect top-k JIT kernels. On a CC 10.7 device, the first request fails with:

```
cute/arch/copy_sm90_tma.hpp:189: static void cute::SM90_TMA_LOAD_3D::copy(...): Assertion `0 && "Trying to use tma without CUTE_ARCH_TMA_SM90_ENABLED."` failed.
```

FlashInfer handles the same situation for its own JIT kernels: `flashinfer.compilation_context.cutlass_supports_sm107()` checks its bundled CUTLASS for `struct Sm107`, and builds the `sm_100f` family target when it is missing.

## Modifications

`python/sglang/kernels/jit/utils/arch.py`: on CC 10.7, when FlashInfer's `cutlass_supports_sm107()` (present in the pinned 0.7.2) is false, the JIT target becomes `10.0f`. The import stays inside the CUDA 10.7 branch, because ROCm and MUSA installs don't provide that function. This gives `-gencode=arch=compute_100f,code=sm_100f` and `SGL_CUDA_ARCH=1000`, so the binary and the arch macro the kernels branch on stay consistent. The `sm_100f` family binary runs on SM107.

Every other architecture is unchanged. On 10.7, the JIT goes back to `sm_107a` automatically once FlashInfer bundles a CUTLASS that declares `Sm107`. The JIT cache key includes the target, so stale `sm_107a` builds are not reused.

## Accuracy Tests

On a CC 10.7 device: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, TP4 / DP4 / EP4 with DP attention, `--moe-a2a-backend megamoe`, `--dsv4-attn-backend trtllm` and DSpark. GSM8K (200 questions, `sglang.test.run_eval`):

- Before: the DeepSelect top-k kernels assert on the first request and the server dies.
- After: 0.985. The JIT cache shows the DeepSelect builds targeting `sm_100f`.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

No speed claim. This trades an `sm_107a` build with TMA and `setmaxnreg` compiled out for a working `sm_100f` build.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).
- [ ] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).
- [ ] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations).
- [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed).

title: [Fix] gguf: Preserve MoE routing, weighting and allocation budgets
author: ch-wan
body:
This PR is part of a stack (oldest at bottom):

* #45681
* #45917
* #45462
* __->__ #45916
* #45915

## Motivation

GGUF MoE must discard padded and nonlocal routes without consuming their expert outputs or NaN scores. Preparing safe IDs and clearing intermediate tensors on every call adds allocations and launches, while an unguarded native projection can form a weight address from a negative ID.

This PR moves CUDA vector-route safety into a local native consumer, shares its format math with the AOT implementation, and preserves per-slot product rounding before the existing MoE reduction. It also restores lazy fallback accumulation and repairs the shared native MMQ bounds/scale indexing.

## Changes

- CUDA MMVQ uses a local JIT entry with negative-ID checks before expert-address formation. Ordinary contiguous int32 routes retain their storage; exceptional layouts/widths normalize explicitly. The quantize/project structure and zeroed projection output remain intact.
- CUDA weighting excludes inactive outputs and scores inside its product kernel, removing activation-sized input copies and separate intermediate clears. Products still round to the output dtype before native `moe_sum`.
- Shared native GGUF code checks MMQ slack bounds before access and indexes Q8_1 scales with the same routed row as the values. Rebuilt MUSA providers can use the native in-place weighting operator; older providers retain their compatibility path.
- The slow fallback adopts the first valid expert result, adds later contributions in order, and zeros the existing final row only when all routes are inactive.
- A local non-flushing FP32 multiply preserves subnormal operands/results and signed zero in CUDA weighting, including SM90 fast-math builds. MUSA multiplication and the reducer are unchanged.
- Shared GGUF headers have one AOT source owner, with JIT forwarding links. Source-distribution staging materializes those headers so the runtime package remains self-contained.

## Review order

1. `python/sglang/srt/layers/quantization/gguf.py`: vector/MMQ/fallback selection, private-buffer lifetimes and final weighting/reduction.
2. `kernels/ops/moe/gguf_moe_vec.py`, `jit/csrc/moe/gguf_moe_vec.cuh` and the shared GGUF headers: preserved format math and negative-ID access guards.
3. `aot/csrc/moe/moe_sum.cu`, `gguf_moe_weights.cuh` and the weighting wrappers: validation, rounding and device registration.
4. `test_gguf_inactive_routes.py`, `test_gguf_moe_weights.py`, then `python/setup.py` for standalone header packaging.

- Define unused CUDA MMQ expert-map capacity in the existing alignment producer. This removes the per-call arange, multiply, comparison and masked-fill sequence while retaining the released provider and buffer sizes.

## CI cadence

The GGUF all-format/AOT numerical regression and weighting/vector microbenchmark now run in `nightly-test-1-gpu-large`. The compact full-entry GGUF tests remain in base CI; the MUSA nightly registration is preserved.

Across the stack, six existing CUDA file registrations move from base CI to extra/nightly, removing 854 estimated GPU-seconds from the default gate (registration estimates, not a measured wall-time saving). All test bodies, cases, inputs, assertions and tolerances are unchanged. Full before/after discovery validates 2,535 files and 3,077 registrations, with every moved file selected in its enabled destination suite. Configured hooks pass; native tests were not rerun for this registration-only update.

## Validation

- Final integrated `e6670af1ad` B300 MMQ comparison against reviewed stack `5ece6073f3`: Q4_0/Q8_0, M65/512, FP16 H256/I256/E4/topk2. Balanced ABBA workers with 32 captured calls × 8 replays × 9 samples show lower GPU time in all four cases: hot graph 10.1–27.7% and cold-L2 graph 11.4–18.7% (256 MiB flush excluded by events). Valid outputs are bitwise identical. Each entry removes 4 GPU launches; allocated peak decreases by 512 bytes at M65 and 2560 bytes at M512. This is a comparison to the reviewed stack; earlier original-main controls below retain their separate baseline and limitations.
- A native Q8_0 identity projection exposed a reference-only Q8_1 rounding-tie error: scalar division had become reciprocal multiplication. The test reference now uses tensor division, with the same inputs and numerical tolerance. No production numerical kernel or math setting changed.

- At integrated `e6670af1ad`, the alignment suite passes 89 tests on 1× H200 and 1× B300, covering count publication, signed IDs, complete expert-map capacity and combined options during graph replay. The GGUF native-entry suite passes 7 tests on B300 with sglang-kernel 0.4.10. H200 uses PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130 for the source-local JIT producer; this is not full native H200 GGUF admission.

Based on #45915 above main `25ad569ff9`. Blackwell checks ran on integrated source `f3a116529a`; the GGUF runtime, production weighting TU/header and registered kernel test match this PR's `b80e51a006` exactly.

On **1× NVIDIA B300, SM10.3**, with PyTorch **2.14.1+cu130**, Triton **3.8.0**, sgl-kernel **0.4.10**, FlashInfer **0.7.2** and NVCC **13.0.88**:

- The registered vector-format/Triton-weighting checks passed **2 tests / 45 subtests**. Vector coverage compares 19 formats against the existing native provider, with FP16/BF16/FP32 coverage for selected formats and inactive/recovery graph states.
- The exact production `moe_sum.cu` was separately compiled with the precise SM100-family `compute_100f/sm_100f` flags. Dedicated process-local registration passed **2 tests / 44 subtests**: native/Triton rounding cases plus native amplified-subnormal, subnormal-result and signed-zero cases, including poisoned inactive routes.
- All **18** generated weighting specializations contain `mul.rn.f32` without FTZ multiplication. Six graph captures passed **24** valid/partial/all-inactive/recovery replays with strided metadata. Ten invalid/overlap cases and three empty shapes passed; FP16 output `[8192, 4096]` required **0 extra allocated peak bytes** for the warmed native weighting call.
- The seven GGUF unit tests, including fallback operation budgets and borrowed input/ID preservation, passed within the combined CPU suite. Normal configured pre-commit hooks passed.

The dedicated weighting library does **not** establish full-provider or model compatibility: the installed provider was unchanged, and CUDA serving uses the local vector entry plus Triton weighting. Full rebuilt-wheel validation, native MUSA/MCC execution, distributed/model parity and GGUF serving performance remain untested. No universal performance claim follows from these operator checks; eager CPU submission overhead is excluded from the performance scope.

## Rebase validation (before the CI registration fix)

This five-PR stack was rebased without conflicts onto main `8b9f72417f`. All five patches retain their stable patch IDs relative to the preceding published stack; the newer main commits do not touch the stack's changed files. The existing removal of the unused `materialized_routing` parameter and its three call-site arguments in #45917 is preserved.

Each rebased PR commit passed its configured pre-commit checks independently. The final stack passes `git diff --check`, and all 72 changed Python files parse successfully. CPU test suites, native GPU tests and performance measurements were not rerun for this rebase. Previously reported results, including those at integrated `e6670af1ad`, remain evidence for those earlier revisions with their stated limits.

## Prior CI registration fix

The GGUF weighting test now uses the existing `nightly-musa-1-gpu` suite with `nightly=True`; at that revision, its CUDA kernel-unit registration was unchanged. The previous nonexistent MUSA suite caused global registry validation to fail before CPU, CUDA and AMD tests could run.

The original collection failure was reproduced. Full registration collection and suite validation now pass on the GGUF component (2,533 files / 3,075 registrations) and the integrated stack (2,535 files / 3,077 registrations), including enabled MUSA nightly and CUDA selection. Configured pre-commit checks pass for the corrected test. This update changes one registration line and is propagated through the existing stack.

## CPU CI follow-up

Run [39935811691](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/39935811691) exposed an upstream Flux2 import test registered in the CPU suite, whose environment lacks the diffusion dependencies. The import chain also queries the active GPU. #45915 moves that check to the existing CUDA diffusion unit suite, which installs those dependencies, while retaining its XPU registration and the real subprocess check that blocks Intel Triton imports. This registration fix is propagated through the stack.

The Flux2 import check passes on 1× NVIDIA B300 with PyTorch 2.14.1+cu130, Triton 3.8.0 and Diffusers 0.37.0; its five Intel-XPU numerical cases are skipped on CUDA and were not rerun on XPU. Full integrated registry collection validates 2,535 files / 3,077 registrations, including the enabled diffusion/XPU selections and the preceding GGUF MUSA fix. Configured checks pass for the changed files. Only three test files change across this follow-up; production code is unchanged. A fresh full CI result is not claimed.

## Merge preparation

Rebased this component onto main `1340044e97` for squash merge. The preceding stack components are already merged into main; only this component is replayed here. No test suites or performance measurements were rerun for this merge. Earlier validation sections describe their named revisions.
