title: [Perf] diffusion: Serve FA4 head sizes on Blackwell instead of falling back to sm80 SDPA
author: mickqian
body:
## Motivation

The CUDA platform decides whether FlashAttention can serve a layer with `FlashAttentionBackend.get_supported_head_sizes()`. That is FA3's list: 32, 64, 96, ..., 256. On Blackwell the FA backend is FA4, which also serves every multiple of 8 up to 128. Other head sizes fall back to `torch_sdpa`. The CUDA platform disables cuDNN SDPA for the whole process, so PyTorch then runs its sm80 FlashAttention-2 kernel (`pytorch_flash::flash_fwd_kernel`).

The Qwen-VL vision towers hit this:
- Qwen3-VL has head size 72. It is the encoder of Qwen-Image-2.1 edit and MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA.
- Qwen2.5-VL has head size 80. It is the encoder of Qwen-Image and Qwen-Image-Edit.

It happens both with the default backend and with `--attention-backend fa`. In both cases the server log shows `Attention backends for text_encoder: torch_sdpa, ...`.

Kernel time on one B300, `[1, H, S, 72]` bf16, non-causal:

| H, S | sm80 FA2 (current) | cuDNN SDPA | FA4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 16, 23808 | 9.64 ms | 2.37 ms | 2.35 ms |
| 8, 23808 | 5.09 ms | 1.27 ms | 1.27 ms |
| 16, 4096 | 0.340 ms | 0.082 ms | 0.106 ms |

## Modifications

`CudaPlatformBase._resolve_flash_attention_backend_cls_str`: on Blackwell, a head size that is a multiple of 8 up to 128 now counts as FA-capable, which matches FA4's own check for sm100.
- Default backend: these layers take the Blackwell default, `dynamic_cudnn_sdpa`. That is cuDNN SDPA, with FA4 as the fallback.
- `--attention-backend fa`: they run FA4, including its packed-varlen path.
- Hopper, SM12x and ROCm are unchanged.

Tests: `test_cuda_attention_backend.py` adds two cases on a mocked platform.
- Blackwell: head sizes 72 and 80 resolve to `dynamic_cudnn_sdpa` by default and to FA4 when FA is requested. Head sizes 68 and 136 still fall back to `torch_sdpa`. On main, the 72 and 80 subtests fail.
- Pre-Blackwell: head size 72 keeps `torch_sdpa`.

## Accuracy Tests

All three kernels take bf16 inputs and accumulate in fp32. Against an fp32 reference on random inputs (H=16, S=23808, D=72), their max abs error is 2.8e-4 (sm80 FA2), 2.7e-4 (cuDNN) and 2.5e-4 (FA4).

The table compares the vision tower's outputs on main and on this PR, with the real checkpoints and the same request inputs. Each value is the relative L2 difference.

| | deepstack (block 8) | deepstack (block 16) | deepstack (block 24) | merger output |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA, 2976x2048 reference, cuDNN | 1.3% | 2.4–2.5% | 3.7–3.8% | 4.7–4.8% |
| Qwen-Image-2.1 edit, `--attention-backend fa` (FA4) | 1.2% | 2.2–2.3% | 3.3–3.6% | 7.1–8.3% |
| Qwen-Image-2.1 edit, default backend (cuDNN) | 1.2% | 2.2–2.3% | 3.4–3.6% | 6.7–7.7% |

The difference grows steadily with depth, which is how bf16 rounding differences add up over 27 blocks. No single layer jumps.

Each kernel against an fp32 reference. The Qwen3-VL vision tower of Qwen-Image-2.1 (27 blocks, head size 72) ran on the benchmark's edit reference (1248x864 after the stage's resize, 4212 patches), once with fp32 weights and math SDPA as the reference, and once in bf16 per attention kernel. Only the attention kernel changes between the bf16 rows. Each value is the relative L2 difference from the fp32 reference, on one B300:

| bf16 attention kernel | deepstack (block 8) | deepstack (block 16) | deepstack (block 24) | merger output |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| sm80 FlashAttention-2 (main on Blackwell) | 2.40% | 5.34% | 7.68% | 15.09% |
| cuDNN SDPA (this PR, default backend) | 2.40% | 5.50% | 7.84% | 13.86% |
| FA4 (this PR, `--attention-backend fa`) | 2.40% | 5.21% | 7.55% | 14.91% |
| memory-efficient SDPA (for scale) | 2.39% | 5.27% | 7.64% | 15.24% |

The new kernels are as close to fp32 as main's kernel. FA4 is closer at every depth. cuDNN is within 0.2 points at the deepstack taps and closer at the output. The 7-8% kernel-to-kernel difference in the earlier table is the size of bf16 rounding over 27 blocks, the same order as each kernel's distance from fp32. (The same check on H200 gives FlashAttention-2 / cuDNN / memory-efficient at 14.39% / 15.28% / 15.20% for the merger output.)

End to end on B300 (Qwen-Image-2.1 edit, B300 `--attention-backend fa` command), this PR ran stacked with four other changes; that stack measured 2.626 / 2.637 s against main's 2.751 / 2.771 s. The changes measured on their own account for all but ~60-67 ms of that difference, which is the stored-PNG change plus this one.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Server runs on B300 with each case's serving command. Main and this PR ran side by side on separate GPUs, with requests sent one at a time. The vision-tower time is synchronized wall time around the tower's forward, and the kernel times come from `torch.profiler`.

**MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA**, 2 GPUs with Ulysses 2. The encoder is TP-folded to 8 heads per rank. The reference is 2976x2048, which gives 23808 patches over 27 blocks.

| | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| attention kernels per tower forward | 137.5 ms (27x `pytorch_flash::flash_fwd_kernel`, sm80) | 34.2 ms (27x `cudnn_generated_fort_native_sdpa_sm100_flash_fprop`) |
| vision tower | 182–188 ms | 84.5–84.7 ms |
| text-encoding stage, two warm requests | | 116 ms and 107 ms shorter |
| end to end, 50 steps | 103.41 s | 102.99 s |

**Qwen-Image-2.1 edit**, 1 GPU. The reference becomes 4212 patches over 27 blocks.

| | main | this PR, `--attention-backend fa` | this PR, default backend |
|---|---|---|---|
| attention kernels per tower forward | 9.4 ms | 2.9 ms (FA4) | 2.3 ms (cuDNN) |
| vision tower | 21.0–21.5 ms | 18.0–20.8 ms | 14.5–16.7 ms |

For this case the vision tower is a small share of the encoding stage. Encoding-stage and end-to-end times stayed within run-to-run noise.

The first request at a new image size pays for building a cuDNN plan once per sequence length, about 45 ms. On the H3 case's first request the tower took 128 ms on this PR, against 182 ms on main. FA4 builds no per-shape plan.

title: [Perf] diffusion: Project LTX-2 prompt K/V once per denoising loop
author: mickqian
body:
Branch: mick/ltx2-prompt-kv-once-per-loop (on main 02b983603d), commit 80375713c2

## Motivation

LTX-2 re-projects the prompt in every block of every denoising step. The 1024-token caption goes through `caption_projection` (two GEMMs, video and audio), and then each block's two prompt cross-attentions (`attn2`, `audio_attn2`) project it to K and V and RMS-normalize K. Neither the text nor the DiT weights change inside a denoising loop: the LoRA phase switch runs before the loop. On 4xB300 (CFG parallel, BCG) these are ~3.4 ms of every 55 ms stage-1 step. TensorRT-LLM caches the same projections per request.

## Modifications

- `models/dits/ltx_2.py`
  - `LTX2Attention.project_context_kv(context)` returns the normed K and the V that `forward` would project. `forward` takes `context_kv=(k, v)` and skips `to_k` / `to_v` / `k_norm`.
  - `LTX2VideoTransformer3DModel.prepare_prompt_kv(encoder_hidden_states, audio_encoder_hidden_states)` runs the caption projections and every block's prompt K/V once. It writes them into persistent per-block buffers keyed by the text shapes and returns that key. The forward takes `cached_prompt_kv=<key>`, skips the caption projections and hands each block its K/V. The buffers keep their addresses across requests, so a breakable CUDA graph captured at warmup reads the current request's K/V.
  - `caches_prompt_kv` is false when the prompt is adaLN-modulated per step (`cross_attention_adaln`, LTX-2.3), whose K/V depend on the step.
- `ltx_2/denoising.py`: on the official CFG path, `_use_cached_ltx2_prompt_kv` prepares the K/V on the loop's first step (`LTX2DenoisingContext.prompt_kv_key`) and passes the key to every step. It keeps the per-step projection under layerwise offload (weights stream per block) and cache-dit.

## Tests

- `test_ltx2_prompt_kv_cache.py`
  - A 2-block LTX-2 forward with `cached_prompt_kv` is bitwise equal to the per-step projection.
  - A second text is written into the same buffers (same data pointers), and the cached forward matches the uncached one for it.
  - `caches_prompt_kv` is false with `cross_attention_adaln`.
  - The stage prepares once per loop and leaves the kwargs untouched for an LTX-2.3 DiT, under layerwise offload and under cache-dit.
- `test_ltx2_bcg_coords.py`: its stub DiT reads the prompt itself, so the step test stubs the new hook.

## Accuracy Tests

4xB300 (2 GPUs used), LTX-2 two-stage 768x512x121, 40 steps, CFG parallel + breakable CUDA graphs. MP4s of 4 requests are byte-identical (md5) to main + #45965 / #45977 / #46047.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Same setup, `SGLANG_DIFFUSION_SYNC_STAGE_PROFILING=1`, median of 3 steady requests:

| | stage 1 (40 steps) | per step |
|---|---|---|
| base | 2.205 s | 55.1 ms |
| this PR | 2.062 s | 51.5 ms |

title: [Perf] diffusion: Drop LTX-2's all-valid prompt mask under lossless quality
author: mickqian
body:
Branch: mick/ltx2-drop-all-valid-prompt-mask (on main 02b983603d), commit 12b5588eb1

## Motivation

LTX-2's text connector replaces every padded prompt token with a learned register, so the mask it returns is all ones. The DiT still received it, and every prompt cross-attention became masked SDPA with an all-zero additive bias. cuDNN serves that with slower kernels. On B300: 1536x1024 tokens at d128 take 53.9 us with the bias and 25.6 us without, and 126x1024 at d64 take 40.2 us against 17.6 us. That is 96 masked calls per stage-1 step. TensorRT-LLM does not pass this mask either.

## Modifications

- `models/adapter/ltx_2_connector.py`: `LTX2TextConnectors.output_mask_is_all_valid` is true when the video connector has learned registers.
- `ltx_2/text_connector.py`: under `quality="lossless"` (the default), the stage stores no prompt or negative mask when the connector's mask is all valid. The DiT then runs unmasked prompt cross-attention. `quality="exact"` keeps the reference mask.

Adding a zero bias changes no attention score. Only the kernel, and with it the rounding, changes.

## Tests

`test_ltx2_prompt_mask_registers.py`: lossless drops both masks with and without CFG; exact keeps the all-ones masks; a connector without registers keeps its mask; `output_mask_is_all_valid` follows the registers.

## Accuracy Tests

4xB300 (2 GPUs), LTX-2 two-stage 768x512x121, CFG parallel + BCG, 4 prompts: PSNR against the masked run 17.9 / 20.6 / 24.4 / 15.1 dB.

Reference band for a rounding-only change on this workload: the same server with `quality="exact"` against the default `lossless` (which already mounts other rounding-moving fusions) gives LTX-2 PSNR 17.0 / 20.6 / 23.1 / 20.8 dB and LTX-2.3 18.1 / 19.3 / 17.6 / 20.4 dB over the same four prompts. The 40-step CFG trajectory amplifies any rounding difference to that level, so the e2e number shows only that the change stays inside the band every rounding change lands in.

CI: `ltx_2_two_stage_t2v` (2xH100) runs the lossless default, so its prompt cross-attention changes kernel on Hopper as well. Its consistency threshold is PSNR 30 dB, tighter than the band above, so its GT likely needs a refresh with this PR (`diffusion-ci-gt-gen.yml`). The LTX-2.3 cases pass no prompt mask and are unaffected.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Kernel times above. Together with the FA4 routing for sub-tile sequences (separate PR), stage-1 steps go from 51.5 ms to 48.5 ms (synced stage timing, on top of the prompt K/V PR).

title: [Perf] diffusion: Route dense attention with a sub-tile side to FA4 on Blackwell
author: mickqian
body:
Branch: mick/blackwell-sub-tile-attention-fa4 (on main 02b983603d), commit cfecddc185

## Motivation

`DYNAMIC_CUDNN_SDPA` sends every dense non-causal attention on sm_10x to cuDNN. When one side is shorter than one 128-row tile and the other is not, cuDNN falls back to `cudnn_generated_fort_native_sdpa_sm80_flash_fprop_wmma`. FA4 is 2-3x faster on those shapes. LTX-2's audio stream has 126 tokens, so audio-prompt, audio-to-video and video-to-audio attention hit this in every block (4 of the 6 attention calls per block in the LTX-2 stage-1 profile).

B300, bf16, no mask, B=1 (B=2 behaves the same):

| q x kv (heads x dim) | cuDNN | FA4 |
|---|---|---|
| 126 x 1024 (32x64) | 17.6 us | 9.5 us |
| 1536 x 126 (32x64) | 13.2 us | 7.5 us |
| 126 x 1536 (32x64) | 24.4 us | 11.6 us |
| 6144 x 126 (16x128) | 35.6 us | 11.7 us |
| 126 x 6144 (16x128) | 84.9 us | 35.3 us |
| 192 x 6144 (32x64) | 32.0 us | 55.6 us |
| 1536 x 1536 (32x128) | 34.7 us | 35.5 us |
| 126 x 126 (32x64) | 6.0 us | 5.6 us |

At 192 tokens and above cuDNN is already on its sm_100 kernels and equal or faster, and with both sides short the two tie.

## Modifications

`layers/attention/backends/sdpa.py`: on sm_10x, `DynamicCudnnSDPAImpl` keeps cuDNN unless exactly one side is shorter than 128 tokens. Those calls go to the FA4 path the backend already holds as its fallback.

Both kernels compute exact softmax attention; only the rounding order changes.

## Tests

`test_dynamic_cudnn_sdpa_routing.py`: both sides at or above a tile, including 192 x 6144, keep cuDNN; one side under a tile routes to FA4; both short keeps cuDNN.

## Accuracy Tests

4xB300 (2 GPUs), LTX-2 two-stage 768x512x121, CFG parallel + BCG, 4 prompts: PSNR against the cuDNN run 16.0 / 19.5 / 23.1 / 14.9 dB.

Reference band for a rounding-only change on this workload: the same server with `quality="exact"` against the default `lossless` (which already mounts other rounding-moving fusions) gives LTX-2 PSNR 17.0 / 20.6 / 23.1 / 20.8 dB and LTX-2.3 18.1 / 19.3 / 17.6 / 20.4 dB over the same four prompts. The 40-step CFG trajectory amplifies any rounding difference to that level, so the e2e number shows only that the change stays inside the band every rounding change lands in.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

LTX-2 stage-1 attention per block drops from 180 us to about 100 us together with the prompt-mask PR. Stage-1 steps go from 51.5 ms to 48.5 ms for the two PRs together (synced stage timing). LTX-2.3 uses the same audio attention shapes at batch 2.

title: [Perf] diffusion: Run LTX-2 stage 2 on a premerged resident DiT
author: mickqian
body:
Branch: mick/ltx2-premerged-stage2 (on main 02b983603d), commit c2002dafe5

## Motivation

LTX-2.3's resident two-stage mode keeps a second DiT with the distilled LoRA merged in. Stage 2 then runs plain weights and needs no LoRA switch. LTX-2 got neither. Its device mode was never resolved, and resident mode did not premerge. So stage 2 ran the rank-384 distilled LoRA dynamically on 1370 layers, which adds about 19% to the stage-2 GEMM FLOPs plus two extra GEMMs per layer. It also paid the LoRA switch (~32 ms) on every request. TensorRT-LLM keeps merged stage-2 weights resident for the same reason.

## Modifications

- `server_args.py`: `_adjust_ltx2_two_stage_device_mode` resolves the mode for every two-stage pipeline that refines with a distilled LoRA (`_is_ltx2_distilled_lora_two_stage_pipeline`: LTX-2 and LTX-2.3, not LTX-2.5, which ships a distilled DiT). LTX-2 now takes the same auto default as LTX-2.3: resident on H200 and on GPUs with at least 130 GiB, original otherwise.
- `ltx_2_pipeline.py`: `should_use_premerged` requires resident mode, a distilled LoRA and no user stage-1 LoRA. It no longer requires LTX-2.3.
- CLI help and the LTX cookbook note now say that resident applies to LTX-2 as well.

The merged weights match the official two-stage pipelines, which fuse the LoRA. Compared with the dynamic delta, only the bf16 rounding of the sum moves.

## Tests

- `test_ltx2_premerged_stage2.py`: resident premerges with a distilled LoRA. Original mode, no distilled LoRA (LTX-2.5) and a user stage-1 LoRA each keep one DiT.
- `test_server_args.py`: an LTX-2 two-stage server resolves resident on a 140 GiB device and original on an 80 GiB one.

## Accuracy Tests

4xB300 (2 GPUs), LTX-2 two-stage 768x512x121: PSNR against the dynamic-LoRA stage 2 is 30.6 / 32.1 / 32.8 / 33.0 dB, audio SNR 11.5-15.2 dB. Only the last 3 steps change.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Synced stage timing, median of 3 requests:

| | LoRA switch | stage 2 (3 steps) | client |
|---|---|---|---|
| before | 0.032 s | 0.439 s | 3.05 s |
| after | 0 | 0.341 s | 2.90 s |

Memory: the second 19B DiT adds about 38 GB per GPU. That is why the default only applies at 130 GiB and above.

title: [Perf] diffusion: Build one LTX-2.3 AdaLN row per sample when every token shares the sigma
author: mickqian
body:
Branch: mick/ltx23-per-sample-adaln (on main 02b983603d), commit 89d01fddaf

## Motivation

LTX-2.3 two-stage passes per-token timesteps (`[B, T]`) even when there is no denoise mask, so every token carries the same sigma. The DiT then runs its AdaLN MLPs on B*T rows. For the two batched guidance passes per CFG rank that builds a `[2, 1536, 9 * 4096]` table, 226 MB per forward. `ltx2_ada_values9` re-reads it in every block (37 us per block per modality), and every modulation and gate becomes a per-token tensor.

## Modifications

`ltx_2/denoising.py`: `_ltx23_token_timesteps` returns one row per sample (`[B, 1]`) under `quality="lossless"`, and the per-token `[B, T]` expansion under `exact`. A denoise mask keeps its per-token path. The DiT already broadcasts `[B, 1]` rows, as it does for LTX-2.

The values are identical. The AdaLN GEMMs run at M = B instead of M = B*T, and the broadcast modulations take the fused kernels, so only rounding moves.

## Tests

`test_ltx23_per_sample_adaln.py`: the lossless rows are `[B, 1]` and expand to the exact rows. A 2-block LTX-2.3-shaped model (prompt AdaLN, gated attention) gives the same outputs within bf16 rounding for per-sample and per-token rows.

## Accuracy Tests

4xB300 (2 GPUs), LTX-2.3 two-stage 768x512x121, 30 steps, official guider: PSNR against main 18.0 / 19.8 / 19.7 / 18.5 dB.

Reference band for a rounding-only change on this workload: the same server with `quality="exact"` against the default `lossless` (which already mounts other rounding-moving fusions) gives LTX-2 PSNR 17.0 / 20.6 / 23.1 / 20.8 dB and LTX-2.3 18.1 / 19.3 / 17.6 / 20.4 dB over the same four prompts. The 40-step CFG trajectory amplifies any rounding difference to that level, so the e2e number shows only that the change stays inside the band every rounding change lands in.

CI: only `ltx_2.3_two_stage_t2v_2gpus` takes this path (threshold PSNR 16 dB, SSIM 0.45). The HQ pipeline (raw-sigma timesteps), the one-stage legacy path and TI2V (denoise mask) keep per-token rows.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Same setup. `ltx2_ada_values9` drops from 36.8 us to 4.2 us per call. Client median: 4.27 s before, 4.07 s with this PR alone. With the FA4 routing PR, stage 1 goes from 3.149 s to 2.918 s (105.0 to 97.2 ms per step).

title: [Perf] diffusion: Cut LTX-2.3 per-block elementwise work (contiguous AdaLN values, gate-folded masks, vectorized head gate)
author: mickqian
body:
Branch: mick/ltx23-block-elementwise (on main 02b983603d), commits 08f4c834c3, 84eaed7e83

## Motivation

LTX-2.3 runs its guidance passes two per CFG rank, so the DiT batch is 2. Three elementwise costs in every block are small at batch 1 and add up at batch 2:

1. `get_ada_values` unbinds a `[B, T, k, D]` sum. With B > 1 every value is strided, so `_ltx2_modulate` copies each scale and shift row to contiguous memory. That is 12 copy launches per block.
2. The modality pass masks the a2v / v2a outputs with a 0/1 per-sample mask, which is a full-size multiply before the gated residual.
3. Gated attention computes `out * (2 * sigmoid(gate_logits))`. The `[B, T, H, 1]` gate is broadcast over the head dim, which PyTorch runs as a non-vectorized strided kernel (26 us at 2x1536x32x128), plus a separate doubling pass. There are six of these per block.

## Modifications

- `get_ada_values` sums value-major (`[k, B, T, D]` via `torch.add(..., out=)`), so every value is contiguous. The audio-video cross-attention tables reuse it instead of an inline copy of the same sum.
- The 0/1 mask commutes with the gate, so it now scales the `[B, T, D]` gate.
- `kernels/ops/diffusion/modulate/head_gate_triton.py`: `head_gate_mul` takes the eager `sigmoid(gate_logits)` and applies the doubling and the product in fp32 with one bf16 rounding, which is what eager does. `LTX2Attention` uses it when the attention output is contiguous and keeps the eager expression otherwise.

All three keep the same operations on the same values, so outputs are bitwise identical.

## Tests

- `test_ltx2_ada_values_layout.py`: the value-major values are contiguous and bitwise equal to the old formula (fp32 and bf16 tables, T = 1 and T > 1). A 0/1 mask on the gate equals the mask on the output, bitwise.
- `test/registered/kernels/ops/diffusion/test_head_gate.py`: `head_gate_mul` is bitwise equal to eager for 4-D and flattened inputs over 4 shapes. Strided, mismatched and fp32 inputs are rejected.

## Accuracy Tests

4xB300 (2 GPUs), LTX-2.3 two-stage 768x512x121, 30 steps, and LTX-2 two-stage: MP4s of 4 requests each are byte-identical (md5) with and without these commits (measured together with the Q/K norm-RoPE vectorization PR).

## Speed Tests and Profiling

`head_gate_mul` on B300: 2x1536x32x128 26.2 to 7.8 us, 2x126x32x64 7.4 to 4.5 us, 2x1536x32x64 16.5 to 6.2 us. With the Q/K norm-RoPE PR, LTX-2.3 stage-1 steps go from 97.2 ms to 91.8 ms, and stage 1 from 2.918 s to 2.754 s (synced stage timing).

title: [Perf] diffusion: Vectorize the LTX-2 Q/K RMSNorm + split-RoPE kernel
author: mickqian
body:
Branch: mick/ltx2-qknorm-rope-vectorize (on main 02b983603d), commit 5dbb8589c1

## Motivation

`ltx2_qknorm_split_rope` (sm_100 path) runs 8 times per LTX-2 block. Its output pass reads x, the norm weight, cos and sin, and writes the output one bf16 element at a time. It is the largest non-GEMM kernel in the LTX-2 profile: 4.3 ms per stage-1 step for LTX-2, and 6.7 ms per forward for LTX-2.3 at batch 2.

## Modifications

`kda_kernels/csrc/diffusion/ltx2_qknorm_split_rope.cuh`: the output pass handles 8 consecutive RoPE pairs per thread with 16-byte loads and stores. It does so when the half head dim, the cos/sin strides and every base pointer allow; otherwise the scalar loop runs. The rstd reduction, the per-element math and the rounding are unchanged.

## Tests

`test_rope_ltx2.py::test_ltx2_qknorm_split_rope_vectorized_matches_scalar`: the same inputs with cos/sin moved off a 16-byte boundary run the scalar loop, and both paths agree bitwise (d128 and d64, batch 1 and 2, odd sequence lengths). The existing exactness and alignment tests pass.

## Accuracy Tests

The new kernel is bitwise equal to the old one on 6 production shapes (B300). LTX-2 and LTX-2.3 MP4s of 4 requests each are byte-identical (measured together with the LTX-2.3 elementwise PR).

## Speed Tests and Profiling

B300, one q/k pair:

| shape (tokens q/k x heads x dim) | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 1536/1536 x 32 x 128 | 30.9 us | 16.6 us |
| 2x1536/1536 x 32 x 128 | 68.8 us | 36.5 us |
| 1536/126 x 32 x 64 | 14.0 us | 8.7 us |
| 2x126/126 x 32 x 64 | 10.1 us | 6.3 us |
| 6144/6144 x 16 x 128 | 69.8 us | 37.4 us |

LTX-2 stage-1 steps go from 48.3 ms to 47.2 ms (synced stage timing).

title: [Perf] diffusion: Keep same-device copies out of the pipelined Ulysses exchange
author: mickqian
body:
Branch: mick/diffusion-ulysses-pipeline-same-device-copies (on main efd2ce8a9d), commit 2aec3e1621

## Motivation

The head-group pipeline (`IpcA2AMultiState.pipelined_attention`) overlaps the Ulysses exchange with attention: group g's peer copies run on the copy engine while group g-1 attends. Two parts of it were same-device copies, and a same-device `cuMemcpy2DAsync` (or `copy_`) runs on the SMs, so it waits out whatever attention kernel is running:

1. **Own rows on the copy stream.** This rank's rows of each group were copied into its own receive slot on the copy stream, interleaved with the peer sends. Each group's own copy waited for the previous group's attention to finish, and the peer sends queued behind it waited with it. Wan2.2 A14B 720p on 4xB300 (CFG 2 x Ulysses 2, 5 head groups) showed a 0.28-0.46 ms gap before every group: 1.76 ms per block between RoPE and the output projection.
2. **Merges after the last group.** Every group's output was copied into the merged output (own rows) and the peers' blocks were copied in after their flags (D2D on the group streams). With the gaps gone these all run after the last attention: 0.63 ms per block.

A microbenchmark on B300 (FA4 or cuDNN attention on one stream, six 38.7 MB pitched copies issued on another): D2D copies finish 0.2 ms after the attention ends; P2P copies finish 0.4 ms after they start.

## Modifications

- `kernels/ops/diffusion/layout/head_group_copy_triton.py`: `copy_head_groups(src, dst)` copies `[group, batch, rows, width]` views with arbitrary strides (last dim contiguous) in one Triton pass.
- `ipc_a2a_multi.pipelined_attention`:
  - this rank's rows of every group go into its slots in one `copy_head_groups` pass per part on the main stream, before the first group; the copy stream carries only peer sends;
  - new `attend_into(q, k, v, out)`: when the backend can write through a strided output, each group attends straight into a token-major `[batch, world * s_local, heads, head_dim]` buffer. This rank's rows of it are the returned output; the peers' rows are sent from it on the copy engine; the peers' blocks come back in one `copy_head_groups` pass per peer. No own merge, one gather per peer.
- `AttentionImpl.forward_into(q, k, v, out, attn_metadata) -> bool` (default False). `FlashAttentionImpl` serves it on FA4 (same call as `forward`, with `out=`); `DynamicCudnnSDPAImpl` delegates when it would take FA4 for those inputs. `out=None` only asks.
- `USPAttention`'s dense Ulysses path passes `attend_into`.

Masked, replicated-row, fill (MiniMax-H3) and cuDNN-served calls keep the previous output path.

## Accuracy Tests

The pipeline checks itself against the sequential exchange on first sight and keeps it only on byte equality; with this change it still passes on Wan2.2 (no "differs from the sequential exchange" in the log). Decoded videos are byte-identical (mp4 md5) to the run without the change for the same requests.

- `test_usp_pipelined_attention_multi_gpu.py`: every Ulysses layout, FA and cuDNN backends, pipelined vs sequential, bitwise, 2 and 4 ranks: passes (the FA4 cases now take `attend_into`).
- `test_ipc_a2a_multi_gpu.py`: passes (2 and 4 ranks, expandable segments without pidfd_getfd).
- `test_layout.py::test_copy_head_groups_*`: both directions vs per-group copies, bitwise; input validation.
- `test_cuda_attention_backend.py` (forward_into cases): FA4 `forward_into` into one head group of a wider buffer equals `forward` bitwise and writes nothing else; backends without it decline.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Wan2.2 T2V A14B 720p, 81 frames, 40 steps, 4xB300, CFG 2 x Ulysses 2, eager, FA4 attention (needs "Prefer FA4 over cuDNN SDPA for long self-attention on B300" for the default backend).

Per transformer block (torch profiler, rank 0):

| | RoPE -> first attention | between groups | after last group | block |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| main | 0.36 ms | 0.28-0.46 ms x4 | 0.18 ms (merges in the gaps) | 56.6 ms |
| own rows in one pass | 0.23 ms | 0 | 0.63 ms (merges) | 54.9 ms |
| + attend into token-major output | 0.23 ms | 0 | 0.14 ms | |

E2E, harness single_e2e (client latency, two measured requests per fresh server, two interleaved rounds), on top of the other B300 Wan changes: without `attend_into` 90.820 / 90.797 s, with it 90.683 / 90.680 s (-0.13 s). The own-rows half was measured together with the FA4 selection change (92.72 -> 91.34 s median, probe client, six requests each).

All four GPUs sit at the 1100 W power cap through the denoise, so idle gaps cost less than their length: removing them raises power and the clocks drop. The e2e gain is smaller than the timeline gain.

title: [Perf] diffusion: Prefer FA4 over cuDNN SDPA for long self-attention on B300
author: mickqian
body:
Branch: mick/diffusion-sm103-fa4-long-self-attn (on main efd2ce8a9d), commit 638be52100

## Motivation

`DYNAMIC_CUDNN_SDPA` sends every dense non-causal call on sm_10x to cuDNN SDPA, a choice measured on B200 ("cuDNN SDPA measured 1.25-1.5x faster than FA4 CuTe"). On B300 (sm_103) FA4 uses the hardware exp2 path and the `tcgen05.ld.red` row max, and long video self-attention is where diffusion models spend most of their step (Wan2.2 A14B 720p: ~67% of a denoising step).

A video DiT on B300 runs at the 1100 W power cap for the whole denoise, so kernels were timed under sustained load (2 s warm-up to the cap, then 2-6 s of back-to-back calls), bf16, B=1 unless noted:

| q x kv, heads x dim | cuDNN | FA4 | FA4/cuDNN |
|---|---|---|---|
| 75600 x 75600, 4 x 128 | 7.411 ms | 7.259 ms | 0.979 |
| 75600 x 75600, 20 x 128 | 36.901 ms | 36.360 ms | 0.985 |
| 37800 x 37800, 10 x 128 | 4.635 ms | 4.549 ms | 0.981 |
| 32760 x 32760, 12 x 128 | 4.281 ms | 4.214 ms | 0.984 |
| 16384 x 16384, 24 x 128 | 2.155 ms | 2.139 ms | 0.993 |
| 8192 x 8192, 24 x 128 | 0.575 ms | 0.577 ms | 1.003 |
| 4608 x 4608, 24 x 128 | 0.185 ms | 0.186 ms | 1.006 |
| 4352 x 4352, 24 x 128, B=2 | 0.338 ms | 0.338 ms | 1.000 |
| 37800 x 512, 40 x 128 | 0.350 ms | 0.338 ms | 0.964 |
| 18900 x 18900, 24 x 64 | 1.928 ms | 2.076 ms | 1.077 |
| 4096 x 4096, 24 x 64 | 0.108 ms | 0.120 ms | 1.114 |

FA4's sm_103 tuning knobs (softmax/correction registers, exp2 emulation, row-max reduction, 2-CTA) were swept at the Wan shape; the defaults are the best of them.

## Modifications

`layers/attention/backends/sdpa.py`: on sm_103, `DynamicCudnnSDPAImpl` takes FA4 for self-attention (`Sq == Skv`) with head_dim 128 and at least 16384 tokens. B200 (sm_100), cross-attention, shorter sequences and head_dim 64 keep cuDNN.

Both are exact softmax attention in bf16 with fp32 accumulation; only the rounding order changes (max |diff| 2.4e-4 on unit-scale inputs).

This touches the same function as "Route dense attention with a sub-tile side to FA4 on Blackwell"; the two conditions are independent and rebase trivially.

## Accuracy Tests

- `test_dynamic_cudnn_sdpa_selection.py`: sm_103 routes 16K and 75.6K self-attention to FA4; 8K, 512-key cross-attention and head_dim 64 stay on cuDNN; sm_100 stays on cuDNN at 75.6K.
- Wan2.2 T2V A14B 720p, 4xB300, same prompts and seeds, video at x264 crf 0, against cuDNN (with the other, bit-identical B300 Wan changes and a 63 dB VAE change in the build): PSNR 27.5 / 22.4 dB, SSIM 0.989 / 0.965 on two prompts. Same scene and composition; the 40-step trajectories drift apart as with any change of rounding order (the subject's pose differs by the last frame).

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Wan2.2 T2V A14B 720p, 81 frames, 40 steps, 4xB300, CFG 2 x Ulysses 2, eager. Attention per block (5 head groups of 4 heads): 38.1 -> 36.8 ms. E2E with the Ulysses pipeline fix: main 92.83 / 92.61 s -> 91.23-91.44 s (6 requests, median 91.34 s). On an older main with NCCL all-to-all, `--attention-backend fa` measured 95.75 s against 97.08 s for the default selection.

title: [Perf] diffusion: Tile the 3D scale-shift Triton kernel by rows
author: mickqian
body:
Branch: mick/diffusion-scale-shift-row-tiles (on main efd2ce8a9d), commit ca74a81722

## Motivation

`fuse_scale_shift_kernel`'s `[B, L, C]` path (`MulAdd` - Wan's FFN gated residual - and the native norm modulation) launches 128x128 tiles, which read each row in 256-byte pieces. On Wan2.2 A14B 720p (`[1, 37800, 5120]` per rank) the kernel moved 1.16 GB in 0.29 ms in isolation and 0.35 ms inside the denoising loop: one of the slowest elementwise kernels in the block.

B300, bf16 x, fp32 gate `[1, 1, C]`, bf16 shift `[B, L, C]`:

| B, L, C | 128x128 | rows x 1024 | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1, 37800, 5120 | 0.2933 ms | 0.1851 ms | 1.58x |
| 2, 4096, 3072 | 0.0449 ms | 0.0273 ms | 1.65x |
| 1, 4608, 3072 | 0.0189 ms | 0.0183 ms | 1.04x |
| 1, 75600, 1536 | 0.1766 ms | 0.1144 ms | 1.54x |
| 2, 8192, 2560 | 0.0681 ms | 0.0435 ms | 1.56x |
| 1, 32760, 4096 | 0.2041 ms | 0.1315 ms | 1.55x |
| 1, 1000, 5120 | 0.0193 ms | 0.0180 ms | 1.07x |
| 1, 37800, 3840 | 0.2209 ms | 0.1392 ms | 1.59x |

## Modifications

`kernels/ops/diffusion/modulate/scale_shift_triton.py`: on NVIDIA GPUs the 3D path launches up to 1024 channels by `4096 / BLOCK_C` rows per program. The per-element arithmetic is unchanged, so the output is bit-identical. ROCm and XPU keep their tiles.

## Accuracy Tests

`test_modulate.py::test_scale_shift_3d_tiling_is_bit_exact`: the new tiling equals a 128x128 launch of the same kernel bitwise (C from 96 to 5120, scale constant 0 and 1), and stays within the existing tolerance of the eager formula.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Wan2.2 T2V A14B 720p, 4xB300, CFG 2 x Ulysses 2: MulAdd 0.349 -> ~0.2 ms per block. E2E, two interleaved rounds of fresh servers, 3 requests each: 91.230 / 91.381 / 91.436 / 91.332 / 91.321 / 91.347 s (median 91.34) -> 91.283 / 91.254 / 91.268 / 91.226 / 91.220 / 91.317 s (median 91.26). The GPUs run at their power cap through the denoise, so a bandwidth-bound kernel's saving shows up at about half its length.

title: [Perf] diffusion: Patchify Wan latents straight into tokens
author: mickqian
body:
Branch: mick/wan-patch-embed-tokens (on main efd2ce8a9d), commit 949d3c9cd6

## Motivation

Wan's `PatchEmbed` is built with `flatten=False`. Its 5D fast path computes the patchify GEMM token-major (`[B, T'H'W', C]`), then writes it out channel-first (`.permute(0, 4, 1, 2, 3).contiguous()`), and `WanTransformer3DModel.forward` immediately transposes it back with `.flatten(2).transpose(1, 2).contiguous()`. At 720p (75600 tokens x 5120) that is two 774 MB copies per forward on every rank, 1.5-2.5 ms each on B300 (`aten::contiguous` on `[1, 5120, 21, 45, 80]` and on `[1, 75600, 5120]` in the profile): 3.3-5 ms per denoising step.

## Modifications

- `layers/visual_embedding.py`: `PatchEmbed.forward(x, tokens=False)`; `tokens=True` returns `[B, T'H'W', C]` whatever `flatten` says (the Conv3d fallback for indivisible grids flattens as before).
- `models/dits/wanvideo.py`: the forward asks for tokens. Subclasses that read the 5D output (Wan-Animate, LingBot) are untouched.

The values are the same, so the output is bit-identical.

## Accuracy Tests

`test_patch_embed_tokens.py`: `tokens=True` equals the flattened channel-first output bitwise for a divisible grid (patchify GEMM) and an indivisible one (Conv3d fallback). The transformer sees the same tensor, minus two copies.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Wan2.2 T2V A14B 720p, 4xB300: the two copies leave the step profile (3.3-5 ms per step). Measured together with "Run the Wan VAE fast path under spatial-parallel decode" (two interleaved rounds, fresh servers, 3 requests each): 91.27 -> 91.03 s median; the decode change alone accounts for ~0.27 s of decode time, so this one is within noise e2e at this resolution.

title: [Perf] diffusion: Speed up Wan's spatial-parallel VAE decode
author: mickqian
body:
Branch: mick/wan-vae-parallel-decode-fast-path (on main efd2ce8a9d), commits 6e09543c4f, 93ccc5dc4f

## Motivation

Multi-GPU Wan decode shards the frame height across ranks (`WanDistResidualBlock`, `SpatialParallelCausalConv3d` with halo exchange). That decoder never got the CUDA fast path ("Wan VAE: spatial-parallel decode; skipping fast path."), and its Conv3d weights stayed NCDHW because the channels_last_3d policy only covers `num_gpus == 1`. In the decode profile of Wan2.2 T2V A14B 720p on 4xB300 (fp32 decode, 1.32 s): cuDNN's own `nchwToNhwc` / `nhwcToNchw` conversions around every conv took 111 ms, the unfused RMSNorm + SiLU chains (`BinaryFunctor`, `silu`, `norm`, adds) ~250 ms, and 4114 `direct_copy` kernels 149 ms.

The spatial-parallel blocks only swap in halo-exchanging convs; the halo exchange slices and concatenates along height, which works in either memory layout.

The mid-block attention gathers the full frame height on every rank and attended every query row of it (21 fp32 `fmha_cutlassF` calls, 143 ms per decode), then kept only its own rows.

## Modifications

- `models/vaes/wan_vae_cuda_opt.py`: the installer accepts the spatial-parallel residual block, resample and attention block classes (`residual_block_cls` is now a tuple of classes) and no longer skips parallel decode.
- `loader/component_loaders/vae_loader.py`: Wan configs convert the VAE's Conv3d weights to channels_last_3d at any GPU count (LTX-2 and Cosmos3 keep the one-GPU rule). On more than one GPU the automatic policy converts the decoder only: cuDNN's TF32 convs round differently in channels_last, and an I2V condition latent that differs by ~3e-3 sends a 40-step 14B trajectory elsewhere (the 2-GPU Wan I2V consistency cases fell to 14-24 dB on the last frame). An explicit `SGLANG_DIFFUSION_VAE_CHANNELS_LAST_3D=1` still converts the whole VAE, as before.
- `models/vaes/wanvae.py`: under spatial-parallel decode each rank attends only its own height shard's query rows (the `tensor_split` chunk the output was cut to) against the whole frame's keys and values.

The fast path is the existing "lossless" quality tier (fp32 ops re-associated, nothing lowered); `quality="exact"` requests still run the reference ops.

## Accuracy Tests

- Wan2.2 T2V A14B 720p, 4xB300, same latents, video saved at x264 crf 0: PSNR 63.2 dB, SSIM 0.99999, max |diff| 4/255, mean |diff| 0.02 against the decode without this change (three requests). No seams at the shard boundaries (rows 180/360/540).
- Row-sharded attention: decoded video byte-identical (mp4 md5 at crf 0, three requests).
- Encoder: with the decoder-only rule, Wan2.1-I2V-14B on 2 GPUs encodes bit-identically to main; with `quality="exact"` (and the decoder's channels_last off) the output mp4 md5 equals main's. The 2-GPU Wan I2V consistency cases pass again (wan2_1_i2v_14b_480P 34.6/37.9/37.5 dB, wan2_1_i2v_14b_720P 36.2/35.9/35.3 dB, wan2_2_i2v_a14b 38.4/36.7/35.5 dB); the Animate cfg-parallel case is bitwise to its GT. Decode on 2 GPUs: main 372 ms, decoder-only 277-283 ms (the encoder no longer gets channels_last's ~8% encode speedup).
- `test_vae_loader.py`: the channels_last_3d policy covers multi-GPU Wan; `test_model_fast_paths.py` passes with the tuple form (33 Wan/Qwen cases); `test_wan_vae_attention_rows.py`: a row range equals those rows of the full-frame block output.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Decode stage with synchronized stage timers, Wan2.2 T2V A14B 720p, 4xB300, fp32 decode (three requests each): 1.284 / 1.266 / 1.269 s -> fast path 1.042 / 1.000 / 1.000 s -> + row-sharded attention 0.972 / 0.942 / 0.938 s (same build without it in the same session: 1.038 / 1.004 / 1.005 s).

title: [Fix] [AMD] dsv4.1: Fix decode graph capture with quantized low-ratio activations
author: kevin-mii
body:
## Motivation

sgl-project/sglang#45407 made `forward_low_ratio_sources` cut `x` and `q_lora` to the hoisted rows on every step (`x[:n]`, `q_lora[:n]`); before, it cut them only when DP attention padded an eager extend. On ROCm, `q_lora` (and on some routes `x`) reaches it quantized, as an `Mxfp8Activation` (q and scale) or an `Fp8GridActivation`: structs that refuse a slice. Since #45407, a DeepSeek-V4.1 server on MI35x fails while capturing its decode graphs (seen with `--monokernel-backend amd`; the failing call is SGLang's own forward, which every decode step of a plain server runs):

```
File ".../layers/attention/deepseek_v4_backend.py", line 3402, in forward_low_ratio_sources
    q_lora = q_lora[:n]
TypeError: 'Mxfp8Activation' object is not subscriptable
```

## Modifications

- `forward_low_ratio_sources` cuts `x`, `positions` and `q_lora` only when DP padding left rows past the hoisted ones, as before #45407. Decode and verify steps, where every row is live, pass them on uncut.
- That cut goes through `_first_rows`, which cuts a quantized struct field by field (`msgspec.structs.replace`) and a tensor with `[:n]`. On CUDA both are tensors here, so CUDA takes the same cut as on main.

## Accuracy Tests

MI350X, TP4, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, this branch on main 74c08f3dc5, with sgl-project/sgl-amd-mono main 52dceb0:

- `test/registered/unit/layers/test_dsv41_late_layer_tail_readers.py`: 13 passed. The new case (DP padding cuts a quantized `q_lora` field by field) fails on main with the error above.
- `test/registered/kernels/ops/attention/dsv4/test_dsv41_decode_glue_hip.py`: 6 passed.
- sgl-amd-mono's `test/e2e/test_deepseek_v41_server.py` (`--monokernel-backend amd`): 9 passed. GSM8K: 0.930 (DSpark verify server), 0.905 (decode server). Both servers step past the monokernels' widths onto this path.
- SGLang alone, without the monokernels, the same two servers, GSM8K (200 questions, 8 shots): 0.895 (DSpark verify), 0.905 (decode).
- sgl-amd-mono's `test/kernels/test_deepseek_v41_kernels.py` against this SGLang (K1, K2 and the FFN launch bit for bit, with and without aiter's preshuffle, every width the spec builds): 6 passed, on 048555d92f.

The other GPU runs used e62ad22f6a. The commits after it change only docstrings and the unit test.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

No speed change intended: decode and verify steps now skip a cut that kept every row. AgentX (InferenceX agentic coding, TP4, concurrency 1, 900 s) with the monokernels, on this PR's first version (048555d92f, same decode and verify path): P90 637.6 tok/s/user, P50 668.0, 6627 tok/s/GPU, acceptance length 3.52.

- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).

title: [Perf] batch-invariant: Fused residual add + RMSNorm kernel
author: aarnetalman
body:
## Motivation

In deterministic mode, RMSNorm with a residual add (both norms in every decoder layer) falls back to eager PyTorch, which takes about ten kernel launches instead of a single fused kernel. This PR adds a fused, batch-invariant add+RMSNorm kernel for that path. It applies to any model whose decoder layers use `RMSNorm` with a residual (Llama, Mistral, Qwen2/3, Qwen3-MoE, Phi, DeepSeek, gpt-oss and most others). Tested on MI350X with Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-30B-A3B and Phi-4: single-request decode throughput with the fused kernel is 56-73% higher and 12-22% higher at concurrency 16, and every determinism check passes on Qwen3-8B (TP1, TP2) and Qwen3-30B-A3B.

The fallback is a large share of deterministic decode time. Profile of a single-request decode (1k-token prompt, 256 output tokens, CUDA graphs off) in deterministic mode on MI350X:

| model | GPU time, deterministic | GPU time, normal mode | eager add+RMSNorm fallback |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen3-8B | 603 ms | 323 ms | about 205 ms (34%) |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B | 678 ms | 298 ms | about 215 ms (32%) |
| Phi-4 | 902 ms | 474 ms | about 205 ms (22%) |

In normal mode the same norms take 12.6 ms on Qwen3-8B as one fused kernel.

Scope: deterministic mode only, on every platform that runs the batch-invariant Triton kernels. The new kernel uses the same float32 math as `forward_native`. Models that use `GemmaRMSNorm` (Gemma, Qwen3-Next/3.5/3.8) take a different path and are not affected. Normal mode is unchanged.

## Modifications

- `batch_invariant_ops.py`: new `_fused_add_rms_norm_kernel` and `fused_add_rms_norm_batch_invariant`, next to the existing `rms_norm` kernel and in the same style. One program per row:
  - adds the residual (and the optional post-residual addend) to the input in float32;
  - stores the sum as the new residual, in the input's dtype or float32 (`fp32_residual`);
  - RMS-normalizes the float32 sum and applies the weight.

  The reduction runs over one row with a fixed block size, so a row's result does not depend on the batch.
- `layernorm.py`: in the batch-invariant branches of `RMSNorm.forward_cuda`, `forward_aiter`, `forward_hip` and `forward_xpu`, calls with a residual use the new kernel where `forward_native`'s math applies. These cases keep falling back to `forward_native` as before:
  - `cast_x_before_out_mul`;
  - a variance-size override;
  - a padded output;
  - the FSDP RL target.
- New `test/registered/unit/batch_invariant_ops/test_fused_add_rms_norm_batch_invariant.py` (per-PR, CUDA and MI35x):
  - every row's output and new residual are bit-identical (`torch.equal`) when computed in batches of 1, 3, 17 and 64;
  - the new residual equals the eager float32 sum exactly, and the output matches the eager path within rounding;
  - covered: hidden sizes 2048/4096/5120/2880, bf16 and fp16, with and without the addend, `fp32_residual` on and off.
- Unchanged: normal mode; batch-invariant calls without a residual; the fallback cases above.

## Accuracy Tests

MI350X, ROCm 7.2.4, `rocm/sgl-dev:v0.5.22-rocm724-mi35x-20261021`.

Unit tests:

```bash
python3 -m pytest -q test/registered/unit/batch_invariant_ops/test_fused_add_rms_norm_batch_invariant.py test/registered/unit/batch_invariant_ops/test_batch_invariant_ops.py
```

```
7 passed, 1 skipped, 86 subtests passed in 16.00s
```

End to end, Qwen3-8B TP1, deterministic mode with AITER prefill and decode attention. These runs use the open MI350X deterministic-mode PRs (#43788, #44045, #44438, #44489, #45599, #45601, #34543), which is the configuration that deterministic mode runs in on MI350X today; "before" is the same tree without this change:

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-8B --enable-deterministic-inference \
  --attention-backend triton --prefill-attention-backend aiter --decode-attention-backend aiter
python3 -m sglang.test.test_deterministic --test-mode {single,prefix,radix_cache} --n-trials 50
```

With this change, Qwen3-8B: `single` 1 output, `prefix` 1/1/1/1 (twice), `prefix --return-logprob` identical, `radix_cache` pass, and a bitwise batch-size check (the same prompt in batches of 1 to 50, 1,275 responses, token IDs and logprobs compared exactly with the batch-size-1 response) 1,275 / 1,275. Qwen3-30B-A3B (same setup): `single` 1, `prefix` 1/1/1/1, bitwise 1,275 / 1,275. Qwen3-8B at TP2: `single` 1, `prefix` 1/1/1/1, bitwise 1,275 / 1,275.

GSM8K (sgl-eval 0.1.2, `--temperature 0 --max-tokens 2048`, all 1,319 questions, Qwen3-8B, deterministic): 93.18% with this change (before: 93.25% deterministic, 93.48% normal mode, same image).

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Deterministic mode (setup above, CUDA graphs on), before vs after on the same node and image, `python3 -m sglang.benchmark.serving --backend sglang --dataset-name random --random-range-ratio 1.0 --request-rate inf --max-concurrency C` (output throughput, median inter-token latency):

| model | workload | before | after | change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen3-8B | 1k in / 256 out, concurrency 1 | 105 tok/s, 9.42 ms | 173 tok/s, 5.64 ms | +65%, ITL -40% |
| Qwen3-8B | 1k / 256, concurrency 16 | 1,663 tok/s, 7.70 ms | 2,033 tok/s, 6.14 ms | +22%, ITL -20% |
| Qwen3-8B | 8k / 256, concurrency 16 | 582 tok/s, 10.71 ms | 653 tok/s, 9.11 ms | +12%, ITL -15% |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B | 1k / 256, concurrency 1 | 94 tok/s, 10.5 ms | 163 tok/s, 6.0 ms | +73%, ITL -43% |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B | 1k / 256, concurrency 16 | 1,070 tok/s, 13.55 ms | 1,282 tok/s, 11.18 ms | +20%, ITL -17% |
| Phi-4 | 1k / 256, concurrency 1 | 72 tok/s, 13.74 ms | 112 tok/s, 8.70 ms | +56%, ITL -37% |

A second alternating round for Qwen3-8B gives the same numbers within 1% (before 105 tok/s / 9.40 ms and 1,655 tok/s / 7.75 ms; after 174 tok/s / 5.64 ms and 2,036 tok/s / 6.11 ms).

For reference, normal mode on the same setup has an inter-token latency of 4.8 ms (Qwen3-8B) and 4.4 ms (Qwen3-30B-A3B) at concurrency 1, so this closes most of the deterministic-mode gap for single-request decode. No change outside deterministic mode.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).
- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).

- [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance).

1. Ping Merge Oncalls to start the process. See the [PR Merge Process](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/.github/MAINTAINER.md#pull-request-merge-process).

title: [Perf] dsv41: Let Mega-mHC write the MegaMoE input under MegaGate
author: kpham-sgl
body:
## Motivation
With MegaGate on (`SGLANG_OPT_DEEPGEMM_MEGA_GATE=1`) the gate writes the routing into MegaMoE's buffer, but every MoE layer still runs `mega_moe_pre_dispatch` to quantize its input: one pass over the bf16 rows per layer that writes the FP8 rows, the per-row routed scales and the paged shared-expert scales. On SM100 those rows come out of the Mega-mHC kernel, which can already emit them as FP8 in both scale layouts (`deep_gemm.mega_mhc` takes `y_routed_sf`, `y_shared_sf` and `shared_sf_block_m`). Follow-up to #43262 and #46071.

## Modifications
- `mega_moe.py`: `mega_moe_input_target` resolves the MoE's buffer views for a batch that will take the MegaGate path (fp8xfp4 with fused shared experts); `MegaMoeInput.mark` tags the normed rows; `run_mega_routed_experts` skips the pre-dispatch when the routing is in the buffer and the rows carry the tag for that buffer and row count.
- `deepseek_v4_mhc.py`: `HcNextBoundary.mega_moe_input`; `_post_fusion` asks the next MoE for its target and hands the views to `mhc_mega_boundary`.
- `deepseek_v4_boundary.py`: the MoE-side read boundary carries the resolver with its forward batch.
- `mhc_mega.py`: `moe_input` through to `deep_gemm.mega_mhc`.

No change with MegaGate off. Prefill, non-fused shared experts, routing that stays out of the buffer and narrowed rows all keep the pre-dispatch.

## Accuracy Tests
GSM8K 5-shot, 1,314 examples, native acceptance, DP attention + EP 4 on GB300, MegaGate + `v41_new` + `--enable-fp32-lm-head`: 0.9711 with this PR and 0.9711 on the base commit. The GB300 `dp2ep2` and `tp2ep2` e2e test files pass (GSM8K 0.975 both, MMMU-Pro 0.815 / 0.79).

## Speed Tests and Profiling
Performance neutral: 0.02 to 0.05 ms per decode step (0.1 to 0.4%), at the edge of what one pair of runs resolves.

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash decode, DP attention + EP 8 on two GB300 nodes, MegaGate + `v41_new` + `--enable-fp32-lm-head`, forced balanced routing, one cached 126,976-token prefix plus 4,096 own tokens per request, 3 drafts at simulated acceptance 3.25, a fixed batch of N requests per rank; step time per rank in ms from the scheduler's own per-step record over a 120 s window, same commit with and without this PR:

| N per rank | base ea226cf782 | this PR | diff |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 8 | 10.761 | 10.745 | -0.017 |
| 16 | 13.029 | 12.976 | -0.053 |
| 32 | 13.654 | 13.622 | -0.033 |
| 64 | 15.483 | 15.433 | -0.050 |
| 128 | 20.141 | 20.123 | -0.018 |
| 256 | 28.867 | 28.844 | -0.023 |

GPU traces (20 steps, rank 0) show why: `mega_moe_pre_dispatch_kernel` drops from 42 to 3 launches per cycle (the 3 are the DSpark draft MoE layers), 0.103 -> 0.007 ms at 64 per rank and 0.207 -> 0.012 at 256; but the FP8-emitting `sm100_mega_mhc_impl` template is slower than the bf16-only one at 256 rows, 1.192 -> 1.313 ms per cycle over 39 layers (about 3 us per launch), and equal at 64 rows (0.600 -> 0.585). Net kernel time -0.11 ms per cycle at 64 per rank and -0.07 at 256. The gain would be about 0.2 ms per step at 256 per rank if the FP8-emitting template cost the same as the bf16 one.

title: [Perf] http: Serialize /v1/embeddings responses with model_json_response
author: anmolgupt
body:
## Motivation

`/v1/embeddings` returns the `EmbeddingResponse` Pydantic model to FastAPI. Without a
`response_model`, FastAPI runs `jsonable_encoder` over it, a recursive pure-Python walk that copies
every float of every embedding, before `ORJSONResponse` serializes the copy. The cost grows with the
number of floats in the response, so it shows most on requests that carry many embeddings. The chat and completions routes already avoid this with `model_json_response`, which serializes the
model once with pydantic-core.

## Modifications

- `python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/http_server.py`: `/v1/embeddings` returns
  `model_json_response(...)`, as `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/completions` do. Error responses
  pass through unchanged.
- `test/registered/unit/entrypoints/test_embedding_responses.py` (new, CPU): the route returns JSON
  bytes equal to `EmbeddingResponse.model_dump_json(by_alias=True)`.

## Accuracy Tests

Ran `Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B` model on one RTX A6000. 32 synthetic texts (8 to 8,430 tokens), sent one per request, as batches in several orders, and concurrently. Each embedding is compared with the FP32 SentenceTransformer reference and the min cosine similarity was ~0.99986 (with and without this change)

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Setup: 1x RTX A6000, `Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B` (1024-dim), `--is-embedding
--tokenizer-worker-num 8`, main = `74c08f3d`, same image and GPU for both. AIPerf 0.13.0 on
`/v1/embeddings` on synthetic dataset, request-count timing: 20 warmup and 200 measured requests per concurrency lane.
Each value is the mean of 3 runs with different dataset seeds

title: [Perf] logits: Cast bf16 logits into the fp32 buffer with a Triton kernel
author: hnyls2002
body:
## Motivation

When a model's lm_head returns bf16 logits and the forward has a shared fp32 logits buffer (CUDA graph decode, speculative verify), `_copy_logits_to_buffer` fills the buffer with `logits_buffer.copy_(logits)`. On Blackwell this dtype-casting copy runs well below memory bandwidth, and at speculative-verify batch sizes (many rows x a full vocabulary) it shows up as one of the larger single kernels of a decode step.

## Modifications

- `softcap.py`: `softcap_inplace_logits_kernel` gains an `APPLY_SOFTCAP` constexpr; the new `cast_to_float32_logits(logits, output)` uses the same launcher without the softcap.
- `activation/__init__.py`: register `activation.cast_to_float32_logits` next to `softcap_to_float32_logits`.
- `logits_processor.py`: in the buffered branch of `_copy_logits_to_buffer`, CUDA fp16/bf16 logits are written by the new kernel; fp32 logits and the unbuffered path are unchanged.

No numerical change: the fp16/bf16 to fp32 conversion is exact, and the buffer contents are byte-identical to the `copy_` result.

## Verification

- Byte-identical fp32 buffer against `copy_` for bf16 and fp16 inputs, contiguous and vocab-padded (sliced) layouts, at several row counts, with inf, NaN, -0.0 and tied maxima in the inputs; argmax of the buffer unchanged.
- `test/registered/rl/test_fp32_lm_head.py` passes on GB300 (covers the buffered path, vocab slicing, softcap and CUDA graph replay).
- Micro benchmark of `_copy_logits_to_buffer` at speculative-verify shapes on GB300 under CUDA graphs: faster at every size tested.

title: [Perf] diffusion: Gather spatial-parallel decode heights on the host
author: mickqian
body:
Branch: mick/diffusion-vae-height-gather-host (on main 005333d029), commit 2a864e5c69

## Motivation

Spatial-parallel VAE decode shards the frame height across the decode ranks. Each output gather (`gather_and_trim_height`) and each height-dependent op (the Wan VAE's row-sharded attention, strided convs) first learns every rank's shard height through `gather_height_sizes`. That helper built a one-element CUDA tensor from a Python int, all-gathered it over the device group and read each element back with `.item()`.

Both the pageable H2D copy and the read-back block the host until every kernel queued before them has run. In the middle of a decode, that drains the GPU queue: the GPU idles while the host relaunches the rest of the decoder. The Wan VAE decodes one latent frame per call and pays this twice per frame. A Cosmos3-Nano 189-frame decode on 4xB300 (48 latent frames) issued 96 stream syncs, which held the host for 590 ms in one profiled request. About 420 ms of the 2.47 s decode window was GPU idle.

## Modifications

- `layers/parallel_conv.py`: `gather_height_sizes` all-gathers the heights as a CPU int64 tensor over the group's gloo `cpu_group` instead of the device group. It does no device work and no stream sync. The values and the call order are the same on every rank, so every decode returns the same result.
- `test_vae_spatial_parallel_decode.py`: `test_height_sizes_are_gathered_on_the_host` runs two gloo ranks with uneven shards (3 and 2 rows) and passes `meta` tensors with no device group. The gather returns `[3, 2]` on both ranks. The old device gather cannot run on meta tensors.
- `test_ltx_vae_parallel_decode.py`: the fake decode group now carries a `cpu_group`.

## Accuracy Tests

The heights are integers and only travel over a different group, so every output is bitwise unchanged. Cosmos3-Nano T2V 720p 189 frames on 4xB300: the MP4s are byte-identical to the base (md5 a494ab96ce / 80597a2763 for two requests). They are also identical at x264 crf 0 together with "Encode Cosmos3 video while it decodes".

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Cosmos3-Nano T2V 720p 189 frames, 4xB300, CFG 2 x Ulysses 2, 4-rank spatial-parallel VAE decode, synchronized stage timers, two requests per build:

| | client e2e | decode stage |
|---|---|---|
| base | 24.251 / 24.300 s | 1.818 / 1.815 s |
| this PR | 24.053 / 24.069 s | 1.619 / 1.621 s |

The decode is 0.2 s (11%) shorter. With "Encode Cosmos3 video while it decodes" on top, the decode stage absorbs the MP4 encode and still takes only 1.717 / 1.730 s. Other affected models: every spatial-parallel decode that gathers heights (Wan family, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image 2.1, HunyuanVideo, FLUX.3, LTX-2 strided convs).

title: [Perf] diffusion: Encode Cosmos3 video while it decodes
author: mickqian
body:
Branch: mick/cosmos3-encode-while-decoding (on main 005333d029), commit f86dd52e1d

Merge note: this PR and #46173 both edit the decode call in `Cosmos3DecodingStage.forward`; whichever lands second needs a trivial rebase.

## Motivation

For causal VAEs, the generic `DecodingStage` passes each run of finished frames to the MP4 encoder while the rest of the clip is still decoding (`EncodeWhileDecoding` over `CudaVideoEncoder`). Only the last frames and the ffmpeg flush are left after the decode.

Cosmos3 runs its own `Cosmos3DecodingStage`, which never set that up. Every Cosmos3 video was decoded to a float32 `[1, 3, T, H, W]` clip (2 GB at 720p and 189 frames) and handed to the worker, and only then encoded. On 4xB300, Cosmos3-Nano T2V 720p 189 frames spent 1.13-1.16 s after the decode stage before the request completed. That was the largest piece of its post-denoise tail.

## Modifications

- `stages/model_specific_stages/cosmos3.py`:
  - `Cosmos3DecodingStage._encode_while_decoding` opens the shared encoder (`streamed_video_output_path` + `EncodeWhileDecoding`) for plain video outputs, using the stage's own `[-1, 1] -> [0, 1]` postprocess as `finish_frames`.
  - The decode passes the encoder as the Wan VAE's `on_frames`. On success the stage returns `OutputBatch(output=None, output_file_paths=...)`, as the generic stage does.
  - An encoder failure falls back to the old save-after-decode path.
  - Outputs that need the decoded frames are not streamed: guardrails, sound, action predictions and transfer displays.
- `test_cosmos3.py`:
  - `TestCosmos3EncodeWhileDecoding.test_streamed_frames_equal_the_saved_output`: a frame-by-frame VAE feeds the encoder frames that are bitwise equal to the clip the non-streamed path returns, and the stage returns the file path.
  - `test_outputs_that_need_the_frames_are_not_streamed` covers guardrails, sound, action and transfer.

## Accuracy Tests

The encoder gets the same values per frame, converted by the same `CudaVideoEncoder` with the same ffmpeg command line, so the MP4 is unchanged. Cosmos3-Nano T2V 720p 189 frames, 4xB300: the base and this change produced byte-identical MP4s (md5 a494ab96ce / 80597a2763 for two requests, default x264 settings).

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Cosmos3-Nano T2V 720p 189 frames, 4xB300 (CFG 2 x Ulysses 2, 4-rank spatial-parallel VAE decode), synchronized stage timers, two requests per build:

| | client e2e | decode stage | after decode |
|---|---|---|---|
| base | 24.251 / 24.300 s | 1.818 / 1.815 s | 1.134 / 1.156 s |
| + this PR + "Gather spatial-parallel decode heights on the host" | 23.076 / 23.062 s | 1.717 / 1.730 s (now includes the encode) | 0.022 / 0.041 s |

Each change on its own, same setup:

| | client e2e | decode stage | after decode | MP4 md5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| base | 24.251 / 24.300 s | 1.818 / 1.815 s | 1.134 / 1.156 s | a494ab96ce / 80597a2763 |
| this PR alone | 23.290 / 23.247 s | 1.919 / 1.920 s (incl. encode) | 0.032 / 0.031 s | same |
| "Gather spatial-parallel decode heights on the host" alone | 24.053 / 24.069 s | 1.619 / 1.621 s | 1.121 / 1.138 s | same |

This PR alone saves 0.96 / 1.05 s per request. The encode now overlaps the decode, and only about 0.1 s of it (the last frames and the ffmpeg flush) is left after the decode.

title: [Perf] diffusion: Run Cosmos3's multi-GPU VAE decode on the lossless fast path
author: mickqian
body:
Branch: mick/cosmos3-vae-decode-fast-path, stacked on #46149 (mick/wan-vae-parallel-decode-fast-path 93ccc5dc4f), commit 638c1f882f

Merge note: this PR and #46172 both edit the decode call in `Cosmos3DecodingStage.forward`; whichever lands second needs a trivial rebase.

## Motivation

Cosmos3 decodes with the Wan 2.2 VAE (`AutoencoderKLWan`, bf16). With more than one GPU, the decode is spatial-parallel over 4 ranks. Two things kept that decode off the CUDA fast path that Wan pipelines use:

1. `vae_loader._should_use_channels_last_3d` gave Cosmos3 channels_last_3d Conv3d weights only at `num_gpus == 1`. With NCDHW weights, cuDNN wraps every conv in `nchwToNhwc` / `nhwcToNchw` conversions (about 200 ms per 189-frame decode on rank 0, profiled). The fused RMSNorm+SiLU kernel only takes channels_last input. The spatial-parallel decoder exchanges halos in either layout (#46149 made Wan multi-GPU channels_last for the same reason).
2. `Cosmos3DecodingStage` never enters `use_vae_fast_path`. The fast path is installed on the VAE at load (since #46149, also on the spatial-parallel decoder), but its gate stays off, so the unfused bf16 `F.normalize -> * scale * gamma + bias -> SiLU` chains run instead.

## Modifications

- `loader/component_loaders/vae_loader.py`: Cosmos3 converts the VAE's Conv3d weights to channels_last_3d at any GPU count. Single-GPU Cosmos3 already did.
- `stages/model_specific_stages/cosmos3.py`: the VAE decode runs under `use_vae_fast_path(vae, quality_allows(quality, "lossless"))`, the same gate the generic `DecodingStage` uses. `quality="exact"` requests keep the reference ops.
- Tests:
  - `test_vae_loader.py`: the channels_last policy now covers multi-GPU Cosmos3.
  - `test_cosmos3.py::TestCosmos3DecodeFastPath`: the gate is on for `lossless` and `high` and off for `exact`.

This touches the same lines in `Cosmos3DecodingStage.forward` as "Encode Cosmos3 video while it decodes". Whichever lands second needs a trivial rebase that keeps both context managers.

## Accuracy Tests

The decode stays in bf16, the official precision. The fused kernel normalizes in fp32 and rounds once, where the reference rounds every bf16 op. The channels_last conv picks different cuDNN algorithms, and the channel reduction runs in a different order. Both changes are float re-association; the precision is not lowered.

| without vs channels_last only (`quality=exact`) | 56.88 / 56.91 dB | 0.086 / 0.084 | 8 / 13 | 0.99999 |
| fp32 VAE vs without this PR (bf16 reference ops) | 52.09 / 52.13 dB | 0.259 / 0.255 | 14 / 18 | 0.99996 |
| fp32 VAE vs with this PR | 52.16 / 52.21 dB | 0.255 / 0.250 | 24 / 23 | 0.99996 |

Mean abs diff and max abs diff are on the 0-255 scale.

Against an fp32 decode of the same latents, this PR is as close as the bf16 reference ops, and slightly closer by PSNR and mean error. The difference between the two bf16 decodes is smaller than either one's distance to fp32. `quality="exact"` keeps the reference ops.

title: [Perf] diffusion: Build spatial-parallel causal conv inputs in one pass
author: mickqian
body:
Branch: mick/diffusion-parallel-conv-halo-in-place, stacked on #46149 (93ccc5dc4f), commit 56c7668c91

## Motivation

Under spatial-parallel VAE decode, `SpatialParallelCausalConv3d` builds each conv input in three full passes over the activation:

1. `torch.cat` of the temporal feature cache.
2. `F.pad` for the width and time padding, plus its zero fill.
3. `halo_exchange`'s `torch.concat` of the neighbours' halo rows.

The single-GPU `WanCausalConv3d` already builds the same input in one channels_last pass (`cat_pad_channels_last_3d`), but the parallel conv had no route to it. The fused NCDHW cat-pad also needs a contiguous input, so channels_last activations fell back to the aten ops.

Profiled 189-frame Cosmos3-Nano decode on 4xB300 (rank 0), out of 1.45 s of GPU busy time:

| op | GPU time |
|---|---|
| halo concat | 134 ms |
| cat/pad fallback (copies, zero fill, cache cat) | 193 ms |

## Modifications

- `layers/parallel_conv.py`:
  - `SpatialParallelCausalConv3d.forward` handles the common case in one pass: a height-preserving conv with channels_last_3d weights, a "zeros" height pad, a matching cache, and no ROCm conv hook. One `cat_pad_channels_last_3d` writes the cache frames, the shard, the width/time padding and zero halo rows.
  - The new `fill_halo_rows_` then exchanges the shard's edge rows with the adjacent ranks, using the same P2P pairs as `halo_exchange`, and copies the received rows into the halo rows in place. The global top and bottom halos stay zero.
  - Every other case keeps the existing path.
- `test_vae_spatial_parallel_decode.py::test_halo_rows_filled_in_place_match_the_concatenated_halo`: two gloo ranks with uneven shards check that `fill_halo_rows_` gives bitwise the tensor `halo_exchange` concatenates. The test uses NCDHW tensors because gloo only sends default-contiguous ones; the channels_last path runs on GPUs and is covered by the md5 checks below.

## Accuracy Tests

Values only move, so outputs are bitwise unchanged.

Cosmos3-Nano T2V 720p 189 frames, 4xB300. The base is "Run Cosmos3's multi-GPU VAE decode on the lossless fast path", which gives a channels_last spatial-parallel decode. Videos are saved at x264 crf 0, two requests per build, and the MP4 md5 is identical in both quality tiers:

| | `quality="exact"` | default (`lossless`) |
|---|---|---|
| base | 9afb4b6195 / a35e3c5382 | 65c152eb33 / d49d169d91 |
| this PR | 9afb4b6195 / a35e3c5382 | |
| this PR + the epilogue follow-up | 9afb4b6195 / a35e3c5382 | 65c152eb33 / d49d169d91 |

The default-crf MP4s are identical too (7d5582dbad / 2f9d13baba).

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Cosmos3-Nano T2V 720p 189 frames, 4xB300, synchronized stage timers, two requests per build. The decode stage includes the MP4 encode streamed during the decode ("Encode Cosmos3 video while it decodes").

| | decode stage | client e2e |
|---|---|---|
| base | 1.266 / 1.286 s | 22.631 / 22.638 s |
| this PR | 1.124 / 1.137 s | 22.463 / 22.461 s |
| this PR + the epilogue follow-up | 1.117 / 1.224 s | 22.469 / 22.522 s |

The passes removed here are the ones profiled on the base (rank 0): the 134 ms halo concatenation and the 193 ms of unfused cat/pad. The decode was not re-profiled with this change.

Wan2.2 multi-GPU decodes run the same parallel conv on channels_last weights since #46149, so they take this path too (not measured here).

title: [Perf] dsv41: Trim per-step DSpark decode overhead
author: hnyls2002
body:
Small per-step DSpark decode costs on DeepSeek-V4.1, each removed without changing any output bit.

- **hc stream mean**: `mhc_stream_mean`, a Triton kernel that averages the four hc streams in torch's order (in-order fp32 sum onto +0); used for the DSpark captures and the replay tail. Unverified shapes and dtypes fall back to `x.mean(dim=1)`.
- **aux packing**: V4 collects the captures in `AuxHiddenStatePacker`, and the mean writes straight into its slot, so the logits processor no longer `torch.cat`s them.
- **markov draft step**: when one rank holds the whole unpadded vocabulary (TP1, or DP attention with `--enable-dp-lm-head`), skip the identity vocab gather so the draft step runs one pass instead of two.
- **draft wo_a**: on Blackwell, target-verify calls outside the TP4 fast path (more rows, other group counts, as in the DSpark draft) use the existing strided bmm instead of `einsum` + transpose copy.

Without DSpark nothing changes.

## Verification

- New `test_mhc_stream_mean.py` pins the kernel bitwise to `x.mean(dim=1)`, including inf, NaN, overflow and all -0 rows.
- Packed captures, markov draft tokens and step logits, and draft wo_a outputs are bitwise equal to the previous code, eager and under CUDA graph replay.
- Existing DSv4 / DSpark unit tests pass.

title: [Perf] dsa: Overlap CP KV gather with indexer computation
author: Fridge003
body:
## Motivation

Overlap attention KV replication with independent DSA indexer computation during interleave CP prefills. Submit KV all-gather as soon as local KV is ready, before indexer projection/compression/scoring, including short prefills that skip MQA/top-k.

## Changes

- Instantiate `DSAInterleaveCPIndexerOverlap` only for DSA interleave CP prefills. Non-CP execution calls the original indexer and KV preparation directly.
- Co-locate the shared orchestration in `cp/interleave.py` and the stable BCG output adapter in `cp/bcg/interleave_bcg.py`. Remove the two standalone overlap modules and the requested unit test.
- Preserve producer readiness, consistent cross-rank collective ordering, the consumer join, FP8 byte transport, and cross-stream storage lifetime.
- Preserve the input-staging fast path for valid contiguous shards, zero padding for uneven shards, and live prefix/padding handling for BCG replay.
- No new server flag or expansion of ordinary-DSA BCG eligibility.

Current candidate: `51cef168bcb0805017ef14220a5992748ae1e897`. The review changes are split into CP gating/rename/test removal (`aab307c818`) and a separately verified pure relocation (`51cef168bc`).

## Validation

Four GB300 GPUs on glm53-dev: Prefill TP2/CP2 interleave + BCG on GPUs 0–1, Decode TP2 + DFlash2 on GPUs 2–3; Mooncake RDMA, FP8 E4M3 KV, chunked prefill 8192. The six PR source files match the tested commit.

### Profile: BS1, ISL2048, OSL20

10 warmups, 24 measured requests, 20 captured prefill steps; radix cache disabled; profiler stacks/shapes disabled. All measured requests have exact input/output lengths, with zero errors/cache hits.

| Prefill rank | Attention KV gathers | KV GPU ms | Covered by indexer compute ms | Weighted overlap | Minimum individual overlap |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| TP0 | 220 | 3.138 | 2.541 | **80.98%** | **65.04%** |
| TP1 | 220 | 3.152 | 2.568 | **81.46%** | **64.76%** |

All 440 eligible gathers exceed 50%. At ISL2048, the model skips MQA/top-k; overlap is with indexer K/compress-gate GEMMs, split-K reduction and normalization. The numerator is the union of GPU time intersections, excluding NCCL, copy kernels, memcpy and memset. Reused-top-k layers keep their original path. This is kernel overlap, not an end-to-end speedup percentage.

The merged Perfetto trace preserves all 514,842 raw events. All 32 downloaded profile evidence files match the remote SHA-256 manifest. Evidence: `/scratch/glm53-review46179-20261024/profile2048-evidence`; raw trace root: `/data/profile/sglang/glm53-review46179-20261024/candidate2048/prefill`.

### Accuracy

Candidate-only validation; no fresh control accuracy run. Same frozen data, prompts, seeds and generation settings as the previous acceptance. Both P/D servers match all 549 static server-info fields after resolving model directory aliases. Router uses `--pool-max-idle-per-host 0 --disable-retries`, as in the previous complete MMMU retest.

| Dataset | Configuration | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AIME26 | 30 questions ×16 seeds42–57; temperature1, top_p.95, max_tokens300000, reasoning_effort max, thinking enabled, concurrency16 | **456/480 (95.00%)**, **0 errors**; all 6 outputs reaching the 300000-token limit retained |
| MMMU-Pro | Same frozen first100 standard10-option examples; temperature0, top_p1, seed42, max_tokens32768, thinking enabled, concurrency8 | **75/100**, **0 errors**; all 17 length-limited outputs retained |

All 480 AIME evaluation prefills used BCG: 466 graph batches, including 30 prefix-hit batches. The 72 one-token eager batches were health probes, with no other eager AIME batch. Logs and metric deltas agree. Max reasoning prompt tokenizations were verified on both P/D servers.

The previous candidate `e6ed9b66e2` scored 462/480 on AIME and 74/100 on the complete error-free MMMU retest. This run is **6 fewer AIME answers and 1 more MMMU answer**; AIME truncations increased from 3 to 6. The saved #43774 AIME reference was 455/480, and earlier PR candidate `9408f417dc` scored 448/480. These are historical references, not a fresh paired control; the candidate-only results do not establish a causal regression or non-regression. No selective retries or sample exclusions were used.

The final audit verifies all 480 AIME question/seed pairs, request settings, MMMU IDs and frozen image bytes, finish reasons, scores/token totals, and the six source hashes. All **115 downloaded accuracy evidence files** match their SHA-256 manifest. Evidence: `/scratch/glm53-review46179-20261024`; archive SHA-256 `1756a6b7af6fad5393dc6e7e5153ec4321947f8b8600e09e835b1f849e6c87c1`. All owned P/D/router processes have exited; the devbox remains allocated.

### Other verification

Pure relocation reproduced byte-for-byte against the exact commit. <details>
<summary>Reproduce the relocation commit (Python ≥3.10, pre-commit)</summary>

From a SGLang checkout containing the PR commits, save the script below as `/tmp/reproduce-overlap.py`, then run:

```bash
python3 /tmp/reproduce-overlap.py --repo "$PWD" --base aab307c8181a1f107ee1c8eb76272d7d7b0c2049 --target 51cef168bcb0805017ef14220a5992748ae1e897
```

The script uses the [proof engine already tracked in this exact commit](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/51cef168bcb0805017ef14220a5992748ae1e897/.agents/skills/mechanical-refactor-verify/scripts/mechanical_refactor_reproduction_utils.py), which byte-matches the engine used for validation. It recreates only the relocation in a temporary worktree, runs formatting/hooks, compares against the fixed target SHA, then removes its temporary worktree. Verified result: **PASS — reproduces the commit byte-for-byte**.

```python
"""Reproduce the interleave-only relocation using faithful move primitives."""
import argparse
from pathlib import Path
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, str(Path.cwd() / ".agents/skills/mechanical-refactor-verify/scripts"))
from mechanical_refactor_reproduction_utils import Repro

def recipe(base, target, repo):
    r = Repro(base=base, target=target, repo_root=repo)
    src = 'python/sglang/srt/layers/cp/indexer_overlap.py'

    after = 'interleave_rows_per_request'

        r.move_symbol(name, src=src, dst=dst, into_class=None, after=after)

    r.add_imported_name(mla, module='sglang.srt.layers.cp.interleave', name='DSAInterleaveCPIndexerOverlap')

    return r

    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()

title: [Perf] dsv41: Read Engram rows from peer device shards
author: hnyls2002
body:
With per-rank Engram tables and DP attention, every lookup all-gathers all DP ranks' hash ids, gathers the owned rows for all of them into a `[DP x tokens]` bf16 buffer, and reduce-scatters it back. The traffic and the buffer grow with the DP size, so wide-EP decode pays a collective per Engram layer that is larger than the lookup itself.

This adds an opt-in path, `SGLANG_OPT_DSV41_ENGRAM_PEER_SHARDS=1`:

- Each TP rank keeps its row shard in exportable device memory (CUDA VMM) and maps every peer's shard after loading: FABRIC handles across an NVLink domain (MNNVL), POSIX fds within a host.
- `engram_gather_peer`: one Triton kernel reads each of a rank's own tokens' rows straight from the owning shard (owner found by binary search over the shard starts). No id gather, no global buffer, no collective; CUDA-graph safe. Covers the TP, DP and prefill-CP lookups.
- Output is bitwise equal to the current path (-0 is written as +0, as the zero-fill + sum leaves it).
- Takes precedence over the host table (a warning says so when both are set). The shard costs `table_size / tp_size` of HBM per GPU, so it suits wide DEP.
- The VMM handle exchange (export, then FABRIC handles or POSIX fds) moves into `cuda_vmm_utils.exchange_shareable_handles`, shared with the DWDP transport; a group spanning hosts without FABRIC handles now fails there with a clear error. Peers are mapped with the existing `import_and_map_alloc`.

Off by default; nothing changes unless the variable is set.

## Verification

- `test/manual/layers/test_engram_peer_shards.py` at the real table size, bitwise equal to the current lookup, eager and under CUDA graph replay: 8 GB300 ranks over two nodes (FABRIC), and 8 B300 GPUs on one host (POSIX fds).
- DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash decode with DP attention over two GB300 nodes: the ReduceScatter and AllGather are gone from the decode step, greedy outputs and accept lengths match, and the reduced KV pool still fits the tested batch.

Related: #45679 (single-node TP4 peer reads).
