title: [Perf] eplb: Fuse expert-count recording into one kernel on CUDA decode graphs
author: weireweire
body:
## Motivation

With `--enable-eplb`, every decode step pays a fixed cost for expert-distribution recording and the logical-to-physical remap. That cost is large enough to cancel the balancing gain on a MegaMoE decode.

`_SelectExpertsSinglePassGatherer.on_select_experts` builds the per-layer count with about eight small elementwise ops: two compares, `&`, `~`, `masked_fill`, two dtype casts and `scatter_add_`. On CUDA the static remap is two more ops (index plus cast). `_on_hook` records whenever a stream is capturing, so all of these go into the decode CUDA graph and run on every replay, even after recording stops.

Measured on GB300, 40 MoE layers in one CUDA graph, 20-120 tokens per rank, extra time over no EPLB:

| path | extra time per forward |
| --- | --- |
| recorder hook only (MegaGate maps in-kernel) | +570 to +720 us |
| torch static remap + recorder hook | +763 to +1069 us |

On DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash DEP32 decode (6x DEP2 prefill, c3018 agentic), dynamic EPLB with 32 redundant experts gave no decode-step gain on an earlier nightly. The placement it computed was near-ideal: the busiest rank carried 1.03-1.07x the mean tokens, against 4.2x with the trivial placement. A matched-batch comparison showed +5.6% step time at 4 running requests per rank and -5.5% at 24: a fixed cost cancelling a load-proportional gain. A static placement computed offline from the same traffic, which runs no recorder, gives the gain.

`eplb_map_and_record_fused` already does the remap and the count in one Triton kernel. It is only reachable on the ROCm prefill-only MegaMoE path, and `get_current_pass_count_buffer` returns `None` during CUDA graph capture, because `_record_current_pass` is only set inside `with_forward_pass`.

## Modifications

- The kernel moves from `srt/eplb/eplb_map_record_fused.py` to `sglang/kernels/ops/moe/eplb_map_record.py` and is registered as `moe.eplb_map_and_record` and `moe.record_physical_counts`. Both entries take tensors only (the dispatch map instead of `ExpertLocationDispatchInfo`). Its GPU test moves to `test/registered/kernels/ops/moe/test_eplb_map_record.py`.
- `eplb_map_record.py`: add `WRITE_IDS` to the histogram kernel. Map+record and the new count-only `record_physical_counts(topk_ids, load_buffer)` share one launch helper. Inputs are made contiguous, since the kernel indexes them flat.
- `expert_location_dispatch.py`: `topk_ids_logical_to_physical_and_record` reads the static dispatch map from the dispatch info and calls the kernel; it returns `None` for non-static algorithms, which keep the torch remap.
- `expert_distribution.py`: `_SelectExpertsSinglePassGatherer.on_select_experts` uses the one-kernel histogram for GPU tensors (CUDA and ROCm) and keeps the torch path for other devices. This covers every recorder caller, including MegaGate's in-buffer path and DeepSeek-V4.1 VL routing. `get_current_pass_count_buffer()` now uses the same gate as `_on_hook` (`_disable_all`, the prefill-only pass check, recording or capturing) on every platform, and returns the recorder's current-layer row, the same row the hook writes. So the fused path is captured into decode graphs.
- `topk.py`: on CUDA, the routed-only branch of `_post_process_topk_ids` uses the fused map+record whenever the recorder exposes a buffer, then applies the usual padded-row mask and skips the separate recorder hook. The ROCm MegaMoE prefill path calls the same helper. All other branches are unchanged.

## Accuracy Tests

The checks below ran on the original revision (aea10915c0). The follow-up commits (kernel move, gate unification, guard removal) were checked by `test_eplb_map_record.py` on 1 GPU and the CPU unit tests at 1da0bdf5d8 only; the last four commits and the ROCm path were not run.

The counts are int32 and must match bitwise. Checked on 1 GPU (GB300) against the previous torch implementation:

- Histogram: 256 cases (T in {1, 7, 20, 60, 120, 144, 1024, 16384}, top-k {6, 8}, 384/416 physical experts, int32/int64 ids, -1 and out-of-range ids, non-contiguous inputs, non-zero initial buffer). 0 mismatches.
- Map + record against remap + padded mask + record: 320 cases (also 256/288 experts, `num_token_non_padded` None/full/T-3/0, padded rows holding -1 or live ids). Output ids and counts are identical in every case. A non-contiguous input gives a contiguous output with identical ids and counts.
- CUDA graph capture with recording started but no forward-pass context: the fused path is captured, and N replays give N times the eager counts. `disable_this_region` and eager-not-recording return `None`.
- Existing tests, identical on base and on this PR: `unit/eplb/test_megamoe_prefill_recorder.py`, `unit/eplb/test_dispatch_dtype_preservation.py`, `unit/layers/moe/test_topk_routing_inputs.py`, `unit/layers/moe/test_mega_moe_deepgemm_api.py`, `moe/test_hash_topk.py` (CPU), and `test_megamoe_prefill_recorder::test_fused_map_record_filters_padding` plus `moe/test_topk_padded_region.py` (GPU; 3 HIP-only skips).
- `torch.compile` bs=1 smoke, DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat TP2/EP2, `--enable-torch-compile --torch-compile-max-bs 1`, EPLB +4 rebalancing every 64 passes (about 1,065 rebalances), GSM8K 200 questions: this PR scores 0.045 at parallel 1 and 0.640 at parallel 32, against 0.045 and 0.655 on the base. The low bs=1 compiled score is already there without EPLB on the base (0.105), so it is unrelated to this change.
- `test/manual/test_expert_distribution.py`: 1 passed (5 subtests) on base and on this PR. `test/manual/ep/test_eplb.py`: 4 passed on base and on this PR.
- Server-level count check, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite-Instruct, TP2 with attention DP2, flashinfer a2a + flashinfer_cutlass, +4 redundant experts from a skewed initial placement, static dispatch, stat recorder, decode in CUDA graphs. Traffic: 16 sequential greedy requests at batch size 1, then an 8-request burst (1,057 forward passes). In the same process, the old torch remap + mask + record ran on the same inputs at every call, including inside the captured graphs, and was compared on device: 0 count mismatches and 0 id mismatches over 27,690 fused calls on both ranks. Comparing separate server runs isn't bitwise reproducible even on the base (two base runs on different nodes differ by up to 35 per expert-layer, two runs of this PR by 12), and base against this PR (13) is within that.
- PD GSM8K, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, DEP4 decode with dynamic EPLB (+32 redundant, rebalance every 200 passes, 42 rebalances during the eval): 96.51% (1273/1319), against 96.82% for the same deployment without EPLB.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Extra time over no EPLB per 40-layer forward, in a CUDA graph on GB300:

| T (tokens/rank) | torch remap + record | fused map + record | record only (MegaGate) | fused record only |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 20 | +763 us | +166 us | +570 us | +168 us |
| 60 | +900 us | +143 us | +638 us | +141 us |
| 120 | +1069 us | +146 us | +720 us | +143 us |

End-to-end, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, 6x DEP2 prefill + DEP32 decode, GB300, agentic c3018, 1800 s from a cold start:

| arm | decode step at matched batch | ITL p50 | ITL p90 | requests (1800 s) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| no EPLB | baseline | 3.53 ms | 3.97 ms | 176,486 |
| no EPLB, repeat | -0.3% | 3.53 ms | 3.91 ms | 173,033 |
| static placement from an offline recording, +32 | -8.7% | 3.18 ms | 3.54 ms | 174,478 |
| **dynamic EPLB +32, this PR** | **-6.8%** | **3.29 ms** | 3.83 ms | 169,837 |

The matched-batch step is the median step time at each per-rank running-request count, weighted over counts, from 600 s on. From 15 minutes in, dynamic gives -6.3% and static -8.2%.

Dynamic EPLB with this PR recovers about three quarters of the static placement's decode gain, with no offline recording. The remaining gap of about 2 points matches the roughly 0.15 ms per step the fused kernels still add, plus a few transient placements in the first rebalances (1.24-1.47x busiest/mean, settling to 1.04-1.06x).

End-to-end request throughput is not better than the no-EPLB control: 3.8% lower here (the control repeat was 2.0% lower than the control), and below the static arm. TTFT p90 is also higher (24.1 s against 14-21 s). The cause is the blocking rebalance itself: about 20 s for the first one and about 0.57 s for each of the 16 that follow. This PR does not change that; #43754 (stop rebalancing after K rebalances) and #45282 (non-blocking rebalance) address it.

## Checklist

- [x] `pre-commit run --all-files`: all Python hooks pass with no changes. The Rust hooks could not run on the test host because cargo is not installed.
- [x] Accuracy and speed results above.

title: [CI] deepep: Add release workflow for sgl-deep-ep-v25 (DeepEP 2.5)
author: Oasis-Git
body:
[codex/claude generated]

## Motivation

DeepEP 2.5 (deepseek-ai/DeepEP#763) removes the V1 `Buffer` API and NVSHMEM, and replaces `ElasticBuffer` with `EPBuffer`, `EngramBuffer`, `PPBuffer`, and `BucketBuffer`. SGLang still needs V1 for the `deepep` backend, so it cannot replace the existing `sgl-deep-ep` package (V1 + DeepEP 2.1, built from `sgl-project/DeepEP@sgl-deepep`).

DeepEP 2.5 is instead packaged separately as `sgl-deep-ep-v25`, built from the new [`sgl-project/DeepEP@sgl-deepep-v25`](https://github.com/sgl-project/DeepEP/tree/sgl-deepep-v25) branch: upstream DeepEP 2.5, plus the manylinux `pidfd` fix and an `sgl_deep_ep_v25/` packaging directory. That wheel installs the Python package `deep_ep_v25`, and its host extension is compiled with the C++ `deep_ep` namespace renamed. As a result, `deep_ep` and `deep_ep_v25` can be installed in, and imported into, the same process. This PR adds the release pipeline for it; the `sgl-deep-ep` release is unchanged.

## Modifications

- `.github/workflows/release-whl-deepep-v25.yml`: a manual release workflow modeled on `release-whl-deepep.yml`.
  - Same Python (3.11/3.12/3.13) x architecture (x86_64/aarch64) matrix; it builds `sgl-deepep-v25` by default.
  - Builds with the CUDA 13.4 manylinux builder, because DeepEP 2.5 needs a CUDA 13.1+ toolkit to build and to JIT-compile kernels at runtime. PyTorch 2.14.1 comes from the cu130 index, matching the SGLang runtime; the extension needs only CUDA 13.
  - Uploads wheels to the `sgl-project/whl` release `sgl-deep-ep-v25-v<version>`. The prefix keeps them out of the `v0.1.x` releases that other packages share.
  - Updates the `cu134/sgl-deep-ep-v25` index.
  - Publishes to PyPI with a new `SGL_DEEP_EP_V25_PYPI_TOKEN` secret.
- `docker/sgl-deep-ep-v25.Dockerfile`:
  - Installs `nvidia-nccl-cu13==2.32.3` with `--no-deps`, because DeepEP 2.5 needs NCCL 2.32.3+ and PyTorch pins an older version.
  - Adds the elfutils headers, which DeepJIT includes. `libdw` is only `dlopen`ed at runtime, if it is present.
  - Drops the NVSHMEM and RDMA build dependencies.
- `scripts/build_sgl_deepep_v25.sh`:
  - Builds in that image and runs `auditwheel repair` without the NVSHMEM/gdrcopy excludes.
  - Writes PyPI wheels that drop the local CUDA version.
- `scripts/update_deepep_whl_index.py`: adds `--package` and `--release-tag-prefix`. The defaults keep the current `sgl-deep-ep` behavior.

SGLang runtime code is unchanged; this PR adds no dependency or import. Switching `deepep_v2` to `deep_ep_v25` will be a follow-up, after the first release.

## Accuracy Tests

Not applicable (release tooling only).

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Not applicable. The package itself was validated with a wheel built from `sgl-deepep-v25` with the same packaging script, outside this workflow, on 4x GB300 (aarch64). The environment was CUDA 13.1 toolkit, PyTorch 2.14.1 cu130, and NCCL 2.32.3:

- `import deep_ep_v25` works, and the wheel contains only `deep_ep_v25`. With only nvcc 13.0 available, the import fails with a clear prerequisite error.
- `deep_ep` (`sgl-deep-ep`, DeepEP 2.1) and `deep_ep_v25` import into one process in either order, with distinct pybind11 types.
- `tests/ep/test_ep.py` on 4 GPUs, NVLink only (`EP_DISABLE_GIN=1`): all 36 correctness cases pass; dispatch/combine run at ~840 GB/s.
- RDMA was not validated. Gin setup failed on that host with an IB-level `IBV_WC_RETRY_EXC_ERR` before any DeepEP kernel ran.

Release tooling checks:

- Both `cuda13.4` builder images put GCC 13 on `PATH`. DeepJIT needs `<format>`, so this matters.
- The shell scripts, including the in-container script, pass `bash -n`, and the workflow YAML parses.
- `update_deepep_whl_index.py` produces the same `sgl-deep-ep` index as before. In a run with both packages' wheels, each index lists only its own package. `ruff`, `ruff format`, and `isort` are clean.
- The builder image and the workflow have not run end to end yet. The first dispatch should use an rc version.

Before the first release:

- Add the `SGL_DEEP_EP_V25_PYPI_TOKEN` repository secret. The `sgl-deep-ep-v25` name is still unregistered on PyPI, so the first upload needs an account-scoped token, or a pending trusted publisher with a matching workflow change.

title: [Perf] paged-experts: fewer host syncs in host-planned steps
author: N3mezis
body:
# [Perf] paged-experts: fewer host syncs in host-planned steps

## Motivation

This PR aims to decrease TTFT.

Currently, Paged Experts (#42557) plans a step on the host when it routes more entries than the K resident slots: prefill, and decode batches past `K // top_k`. Such a step runs in waves, and each MoE layer syncs with the GPU 6 times plus once per wave (twice on the compacted Marlin path): two reads of the device LRU state, `torch.unique().tolist()`, a blocking upload of each wave's slot map, a `nonzero()` per compacted wave, `step.item()`, and two blocking uploads of the state back.

Profiling Qwen3-30B-A3B-GPTQ-Int4 at K=92 on an RTX 5070 Ti, the GPU sat idle for 24.5 ms of a 79 ms TTFT on a 60-token prompt, inside these MoE layers. The page-in copies themselves already ran at the PCIe ceiling (51.8 GB/s); the idle time was host round trips.


## Modifications

**One host sync per host-planned MoE layer** (`residency.py`, `executor.py`, `runners.py`).
- The step's routed entries per expert are counted on the GPU (`scatter_add_`) and read together with the device LRU state in one copy; all waves are planned from the counts.
- Every wave's slot map goes up in one pinned copy that does not wait for the GPU.
- A Marlin wave is compacted to the entry count the host already has (`nonzero_static`), so it needs no `nonzero()` sync.
- The state goes back in one such copy; the step counter it needs was read with the state.

The device state tensors, the decide kernel of the captured path and the per-expert page-in copies are unchanged.

## Accuracy Tests

**Unit and kernel tests.**
- Multi-wave paged forward on CPU equals the unpaged reference, for both the masked (triton) and the compacted (Marlin) runner contracts; on Marlin, a wrong entry count would drop or duplicate rows.
- The device state round-trips through the host LRU policy and returns the step's counts.

**Paged vs unpaged, 4-layer test models** (E=32, top-4, K=8; prompt and greedy decode logprobs; RTX 5070 Ti; main 2d3de82633 and this PR in one run):

| model | runner | this PR | main |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-MoE bf16 | triton | identical | identical |
| AWQ int4 | Marlin | decode max 0.014 | decode max 0.014 |
| compressed-tensors NVFP4 | Marlin | median max 0.050, unpaged floor 0.055 | median max 0.050, unpaged floor 0.046 |

Marlin is not run-to-run reproducible, so the Marlin formats are judged against the spread of two unpaged servers (the floor); bf16 on triton is bit-identical. Each check has a negative control that must fail (a perturbed RMSNorm eps on bf16 and AWQ, unnormalized top-k weights on NVFP4), and all three do.

**GSM8K (200 questions), Qwen3-30B-A3B-GPTQ-Int4, K=92:** main 0.945 / 0.945, this PR 0.950.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Same machine as #42557: RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB (PCIe 5.0 x16, 62 GB RAM), Qwen3-30B-A3B, 10,240 KV tokens and 4 slots, prefix caching off, 16 ShareGPT warm-up requests discarded. Decode tok/s is `1000 / median TPOT` over 8 ShareGPT prompts sent one at a time (256 output tokens each); TTFT and ITL are from the same requests. 4 requests: 16 ShareGPT prompts from 4 clients at once (output tok/s). 2k TTFT: 4 natural ~2,048-token prompts. main (upstream 2d3de82633) is measured first and last in the same run as this PR; both values are shown, and a difference inside their spread is no difference. Prefill is host-planned in every phase; decode with 4 requests stays captured (4 ≤ `K // top_k` = 11, 5 and 10 here).

| config | decode tok/s | TTFT p50 / p99 | ITL p50 / p99 | 4 requests: out tok/s | 2k TTFT p50 / p99 | peak VRAM |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| int4, K=92: main | 212.3 / 212.7 | 50 / 86, 50 / 82 ms | 4.70 / 5.35, 4.69 / 5.33 ms | 399 / 399 | 239 / 275, 246 / 274 ms | 14.8 GiB |
| int4, K=92: this PR | 212.2 | **40 / 75 ms** | 4.70 / 5.29 ms | 403 | **232 / 262 ms** | 14.9 GiB |
| FP8, K=40: main | 90.3 / 90.3 | 213 / 301, 213 / 300 ms | 10.50 / 20.70, 10.50 / 20.75 ms | 100 / 100 | 427 / 481, 427 / 481 ms | 13.3 GiB |
| FP8, K=40: this PR | 90.2 | **196 / 281 ms** | 10.52 / 20.76 ms | 101 | **410 / 465 ms** | 13.4 GiB |
| NVFP4 (Marlin), K=85: main | 189.6 / 190.6 | 73 / 112, 74 / 118 ms | 5.20 / 6.50, 5.18 / 6.41 ms | 347 / 343 | 257 / 285, 246 / 283 ms | 14.5 GiB |
| NVFP4 (Marlin), K=85: this PR | 189.3 | **62 / 100 ms** | 5.20 / 6.39 ms | 356 | **232 / 272 ms** | 14.5 GiB |

TTFT p50 drops 20% (int4), 8% (FP8) and 16% (NVFP4) for ShareGPT prompts, and 4%, 4% and 8% for a natural 2k prompt, against the mean of the two main runs. Decode, ITL and 4-request throughput are unchanged: captured decode does not take this path.


## CI

The unit tests check multi-wave forward against the unpaged reference on both runner contracts, and the state round trip. `test_paged_experts.py` already runs paged prefill end to end on GPTQ, FP8 and gpt-oss MXFP4.

title: [Perf] [NVIDIA] minimax-sparse: Run the decode indexer CP on Hopper at TP4 and TP8
author: ischencheng
body:
## Motivation

On Hopper every attention-TP rank keeps the whole MiniMax index K (one head) and every sparse layer scores all of it on each decode step. Index top-k sharing only runs on gfx95, so on CUDA every layer scans. At 128K context that is 33.5 MB per request per layer on each rank, and it grows with concurrency.

The opt-in indexer CP from #41488 and #42614 splits that scan across the ranks, but it only turns on for gfx950 at TP4. This PR turns it on for SM90 at TP4 and TP8. The three kernels are unchanged. MiniMax-M3 and M3.1 both take this path on Hopper. With DSPARK the gate keeps CP off, so this applies to runs without speculation or with EAGLE top-k 1.

## Modifications

- `unsupported_reason` takes an `sm90` flag. On SM90 it allows attention TP4 or TP8 with attention CP/DP size 1. The gfx950 gate stays TP4.
- `MiniMaxIndexerCP` sizes its gather buffers from the group (4 or 8 ranks). At TP8 two ranks serve each index head, so 8 query rows are gathered. K is still read once per block, and each rank reads 1/8 of the blocks.
- Still opt-in with `SGLANG_MINIMAX_M3_INDEXER_CP=1`. At batch 1 the two all-gathers per layer cost more than the scan they save, see the tables below.

## Accuracy Tests

- New `test_minimax_indexer_cp.py` (SM90): the merged CP selection for every rank equals the native page-128 selector at W=4 and W=8, BF16 and FP8, plus chain verify rows across a block boundary. Passes on 1x H200. Gate cases added to `test_minimax_indexer_cp_gate.py`.
- Real TP8 and TP4 groups on 8x H200: on every rank the CP selection equals the native selector, eager and in a CUDA graph replayed with changed seq_lens, BF16 and FP8, batch 1-32, 32K and 128K context. 0 rows differ.
- End to end on the dummy-weight model below, the first 32 greedy output ids of every request at batch 8 match across all 4 servers (CP off, on, on, off).
- Exact ties: since #45174 the CUDA radix top-k keeps the lowest block ids, which is what CP does. Checked once on 1x H200 with index K filled from 3 repeated block patterns (W=4 and 8, 32K and 128K context, BF16 and FP8): 0 rows differ. That check isn't in the test file.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Measured on 10-26, before merging the latest main, and not re-run since.

Per layer per rank, 8x H200, real TP8, BF16 index K, 128K context, us. CUDA graph with 8 calls per replay on disjoint requests, max over ranks, median of 20 replays. CP includes both all-gathers. "% of floor" is index K bytes over 4.8 TB/s.

| batch | native | native % of floor | CP, TP8 | change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 19.8 | 35% | 47.4 | +139% |
| 8 | 73.0 | 77% | 65.3 | -11% |
| 16 | 133.6 | 84% | 80.5 | -40% |
| 32 | 255.5 | 88% | 100.9 | -61% |

The two all-gathers alone take 42-48 us at TP8 and 30-42 us at TP4, so most of the CP time is communication. TP4: batch 16 133.2 -> 85.7, batch 32 252.5 -> 112.8. FP8 index K at TP8: batch 32 137.0 -> 87.0, batch 8 45.5 -> 64.1.

End to end on a 16-layer MiniMax-M3 dummy-weight model with the M3.1 layer layout (every layer sparse, first 3 FFNs dense), TP8 on 8x H200, BF16 KV and index K, page 128, 131K input, 160 greedy output tokens, decode CUDA graph. CP off and on alternated twice in the same container. Decode step in ms, median of 14 log windows of 10 steps each:

| batch | off (2 runs) | on (2 runs) | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2.25 / 2.23 | 2.38 / 2.31 | +4.7% |
| 4 | 2.62 / 2.62 | 2.63 / 2.63 | +0.3% |
| 8 | 3.52 / 3.52 | 3.17 / 3.16 | -10.0% |
| 16 | 4.96 / 4.98 | 3.87 / 3.85 | -22.3% |
| 24 | 6.52 / 6.52 | 4.58 / 4.59 | -29.7% |

That is 69 us per layer at batch 16 and 121 us at batch 24, so the full 60-layer model should save roughly 4 ms per step with 16 concurrent 128K requests. It's worth turning on for long-context serving with more than a few requests in flight.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).
- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).
- [ ] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations).
- [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed).

title: [Fix] kernel-plugins: Serve the MSA plugin behind --enable-nvidia-megakernel
author: ispobock
body:
## Motivation

#45389 moved the monokernel registry to `sglang.kernels.plugin_kernels.amd.spec`, fixed its backend to `amd` and narrowed `--monokernel-backend` to `amd`. The MSA plugin, which serves MiniMax-M3.1 on NVIDIA Blackwell, registers its specs under `msa` through `sglang.srt.monokernels.spec`. On main the plugin therefore fails to load (`No module named 'sglang.srt.monokernels'`), and the MiniMax-M3.1 B300 / GB300 Low-Latency recipe, which passes `--monokernel-backend msa`, fails at argument parsing.

## Modifications

- `--enable-nvidia-megakernel` also serves the MSA plugin: a model whose architecture the plugin registers (MiniMax-M3 / M3.1 and their DSpark draft) runs through the monokernel binding, and every other model keeps the sgl-nvidia-mega path. The MSA repository needs no change.
- `--monokernel-backend amd|msa` stays as a deprecated alias of `--enable-amd-monokernel` and `--enable-nvidia-megakernel`, on the CLI and in config files, so the published recipes keep working.
- `sglang.srt.monokernels.spec` re-exports the contracts for the MSA plugin pinned by `MSA_COMMIT` in `docker/Dockerfile.cu134`, until the plugin imports the new path.

## Verification

- `test_mono_framework.py` and the monokernel cases of `test_server_args.py`: 22 passed.
- 4x B300, `MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash`, MSA at the Dockerfile pin (1e7bf76), the cookbook B300 Low-Latency recipe: an earlier revision of this change, which selected the same monokernel path under its own flag, logged `minimax_m3_msa_v1 on sm_103, widths [8]` and scored 0.955 on sgl-eval GSM8K (200 examples, temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95). The run with `--enable-nvidia-megakernel` and `--monokernel-backend msa` is in progress.

title: [Perf] speculative: Rotate multi-layer EAGLE prefill input_ids 4096 ids per trip, not 8
author: Monishver11
body:
## Motivation

In short: `rotate_input_ids` shifts each request's `input_ids` left by one in place for the multi-layer EAGLE draft. On the prefill path it moves only 8 ids per loop trip, so a 16384-token chunk takes 2048 serial trips with two CTA barriers each. This PR uses the 4096-id block that the decode path already uses. The output is bit-identical. On an H100 PCIe one prefill call goes from 824 to 6.4 us at 16384 tokens, and inside a server from 763 to 6.0 us per launch.

Details:

`rotate_input_ids` (`python/sglang/kernels/ops/speculative/multi_layer_eagle.py`) runs one program per request. Each loop trip loads `BLOCK_SIZE` ids, hits `tl.debug_barrier()`, stores them one slot to the left, and hits a second barrier. The launcher picks `BLOCK_SIZE = 4096 if select_index is not None else 8`. `select_index` is set on the decode calls and is `None` on the prefill calls, so prefill gets 8. Both values came in with the day-0 MiMo-V2-Flash support in #15207, with no stated reason for 8.

In `multi_layer_eagle_worker_v2.py` the prefill draft extend calls it once before the first draft step and once after every step, so a prefill chunk pays `speculative_num_steps + 1` calls. Each call takes `max request length / 8` trips. Measured on an H100 PCIe that is about 0.40 us per trip, so 0.82 ms per call at 16384 tokens and 1.65 ms at 32768.

Recipes that reach it, from the cookbook (MTP on, which sets `--enable-multi-layer-eagle`). The chunk is per attention-DP rank, since DP attention divides `--chunked-prefill-size` by `--attn-dp-size`:

| recipe | prefill chunk per rank | draft steps | calls per chunk |
|---|---|---|---|
| MiMo-V2-Flash (DP 2 by default) | 8192 | 3 | 4 |
| MiMo-V2.5 | 8192 on Hopper (DP 2), 16384 on Blackwell; V2.5-Pro 16384 | 3 | 4 |
| Step-5-Preview | 16384 (8192 in the DP 2 rows) | 3 | 4 |
| Step-3.5, Step-3.7-Flash (MTP opt-in) | default: 8192 on H200, 16384 on B200 and MI300-class | 3 | 4 |
| Inkling, Inkling-Small | default: 8192 on H200, 16384 on B200/B300 | 8 | 9 |

## Modifications

In short: `BLOCK_SIZE = 4096` for both paths. One line, plus a test.

Why any block size gives the same bytes: each trip reads `[off + 1, off + B + 1)` and writes `[off, off + B)`. All loads of a trip complete before the barrier, and the stores come after it. The next trip reads only ids past every slot written so far. So no trip reads an id that an earlier store overwrote, for any `B`. (The decode path already uses 4096, but its windows are 4-9 ids, so it never runs more than one trip.)

`num_warps` stays at the default 4. I swept `BLOCK_SIZE` 1024-8192 x `num_warps` 4/8/16. 8192 x 16 warps is 1.1-2.4 us faster for one request of 16384-32768 tokens (5.31 vs 6.40 us at 16384, 9.02 vs 11.39 us at 32768), which is small next to the 0.8-1.6 ms saved. So I kept the decode path's 4096 x 4 and left one config for both paths.

New test `TestRotateInputIds.test_in_place_shift_across_blocks` in `test_boundary_kv_fix_kernels.py` (the GPU test file for the multi-layer EAGLE kernels; there was no GPU test for this kernel). It compares against a torch reference for one batch with request lengths 0, 1, 2, 4095, 4096, 4097 and 8197: 4097 shifts exactly one full block, and 8197 runs three trips, so later trips must read ids that earlier trips did not overwrite. Sentinel slots between requests catch writes outside a request's window. It runs with `select_index` `None` and set.

Not a duplicate: no open PR changes this kernel. #46385 moves draft-proposal sampling into the per-step draft-extend graphs and patches in a Python reference of the rotate for its unit test; it does not touch the Triton kernel. #43052 changes the draft-extend buffer prep kernel in the same file, not `rotate_input_ids`.

## Accuracy Tests

The output is bit-identical to main, so model accuracy can't change. Checked at the kernel level and in a server:

- Bitwise vs main 9f6678aa3d, CPU-seeded inputs, whole `input_ids` buffer hashed: **192 of 192 identical**. Lengths 1-32768 (including 7, 8, 9 and 4095, 4096, 4097), with 1, 4 or 32 requests, or a random split with an empty and a 1-id request; int32 and int64 index tensors; `select_index` `None` and set. All 192 also match a torch reference.
- Every swept `BLOCK_SIZE` x `num_warps` config vs `BLOCK_SIZE` 8 on the same 192 cases: 2304 of 2304 identical.
- `test_boundary_kv_fix_kernels.py`: 2 passed (6 subtests). I checked the new test fails on 5 broken kernels (mask `<=`, a short loop bound, a write for an empty request, `select_index` ignored, read offset +2).
- Registers: 113 per thread at 4096 x 4 warps, 0 spills.
- In a server: `thinkingmachines/Inkling` revision `test` (the 4.4 GB checkpoint with 2 MTP heads from `TestUnifiedHybridMTPBitExact`), its server args (deterministic inference, `--enable-multi-layer-eagle`, 2 steps, `--chunked-prefill-size 16384`). 6 greedy prompts of 7 to 25206 tokens, 64 new tokens: output ids and `spec_accept_length` identical on 6 of 6.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

H100 PCIe (350 W limit, 310 W default), driver 595.71, torch 2.14.1+cu130, triton 3.8.0, main 9f6678aa3d. `sglang.kernels.jit.benchmark.marker.do_bench` (CUDA graph, `input_ids` copies rotated so L2 is cold), median of 3 rounds that interleave all configs in one process. "main" is the same kernel launched with `BLOCK_SIZE=8`, the only difference in the diff. Contiguous requests, int32 index tensors.

| prefill shape | main | this PR | speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1024 tokens, 1 request | 52.56 us | 2.17 us | 24x |
| 4096 tokens, 1 request | 207.02 us | 2.60 us | 80x |
| 8192 tokens, 1 request | 412.52 us | 3.86 us | 107x |
| 16384 tokens, 1 request | 824.10 us | 6.40 us | 129x |
| 16384 tokens, 4 requests | 213.70 us | 2.82 us | 76x |
| 16384 tokens, 32 requests | 31.51 us | 2.42 us | 13x |
| 32768 tokens, 1 request | 1646.03 us | 11.39 us | 145x |

Over 18 prefill shapes (1024-32768 tokens, 1, 4 or 32 requests): geomean 23.3x, range 1.44x (1024 tokens in 32 requests) to 145x. The decode calls run the same 4096 x 4 config on main and this PR (2.29-2.78 us at batch 1-256, width 4 and 9).

When one request fills the chunk, that is 0.41 ms saved per call at 8192 tokens and 0.82 ms at 16384. Per chunk:

| chunk per rank | 3 draft steps (4 calls) | 8 draft steps (9 calls) |
|---|---:|---:|
| 8192 | 1.6 ms | 3.7 ms |
| 16384 | 3.3 ms | 7.4 ms |

These are H100 PCIe per-call times x calls per chunk, not measured on those models.

In a server, same Inkling test checkpoint and args as above, torch profiler over 8 requests of 16000 input tokens: 24 `rotate_input_ids_kernel` launches (8 chunks x 3 calls), median 763 -> 6.0 us per launch, total 18.09 -> 0.14 ms, 4.15% -> 0.03% of GPU kernel time. This checkpoint is small, so I expect that share to be lower on the full models. The per-launch time depends on the GPU and the longest request in the chunk, not on the model weights.

`sglang.benchmark.serving`, random 16000 in / 1 out, 64 prompts, request rate inf, 3 interleaved rounds:

| round | main input tok/s | this PR input tok/s |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | 269588 | 294714 |
| 2 | 286508 | 292351 |
| 3 | 285938 | 295081 |

Rounds 2-3: 286.2k -> 293.7k tok/s (+2.6%). All rounds: 280.7k -> 294.0k (+4.8%). Main round 1 was the first server launch on the box (240 s to start vs 50 s for the others), which is why I quote rounds 2-3.

Not tested: NPU. The Ascend MiMo recipes run this Triton kernel too, and the decode calls in the same worker already use 4096 there.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).
- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).
- [ ] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations). (no user-facing change)
- [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed). (bitwise, microbench, profile and serving)
- [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance).

I used Claude Code for this change. I reviewed every line and ran the tests and benchmarks above myself.

title: [Perf] MOSS-Image: Fuse joint-block QKV projections in high quality
author: BBuf
body:
## Motivation

MOSS-Image joint blocks run three separate Q/K/V GEMMs for every conditional and unconditional denoising pass. This PR packs those projections for `quality=high` and lets the existing ordered RMSNorm+RoPE kernel read their strided Q/K views directly. The latter avoids copying Q and K back to contiguous storage after each packed GEMM.

The measured scope is MOSS-Image-Base, 1024×1024, 50 steps, batch 1 / concurrency 1 on one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition. Four repeated temporal pairs give a geometric-mean E2E speedup of **1.0141× over main** (1.386% lower latency) and **1.0222× over native Omni**; every pair is faster. The primary timed input is the fixed short product-photograph prompt; the long and Chinese prompts are quality checks. This is an eager optimization; it does not add or claim BCG coverage.

- Frozen main baseline: `af21e2b989e482cfdce39689126562f2209d53ac`.
- Tested PR head: `d752066eaa6f5091fa4c8daa2ba1d5d43a3928cd`.
- Native vLLM-Omni comparator: `817d4c17feb702289a2d2b2cbacfd594c262b7a7`.
- Common checkpoint: `OpenMOSS/MOSS-Image-Base@85975793d8b3d432f1b6e27f352abaa4c2a4c0d3`; all downloaded files were verified against the pinned file hashes.

## Modifications

- Reuse the existing checkpoint name mapping to merge Q/K/V in that order into one weight. There is no duplicate model weight or persistent view cache.
- Pass the quality choice through the request's denoising branch. `high` uses one packed GEMM; `exact/lossless` use three separate `F.linear` calls with fresh slices of the packed weight. A later request can change quality without reloading weights or mutating a module-wide mode.
- Extend the existing ordered norm+RoPE kernel to accept contiguous heads with a regular token stride. Reduction order and BF16 rounding in this kernel are unchanged; its result remains contiguous. Other layouts keep the existing fallback.
- Extend existing loading-order, quality-dispatch, offload/stream and numerical/stride tests; document the quality policy in the existing MOSS cookbook.

## Accuracy Tests

A wider GEMM changes BF16 rounding. The first unconditional version failed the task's lossless byte-exact gate, so packing is explicitly restricted to `high`.

Final committed-head serving checks under the selected cuDNN configuration pass: all three lossless prompt outputs match actual main lossless byte for byte, both before and after high requests. Each short → long → Chinese → short sequence also repeats the first PNG exactly. Final main/PR high outputs match their respective paired-benchmark outputs; collecting a Torch profile preserves the same high PNG.

High-quality main/PR comparison, using the actual final-head outputs shown below:

| Prompt | SSIM | PSNR (dB) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Short product photograph | 0.993826 | 38.0795 |
| Long still life, worst main/PR sample | 0.971474 | 32.2421 |
| Chinese café poster | 0.996791 | 37.7274 |

The task's predeclared image-alignment thresholds are SSIM ≥ 0.95 and PSNR ≥ 28 dB. These are numeric alignment gates, supplemented by visual inspection, not a broad perceptual-equivalence study. The long sample preserves a baseline prompt mismatch: both show two visible pears although the prompt asks for three. Short → long → Chinese → short checks repeat the first PNG exactly within each process. All 12 process-level quality gates passed. Within each arm, all three prompt PNGs are also identical across its four restarts. Across all main/candidate/Omni reference checks, the lowest SSIM is 0.969576 and lowest PSNR is 28.4811 dB (main vs Omni). Candidate vs matched main has the per-prompt metrics above; candidate vs Omni has minimum SSIM 0.985401 and PSNR 28.5654 dB.

All figures below paste the complete source PNGs at their original pixel scale, with labels outside image bounds. Both sides use seed 1101, 1024×1024, 50 steps, CFG 3, flow shift 5, skip layer 22 / SLG window 0.01–1.0, BF16 DiT/text encoder, FP32 VAE/solver, high quality and transformer cuDNN SDPA.

![Actual main and PR short-prompt outputs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BBuf/sglang/8df03e213fe39d57c723da266338b5236674f144/00-image-short-main-vs-pr.png)

![Actual main and PR long-prompt outputs, worst paired quality sample](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BBuf/sglang/8df03e213fe39d57c723da266338b5236674f144/01-image-long-main-vs-pr.png)

![Actual main and PR Chinese-poster outputs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BBuf/sglang/8df03e213fe39d57c723da266338b5236674f144/02-image-text-main-vs-pr.png)

Exact prompts and media hashes: [evidence branch](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/tree/bbuf/rtx6000-diffusion-20261026-moss-qkv-evidence).

Validation executed on the actual SM120 GPU after cleanup:

- Existing MOSS norm tests: 30 passed, including packed nonzero offsets, batch/odd sequence lengths, extreme values and rejected strides.
- MOSS model and CPU-distributed tests: 115 passed, including loading order, quality dispatch and high/separate projection offload with alternate streams. The CPU-distributed tests do not establish GPU multicard performance.
- Repository-selected Ruff rules, Ruff formatting and isort passed; `mint validate` and `mint broken-links` passed.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

| Arm | Denoise p50 (s) | HTTP E2E p50 / p95 (s) | Sequential requests/s | Peak NVML (GiB) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| SGL main, eager high + cuDNN | 14.5002 | 14.7131 / 14.7194 | 0.067966 | 32.2065 |
| PR final head, eager high + cuDNN | 14.2931 | 14.5095 / 14.5145 | 0.068920 | 32.2787 |
| Native Omni, regional compile + cuDNN | 14.4178† | 14.8269 / 14.8480 | 0.067423 | 32.5034 |

PR peak NVML memory is **74 MiB higher than main**. The primary E2E results contain 16 measured requests from four processes per arm. Per-process measured CV ranges are main 0.00768–0.03252%, PR 0.01970–0.03256%, Omni 0.01309–0.04414%.

| Temporal pair | Main / PR | Omni / PR |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Cycle 1 forward | 1.013838× | 1.022582× |
| Cycle 1 reverse | 1.014105× | 1.021613× |
| Cycle 2 forward | 1.014191× | 1.021622× |
| Cycle 2 reverse | 1.014079× | 1.023077× |
| Geometric mean | **1.014053×** | **1.022223×** |

Process launch-to-ready ranges: main 56.04–56.05 s, PR 54.05–56.05 s, Omni 32.02 s, observed with 2-second readiness polling. Eight additional thermal-warmup requests take 117.41–117.55 s / 115.83–115.87 s / 118.39–118.49 s respectively. Compiler/JIT caches are reused across process restarts; these are not isolated cold-compile estimates. BCG is disabled, with no new graph capture/replay claim.

The protocol runs two symmetric main / PR / Omni / Omni / PR / main cycles on the same physical GPU: four fresh processes and 16 measured requests per arm. Each process first passes the three-prompt and repeated-short quality gate, then runs eight thermal warmups and four timed requests. All rows, including failed configuration screens, are retained. GPU0 UUID and owned PIDs are checked in archived NVML samples; GPU1 remains idle. No Torch/Nsight profiler runs during these timings.

HTTP E2E covers submission through receipt of all response bytes; client PNG decoding/writing is outside the timer. Startup and warmups are reported separately. Launch-to-ready uses each framework's native readiness boundary: SGL includes its configured 50-step built-in warmup, while Omni's health readiness precedes the qualification requests. This is not a same-work cold-start comparison. Both then receive the same quality sequence and eight extra thermal warmups. SGL native stage timing is enabled equally for main and PR. Its denoise stage includes the scheduler. † Omni denoise-core p50 is **14.417836 s** across four separately instrumented requests. Its default profiler did not time the actual MOSS full-forward loop, so an isolated diagnostic checkout adds four lines configuring the existing native profiler targets: `predict_noise_with_slg`, `scheduler_step_maybe_with_cfg`, encoder and VAE. Logs verify exactly 50 prediction and 50 Euler calls per request, and their sums agree with response metrics. This boundary excludes the surrounding Python loop/setup, unlike the SGL denoise stage. The primary Omni checkout and all primary E2E timing rows are unchanged. No cross-framework denoise speedup is inferred from these different boundaries.

Both SGL arms use the faster qualified explicit transformer cuDNN configuration. Omni's native Blackwell default already selects `CUDNN_ATTN`; it keeps regional compilation enabled with `TORCHINDUCTOR_EMULATE_PRECISION_CASTS=1`. The default compile configuration without cast emulation failed the restart quality gate (PSNR 27.449 < 28), so its timing is not used as a qualified comparison. SGL MOSS rejects torch.compile in this pinned source.

Library stacks are native to each framework and disclosed rather than silently equated:

| Component | SGL main / PR | Omni |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PyTorch / CUDA wheel | 2.14.1+cu130 | 2.13.0+cu130 |
| Triton | 3.8.0 | 3.7.1 |
| cuDNN | 9.24.0.43 | 9.20.0.48 |
| Transformers | 5.19.0 | 5.19.0 |
| Diffusers | 0.37.0 | 0.40.0 |
| FlashInfer Python | 0.7.2 | 0.7.0.post1 |

Driver 595.84, stock 600 W power limit; one 97,887 MiB RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition. Both use the same physical GPU, weights, input, seed, precision and generation contract. No quantization or offload is enabled in the measured cell.

Final-head cuDNN traces compare complete GPU `ProfilerStep#2/#3/#4` for the same short request. Average diagnostic values:

| Per denoising step | Main | PR |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| GPU step annotation | 289.527 ms | 285.502 ms |
| GEMM launches | 502 | 336 |
| GEMM summed kernel time | 214.864 ms | 209.459 ms |
| Norm+RoPE launches | 166 | 166 |
| Norm+RoPE summed kernel time | 2.455 ms | 4.640 ms |
| BF16 copy launches | 9 | 9 |
| cuDNN attention launches | 83 | 83 |

Strided norm+RoPE is **slower** than contiguous norm+RoPE, but removes the extra copies a packed-only implementation would require. The earlier packed-only prototype's Torch-flash trace added 166 BF16 copies per step (~5.75 ms total copy time); the final implementation preserves main's nine small copies. The model-level paired result above is the net benefit. These independent traces are diagnostic, not latency benchmarks. Whole-trace kernel sums contain different work outside the matched annotations and are not compared as E2E time. Both final traces have zero CUDA-graph launches.

Cleanup removed an unused test allocation and added the quality-policy documentation; production code was unchanged from the validated strided version. Same-configuration before/after A/A p50: 14.684656 s → 14.682991 s (ratio 0.999887), with CV 0.03669% / 0.02480%; all repeated outputs were identical. This is a cleanup regression check, not a substitute for the final-head paired main comparison above. Full diff was self-reviewed using BBuf cleanup source/review references [#39293](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39293), [#42391](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/42391), and [#40265](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40265).

### Reproduction

Use separate source checkouts at the exact baseline/head SHAs, installed into the same SGL environment. Put the verified checkpoint at `/task/cache/common/MOSS-Image-Base` and use the public `moss-workloads.json` unchanged.

```bash
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 FLASHINFER_DISABLE_VERSION_CHECK=1 \
SGLANG_DIFFUSION_SYNC_STAGE_PROFILING=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=8 \
sglang serve --model-path /task/cache/common/MOSS-Image-Base \
  --backend sglang --num-gpus 1 --tp-size 1 --ulysses-degree 1 --ring-degree 1 \
  --performance-mode speed --disable-autocast true \
  --component-attention-backends transformer=torch_cudnn_sdpa \
  --enable-torch-compile false --enable-breakable-cuda-graph false \
  --warmup-resolutions 1024x1024 --warmup-steps 50 --host 127.0.0.1 --port 31030

# In the pinned Omni environment, after stopping the SGL server:
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 FLASHINFER_DISABLE_VERSION_CHECK=1 \
TORCHINDUCTOR_EMULATE_PRECISION_CASTS=1 VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD=spawn \
OMP_NUM_THREADS=8 vllm serve /task/cache/common/MOSS-Image-Base \
  --omni --num-gpus 1 --host 127.0.0.1 --port 31031
```

Immutable evidence: [primary paired data](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/tree/2356205dd857a1727453c079d1cd05afa9b9e54d/results), [final diagnostics and traces](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/tree/2356205dd857a1727453c079d1cd05afa9b9e54d/diagnostics), [exact harnesses](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/tree/2356205dd857a1727453c079d1cd05afa9b9e54d/reproduce), [validation logs and version pins](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/tree/2356205dd857a1727453c079d1cd05afa9b9e54d/validation). The archive includes exact launch environments, all 12 process blocks, the predeclared order, request bodies, stage/NVML measurements, source/output hashes, dependency pins, final traces, mode-switch checks and the native-profiler-only patch. Public response JSON omits repeated base64 PNG payloads; complete original responses, PNGs and server logs remain in the task archive. Profiling uses separate requests and does not contribute primary timing rows.

Limits: this PR establishes the measured Base single-GPU eager high cell. It does not establish SFT, multicard, concurrent serving, other resolutions, quantization, or BCG gains. Existing MOSS quantization restrictions remain. High numerical differences are expected and documented. Lossless/exact retain separate projections; no new quality guarantee across attention backends is implied.

## Checklist

- [x] Follow repository formatting and code style.
- [x] Extend existing tests for the actual loading, numerical and lifetime risks.
- [x] Update the model cookbook and validate documentation.
- [x] Complete final-head paired performance, mode-switch, profiles and native Omni diagnostic.
- [x] Verify that all three embedded actual-output figures render on the official Draft PR page.

title: [Fix] elementwise: Avoid data-dependent token-count guards in sigmoid-mul launchers
author: rayanht
body:
## Motivation

`fused_sigmoid_mul` and `_launch_fused_gate_sigmoid_mul` pick their launch config
in Python with `num_tokens >= 1024`. Under `torch.compile(fullgraph=True)` with an
unbacked token count (e.g. `torch._dynamo.mark_unbacked` on the token dim), Dynamo
fails with `Could not guard on data-dependent expression u0 >= 1024`. Hit in the
Qwen3.5 attention output gate and shared-expert gate.

## Modifications

- Wrap both checks in `torch.fx.experimental.symbolic_shapes.guard_or_false`.
- Backed sizes (eager, and `torch.compile` without unbacked dims) evaluate the
check exactly as before. Unbacked sizes take the small-batch config instead of
failing to trace. The threshold only selects `BLOCK_H` / `num_warps`, so outputs
are unchanged either way.

## Accuracy Tests

Not applicable. Only the launch config can change, and only for unbacked sizes.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Not applicable. Eager and backed-shape configs are unchanged.

## Checklist

- [ ] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).
- [ ] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).

title: [Doc] [AMD] GLM-5.3: Enable MTP on MI355X and add the agentic recipe with the AMD monokernel
author: jhinpan
body:
Depends on an SGLang pin of sgl-amd-mono at or after [`0a107f1`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sgl-amd-mono/commit/0a107f15362714c45be34ca37e4dec286fa3d303) ([sgl-amd-mono#60](https://github.com/sgl-project/sgl-amd-mono/pull/60)): done. [sglang#45202](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/45202) (merged 2026-11-05) pins sgl-amd-mono [`e52803f9`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sgl-amd-mono/commit/e52803f9d2b7dabff4bfd2f53ec25c03d56af947), which also contains [sgl-amd-mono#85](https://github.com/sgl-project/sgl-amd-mono/pull/85) and [#86](https://github.com/sgl-project/sgl-amd-mono/pull/86) (`ca929b7d`). The first MI35x image with this pin is `lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:v0.5.23-rocm720-mi35x-20261105` (`sha256:33efb7dc35be`). The MI355X FP8 agentic recipe names this image, and the published-image tables below measure its command on it.

## Motivation

The GLM-5.3 page keeps MTP off on MI355X. No AMD Deploy cell has MTP flags, the Playground turns off both MTP presets on AMD, and the reasons say that more than 3 steps hit a build issue on gfx950. On the page's own MI355X image with the FP8 cells' flags, EAGLE 1-1-2, 3-1-4, and 5-1-6 serve at the GSM8K score of no MTP, and 3-1-4 decodes one request 2.2 times as fast as no MTP. Only 5-1-6 on the high-throughput cell fails: it runs out of memory at startup (tables below).

The page's MI355X agentic recipe ([#46825](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/46825)) serves AMD's MXFP4 checkpoint. No agentic recipe serves the official FP8 checkpoint `zai-org/GLM-5.3` on MI355X, and none uses the AMD monokernel, which accepts only FP8 block-128 weights. On one MI355X node at TP8, EAGLE 3-1-4 with `fp8_e4m3` KV runs on the FP8 checkpoint, and adding the monokernel improves all three InferenceX AgentX headline metrics (throughput, P90 interactivity, P90 E2EL) at concurrency 1, 2, 4, and 10 (tables below).

InferenceX accepts a recipe only when its production-useful flags are on a merged cookbook page, as [#45693](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/45693) did for DeepSeek-V4.1 before [InferenceX#4367](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/4367). This page change comes before the GLM-5.3 MI355X submission.

## Modifications

- `glm-5.3.jsx`:
  - The MI355X FP8 low-latency Deploy cell serves EAGLE 3-1-4. At one request, 3-1-4 decodes faster than 5-1-6 and 1-1-2 on MI355X, and the MI355X FP8 agentic recipe uses the same draft.
  - The Playground's two MTP presets are on for the MI355X FP8 cells, except 5-1-6 on the high-throughput cell (startup OOM). They stay off for BF16 on MI355X and for MI300X and MI325X, which did not run. The reasons no longer say that more than 3 steps hit a build issue.
  - The AMD cell comment says which cell serves MTP.
- `GLM-5.3.mdx`: a new subsection, "MI355X FP8 deployment with the AMD monokernel", follows the MXFP4 recipe of [#46825](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/46825) under Agentic Long-Context Deployment, in the same form. It gives the command and the admission limit per concurrency, and names the first MI35x image that runs the command, `v0.5.23-rocm720-mi35x-20261105`. It states that the monokernel accepts only FP8 block-128 weights. On that image, the command with the MXFP4 checkpoint stops at startup: SGLang raises `ValueError: --enable-amd-monokernel cannot run this setup: needs the FP8 block-128 checkpoint, got 'quark' None` while it resolves the server arguments. The section-2 AMD tip now says which MI355X cell serves MTP, where the presets run, and where MTP is not validated. It also keeps the MXFP4 AgentX commands that [#46825](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/46825) added to the same tip.
- Unchanged: the images, the benchmarks, the other AMD cells, `verified: false` on all AMD cells, and the text of the MXFP4 recipe. The BF16 cells keep no MTP because no BF16 checkpoint ran. `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3` lowers KV precision, so it goes in the agentic recipe and not in a Deploy cell.
- Left out of the agentic command: harness-only settings (served model name, metrics, keep-alive, and the synthetic acceptance `SGLANG_SIMULATE_ACC_*`), and `SGLANG_OPT_USE_TOPK_V2=false`, which [`model_hook.py`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/1305b1830a1285fdfa9e4f6dbe40f51563d5576e/python/sglang/srt/arg_groups/model_hook.py#L450-L453) already sets for DSA models on HIP.
- No test: documentation-only change.

## Accuracy Tests

### sgl-amd-mono #85 and #86 on the agentic command (local, overlay)

title: [Perf] radix-tree: Keep the GIL for tree-core flag, size and digest reads unless the core is busy
author: metamergebot
body:
## Motivation

The Python bindings of the Rust tree core (`rust/sglang-radix-tree/src/python_bindings.rs`) released the GIL around every O(1) read the radix cache makes on its scheduler-step paths: the tier config flags (`enable_hicache`, `enable_storage`, `has_swa_host_pool`, `is_write_back`, `write_through_threshold`, `is_host_memory_buffer_only`, `enable_external_cache_linker`), the evictable/protected size counters, `has_ongoing_insert` and the write-back coexist reclaim digest. Each is a single field load under the core mutex, but `py.detach` hands the GIL to any waiting Python thread, so the reader can stall for up to a switch interval (5 ms by default) before it gets the GIL back. The cache reads these per scheduler step, per insert and once per evicted leaf, so next to a busy Python thread the stalls add up.

## Modifications

These 15 getters now lock the core through a new `core_attached(py)` helper built on `pyo3::sync::MutexExt::lock_py_attached`: it takes the lock while still attached to the interpreter when the core is free, and only detaches to block when another thread holds the core. Waiting with the GIL held would not be safe: a native call that holds the core can drop tensors Python still references, and libtorch needs the GIL to release their Python objects, so a `reset()` racing a flag read would deadlock.

Setters, `total_size`, the per-node reads and every other binding method still release the GIL around native work. Return values and the Python adapters are unchanged.

## Test plan

- `cargo fmt --check`: clean.
- `cargo build --locked --features python-extension`: builds.
- `cargo test --locked --features inspection`: all tests pass, same count as `main`.
- `cargo clippy --locked --all-targets --features python-extension,inspection`: no new warnings.
- The existing Python/Rust cache suite (`test_rust_tree_core_integration.py`) is unchanged and runs in CI.

title: [Perf] [AMD] dsv4.1: Wire up 32x32-block fp8 wo_a GEMM
author: RolaoDenthu
body:
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->

<!-- PR title: [Type] scope: title, or [Type] [Hardware] scope: title.
Type: Feat, Fix, Refactor, Perf, Doc, Test, CI, or Chore.

Hardware: optional single tag without spaces. Use uppercase hardware tags (AMD, NVIDIA, NPU, MI300X), except for exactly these four spellings: Intel, Apple, Huawei, Ascend.
Title: no letter-case restriction.
Reverts: use GitHub's default title, Revert "original title".
Examples: [Fix] attention: Fix KV cache indexing; [Perf] [AMD] flash-attn: Optimize decode performance. -->

## Motivation
DeepSeek-V4.1's checkpoint stores `wo_a` as fp8 with 32x32 block scales (`weight_block_size: [32, 32]`, `scale_fmt: ue8m0`). On ROCm, sglang's fp8 `wo_a` path only took DeepSeek-V4's 128x128 blocks, so V4.1's `wo_a` is dequantized to bf16 at load and runs as a bf16 batched GEMM (split-K partial + reduce on decode), reading twice the weight bytes of the fp8 checkpoint.

aiter now supports this fp8 shape: `batched_gemm_a8w8_mxscale_bpreshuffle` runs 32x32 block scales on gfx950 and ships tuned configs for V4.1's `wo_a` shapes (ROCm/aiter#5896).

This PR switches V4.1's `wo_a` to that kernel: the fp8 weight is kept as is, re-laid out at load, and the activation is quantized per 32 to match.

## Modifications
DeepSeek-V4.1's `wo_a` is fp8 with 32x32 blocks. To wire it up, the weight is shuffled into the (16, 16) layout at load time, leaving the fp8 values and e8m0 scales unchanged; in forward, the activation is quantized per 32 and the GEMM runs on aiter's `batched_gemm_a8w8_mxscale_bpreshuffle`. The scale shape decides which GEMM is used, so DeepSeek-V4's 128x128 path is unaffected.

<!-- Detail the changes made in this pull request. -->

## Accuracy Tests
gsm8k 1319: 0.904

Baseline is `SGLANG_OPT_FP8_WO_A_GEMM=0`.

title: [CI] [AMD] diffusion: Skip the CUDA-only Nomas fused-kernel and FlexAttention unit tests on ROCm
author: michaelzhang-ai
body:
## What

Three tests in `test_nomas.py` are skipped only when `torch.cuda.is_available()` is False, and that is also True on ROCm. They now also require `current_platform.is_cuda()`, so they skip on ROCm and still run on NVIDIA:

- `test_fused_qk_norm_rope_and_modulate_cast_are_bitwise_exact` and `test_pixelumm_fused_norm_and_swiglu_are_bitwise_exact` assert that the `torch.compile(..., emulate_precision_casts=True)` helpers match eager output bit for bit. On ROCm, the Inductor kernels round differently, and `torch.equal` returns False.
- `test_growing_history_across_twelve_segments` uses the FlexAttention backend. On ROCm, compiling `create_block_mask` with dynamic shapes in `nomas_kv_cache.py` fails with `InductorError: AssertionError: failed to set ranges [s55, s55]`.

The other `test_nomas.py` tests, including the CPU/SDPA reference cases, still run on ROCm.

## Why

The file was added in #46124. On the AMD `multimodal-gen-test-1-gpu-amd` stage, it has failed on every run since then, with the same three tests failing on both pytest attempts:

- rocm10: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/40250572724/job/121341392522

title: [Perf] disaggregation: Restore host-received decode KV without blocking the scheduler
author: metamergebot
body:
## Motivation

A PD decode with `--disaggregation-decode-host-receive-threshold` below 1 receives a request's KV cache into host memory and copies it to the device when the request joins a batch. The scheduler submitted that copy as the request was admitted and then called `finish_event.synchronize()`, so it waited for the in-flight forward and then for the copy while the forward stream idled. This PR removes that host wait: the copies start early, and a request joins a batch once its copy has finished on every rank that shares it.

## Modifications

- **Copies start before admission.** At the start of decode batch assembly, `_start_host_restores` starts the host-to-device copy of every waiting host-received request (`start_restore_kv_cache`), ordered after the in-flight forward. Each request keeps its copy's finish event in `ReqKvInfo.restore_done_event`.
- **All ranks admit together.** `_host_restores_ready` checks each rank's events with a non-blocking `query()`, then combines the answers with a MIN all-reduce over the attention-TP CPU group and then the attention-CP CPU group, so all ranks of a DP shard admit the same requests. PP stages cannot all-reduce there (a stage selects a microbatch's batch before the next stage starts that microbatch), so under PP every pending restore counts as ready and admission (`finish_restore_kv_cache`) waits for the copy on the host, as the synchronous restore did.
- **Moves and frees wait for the copy.** The finish event is registered with the allocator, so device page moves and frees are ordered after the copy on the device. The host slots return once the request is admitted or its row is freed; `UnifiedRadixCache.free_kv_row` waits for an in-flight copy first, and a full cache reset finishes the pending restores before destroying the tree.
- **No host waits on the restore path.** The restore's SWA window check runs on the device (`torch._assert_async`), and `restore_kv_cache` for a retracted request makes the current stream wait for the copy instead of synchronizing the host.
- **Forward-stream restores with the kernel backend.** With `--hicache-io-backend kernel` the restore copies run on the stream the forwards run on, after the in-flight forward and before this iteration's forward, through the new `L2TransferEngine.on_current_stream()` context. The direct backend reads the device indices on the host while preparing a copy, which on the forward stream would wait for the in-flight forward, so it keeps the engine's copy stream and, with overlap scheduling, fences only that stream on the forward stream.
- **Index preparation on its own stream.** `L2TransferEngine` prepares transfer indices on a new `index_stream`, and the copy stream waits for that preparation, so a host read of the indices waits only for their producer, never for copies queued earlier on the transfer stream.
- Tests: `test_decode_retraction_backup.py` returns the restores' host slots explicitly after each restore (the restore no longer does so synchronously), and `TestTransferStreamOrdering` in `test_unified_hicache_regressions.py` expects index translation on the index stream.

Files: `python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/decode.py`, `python/sglang/srt/managers/schedule_batch.py`, `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/common.py`, `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/l2_transfer.py`, `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/unified_radix_cache.py`, and the two unit test files above.

## Accuracy Tests

Not run for this PR: the change moves when a copy is waited for, not what is copied; the unit tests below check the restored KV contents.

Run locally on one GPU against this branch: `test/registered/unit/mem_cache/test_decode_retraction_backup.py`, `test/registered/unit/mem_cache/test_unified_hicache_regressions.py`, `test/registered/unit/disaggregation/test_admission_abort_not_enqueued.py` and `test/registered/unit/mem_cache/test_hicache_staged_write_back_dispatch.py`: 53 passed, 1 skipped. `pre-commit` (isort, ruff, ruff-format, codespell) passes on the changed files.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Not included.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).
- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests). (Existing retraction-backup and transfer-ordering tests updated for the non-blocking restore.)
- [ ] Update documentation / docstrings / example tutorials as needed, according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations).
- [ ] Provide throughput / latency benchmark results and accuracy evaluation results as needed.
- [ ] For reviewers: If you haven't made any contributions to this PR and are only assisting with merging the main branch, please remove yourself as a co-author when merging.

title: [Feat] [AMD] minimax: gfx950 sparse attention, NVFP4 KV and DSpark verify kernels
author: kevin-mii
body:
> Part of the MiniMax-M3.1-Flash AMD series that replaces #45936 (closed with its base branch `minimax-m3.1-flash`): kernel PRs #46690 (attention), #46691 (MoE / GEMM) and #46692 (quick all-reduce), each on `main`; then #46693 with the M3.1 call sites and #46694 (indexer CP). It follows the DeepSeek-V4.1 AMD layout (#41018-#41021, then #41308).

## Summary
- **NVFP4 KV (MSA-v1 layout).** `minimax_sparse/common/nvfp4.py` reads the packed rows for the Triton kernels and `nvfp4_gfx950.py` dequantizes them in Gluon. The kernel tests build their packed caches with a torch quantizer in `NVFP4KVQuantizeUtil`'s layout (`nvfp4_kv_quantize` in `sglang/test/quant_ref_utils.py`).
- **Sparse decode.** `decode/nvfp4_decode_gfx950.py` runs sparse decode over the packed NVFP4 K/V in Gluon (one program per row, top-k chunk and KV head; per-warp online softmax). `topk_sparse.py` dispatches an `Nvfp4Cache` to it, and the NVFP4 verify scorer sits beside the bf16 one in `decode/verify_topk_idx.py`.
- **Verify indexer.** `decode/verify_topk_idx.py` scores a linear draft chain against one shared prefix; `decode/verify_topk_gfx950.py` fuses the per-block max score with a streaming top-k on MFMA tiles.
- **Prefill.** `prefill/index_topk_gfx950.py` is the fused prefill indexer; `prefill/gluon_prefill_pair_gfx950.py` runs two queries per program over the union of their top-k blocks; `prefill/nvfp4_prefill.py` gathers the NVFP4 cache into the Gluon prefill's paged layout; `prefill/gluon_prefill.py` and `prefill/flash_with_topk_idx.py` take the new cache.
- **fp8 O epilogue.** `common/out_quant_gfx950.py` is shared by the Gluon decode and pair prefill: they can write O directly as the fp8 o_proj input, with the same bytes and scales as aiter's separate per-token or 1x128 quant.
- **QK-norm + RoPE.** `minimax_m3_qk_norm_rope.py` adds the gfx950 fused Gemma Q/K RMSNorm + partial RoPE + KV-cache write.
- **HiCache.** The NVFP4 page-row copy takes its CTA quota as a template argument: 32 on HIP (MI350X needs 16+ to saturate PCIe), 2 on CUDA as before.
- **Windowed verify.** `verify_mla_window.py` lets the gfx950 grouped-head split-KV verify serve the DSpark draft's sliding window (its non-causal draft block, window 4095) with a one-pass combine, as a `VerifyMLA` subclass; `num_stages=2` was 13-26% faster for that window. The shared `verify_mla.py` only gains the stage-1 window mask (a constexpr, compiled out without a window), the caller's opt-in in `can_handle`, and the two class hooks the subclass sets; Qwen3.5 and Kimi-K3 verify outputs are bitwise unchanged.
- The M3.1 call sites (NVFP4 pool, verify indexer, fp8 O for `o_proj`, windowed draft verify) are in the integration PR.

## Serving gain of each kernel
Measured in the integration PR at TP4 on MI350X (NVFP4 KV, DSpark acceptance simulated at 3 tokens per step, 32K-token contexts), each change turned off alone; the share decode TPOT or prefill latency grows without it, mean of two GPU sets:
- Windowed draft verify (`verify_mla_window`): decode TPOT +20.6% at 1 request, +8.2-9.6% at 8-64.
- Two-queries-per-program Gluon prefill (`gluon_prefill_pair_gfx950`): 32K-token prefill +10.3%, decode +4.2-5.4% at 8-64.
- Gluon prefill over an FP8 KV pool (`SGLANG_MINIMAX_M3_AMD_KV_FORMAT=fp8`): prefill +11.7% (32K tokens) and +12.4% (eight 8K requests).
- NVFP4 KV itself (kernel level, CUDA-graph replay, per layer): the verify indexer at 110K context takes 0.75-0.84x FP8's time from 8 requests and sparse decode 0.42-0.68x, with 1.78x the tokens per GB of KV.

## Changes to existing kernels
On CUDA nothing changes: `topk_sparse` only dispatches the new `Nvfp4Cache` type, the decode top-k only moves into `select_decode_topk`, and the page-row quota stays 2.

On gfx950, main's MiniMax-M3 layers switch kernels when this merges, with no new call site:
- QK-norm + RoPE + cache store (`sparse_qk_index_gemma_rmsnorm_rope_cache`) runs the tiled kernel for M3's 128-wide head with 64-dim neox RoPE; its bf16 outputs equal the per-head kernel's bit for bit.
- The Gluon sparse prefill pairs two queries per program for bf16 batches from 2048 tokens (16 query heads), and now also serves an fp8 KV pool at its per-tensor k/v scales, which `minimax_sparse_prefill` now passes on; before, an fp8 pool stayed on Triton. Both match the Triton kernel up to bf16 rounding.
- The prefill indexer uses the fused gfx950 index top-k for score-only max layers at unit scales and 128-aligned pages; on these bf16 / fp8 index caches it emits the Triton two-pass indexer's block ids exactly. It keeps Triton when Gluon's CDNA4 module is missing.

On other ROCm GPUs, the per-head QK-norm kernel, which serves them (and gfx950 heads other than M3's), no longer writes main K/V to slot 0, the reserved CUDA-graph padding slot. The unfused `store_cache` already skips it, and no real token is stored there.

## Verification
- MI350X (ROCm 7.2 image `rocm/sgl-dev:v0.5.20-rocm720-mi35x-20260926`, AITER `acf8fdf93`, `SGLANG_USE_AITER=1`), this branch alone on `main`: `test_minimax_gfx950_prefill` 35 passed, `test_minimax_m3_qk_norm_rope` 55, `test_minimax_nvfp4_sparse_decode` 13, `test_minimax_verify_topk_idx` 68 (the kernel cases; the integration PR adds 8 more), `test_verify_shared_kv` 10. pre-commit clean; main's callers of every modified kernel module import.
- Not executed on this branch alone: CUDA (shared files keep main's behavior there), end-to-end serving.

title: [Feat] [AMD] minimax: gfx950 MoE, router GEMV, block-fp8 GEMM and fp8 producer kernels
author: kevin-mii
body:
> Part of the MiniMax-M3.1-Flash AMD series that replaces #45936 (closed with its base branch `minimax-m3.1-flash`): kernel PRs #46690 (attention), #46691 (MoE / GEMM) and #46692 (quick all-reduce), each on `main`; then #46693 with the M3.1 call sites and #46694 (indexer CP). It follows the DeepSeek-V4.1 AMD layout (#41018-#41021, then #41308).

## Summary
- **MoE sorting + quant.** `moe/moe_sort_quant.py` (one launch for decode batches) and `moe/moe_sort_quant_large.py` (four launches for prefill) sort and MXFP4-quantize the stage-1 activations bit-for-bit like aiter's multi-phase path; `moe_sorting_small.py` hands them to aiter as runtime patches.
- **Shared-expert fold.** `moe/aiter_moe_addend.py` folds the shared-expert output into aiter's stage-2 reduction as a runtime patch, applied only when aiter's signature matches.
- **Router.** `gemm/router_gemv.py` raises the gfx950 split-K GEMV to 512 rows with a reduce launch past 16 rows, exposes its split-K partials, and fuses them with the shared expert's fp8 SwiGLU in one launch; `moe_fused_gate.py` accepts those partials and sums them in order. `moe/smallm_router_gfx950/m31_router.*` is a one-launch decode router for 1-16 tokens, bitwise equal to router GEMV, gate and aiter's sort.
- **GEMM.** `gemm/aiter_asm_blockscale.py` launches aiter's asm block-fp8 split-K GEMM into an output its producer already zeroed (aiter always memsets it first; ROCm/aiter#6786 adds `out_zeroed`), and `jit/utils/hipcc.py` launches the 2-D grid it needs. `smallm_fp8_gfx950` gains the M3.1 shared expert's 1536 x 6144 gate_up and exposes its kernel body, which `m31_router` runs in its fused launch.
- **fp8 producers.** `quantization/aiter_fp8_quant_triton.py` holds Triton epilogues that write exactly aiter's per-token and 1x128 fp8 bytes and scales; `layernorm/minimax_m3_rmsnorm.py` adds the Gemma RMSNorm (+ residual) producers that use them.
- Merged with main's Beam FP32-gate path (#45254): FP32 gates keep their CUDA configs and one-row tile; BF16 gates stay gfx950-only.
- The M3.1 call sites (fused routers, fp8 producers, shared-expert fold, pre-zeroed GEMM launch) are in the integration PR.

## Serving gain of each kernel
Measured in the integration PR at TP4 on MI350X (NVFP4 KV, DSpark acceptance simulated at 3 tokens per step, 32K-token contexts), each change turned off alone; the share decode TPOT or prefill latency grows without it, mean of two GPU sets:
- Shared-expert fold into aiter's stage-2 reduction: 32K-token prefill +15.9%, decode +1.9-5.0% at 8-64 requests. Not bit-identical to adding the shared output afterwards (its test bounds the relative error at 1e-2).
- Gemma RMSNorm producers writing the next GEMM's fp8: decode +8.5% at 1 request, +1.5-2.9% at 8-64.
- SwiGLU writing the down projection's fp8: decode +4.4% at 1 request, prefill +5.3%.
- Fused decode routers (`m31_router`, router GEMV partials): decode +4.2% at 1 request, +1.5% at 8. Bitwise equal to the unfused chain.
- The MoE sort + quant kernels were not toggled on their own; they are bitwise equal to aiter's multi-phase path.
- The pre-zeroed asm split-K launch is bit-exact and saves one memset launch per prefill block-fp8 GEMM; end to end it measured within run-to-run noise.

## Not in this PR
- `moe_sorting_small.sorting_impl_wrapper` is ~160 lines; its two one-launch branches could share a helper.
- `m31_router` keeps module-level kernel caches and `global _disabled`, like its `smallm_moe_gfx950` / `smallm_fp8_gfx950` siblings.

## Changes to existing kernels
`router_gemv`, `moe_fused_gate`, `moe_sorting_small` and `smallm_fp8_gfx950` keep their signatures. On CUDA, `router_gemv`'s FP32-gate path runs main's kernel body and tiles, with a split-K scratch now sized for its own tiles (64 KiB at N = 256, against main's 512 KiB), and `moe_fused_gate`'s 2-D path is unchanged; split-K partials never take its SM120 or radix fast paths.

On gfx950, existing callers change when this merges, with no new call site:
- `router_gemv`'s bf16 tiles change for its callers (MiniMax-M3, Beam, DeepSeek-V4.1 VL routing), which changes the fp32 summation order; the fp64 accuracy and determinism test covers them.
- main's aiter MoE runner applies `moe_sorting_small`'s patch, which now sorts 128-expert top-4 routing at hidden 6144 in one launch with the stage1 MXFP4 activation quant: `moe_sort_quant` up to 1024 tokens, `moe_sort_quant_large` above (aiter's sort again past 349,525 tokens, the large sort's int32 offset limit), both bitwise equal to aiter's multi-phase sort. It no longer emits an mxfp8 quant for separated-SwiGLU MXFP4 weights, which never read one, and it stays off, with an info log, when aiter's sort or quant signatures differ from the ones it wraps.
- `smallm_fp8_gfx950` gains (1536, 6144), which main's per-token fp8 linear also dispatches up to 16 rows; it stays within one bf16 ulp of aiter's `gemm_a8w8_bpreshuffle` there.

## Verification
- MI350X (same stack), this branch alone on `main`: `test_minimax_m3_rmsnorm` 32 (the kernel cases), `test_aiter_asm_blockscale` 1 (the launch case), `test_aiter_moe_addend` 3, `test_m31_router_gfx950` 6, `test_moe_sort_quant_large` 3, `test_moe_sorting_small` 7 (192 subtests), `test_router_gemv_gfx950` 4, `test_aiter_fp8_quant_triton` 7, main's `test_smallm_fp8_proj_gfx950` 7 (with the M3.1 shape). Main's FP32-gate path run on gfx950 through the merged kernel: max error 3.9e-7 to 6.2e-7 against fp64 at 1-8 rows (main's bound 2e-6), deterministic. pre-commit clean.
- Not executed: main's CUDA `test_router_gemv.py` (needs CUDA), end-to-end serving.

title: [Feat] [AMD] distributed: JIT quick all-reduce for TP4 on gfx950
author: kevin-mii
body:
> Part of the MiniMax-M3.1-Flash AMD series that replaces #45936 (closed with its base branch `minimax-m3.1-flash`): kernel PRs #46690 (attention), #46691 (MoE / GEMM) and #46692 (quick all-reduce), each on `main`; then #46693 with the M3.1 call sites and #46694 (indexer CP). It follows the DeepSeek-V4.1 AMD layout (#41018-#41021, then #41308).

## Summary
- A JIT copy of sgl-kernel's quick all-reduce (`jit/csrc/distributed/quick_all_reduce/`, `quick_all_reduce_hip.cuh`, `ops/communication/quick_all_reduce_hip.py`), restructured for latency (the per-tile wire layout is wave-major) and cut to the INT4 / INT8 codecs at TP4 on bf16 data. It keeps sgl-kernel's buffer sizes, flags and arithmetic, so at the level it runs its outputs are bitwise equal to sgl-kernel's, including a partial last tile and bf16 values past fp16's range. Asked for INT4, it runs all-reduces below `SGLANG_ROCM_QUICK_REDUCE_INT8_BELOW_MB` (default 64 MiB; 0 keeps INT4 at every size) in INT8, about 1/16 of INT4's error, and logs that once at init; the JIT INT4 column below 64 MB in the table is the kernel called at INT4 directly. `jit_serves()` takes only gfx950, and `qr_supports(fa, dtype)` tells a caller that a JIT handle reduces bf16 only.
- Nothing in this PR calls the module: #46693 wires it in (`custom_all_reduce_ops` behind `SGLANG_ROCM_QUICK_ALL_REDUCE_JIT`, on gfx950 only, the GPU it is validated on; `QuickAllReduce` asks `qr_supports()` so float16 goes to the next all-reduce). Review it here as a kernel; the serving numbers below come from #46693.

## Changes to existing kernels
None; every source file is new and HIP-only. The existing `test_quick_allreduce_bf16_range` gains the JIT cases.

## Not in this PR
- Each communicator allocates twice its max size (4 GiB per GPU at the 2 GiB default), as sgl-kernel's does, although the kernel indexes its slots by block and so uses at most 256 tiles per phase. Shrinking it would return that memory to the KV cache; it is left for a follow-up.
- sgl-kernel's own `quick_all_reduce.h` keeps `data_buffer_size` function-static, so the first communicator's size sticks process-wide; this JIT copy sizes it per communicator and leaves the original untouched.

## Verification
- MI350X (ROCm 7.2 image, AITER `acf8fdf93`), this branch alone on `main`: `test_quick_allreduce_bf16_range` 3 passed (8 GPUs). pre-commit clean.
- Latency at TP4 on MI350X, bf16 messages, eager, us per all-reduce (sgl-kernel = the AOT `qr_all_reduce` this replaces):

| Message | aiter bf16 custom AR | sgl-kernel INT8 | JIT INT8 | JIT / sgl-kernel | sgl-kernel INT4 | JIT INT4 | JIT / sgl-kernel |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 MB | 18.4 | 29.6 | 14.2 | 0.48 | 26.9 | 13.7 | 0.51 |
| 2.4 MB | 28.1 | 40.5 | 20.1 | 0.49 | 31.9 | 16.7 | 0.52 |
| 8 MB | 79.2 | 92.8 | 51.3 | 0.55 | 56.7 | 38.3 | 0.68 |
| 32 MB | 389.3 | 267.8 | 177.6 | 0.66 | 157.9 | 104.2 | 0.66 |
| 63 MB | 576.8 | 446.8 | 345.9 | 0.77 | 261.7 | 194.8 | 0.74 |
| 128 MB | | 1003.0 | 699.5 | 0.70 | 462.2 | 391.7 | 0.85 |
| 400 MB | | 2308.6 | 2181.6 | 0.94 | 1415.5 | 1249.5 | 0.88 |

  The JIT INT8 beats aiter's bf16 custom all-reduce from 1 MB, where sgl-kernel's INT8 does not until about 16 MB; that is what lets the integration PR lower aiter's custom-AR cutoff to 2.4 MiB. One run; single-size outliers in other columns (RCCL at 8 MB, sgl-kernel INT4 at 16 and 256 MB) were left out.
- Serving, measured in the integration PR (MI350X TP 4, NVFP4 KV, DSpark acceptance simulated at 3 tokens per step, 32K-token contexts, two repeats on each of two GPU sets). With sgl-kernel's quick all-reduce instead (`SGLANG_ROCM_QUICK_ALL_REDUCE_JIT=0`) at the same 2.4 MiB custom-AR cutoff, decode TPOT grows 4.0% at 32 concurrent requests and 2.6% at 64, and 32K-token prefill 1.9%. With main's 64 MiB cutoff as well: 3.6%, 6.7% and 4.3%. At 1 and 8 requests every all-reduce stays under the cutoff, on aiter's custom all-reduce.
