Tests were then trimmed to the core cases (stock / disabled / no-provider fallback and the provider entry for each commit; 265 added test lines, previously 601), formatted with the repository pre-commit hooks, and rerun per commit with no new failures; production code is unchanged.

| ID | Commit | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| B1a | `56b85c7d96` | Define speculative provider contracts |
| B1b | `52f19a096e` | Bind provider factories to stock defaults |
| B1c | `c2f6e30088` | Bind an always-present DSpark draft strategy |

| — | `87750d0776` | Document `SGLANG_NVIDIA_MEGAKERNEL_SLOTS` with the plugin settings |

### Performance per commit

This PR is a binding layer: by itself it routes every call to the stock SGLang path, and its speedup appears only when the NVIDIA plugin provides the megakernel entries it exposes. The commits are not independently switchable for that path (B1b supplies the factories, B1d the EAGLE entry points that use them), so the gain is measured for the PR as a whole together with sgl-project/sgl-nvidia-mega#33.

| ID | Production / test lines | Effect on the measured Qwen3.5 points |
|---|---:|---|
| B1a | +272/−2 · +23/−0 | No runtime change by construction |
| B1b | +154/−0 · +117/−0 | Required for the plugin's sharded-verify local keys; part of the stack gain below |
| B1c | +143/−48 · +19/−4 | DSpark path; not exercised by the Qwen3.5 EAGLE runs below (no effect on these numbers) |
| B1d | +219/−131 · +44/−9 | Required for the plugin's draft / draft-extend entries; part of the stack gain below |
| B2 | +90/−3 · +68/−4 | Required for the plugin's PD prefill split convolution; not measured separately |
| docs | +8/−0 (docs) | None |

AgentX, Qwen3.5 on GB300, PD, one 1200 s run per arm, same request window and fixed acceptance length in every arm (TPS/user P50, change vs `main`; run-to-run noise about 2% at TP8 c16 and 1.4% at TEP8 c272):

| Arm | TP8 decode, c16 | TEP8 decode (EP4), c272 |
|---|---:|---:|
| `main` | 686.7 | 86.2 |
| `main` + this PR + plugin #33 | 1180.4 (+71.9%) | 104.1 (+20.7%) |
| `main` + this PR + #47200 + plugin #33 | 1381.5 (+101.2%) | 123.8 (+43.6%) |

With the plugin off, `main` + this PR is within noise of `main` (TPS/user P50 +0.7%, P90 +3.9%; DEP8 PD, same rack).

### Notes for reviewers

- **`speculative_runtime_hooks` is read as a declared member** (commit `faca41e854`, +8/−11 production, +1 test). SGLang already rejects any plugin whose `MEGAKERNEL_API_VERSION` differs, so the plugin and SGLang move together; like `draft_sampler` and `graph_variants`, every built object must define the member (`None` when it offers no factory). The matching plugin change declares it on all built classes (sgl-project/sgl-nvidia-mega#33, `72f0cd25`); that plugin commit should land together with or before this PR. Per-commit CPU tests: no new failures.
- **`id(runner)` in `EagleMegakernel`.** The draft and draft-extend graph caches key on `id(runner)`, as on `main`. The key is used only inside SGLang to find the graphs a runner captured; the runner object itself is never passed to the plugin. Providers receive only the buffers and batch sizes documented in `spec.py`.
- **`SGLANG_NVIDIA_MEGAKERNEL_SLOTS` is not a child of the runtime master switch.** SGLang only registers and documents the variable; the plugin reads it to choose which of its kernels to build under `--enable-nvidia-megakernel`. That choice is independent of SGLang's runtime optimizations: a deployment can run plugin kernels with the master switch off, and turning the master switch off should not silently change the kernel selection. Making it a Boolean child would also not fit its type, since it is a tuple of slot names whose empty value already means "stock paths".

title: [Refactor] [NPU] quant: Refactor shared quantization utilities and DSpark weight mapping
author: hanwlax

title: [Fix] kernels: Support OOT fused ops under torch.compile
author: rumitdesai
body:
## Motivation

Before this change, out-of-tree (OOT) platform plugins register eager fused-op implementations through
[`BaseFusedOp.register_oot_forward()`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/46caa54562a97e71d9b937c62875c90b39274b0d/python/sglang/kernels/fused_op.py#L375).
[`BaseFusedOp._resolve_forward_method()`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/46caa54562a97e71d9b937c62875c90b39274b0d/python/sglang/kernels/fused_op.py#L539)
selects the function for the active platform and binds it to the operator with
`registered.__get__(self)`. This works eagerly without adding a
`forward_<platform_key>` method to the operator class.


Out-of-tree platform plugins can register eager fused-op implementations without defining platform-specific methods on operator classes. However, model compilation currently has no equivalent registration API.

Eager dispatch also binds registered functions directly to the operator instance. When PyTorch saves compiler guards, it can look up a bound method by name. A registered function may have no matching class attribute, causing serialization to fail.

Provide an explicit OOT compile registration API and store plugin functions in a form that supports both eager execution and compiler guard serialization. Plugins can choose their compile implementation independently while keeping normal PyTorch tracing behavior.


## Modifications

- Add `BaseFusedOp.register_oot_compile_forward(op_cls, fn, platform_key)`.
  Selection uses the exact operator type and active OOT platform, before the
  existing subclass compile-selection method.
- Store registered functions without binding them to the instance.
  `_forward_oot()` and `_forward_oot_compile()`, defined on `BaseFusedOp`, call
  them with the operator instance as `self`. The active and saved forward
  methods can therefore be resolved by name during guard serialization.
- Preserve eager dispatch precedence, rebinding of registered Python methods,
  compile fallback behavior, explicit/forced backend priority, trace labels,
  and repeated enter/leave restoration.
- Trace the registered function's body as part of the enclosing model.
  Unsupported tracing operations still fail with `fullgraph=True`; normal
  graph-break behavior applies with `fullgraph=False`.
- Add test cases using a fake OOT platform and tensor operations,
  including the guard-serialization regression. Document the registration API.

A plugin can register the same function for both modes, or use separate
implementations with the same signature and behavior:

```python
BaseFusedOp.register_oot_forward(Op, eager_forward, platform_key)
BaseFusedOp.register_oot_compile_forward(Op, compile_forward, platform_key)
```

## Accuracy Tests

### CPU functional checks — passed

Verified with Python 3.12 and PyTorch 2.14.1+cu130:

```bash
python -m pytest test/registered/unit/kernels/test_fused_op_dispatch.py -q
python -m pytest test/registered/unit/kernels/test_fused_op.py -q
python -m pytest test/registered/unit/kernels/test_kernels_namespace.py -q

python -m pytest test/registered/unit/platforms/test_platform_interface.py -q
python -m pytest test/registered/unit/model_executor/runner_backend/test_full_cuda_graph_backend.py -q
python -m pytest test/registered/unit/model_executor/test_cuda_graph_config_backends.py -q
python -m pytest test/registered/unit/compilation/test_torch_compile_decoration.py -q
```
**293 tests passed, plus 25 platform subtests**.

- 293 tests passed, plus 25 subtests.
- Includes 73 dispatch tests, with 38 new cases covering OOT registration, compilation, restoration, and guard serialization.
- The serialization regression failed before the fix and passed afterward.
- The compiler matrix covers eager/Inductor, both fullgraph settings, caching enabled/disabled, and cold/warmed instances.

### GPU numerical parity and model accuracy

```bash
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python -m pytest test/registered/kernels/ops/activation/test_fused_op_gpu_parity.py -v -ra
```

**13 passed, 17 warnings**


### Additional compiler integration check
```bash
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python -m pytest test/registered/e2e/models/test_transformers_backend_eval.py -v
```

**1 passed, 20 warnings**


## Speed Tests and Profiling

Two-GPU throughput check

CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1 python -m pytest test/registered/basic_perf/test_torch_compile_throughput.py -v
```
**1 passed, 19 warnings**

CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python -m pytest test/registered/moe/test_torch_compile_moe.py -v -k mmlu
```

title: [Perf] [AMD] moe/topk: Use the Triton softmax top-k router for Qwen3-Next (hidden 2048)
author: chennyiiis
body:
## Motivation

`_use_rocm_triton_softmax_topk` in `python/sglang/srt/layers/moe/topk.py` selects the Triton softmax router over AITER `aiter_fused_topk` on gfx950 for decode-sized rows. #39986 scoped it to the Qwen3.5 envelope it measured, which includes `hidden_states.shape[1] == 4096`.

Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B has the same router shape that the rest of the envelope checks: 512 experts, top-10, bf16 logits, no correction bias, no fused shared-expert slots and no packed output. Only its hidden size differs, 2048, so its decode router never reaches the Triton path. The hidden size does not enter the router computation: the Triton router reads only `gating_output`, and `hidden_states` contributes its row count.

## Modifications

- `topk.py`: accept hidden size 2048 as well as 4096. Every other condition, including the 128-row limit and the gfx950 requirement, is unchanged.
- `test/registered/amd/test_qwen35_moe_softmax_topk.py`: `test_triton_dispatch_matches_aiter` now runs at hidden 2048 and 4096; on main the 2048 cases reach AITER and fail the test's bypass assertion. `test_dispatch_envelope_is_narrow` accepts 2048 and still rejects a width outside the measured set (3072).

## Accuracy Tests

The router change does not alter which experts are chosen. `test_qwen35_moe_softmax_topk.py` on MI355X (gfx950), torch 2.11.0+rocm10.0.0:

| code under test | result |
|---|---|
| main `58214f6` | 4 failed, 1 passed, 3 subtests passed: every hidden-2048 case raises `AITER top-k should be bypassed`, and the envelope test rejects 2048 |
| this PR | 2 passed, 6 subtests passed: expert ids identical to `aiter_fused_topk` and weights within 1e-5 at 4, 12 and 128 rows for hidden 2048 and 4096 |

A Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-FP8 server (TP2) started from this branch takes the Triton router at every decode-sized batch it captures (1 to 128 rows, both ranks) and keeps AITER above 128 rows.

GSM8K, all 1319 questions, through sgl-eval 0.1.3 against the same TP2 server. sgl-eval has no preset for this model, so the model card's recommended sampling was passed explicitly: `--temperature 0.7 --top-p 0.8 --max-tokens 16384`, with `--seed` 0, 1 and 2 for each arm:

| seed | main | this PR |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 96.13% | 95.98% |
| 1 | 95.98% | 95.91% |
| 2 | 96.13% | 95.91% |
| mean | 96.08% | 95.93% |

The 0.15-point gap is two questions out of 1319, inside the ±0.5-point standard error of a single run at this score, and both arms sample at temperature 0.7, so this shows no regression rather than a measurable difference. The router change selects the same experts as AITER in the unit test and the microbenchmark below.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Router microbenchmark on MI355X (gfx950), both arms through `topk.fused_topk` with only the dispatch predicate differing, per-call device time under CUDA graph replay with 50 calls captured per graph; 512 experts, top-10, bf16:

| rows | AITER (us) | Triton (us) | speedup | expert ids equal |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 1 | 9.539 | 4.869 | 1.96x | yes |
| 2 | 9.370 | 5.074 | 1.85x | yes |
| 4 | 8.620 | 5.092 | 1.69x | yes |
| 8 | 8.961 | 5.063 | 1.77x | yes |
| 16 | 9.471 | 5.106 | 1.85x | yes |
| 32 | 9.309 | 5.089 | 1.83x | yes |
| 64 | 9.773 | 5.122 | 1.91x | yes |
| 128 | 9.900 | 5.169 | 1.92x | yes |

That is hidden 2048. The same benchmark at hidden 4096, the Qwen3.5 shape #39986 enabled, gives 1.74x to 1.97x with the same median, 1.85x, which is what you expect when the hidden size never enters the router.

End to end: `sglang.bench_serving` on Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-FP8, MI355X, TP2, random 1024 in / 1024 out, a fresh server per block in the order main, PR, PR, main, four runs per block with the first discarded; each block reports the median of runs 2 to 4, and each arm averages its two blocks:

| concurrency | metric | main | this PR | change | main block-to-block | PR block-to-block |
|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 16 | output tok/s | 2292.4 | 2354.3 | +2.70% | 0.62% | 0.16% |
| 16 | median TPOT (ms) | 6.73 | 6.55 | -2.56% | 0.25% | 0.15% |
| 16 | median TTFT (ms) | 298.1 | 296.1 | -0.66% | 1.30% | 1.19% |
| 64 | output tok/s | 5507.0 | 5601.2 | +1.71% | 0.31% | 0.04% |
| 64 | median TPOT (ms) | 10.98 | 10.77 | -1.92% | 0.24% | 0.15% |
| 64 | median TTFT (ms) | 613.1 | 607.5 | -0.91% | 1.22% | 0.34% |

The throughput and TPOT changes are several times the drift between the two blocks of the same arm; TTFT moves less than that drift, as expected for a change that only touches decode-sized batches. TP2 rather than the cookbook's TP8 because the measurement used two GPUs.

title: [Perf] detokenizer: Send per-request decode inputs once and keep them in the detokenizer
author: hnyls2002
body:
The scheduler sent, on every decode step and for every emitted row, values that do not change during a request: a decode-id delta that copies `output_ids`, the read offset, three decode flags, and the tokenizer worker route. It also kept the prompt tail and all output ids just to slice that delta. These values are now sent once and kept by the detokenizer.

## Changes

- **Header once.** A request's first emitted row carries a `DetokenizeHeader`: the prompt tail, `skip_special_tokens`, `spaces_between_special_tokens`, `no_stop_trim`, and `http_worker_ipc`. The detokenizer keeps it in a per-request `DetokenizeState` (`incremental_detokenize.py`) and extends the decode ids from each row's `output_ids`. The scheduler drops `surr_offset`, `read_offset`, `send_decode_id_offset` and `init_incremental_detokenize`.
- **State lifetime.** A new header replaces any state left under the same rid. A request ended outside the output stream (`send_abort_output`) sends a `DetokenizeReleaseReq`.
- **Routing.** `MultiDetokenizerRouter` routes by rid. Finished rows carry their own `http_worker_ipc`, so they reach their tokenizer worker even without stored state.
- **Continuity alarm.** For each non-beam row the detokenizer checks the ids received so far against `completion_tokens`; a mismatch logs a warning (raises in CI) and resyncs.
- `--skip-tokenizer-init` and the Rust server are unchanged: they send no header and no release.

## Behavior changes

- A request that reuses a rid no longer decodes on top of stale state. Finished rows are delivered when one rid is in flight on two tokenizer workers, or after more than `SGLANG_DETOKENIZER_MAX_STATES` live requests, where main crashed.
- An unfinished row with no stored state gets empty text and a warning: after eviction, or a late row after `send_abort_output`.
- With several detokenizer workers, rows are assigned by rid instead of by tokenizer worker.
- The continuity alarm fires on `input_embeds` requests retracted after streaming, a path already inconsistent on main (`reset_for_retract` empties `output_ids` but keeps `send_token_offset`). Outputs there are unchanged.

## Verification

- Unit tests for the header, the release, decoding from stored state, rid reuse, missing state, routing through the streamer, the multi-detokenizer split and the multi-tokenizer fan-out, the continuity alarm, and the msgpack round trip.
- Differential test: 20,000 random request lifecycles through the real streamer, routers, detokenizer and fan-out with a Qwen3 tokenizer (multibyte characters split across tokens, special tokens, stop strings, speculative steps, stream intervals, retraction, aborts, beam search, skip-init, 1-3 workers). 0 differences from main over 542,499 rows, apart from the rid-reuse fix. Stress runs with one rid on two tokenizer workers and with 1-4 detokenizer states delivered every finished row; main crashed in both.

## Micro benchmark

CPU only, one steady decode step for 512 streaming requests with 512-token prompts, real tokenizer, pickle IPC.

| | scheduler build (us/step) | pickle (us/step) | unpickle (us/step) | detokenizer decode (us/step) | message (KB) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| main | 705-732 | 398-404 | 293-298 | 1508-1530 | 51.0 |
| this PR | 500-524 | 219-223 | 163-168 | 1554-1564 | 28.4 |

The scheduler side (build + pickle) drops by about 35%; detokenizer decode is 2-3% slower (stored-state lookups, the route list and the continuity check).

title: [Fix] attention: Keep fused RoPE KV writes off DCP layouts
author: LLLL114
body:
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->

<!-- PR title: [Type] scope: title, or [Type] [Hardware] scope: title.
Type: Feat, Fix, Refactor, Perf, Doc, Test, CI, or Chore.
Scope: any module or model name (no fixed list or letter-case restriction), e.g. attention, qwen3, or flash-attn.
Hardware: optional single tag without spaces. Use uppercase hardware tags (AMD, NVIDIA, NPU, MI300X), except for exactly these four spellings: Intel, Apple, Huawei, Ascend.
Title: no letter-case restriction.
Reverts: use GitHub's default title, Revert "original title".
Examples: [Fix] attention: Fix KV cache indexing; [Perf] [AMD] flash-attn: Optimize decode performance. -->

## Motivation
Qwen3-30B-A3B with TP8/DCP2, Triton attention and BF16 KV can write DCP logical slot IDs directly into a rank-local KV buffer through fused RoPE + KV storage. This causes incorrect output and can produce CUDA illegal memory accesses as the cache allocation advances.
<!-- Describe the purpose and goals of this pull request. -->

## Modifications

<!-- Detail the changes made in this pull request. -->
`enable_fused_set_kv_buffer()` checks `forward_batch.dcp_kv_mask` to avoid DCP, but eager batch construction only populates that mask on HIP. CUDA batches can therefore have DCP enabled with a `None` mask.

Qwen3 MoE then selects fused RoPE storage, whose `FusedSetKVBufferArg.cache_loc` is the unchanged `out_cache_loc`, and skips the attention backend's KV store. That bypasses the Triton DCP path's owner mask and `loc // dcp_size` translation. 
- Reject the generic fused RoPE KV-store path when `get_parallel().dcp_enabled` is true. The existing attention backend performs the DCP-aware store.
- Add a regression to the existing gate test for CUDA/HIP, DCP1/2/4, and an absent batch mask. Keep DCP1 eligible for fusion.

- Chat API, 5-shot prompting, `enable_thinking=False`, temperature 0, `top_p=1`, `max_tokens=1024`, server seed 42.

title: [Fix] diffusion: recover LTX eager performance without disabling fusion
author: mickqian
body:
## Motivation

Fix LTX-2.3 eager regressions without globally removing the fused head-gate or RMSNorm/modulation kernels.

Image-conditioned stage 1 splits guidance into batch-1 forwards. Video retains per-token timesteps, but audio uses per-sample AdaLN and enters RMSNorm modulation fusion. GPU-only timings do not characterize this host-bound path.

The initial version of this PR addressed launch overhead but did not establish recovery against the original good revision. Further same-machine interleaved comparisons identified redundant AdaLN layout work and a separate Blackwell stage-2 sharding regression. Companion #47301 handles shared Blackwell attention routing; this PR alone is not the complete Blackwell fix.

## Changes

- Reuse `replay_launches` for head-gate and RMSNorm modulation, caching launch metadata rather than tensors or outputs. Keep both fused kernels.
- Move head-gate eligibility/fallback inside the cached operator instead of repeating it in the model.
- Avoid the value-major allocation for singleton AdaLN rows, which are already contiguous. Preserve per-token layout where the broadcast-only fused consumers cannot apply; retain contiguous batched broadcast rows.
- Use automatic stage-2 CFG-rank Ulysses on Hopper and on Blackwell with BCG enabled. Blackwell eager does not amortize the extra dispatch; disabling it for graph mode as well would lose an existing benefit. Preserve explicit sequence parallelism and the existing token threshold.
- Extend launch-cache, fallback, fresh-input, graph, compile, AdaLN-layout and CFG/SP topology tests. Document existing image-conditioned BCG warmup and automatic stage-2 platform selection.

No new knobs, kernel arithmetic changes, quality-tier changes, GT updates, or performance-baseline changes. Existing production-file churn: +35/-12 across four files; no new production files. Tests/docs: +174/-14.

## Validation and Provenance

Original good: `02b983603d34c6af09e554ed2b8bf8d85290d9ae`. Current base: `58214f648c812c70bfd57f0b4196de494f75c0bc`.

Same task-owned H200/B300 machines and dependencies, public `Lightricks/LTX-2.3`, 768x512x121, seed 42, official two-stage schedule, CFG2, TP/SP1, `quality=lossless`, compile disabled, explicit `--ltx2-two-stage-device-mode original`; DiT resident, text/image encoder and VAE layerwise offloaded. Stage timing synchronization is enabled identically. No profiler requests are used for performance medians. Each process has one warmup followed by changing-input measured requests.

Initial measured runtime candidate: `7ad0ae895ae701894dd68fc906362a51ff9a6c54`. Final combined head `02dc569408cd24bd6fee91086c93829cd076b1ef` includes model head `698a5afb05c3e9f0738df4a59b66acc5847d4360` and attention head `115643e05b80622fc0a887dc8a8dbec570cde35e`. It preserves Blackwell stage-2 sharding in graph mode and exact-quality attention routing. Each run records its SHA; intermediate results are distinguished below.

H200, five measured requests per run:

| Workload | Original good stage 1 / stage 2 | Fixed stage 1 / stage 2 | Fixed client E2E |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| TI2V eager | 8.649-8.882 / 1.416-1.420 s | 8.665 / 0.962 s | 10.950 s |
| T2V eager | Not rerun on original good | 5.368 / 0.948 s | 7.604 s |
| TI2V, matching-image BCG warmup | Not rerun on original good | 6.100 / 0.844 s | 8.322 s |
| T2V BCG | Not rerun on original good | 5.288 / 0.805 s | 7.408 s |

The last three configurations are neutral against the initial #47270 head. Ranges are independent-run medians, not confidence intervals. H200 behavior does not depend on the companion Blackwell attention patch.

B300, 9-request good/fixed/good comparison: stage 1 **9.262 / 9.039 / 9.382 s**, stage 2 **0.767 / 0.749 / 0.767 s**, client E2E **11.355 / 11.148 / 11.446 s**. The fixed run uses the combined candidate `7ad0ae895ae701894dd68fc906362a51ff9a6c54`. Earlier smaller runs varied; the interleaved comparison supports recovery, not a hardware-independent extra percentage gain. Disabling both fused paths did not recover the original performance; attention routing and stage-2 communication mattered independently.

The execution mode matters for stage 2 too: B300 T2V BCG takes approximately 0.465 s with CFG-rank sharding versus 0.671 s without it. The final patch preserves this graph-mode benefit while avoiding the roughly 0.3 s loss in eager. Final combined head `02dc569408cd24bd6fee91086c93829cd076b1ef` passed both graph configurations with five changing-input requests each:

| B300 workload | Stage 1 | Stage 2 | Client E2E |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| TI2V, matching-image BCG warmup | 3.374 s | 0.487 s | 5.073 s |
| T2V BCG | 2.742 s | 0.467 s | 4.469 s |

The same final combined head was rerun for nine eager requests: stage 1 **9.161 s**, stage 2 **0.753 s**, client E2E **11.251 s**. This remains within the matched original-good range.

Accuracy scope:

- Focused operator tests cover fresh tensors, JIT-dispatch avoidance for warmed signatures, real graphs, Inductor, and CPU/strided/broadcast fallbacks.
- AdaLN tests preserve values exactly while checking the required layouts and avoiding redundant allocation.
- H200: five final-layout videos match the preceding candidate pixel-for-pixel; those five also match the original public PR head. Audio is not universally bit-identical (final-layout comparison MSE 0 to 4.52e-7); unchanged baselines also vary. No GT was changed.
- B300: switching attention backends and stage-2 reduction topology is not bit-exact. Against the initial PR head, five matched videos have full-video PSNR 25.63-31.31 dB and audio MSE 0.000328-0.008539. These are observed differences, not a quality pass or proof of closer agreement with the official reference. Fresh-input operator tests compare captured FA4 against cuDNN with the existing BF16 tolerance; full server consistency results are reported separately.
- These isolated comparisons do not establish bitwise equivalence against every intervening optimization since original-good, nor do H200/B300 establish recovery of all historical H100 cross-runner timing differences.

An additional B300 `exact` TI2V check isolates the model patch from attention routing: model-only head `698a5afb05c3e9f0738df4a59b66acc5847d4360` produces the same decoded video SHA256 as the preceding `61bb5547b67db0aebbcba15017e5e6921a56e9c6` (`2743239da33f0fdbd15c140fa33df165a52cb3c50f5b38b193ea39bae5c21482`). An ungated companion attention candidate changed this output and failed the existing official-reference CLIP threshold; it was fixed before publication. Final combined head `02dc569408cd24bd6fee91086c93829cd076b1ef` matches all 25 video frames and decoded audio samples bit-for-bit. Existing pinned official GT (`c7258eb56e9951878c66fc0fb3673d9f4775b0b2`) passes unchanged thresholds: CLIP 0.5749, SSIM 0.3431, PSNR 12.0377, max MAD 43.2833.

Standard-server limitation: B300's `b200.json` has no LTX performance baseline, and existing official TI2V images lack a `case_map.json` entry. The direct pinned-image comparison above uses existing metrics and thresholds but does not turn the standard server test into a pass.

Pre-commit passed. H200 focused tests passed at model head `15e7a2c8d8eedd2325b3d6613b61963060d794b1`; the subsequent model change only restores the Blackwell graph-mode branch. Final combined head `02dc569408cd24bd6fee91086c93829cd076b1ef` passed the full focused suite on B300, including real CFG/SP folding and registered graph routing. Additional shared-context/CFG/LoRA/cache/model coverage: 69 passed, 4 subtests. Exact CI status is reported separately; pending CI is not treated as passed.

title: [Fix] [AMD] deepseek-v4: Respect AITER selection for Q-LoRA quantization
author: lunarwhite
body:
## Motivation

On gfx95/gfx1250, DeepSeek V4 can select fused Q/K normalization and RoPE while `SGLANG_USE_AITER=0`. When the non-e8m0 producer is selected, both Q-LoRA prepare paths call the fused quantizer, although `fused_rms_fp8_group_quant` is imported only when AITER is enabled. This raises `NameError` before attention preparation completes.

## Modifications

Gate the AITER-dependent producer on the AITER switch and reuse the existing normalization/projection fallback when it is disabled. Keep the independent e8m0 producer available and preserve the downstream Q/K normalization, RoPE and cache-store path. Add a regression test for both prepare methods and the AITER/e8m0 choices.

## Accuracy Tests

On MI355X, PyTorch 2.11.0 with ROCm, using upstream `5007cbd6a57515bf5e008ff2fd2bdb834356b53c` and the patch:

- Both real prepare methods at batch sizes 1 and 5: all four AITER-off baseline cases reproduce the exact `NameError`; all four patched cases pass normalization, Q/RoPE, KV-cache and indexer checks using real block-FP8 projections.
- AITER-on: four base/head pairs complete, with all saved outputs compared byte-for-byte by the validation runner.
- Existing e8m0 tests pass: eight producer and two consumer cases, with no skips.
- The same 12-case dispatch regression yields four expected baseline failures and no patched failures.

These are fixed-weight component tests using DeepSeek-V4-Flash-FP8 configuration dimensions, not full-model accuracy or gfx1250 hardware results. AITER is installed; the disabled-switch cases use the existing Triton block-FP8 path.

The branch is aligned with upstream `68e57f40057175ff22a17ea0bdbe7ecbc69d9d91`; the changed model file and regression test are byte-identical to the GPU-validated versions. The local dispatch control was rerun after alignment; GPU results belong to the stated baseline.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

No performance improvement is claimed. This fixes a failing dispatch and leaves the AITER-on producer unchanged.

title: [Perf] diffusion: Fuse SANA-Video depthwise convolution and GLU on SM120
author: BBuf
body:
## Motivation and change

SANA-Video applies a BF16 depthwise 3×3 convolution followed by bias and GLU to large channel-last activations. The tested `[21, 13440, 30, 52]` activation materializes an approximately 840 MiB convolution intermediate. A complete CFG iteration contains 40 depthwise convolutions and 40 separate GLU kernels in the frozen baseline.

This PR fuses those operations in one Triton kernel. Four adjacent output rows reuse input loads. It preserves row-major FP32 FMA accumulation and the native BF16 convolution, bias and SiLU rounding boundaries. Dispatch uses the existing per-signature exactness gate and is restricted to SM120 inference with the supported large BF16 channel-last convolution. Unseen signatures during capture, unsupported convolution/layout settings, gradients, compilation and disabled cuDNN retain the reference path. A failed exactness verification disables the fusion. SANA-WM remains unchanged because its biased-convolution arithmetic differs.

The implementation lives in the KDA backend and is exposed through the existing lazy diffusion facade. This independent change does not include the separate eager-LN optimization. Existing RoPE and bias-SiLU fusions remain in place.

## Final-head benchmark

Frozen SGLang main: `af21e2b989e482cfdce39689126562f2209d53ac`. Final tested PR head: `f248594caca5c533c94612b6848ff3512ed98e08`. Frozen vLLM-Omni: `817d4c17feb702289a2d2b2cbacfd594c262b7a7`.
The [independent raw audit](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/blob/cc6d5a134821364c9244a6aaea8a75dd0fe22558/evidence/preflight/sana-video-depthwise-final-primary1-raw-audit.json) checks every saved request, native MP4, runtime commit and GPU ownership sample and recomputes the original statistics. It does not change the frozen samples or thresholds.

One NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (SM120, 97,887 MiB, 600 W), GPU 0 only; GPU 1 idle. Checkpoint `Efficient-Large-Model/SANA-Video_2B_480p_diffusers@db5f398b13ca086d09a50ce156c20527773841b1`. Native SGLang and Omni backends; BF16 DiT/text encoder, FP32 VAE/noise/solver. Workload: 832×480, 81 frames at 16 fps, 50 steps, CFG 6, CPU seed 1101, empty negative prompt, 300-token cap, batch/concurrency 1.

| Configuration | Prompt | n | Mean / p50 / p95 E2E (s) | Serial req/s | Request peak GiB | Separate synchronized denoise / decode (s) |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| omni_eager | short | 6 | 85.2435 / 85.1708 / 85.4637 | 0.01173 | 31.011 | 81.1538 / 3.2919 (n=1) |
| omni_eager | long | 6 | 85.2417 / 85.1557 / 85.4571 | 0.01173 | 31.011 | 81.1240 / 3.2956 (n=1) |
| main_eager | short | 6 | 63.5638 / 63.5646 / 63.5718 | 0.01573 | 23.054 | 58.4761 / 5.0376 (n=4) |
| main_eager | long | 6 | 63.5655 / 63.5674 / 63.5722 | 0.01573 | 23.054 | 58.4810 / 5.0345 (n=2) |
| v1_eager | short | 12 | 61.3030 / 61.3000 / 61.3237 | 0.01631 | 23.025 | not collected here |
| v1_eager | long | 12 | 61.3000 / 61.2966 / 61.3201 | 0.01631 | 23.025 | not collected here |
| final_eager | short | 12 | 61.3031 / 61.3028 / 61.3103 | 0.01631 | 23.025 | 56.1882 / 5.0333 (n=4) |
| final_eager | long | 12 | 61.3054 / 61.3074 / 61.3156 | 0.01631 | 23.025 | 56.1962 / 5.0347 (n=2) |

Primary values use every predeclared measured request. NVML is sampled every 250 ms during requests; these are observed device-memory peaks, not exact allocator maxima. Denoise is from a separate synchronized diagnostic, not a component subtracted from primary E2E. V1 is retained for cleanup comparison. Omni denoise/decode reuses the already archived native stage diagnostic at the unchanged frozen source/checkpoint/configuration, with one steady request per English prompt. All primary E2E samples are new. Native stage boundaries differ across frameworks; no diagnostic timing replaces primary E2E.

| Prompt | Final mean E2E reduction vs main | Omni / final mean E2E | V1 → final mean latency change | Cleanup paired-t 95% regression upper bound |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| short | 3.55649% | 1.390525× | +0.00028% | 0.02661% |
| long | 3.55557% | 1.390443× | +0.00892% | 0.03643% |

| Comparison | Prompt | Process pairs | Paired median geometric ratio | Paired-log-t 95% interval |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| main_vs_final | short | 2 | 1.036879 | [1.036786, 1.036973] |
| omni_vs_final | short | 2 | 1.391066 | [1.355012, 1.428079] |

| v1_vs_final_cleanup | short | 4 | 0.999996 | [0.999734, 1.000258] |

The prospectively frozen order is M–V1–F–O–V1–F–F–V1–O–F–V1–M, with one excluded warmup and three measured requests per English prompt per process. Prompt order reverses in the second half. Main/Omni have n=6 per prompt and V1/final n=12. HTTP E2E includes request submission, native polling where applicable, encoding and complete MP4 transfer, but excludes validation and disk writes. The primary SGLang process has no profiler, observer or added stage synchronization. All original samples and warmups are retained.

The final table includes the complete paired results and uncertainty. Two main/final and Omni/final process pairs limit interval precision.

## Actual execution and compatibility

| Configuration | GPU kernels / CFG iteration | Kernel sum (ms) | Depthwise+GLU | Native depthwise | Separate GLU | Graph launches |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| main_eager | 2309 | 1170.332 | 0 | 40 | 40 | 0 |
| v1_eager | 2269 | 1124.244 | 40 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| final_eager | 2269 | 1123.985 | 40 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| main_bcg | 2103 | 1135.238 | 0 | 40 | 40 | 2 |
| final_bcg | 2063 | 1090.626 | 40 | 0 | 0 | 2 |

Profiles are separate synchronized diagnostics. CPU `ProfilerStep#3` launch correlations identify a complete CFG iteration and the actual kernels inside graph launches. The final eager path retains all 82 ATen LayerNorm calls; the existing BCG path uses its 82 fused LN calls. Both retain 40 RoPE and 40 bias-SiLU calls. Kernel sums are not primary serving latency.

| Configuration | Serving requests | Model replays | Serving captures | Warmup graph captures | Capture time sum (s) | Launch-to-ready (s) | Full diagnostic process peak (MiB) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|

The compatibility sequence switches short/long/Chinese prompts and lossless/exact/high modes, including repeated requests and return to lossless. Exact/high use uncaptured quality-specific eager runners; returning to lossless reuses the graph without serving capture. Final BCG profiles place all 40 new depthwise+GLU kernels inside graph replay. These results establish compatibility with existing BCG, not a new beneficial BCG scenario. Full-process diagnostic memory includes loading, warmup, quality switching and profiling; it does not isolate serving-only BCG overhead. Launch/capture observations are cached individual runs, not cold-start distributions.

## Quality and actual generated results

All 96 final primary MP4s match their qualified native-arm reference hashes. The 51 compatibility MP4s match the same-quality main outputs, including every decoded frame. Native input auditing checks actual token IDs/masks, CPU noise and schedules. English cross-framework workloads pass the frozen quality criteria. Chinese cross-framework PSNR fails at frames 26–28 (minimum 23.5768 dB below 24 dB); its outputs and failure are retained and excluded from primary timing admission. Main/PR Chinese outputs remain exact.

Native SGLang main versus native Omni, with all 81 decoded frames evaluated per request. Frozen admission requires every frame to have SSIM ≥ 0.92 and PSNR ≥ 24 dB; passing an average alone is insufficient.

| Request | SSIM mean / minimum | PSNR mean / minimum (dB) | All-frame admission |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| 00-short | 0.956517 / 0.930914 | 30.7329 / 28.4207 | pass |

| 02-chinese | 0.939182 / 0.920909 | 26.7774 / 23.5768 | FAIL; excluded from primary timing |
| 03-short | 0.956517 / 0.930914 | 30.7329 / 28.4207 | pass |

The panels below show actual main/final frames 0/40/80 at 0/2.5/5 seconds with identical prompts and generation settings. Representative frames were manually reviewed; full-motion review is not claimed. title: [Perf] cuda-graph: Upload each deduplicated executable on a private stream before its first launch
author: metamergebot
body:
## Motivation

A CUDA graph executable that has never been launched is uploaded to the device implicitly by its first `cudaGraphLaunch`, through the launch stream. When that stream already has work queued, the implicit upload can block the host until the stream drains. A server that first-launches many executables while it is already serving traffic (for example when the dedup fallback keeps many graphs in separate executables) pays those stalls on the request path.

CUDA provides `cudaGraphUpload` to upload an executable ahead of its launch. Uploading every executable eagerly at capture or seal time would avoid the stalls but adds the full upload cost to startup, so this change uploads lazily instead, right before the first launch.

## Modifications

- `DedupedCudaGraphRegistry.replay` now uploads a group's executable with `cudaGraphUpload` before its first launch, on a private non-blocking stream created lazily by the registry. An event is recorded on that stream and the launch stream waits on it, so ordering is unchanged and the host does not block.
- `GraphExecGroup` gains an `uploaded` flag; the upload happens once per executable, at its first replay.
- `close()` destroys the private stream and event along with the executables.
- Capture, `register` and `seal` are untouched, so startup time is unchanged.
- `test_cuda_graph_dedup.py`: the shared-executable test now also asserts that two graphs sharing one executable upload it exactly once, at the first replay.

## Accuracy Tests

No change to kernels or outputs: the same executable is launched on the same stream, after an explicit upload that the implicit path would have done anyway. The unit test checks replay outputs are unchanged.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Not a kernel change. The only runtime difference is where the one-time upload of each executable happens: on a private stream before the first launch instead of implicitly inside it, so the first replay of an executable no longer blocks the host behind work queued on the launch stream.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).
- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests). `test/registered/unit/model_executor/runner_backend/test_cuda_graph_dedup.py` covers the change and runs in the `base-b-kernel-unit` stage.
- [ ] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations).
- [ ] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed).

title: [Fix] TensorMatcher: keep symbol device/dtype options; use kDLGPU aliases
author: DarkSharpness
body:
> (auto generated by Claude)

## Motivation

`TensorMatcher::with_device<Codes...>(sym)` and `with_dtype<Ts...>(sym)` called `set_options` even with an empty pack, which replaced the symbol's options with an empty list (= anything allowed). The common launcher idiom `device.set_options<kDLCUDA>(); TensorMatcher(...).with_device(device).verify(x);` therefore never checked the device type, so a CPU tensor passed. About 200 of 260 `SymbolicDevice` declarations under `python/sglang/kernels/jit/csrc/` used this idiom. The same bug affected the dtype restriction in `distributed/nvlink_comm.cuh`.

Introduced in #14570, which added the `set_options` call to the symbol overloads; before that (#13453) they left the symbol's options untouched, so every launcher written with this idiom since has had an unchecked device type.

## Modifications

- `tensor.h`: `with_device(sym)` / `with_dtype(sym)` only override options when the pack is non-empty. `set_options` now re-checks a value that is already bound, so a runtime `DLDevice` / `DLDataType` passed together with a type list (e.g. `.with_device<kDLGPU>(x.device())`) is checked too; that path was also unchecked before.
- Replace hard-coded `kDLCUDA` / `kDLCUDAHost` with `kDLGPU` / `kDLGPUHost` in JIT launchers and headers (`jit/csrc`, `jit/include`, `kda_kernels/csrc`), so the check is correct on ROCm. `moe/paged_experts.cuh` needed `using sglang::kDLGPU;` because it only imports `sglang::host`.
- Left as `kDLCUDA` because they are CUDA-only and don't include `sgl_kernel/utils.cuh`: `jit/csrc/moe/tvm_ffi_utils.h` (`cudaGetDevice` + CUDA stream helper), the vendored `ops/lora/moe/trtllm_lora_temp/data/csrc/trtllm_fused_moe_kernel_launcher.cu`, and the device-name table in `tensor.h`.
- `add-jit-kernel` skill examples updated to `kDLGPU`, plus a note that options set on a symbol stay in force.
- New `test/registered/unit/kernels/test_tensor_matcher.py`: JIT-compiles a small launcher and checks that a CPU tensor or a wrong dtype is rejected through both the symbol path and the runtime-value path. All 4 cases fail on the old header.

## Fallout

No launcher started rejecting its inputs: no test anywhere hit `not in the allowed options`, so no call site or declared option needed changing.

Note: `moe/expert_specialization/es_sm100_mxfp8_blockscaled_{group_quant,moe_group_gemm}.cuh` are not referenced by any JIT loader and already fail to compile on main (`host` is not visible there). They were only touched by the rename.

## Accuracy / tests

- All `test/registered/kernels/ops/**` and `test/registered/unit/kernels/**` on 1x B200. Every failure reproduces on main with identical counts (`paged_mqa_metadata`, `q8kv8_sparse_prefill_backend`, `tilelang_dsa_zero_rope`, `model_fast_paths`, diffusion `test_rope`, `hy4_decode_kernels`, `lanczos`, `moe_topk_softmax`, `per_token_group_quant_8bit_v2`). The rest are multi-GPU or ROCm-only tests that can't run on a single CUDA GPU.
- Multi-GPU communication tests on 4x H200: `all_reduce_residual_norm`, `deterministic_reduce_scatter`, `fp4_allgather_moe_reduction`, `tp_qknorm`, `custom_all_reduce`, `symm_mem_all_gather` pass. `ar_fusion` and `beam_all_reduce` need 8 GPUs (left to CI).
- Every changed header compiled standalone for sm_100a on this branch vs main: no new failures.
- ROCm not run locally; relying on AMD CI.

## Follow-up (not in this PR)

Hand-written checks that should become matcher expressions (`RuntimeCheck(t.dim() == ...)`, stride / contiguity / alignment checks, raw dtype `.code` / `.bits`, `TVM_FFI_ICHECK`) remain in about 90 files under `jit/csrc`, e.g. `distributed/custom_all_reduce.cuh`, `gemm/fp8_blockwise/fp8_blockwise_scaled_mm_sm120.cuh`, `elementwise/fused_qknorm_rope.cuh`, `inkling/inkling_all_reduce.cuh`, `deepseek_v4/hash_topk.cuh`.

title: [Perf] dsv41: Drop per-layer routing glue under simulated routing with EPLB
author: zcnrex
body:
## Motivation

DSV4.1 decode baselines run with `SGLANG_SIMULATE_ROUND_ROBIN_EXPERTS=1` plus EPLB (`--ep-num-redundant-experts 64 --ep-dispatch-algorithm dynamic`). In that setup every MoE layer ran six small kernels between MegaGate and MegaMoE that production never runs:

`randint` → `triton_poi_fused_index_randint_remainder` → `_fill_padded_rows` → int32 `direct_copy` → routed-scale `Mul` → `mega_moe_pre_dispatch`

`run_mega_gate` dropped the in-buffer routing path whenever simulation and EPLB were both on, because the simulation wrote logical ids. So the benchmark overstated decode step time.

Separately, `_physical_dispatch_maps` cast the int64 EPLB maps to int32 on every call. That is 2 cast kernels per MoE layer per step, on the production path too.

## Modifications

1. **Simulation writes physical ids.** `_simulate_balanced_routing_kernel` optionally maps logical ids to physical slots with MegaGate's replica pick (`(ep_rank + token * 23333) % logical_count`). `run_mega_gate` passes the maps and keeps `in_buffer` under simulation. `moe_ep_rank` is read only when a map is passed.
2. **Cached int32 dispatch maps for MegaGate.** `ExpertLocationMetadata.mega_gate_maps(algorithm)` builds MegaGate's int32 `(physical map, replica count)` once per dispatch algorithm, on first use and outside graph capture. `update()` refreshes the cached maps in place, so captured CUDA graphs see rebalances. When MegaGate is on, `ExpertLocationDispatchInfo` carries this layer's slice in one `mega_gate_maps` field. Without it, for example when another backend is in use or in existing tests, the gate still casts per call. Nothing is allocated unless MegaGate and a static/dynamic dispatch algorithm are both enabled.

## Accuracy Tests

No numerics change in production. (1) only touches the benchmark-only simulation path, and (2) replaces casts with identical int32 values.

## Benchmarking and Profiling

DSV4.1-Flash, DEP16 (4 nodes × 4 GPUs), DSpark spec with simulated acceptance 3.25, round-robin simulated routing, 64 redundant experts with dynamic dispatch.

Same job, baseline vs. this PR, bs256 per rank, 2k-token prefix:

| | base | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| step time | 19.09 ms | 18.50 ms (−3.1%) |
| kernels / step (rank 0) | 1155 | 913 |
| elementwise kernels / step | 324 | 122 |

Removed per step (×40 layers each): `mega_moe_pre_dispatch` (302 µs), `triton_poi_…randint…` (101 µs), `randint` (95 µs), `direct_copy` (80 µs), `Mul` (57 µs), `_fill_padded_rows` (52 µs). Each layer now runs MegaGate → simulation → MegaMoE.

At a 126k prefix (commit 1 only, vs. an earlier baseline run): bs8 8.09 → 7.84 ms, bs64 10.15 → 9.83 ms, bs256 19.91 → 19.45 ms.

## Tests

- Existing tests passed on GPU with this change: `test_round_robin_ep_balance.py`, `test_mega_gate.py`, `test_topk_routing_inputs.py`, `test_dispatch_dtype_preservation.py`, `test_expert_location_weight_loading.py`, `test_hash_topk.py`, `test_flashinfer_dispatcher.py`, `test_mega_moe_deepgemm_api.py`.
- Checked end to end with the bs256 decode profiles above: no glue kernels, and no int32 cast kernels before MegaGate.

title: [Perf] allreduce: enable FlashInfer AllReduce Fusion auto-enable for Kimi-K3
author: brandonfzhang
body:
## Motivation

`_flashinfer_allreduce_fusion_auto_enable` arms
`flashinfer_allreduce_fusion_backend="auto"` only for architectures in
`_FLASHINFER_ALLREDUCE_FUSION_ARCHS` (`python/sglang/srt/arg_groups/
overrides.py`). `KimiK25ForConditionalGeneration` is listed;
`KimiK3ForConditionalGeneration` is not (checked at current main, b960aa9),
so Kimi-K3 serves run every TP all-reduce on the stock path even though all
other auto-enable conditions pass on the measured deployment (SM100-family,
TP > 1, no DP attention, `moe_a2a_backend == "none"`; multi-node is allowed
on SM100 by the existing gate).

Measured end-to-end on a 2-node TP8 GB300 NVL (SM103) serve of Kimi-K3
NVFP4, enabling the fusion backend gives **+9.1% mean / +9.7% median p90
per-user interactivity** (normalized output tok/s per user) over a 5-point
concurrency ladder, 4 of 5 points positive, zero request errors everywhere.

Users can already opt in today with
`--flashinfer-allreduce-fusion-backend auto` (the flag sets exactly the
field the auto-enable pass sets; all evidence below was collected through
that route with an otherwise byte-identical serve). This PR only makes the
measured-better configuration the default for this architecture.

## Modifications

One line in `python/sglang/srt/arg_groups/overrides.py`:

```python
_FLASHINFER_ALLREDUCE_FUSION_ARCHS = frozenset(
    {
        ...
        "KimiK25ForConditionalGeneration",
        "KimiK3ForConditionalGeneration",   # <-- added
        ...
    }
)
```

No other behavior changes. FlashInfer strategy-threshold changes and
engine-side completion-mode changes investigated in the same study are
explicitly NOT part of this PR (separate tracks); the enabled arm below runs
stock FlashInfer strategy selection.

## Accuracy Tests

All-reduce fusion swaps the kernel, not the reduction semantics. Request
error rates were zero in every run and output-length distributions matched
between arms, but no pinned accuracy set exists for this serve recipe —
flagged for reviewers rather than waived. (Happy to run a maintainer-
suggested accuracy suite on the same deployment.)

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Serve: Kimi-K3 NVFP4, TP8 (+ decode-context-parallel 8) across 2x GB300 NVL
nodes (4 GPUs each); agentic-coding replay (900 s windows, fixed seed);
metric `e2e_normalized_interactivity_tps` (higher is better). One run per
arm per point, arms of a pair launched back-to-back.

| conc | arm | p50 | p90 | p99 | completed reqs (errored) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | stock | 90.51 | 53.50 | 31.03 | 106 (0) |
| 1 | enabled | 96.64 | **64.28 (+20.2%)** | 31.69 | 106 (0) |
| 8 | stock | 45.07 | 29.43 | 8.02 | 312 (0) |
| 8 | enabled | 44.05 | 28.13 (−4.4%) | 9.23 | 320 (0) |
| 8 (repeat pair, different day + node pairs) | stock | 47.67 | 28.48 | 8.83 | 320 (0) |
| 8 (repeat pair, different day + node pairs) | enabled | 49.32 | **31.54 (+10.7%)** | 14.96 | 322 (0) |
| 20 | stock | 24.42 | 10.86 | 2.25 | 523 (0) |
| 20 | enabled | 26.30 | **11.88 (+9.4%)** | 2.53 | 538 (0) |
| 40 | stock | 8.07 | 1.13 | 0.34 | 249 (0) |
| 40 | enabled | 6.46 | 1.24 (+9.9%) | 0.50 | 253 (0) |
| 60 | stock | 5.13 | 0.64 | 0.28 | 247 (0) |
| 60 | enabled | 6.69 | 0.70 (+8.9%) | 0.07 | 261 (0) |

Pooled p90 delta over the six measurements: **+9.1% mean / +9.7% median,
sign 5/1**. The single negative (−4.4% at concurrency 8) sign-flipped to
+10.7% in a full repeat of that pair on different node pairs a day later —
i.e. the c8 point is run-to-run noise, not a stable regression; both pairs
are shown above. An earlier
independent 3-point A/B of the same flag on the same topology measured p50
+0.4% / +1.5% / **+24.2%** at concurrency 8/20/40 with identical record
counts, corroborating the direction.

Noise context measured in the same campaign: a repeated stock baseline on
this 2-node topology reproduced p90 to ±5.4%; an identical-arm control pair
(a TP1 serve where the flag changes nothing) differed by −4.2% p90. The
c1/c20/c40/c60 gains sit at or beyond that band; the single −4.4% point is
inside it and did not reproduce (repeat pair: +10.7%). Concurrency 40/60 run deep in queue saturation (absolute p90
~0.6–1.2 tok/s/user), so their relative deltas carry small absolute
magnitudes; c1 and c20 carry the practical win.

Dispatch verification: per-rank FlashInfer API census — stock arm logs
**zero** `allreduce_fusion` calls; enabled arm logs **264,048** calls across
the 8 TP ranks in the concurrency-8 window alone (equal per rank), with the
serve log attesting `flashinfer_allreduce_fusion_backend='auto'`. MNNVL
workspace rendezvous succeeded across both nodes in every enabled run; on
topologies where MNNVL is unavailable the existing
`_flashinfer_allreduce_unavailable` plumbing falls back to the stock path,
so the default change is safe there.

Scope caveats:
- Measured on GB300 NVL (SM103) 2-node TP8 over the MNNVL fabric only; the
  auto-enable gate already restricts to SM90/SM100-family (multi-node:
  SM100).
- One run per cell, arms on different node pairs (the repeat-band numbers
  above quantify that); more repeats would tighten the c8 point.
- GLM-5.3 (`Glm5NextForConditionalGeneration`) was ALSO tested and is
  deliberately NOT included: its deltas did not reproduce across the ladder
  (one +28.5% p90 cell at concurrency 8, −14.7% at 20, ~0 elsewhere). This
  PR adds only the architecture with reproducible evidence.

title: [Perf] [NVIDIA] deep_select: Add a 3-CTA tier for the paged indexer top-k
author: zcnrex
body:
## Motivation

`topk_select` runs one CTA per row, so it takes `ceil(rows / (SMs * occupancy))` rounds. At occupancy 2 on VR the grid quantizes to **2 × SMs rows**, and a DSv4.1 decode step at batch 128 asks for 512 — two full rounds for barely more than one round of work. The jump is visible in the raw timings: 512 rows costs 1.8× what 2 × SMs rows costs.

## What this does

Adds a third config to `TopkNormal` at occupancy 3, moving the grid to `3 * SMs`.

Fitting the plan under `(opt-in smem) / 3` caps `reconstruct_threshold` at 2048, which costs per-CTA throughput — so the tier is **taken only when it removes a round**. `TopkNormal` compares the two round counts and otherwise keeps the existing config.

A threshold that small leaves `NUM_EXTRA_SLOTS` under what the index-sort window delta table needs. That table is built only under `SORT_BY_INDEX`, so the assert is narrowed to the feature it protects rather than the bound being weakened — `MAX_VOCAB_SIZE` is untouched and no caller's vocabulary reach changes.

Three files, +18/-2.

## Measurements

VR (sm_100f), time per call after vs before, topk 512, `--check` against `torch.topk` at every point. The tier is read back out of the kernel's own template arguments, so this is the dispatch decision rather than an inference from timings:

| rows | rnd2 | rnd3 | tier chosen | after vs before |
|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|
| 128 | - | - | `occ=1 rt=4096 d=5` | +0.9% |
| SMs | - | - | `occ=1 rt=4096 d=5` | +0.7% |
| 256 | 1 | 1 | `occ=2 rt=4096 d=4` | +0.2% |
| 2 × SMs | 1 | 1 | `occ=2 rt=4096 d=4` | +0.0% |
| 512 | 2 | 1 | **`occ=3 rt=2048 d=2`** | **-25.6%** |
| 3 × SMs | 2 | 1 | **`occ=3 rt=2048 d=2`** | **-29.6%** |
| 4 × SMs | 2 | 2 | `occ=2 rt=4096 d=4` | +0.3% |
| 1024 | 3 | 2 | **`occ=3 rt=2048 d=2`** | **-20.9%** |

<sub>vocab 65536. At vocab 131072 the same tiers are chosen and the wins are -27.7%, -25.8% and -14.9%.</sub>

Rows where `rnd3 == rnd2` keep the existing tier and land within 1% of the old time. 16/16 correct.

On a DSv4.1 decode step: **0.31% at batch 128, 0.19% at batch 256**. The benefit tracks rounds rather than batch size, so it is non-monotone — batches whose rows fall between 2 × SMs and 3 × SMs, or above 4 × SMs, gain; those between 3 × SMs and 4 × SMs do not.

## Scope

Measured on sm_107 only. Nothing in the mechanism is architecture-specific — every arch in `SUPPORTED_CUDA_ARCHS` reports the same 232448 B opt-in cap and the same register file, and the rule reads the SM count at runtime — but the per-CTA cost of the smaller threshold has not been measured on sm_90 or sm_100. The rule is self-limiting (it fires only when a round is saved, worth 33-50%, against a penalty measured at 8-14% here), so the sign should hold, but a confirmation on B200 or H100 would be welcome.

title: [Perf] [NVIDIA] glm5: Route small-M BF16 GEMMs to FlashInfer warp split-K with PDL on SM107
author: akhilg-nv
body:
[by Claude Code]

## Motivation

On SM107 (Vera Rubin NVL72), GLM-5 TP4 decode with EAGLE runs its dense BF16 GEMMs on 1 to 20 tokens per step: o_proj, fused_qkv_a, the DSA indexer's fused wk + weights_proj, and the shared expert's gate_up and down. Today they go to the CuTe DSL TGV kernel, to cuBLAS (for the shared expert and the indexer often a split-K GEMM plus a separate reduce kernel), or, for fused_qkv_a at M <= 16, to SGLang's fused_a JIT kernel. At these sizes each GEMM takes a few microseconds and mostly streams weights, so how much of its start-up overlaps the previous kernel matters as much as the kernel body.

FlashInfer's warp split-K BF16 GEMM, which main already runs for its Muse Spark keys in `_BF16_WARP_SPLITK_TUNED_TACTICS`, launches with PDL (programmatic dependent launch): it starts while the previous kernel is still finishing, issues its weight loads, and waits for the previous kernel only before it reads the activations. With PDL it is faster per call than the current route at all of these shapes; without PDL it is slower than TGV at o_proj (tables below).

This PR, on SM107 only:
- adds 16 GLM-5 TP4 decode keys `(M, N, K)` to the warp split-K table, so these GEMMs take main's existing split-K route (`pdl=True`, FlashInfer's default tactic per key). M = 1, 4, 5, 20 are the draft and verify sizes at batch 1 and 4 with EAGLE 4-1-5 (verify M = 5 x batch);
- moves fused_qkv_a at M = 1, 4, 5 off the fused_a JIT kernel onto that route (q_b_proj keeps fused_a);
- compiles the 16 tactics before CUDA graph capture in `GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM.precompile_kernels_after_loading`, as Qwen4-Exp does for its keys.

Other GPUs, other shapes and the kernel itself are unchanged. Like main's table, the keys match on shape alone, so on SM107 any model whose BF16 GEMMs have exactly these shapes takes the same route. `SGLANG_ENABLE_BF16_SPLITK_GEMM=0` still turns the whole split-K route off, including the fused_qkv_a move.

**Impact**
- **Performance:** AgentX GLM-5.3-NVFP4 TP4 c1 on Vera Rubin NVL72 (low-latency point, EAGLE 4-1-5): per-request decode time per output token **-2.51%** [95% CI -2.80%, -2.16%]; the two base/PR pairs gave -2.54% and -2.47%, A/A noise +/-0.14%. Interactivity (1000 / p90 ITL) +2.6%, within this run's noise (A/A +/-2.5-2.9%); TTFT unchanged within noise. About 1 point of the -2.51% comes from the fused_qkv_a move (estimate, not measured separately: its share of the main-stream per-call savings, weighted by calls per decode cycle).
- **Per call** (decode profile on Vera Rubin NVL72; main stream timed from the previous kernel's end to the GEMM's end, side stream by kernel time): o_proj M=5 5.79 -> 4.93 us, fused_qkv_a M=5 4.51 -> 3.55 us, indexer wk M=5 4.48 -> 2.88 us on the main stream; shared expert gate_up M=5 8.35 -> 4.10 us and down M=5 4.10 -> 2.82 us on the side stream.
- **Accuracy:** GSM8K (sgl-eval, 300 questions, with a superset of these keys) 98.00% -> 98.00%; with `--max-running-requests 1`, so every decode step runs on the new keys, 98.33% -> 98.33%. All 16 keys match an FP32 reference within BF16 tolerance, with PDL on and off.
- **Accuracy (GPQA-Diamond, GB300 proxy):** 90.40% -> 91.92%, paired difference +1.52 points [95% CI -1.52, +4.55], within a 5-point non-inferiority margin set before the run (it rules out gross breakage only; details below).

## Modifications

**+74 / -8 runtime code (3 files), +234 tests (1 file).** No kernel changes.

- `_BF16_SM107_WARP_SPLITK_TUNED_TACTICS` (16 keys) is added to the active warp split-K table when split-K is enabled and `get_platform().device_sm == 107`: `initialize_bf16_gemm_config` rebinds `_active_warp_splitk_tactics` (the base table, or the base table plus these keys on SM107), which `use_bf16_splitk_gemm`, `_bf16_splitk_gemm_out` and `precompile_splitk_tactics` read; neither table is modified (`layers/quantization/unquant.py`). A key was kept only where FlashInfer with PDL beat the current route per call in a decode profile (table below); the indexer's wq_b (no gain at M=5; at M=20 it shares its shape with q_b_proj, which got 12.5% slower) and shared expert down at M=20 (+8.7%) keep their current routes. Each key uses FlashInfer's default tactic: an in-situ sweep over the 88-110 valid tactics per shape, at M = 1 and 5, found none more than 1.5% faster.
- `prefer_bf16_splitk_over_fused_a()` (`unquant.py`) and its call in `DeepseekV2AttentionMLA.prepare_qkv_latent` (`models/deepseek_v2.py`): fused_qkv_a at M = 1, 4, 5 (N=2624, K=6144) runs through the linear layer, and so through the split-K route, instead of the fused_a JIT kernel. It returns False unless the SM107 keys are active, so other GPUs never reach the shape check.
- `precompile_splitk_tactics(keys=...)` takes an optional key subset; `precompile_sm107_splitk_tactics()` compiles only the SM107 keys and is called from `GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM.precompile_kernels_after_loading` (`models/glm4_moe.py`), so GLM does not compile the Muse Spark and GB300 tables.
- `test/registered/unit/layers/quantization/test_unquant_sm107_splitk.py` (CPU): the routing on SM107 vs SM100/SM103, the fused_qkv_a condition, and the `prepare_qkv_latent` call site (Accuracy Tests).

## Accuracy Tests

**GSM8K** (sgl-eval 0.1.3, gsm8k, 300 examples, temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95, max_tokens 16384, seed 0, thinking on; real decoding, no simulated acceptance; server flags of the AgentX GLM-5 TP4 c1 configuration below):

| run | base | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| normal batching (a superset of these keys; about 42% of decoded tokens at batch sizes that hit a key) | 98.00% | 98.00% |
| `--max-running-requests 1` (every decode step on the new keys: verify M=5, draft M=1, draft extend M=5) | 98.33% (295/300) | 98.33% (295/300) |

**GPQA-Diamond (GB300 proxy).** CI and our Rubin capacity cannot run this branch on SM107 right now, so the same 16 keys were forced on SM103 with a test-only switch that is not part of this PR (the FlashInfer warp split-K kernel is the same code, compiled for sm_103a). GLM-5.2-NVFP4 (its GEMM shapes match GLM-5.3 at all 16 keys), TP4 on GB300, EAGLE 4-1-5 with real decoding, `--max-running-requests 4` so that 97% of decode steps run at batch 4 and hit the keys (verified in a 40-step profile: 9,840 warp split-K launches per rank), sgl-eval 0.1.3 gpqa, 198 questions x 1, temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95, thinking on, max_tokens 200,000. Each arm ran in two halves of the question set.

| | base | this change (keys forced on) |
|---|---|---|
| GPQA-Diamond pass@1 | 90.40% (179/198) | 91.92% (182/198) |
| paired difference, 95% bootstrap CI (10,000 draws) | | +1.52 points [-1.52, +4.55] |
| truncated responses | 1 | 0 |
| mean completion tokens | 23,822 | 23,634 |

The non-inferiority margin (5 points) was fixed before the run; at this sample size the check detects gross breakage only.

**Element-wise, all 16 keys, PDL on and off (Vera Rubin NVL72):** tolerance |out - ref| <= 2^-7 |ref| + 2^-9 rms(ref), with ref an FP32 matmul of the same BF16 inputs, two input sets, poisoned outputs: 32/32 pass (worst error 0.44 of the bound, no non-finite values). The output through SGLang's route is bit-equal to a direct FlashInfer call at all 16 keys. The checker catches injected errors (shifted weight row, dropped last K tile, 2% scale, one unwritten row) in 64/64 cases. PDL chain test (CUDA graph of a producer that triggers its dependents early, the GEMM, and a consumer): 0 wrong outputs in 1,600 replays. compute-sanitizer memcheck and initcheck: 0 errors.

**Unit test** (`test_unquant_sm107_splitk.py`, CPU, FlashInfer and CuTe DSL entry points replaced by CPU stand-ins that record the route):
- On SM107, GLM keys (o_proj M=5, shared down M=4, fused_qkv_a M=20) and a Muse Spark key take the warp split-K route with `pdl=True`, and the output matches `F.linear`.
- On SM100 and SM103 the same GLM keys keep their current route, while the Muse Spark key still takes split-K. Fails if the SM107 gate is dropped or widened.
- Initializing on SM107 and then on SM100 routes the GLM keys back to their current route and leaves the shared warp split-K table unchanged.
- fused_qkv_a leaves fused_a only when split-K will take the call: SM107, split-K on, M in {1, 4, 5}; not for M = 2 or 16, not with `SGLANG_ENABLE_BF16_SPLITK_GEMM` off (that would send it to cuBLAS), and not on SM100/SM103.
- `prepare_qkv_latent` uses the linear route for those keys and fused_a otherwise.

Each case was checked to fail when its condition is broken (gate widened to every SM10x, merge removed, keys merged into the other table, fused_qkv_a condition ignoring the split-K switch, M check removed, call-site condition inverted).

Existing GPU tests on these paths (`test_unquant_apply_with_addend.py`, `test_dsv3_fused_a_gemm.py`, `test_cutedsl_dsv3_fused_a_gemm.py`) see unchanged routes on the GPUs CI runs; CI has no SM107 runner, so the new route itself runs only in the Vera Rubin NVL72 checks above.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

**Pareto point:** the low-latency end (c1 with EAGLE). The change only touches GEMMs on at most 20 tokens, that is batch <= 4 with EAGLE 4-1-5; larger batches keep their routes. These decode steps are dominated by small, weight-streaming kernels and launch gaps, which is where PDL overlap pays.

**Why AgentX:** the kernel effect depends only on batch shape, so a static workload isolates it (static results below), but the deployment this targets is the AgentX GLM-5 c1 configuration, so the deciding run used AgentX traffic (multi-turn requests with prefix-cache hits and varying context lengths).

**Setup:** one Vera Rubin NVL72 compute tray (4 GPUs), GLM-5.3-NVFP4, TP4, AgentX GLM-5 TP4 c1 configuration: `--bf16-gemm-backend cutedsl`, `--disable-shared-experts-fusion` (so the BF16 shared expert runs as its own GEMMs), EAGLE (4 steps, top-k 1, 5 draft tokens), HiCache, FP8 KV cache, `--max-running-requests 8`, simulated acceptance length 3.33 in both arms (draft tokens are real, acceptance is matched to the recipe's expected length). Base: main 86f72e5; PR: the same main plus an earlier revision of this change with the same 16 keys, tactics and routing. This branch is that revision rebased onto current main and simplified (no override env var; the fused_qkv_a check sits in its caller instead of the fused_a helper); it launches the same kernels and was not re-measured. Order base, PR, PR, base, 900 s each, 125 requests paired across all four runs. Every PR server compiled the 16 tactics before graph capture, and no kernel compiled during serving.

| metric (paired over 125 requests) | PR vs base, pair 1 | pair 2 | pooled [95% CI] | A/A (base, PR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| decode time per output token, median of per-request values (primary) | -2.54% | -2.47% | **-2.51% [-2.80, -2.16]** | -0.14%, +0.14% |
| decode time per output token, p50 | -2.89% | -2.75% | -2.81% [-3.29, -2.27] | -0.29%, -0.15% |
| decode time per output token, p90 | -4.06% | +0.27% | -1.89% [-6.88, +1.56] (noise) | -2.06%, +2.36% |
| interactivity, 1000 / p90 ITL | +5.23% | -0.33% | +2.59% [-1.46, +7.11] (noise) | +2.50%, -2.92% |

Batch 4 (keys at M = 4 and 20) has no AgentX run. Supporting static results (random 8K in / 1K out, simulated acceptance with real draft tokens):
- this change with a superset of the keys, one server per arm (indicative only): TPOT -3% at concurrency 1, -2% at concurrency 4;
- an earlier integration of the same kernel with PDL at an overlapping set of sites (o_proj, the shared expert, the indexer's wq_b and wk, and fused_qkv_a at M = 24 only; EAGLE 5-1-6, so M = 6 and 24; 2 servers x 3 runs per arm): decode cycle time -1.22% [-1.56, -0.88] at concurrency 1 and -0.62% [-0.92, -0.32] at concurrency 4.

**Per call, every key** (TP rank 0, mid-decode profiles at concurrency 1 and 4, base vs a build with a superset of these keys; main = main stream, timed from the previous kernel's end to the GEMM's end so that PDL overlap counts; side = shared-expert stream that overlaps the routed experts, timed by kernel duration):

| GEMM (N x K) | M | current route | current (us) | this PR (us) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| o_proj (6144 x 4096), main | 1 / 4 / 5 / 20 | TGV | 5.76 / 5.63 / 5.79 / 7.04 | 4.61 / 4.64 / 4.93 / 6.18 |
| fused_qkv_a (2624 x 6144), main | 1 / 4 / 5 | fused_a JIT | 5.22 / 5.63 / 4.51 | 4.29 / 4.67 / 3.55 |
| fused_qkv_a (2624 x 6144), main | 20 | TGV | 5.89 | 5.63 |
| indexer wk + weights_proj (160 x 6144), main | 5 | cuBLAS split-K + reduce | 4.48 | 2.88 |
| shared gate_up (1024 x 6144), side | 1 / 4 / 5 / 20 | cuBLAS split-K + reduce | 7.71 / 8.16 / 8.35 / 9.09 | 3.94 / 4.64 / 4.10 / 6.69 |
| shared down (6144 x 512), side | 1 / 4 / 5 | cuBLAS | 7.65 / 4.00 / 4.10 | 2.78 / 2.75 / 2.82 |

A decode profile with a superset of these keys has no added copy, cast or fill kernel: each FlashInfer launch replaces one TGV, fused_a or cuBLAS GEMM, and the cuBLAS split-K reduce kernels go away (2,135 -> 2,034 kernels per decode cycle at c1).

**Why PDL matters** (in-situ microbenchmark on Vera Rubin NVL72: CUDA graph of [predecessor -> GEMM -> successor] chains with predecessors and successors like those in the model, >= 512 MB of distinct weights so L2 is cold, 15 x 10 replays; marginal GEMM time per call; M from the earlier EAGLE 5-1-6 recipe):

| GEMM | M | current route (us) | FlashInfer, PDL off (us) | FlashInfer, PDL on (us) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| o_proj | 1 / 4 / 6 | TGV 6.11 / 5.99 / 6.06 | 6.24 / 6.24 / 6.39 | 4.70 / 4.70 / 4.69 |
| fused_qkv_a | 24 | TGV 7.10 | 6.62 | 5.64 |
| shared gate_up | 4 / 6 / 24 | cuBLAS split-K + reduce 6.34 / 6.24 / 5.63 | 3.99 / 3.89 / 4.64 | 3.30 / 3.31 / 4.02 |
| shared down | 1 / 4 / 6 | cuBLAS 3.40 / 3.33 / 3.21 | 2.76 / 2.91 / 2.81 | 2.50 / 2.34 / 2.28 |
| wk + weights_proj | 24 | cuBLAS split-K + reduce 4.81 | 4.55 | 3.79 |

Without PDL the kernel cannot overlap its start-up with the predecessor, and at o_proj it is slower than TGV, which already overlaps.

**Known issue (pre-existing, not changed here).** FlashInfer's warp split-K kernel, which main already runs with PDL for the Muse Spark keys, has three synchronization orderings that the PTX memory model does not guarantee (output stores under PDL, the shared-memory stage release, and loader exit with copies in flight). None depends on this PR or showed up in the checks above. Reported in flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#8080, fixed in flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#8081 (outputs bit-identical; per-call cost within about +-1% at most of these shapes).

title: [Perf] [NPU] attention: Support mlaprolog for kimik3
author: LinyuanLi0046
body:
## Motivation

Enable MLAProlog for Kimi K3’s no-RoPE MLA on Ascend, supporting BF16 and MXFP8 projection weights with BF16 KV cache.

- The existing MLAProlog path assumes a rotary embedding, but Kimik3 does not need rope. 
- Use mlaprolog V4 kernel to support mlaprolog without rope.

## Modifications

- Integrate `sgl_kernel_npu.operators.attention.mlaprolog_v4` for MLA without RoPE, passing `None` for sine and cosine inputs.
- Route A5 MLA preprocessing through MLAProlog, reusing existing BF16 and MXFP8 weight preparation.
- Correct the `v_head_dim` argument passed to `NPUFusedMLAPreprocess` and consume the common Q/K outputs without assuming a fixed return-tuple length.
- Automatically select the existing split QKV/G path when ModelSlim metadata indicates different quantization precisions for Q and G, keeping construction, forward execution, and weight loading consistent.

## Accuracy Tests

title: [Perf] [NVIDIA] dsv41: Balance the SM90 paged decode indexer's tiles across the GPU so one long context no longer sets the step time
author: latrawy
body:
## Motivation

On SM90, DeepSeek-V4.1 decode scores each query row against its whole visible compressed context with `fp4_index_logits_paged`. The grid gives every row a fixed `min(cdiv(max_len, 64), cdiv(num_sms * 4, rows))` CTAs, which scan the row's tiles serially, so a single long request sets the kernel time while most SMs are idle. Under DP attention every rank waits for the slowest one, so one long context slows every request on the node.

## Modifications

- `_fp4_index_logits_paged_balanced_kernel`: a persistent grid of `num_sms * 8` programs that splits all rows' tiles into equal contiguous shares. The grid does not depend on lengths, so CUDA graph capture and replay work as before.
- Per tile: queries and head weights are loaded once per row, scales are read as 4 bytes per position, e2m1 is decoded from its bit pattern, and `BLOCK_L` is 128.
- The dot shapes, bf16 rounding points and head sum are unchanged, so the scores are bitwise identical to the per-row kernel.
- `fp4_index_logits_paged` uses it behind `SGLANG_OPT_DSV41_FAST_DECODE_INDEXER` (default on; `0` restores the per-row kernel), for up to 4096 rows.

## Accuracy Tests

The scores are bitwise identical, so outputs do not change. New `test_fp4_paged_logits_balanced_matches_per_row_replay` compares the two kernels bit for bit across CUDA graph replays (32 / 64 heads, ratio 1 / 2, with and without a candidate mask, lengths 0, 1, tile edges and past `max_len`).

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Kernel, H200, one call, 32 heads, 48 query rows:

| Rows | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| 48 × 3K | 0.055 ms | 0.051 ms |
| 48 rows, 30K-220K | 1.924 ms | 0.713 ms |
| 43 × 3K + one 900K request (5 rows) | 6.172 ms | 0.584 ms |

End to end, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on 8×H200 with DP attention and DSpark, 80 concurrent requests, decode tok/s:

| Workload | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| 80 × 3K | ~11.0K | ~10.8K (within noise) |
| 80 × 30K-200K | 8.8K | 10.2K (+16.5%) |
| 79 × 3K + one 900K | 6.8K | 10.2K (+49%) |

title: [Perf] detokenizer: Send each step's output ids as one flat column with row offsets
author: hnyls2002
body:
- `BatchTokenIDOutput` and `BatchStrOutput` carry a step's output ids as one flat `array("q")` (`output_ids_flat`) plus row offsets (`output_ids_offsets`) instead of one array per row, so each IPC hop encodes two objects per batch instead of one per request.

- The Rust server push sends `output_ids_flat` as one buffer and derives the per-row lengths from the offsets.

title: [Perf] kimi-k3: Allow residual bank shards with NCCL
author: Codoge
body:
## Motivation

`SGLANG_K3_SP_ATTN_RES` keeps post-MoE residual streams and bank operations on each rank's token shard, then gathers the normalized attention input. Its eligibility check also requires K3's custom collective backend, preventing NCCL deployments from using an existing layout that already has ordinary ReduceScatter/AllGather fallbacks.

## Modifications

- Remove the custom-collective requirement from bank-slice eligibility. Preserve the existing opt-in switch, SP-MoE and residual-bank requirements, PP=1 restriction, consecutive-MoE guard, and speculative hidden-state capture exclusions.
- Keep fused bank/communication paths conditional on custom collective availability. At the terminal bank read, skip custom fusion preparation when no custom gather callback exists; this avoids preparing a pending residual add only to fall back to the ordinary read.
- Use the actual eligibility helper throughout the stage-planning tests, including the terminal read, and check NCCL fallback behavior without a custom communicator.
- Update the existing switch's documentation. No new flags, device-name checks, private communicators, tuning-table bypasses, or communication kernels are introduced.

This reduces the bank rows read and written; it does not shrink the physical bank allocation. The contiguous-QKV convolution optimization is independent and is not included in either measurement arm.

## Accuracy Tests

Validated revision `34f21eebabbcf8130d6adb331f289f7b88a1e8c9` against common base `17e94c4677d7beb58a89b104fd61b3768994e45e`:

- CPU stage-planning and bank-residual suites: **17 passed, 27 subtests**. Tests exercise the real eligibility helper, ordinary NCCL boundary moves, custom-collective fallbacks, terminal output ownership, and rejection of stale full-bank reads.
- The terminal-read regression checks that NCCL-only execution never enters custom fusion preparation while a supplied custom gather still permits a fusion attempt.
- isort, Ruff formatting and repository-configured lint rules, registered-test lint, AST parsing, and `git diff --check` passed.

<!-- accuracy-results:start -->
Real-routing model regression on B300: ISL 257/4096 with OSL 16 and ISL 65536 with OSL 1, each repeated twice. All 66 generated token IDs and their per-step top-20 token IDs/logprobs match the common baseline exactly (maximum absolute logprob difference 0). Repeated probes within each arm also match exactly. These synthetic regression probes are not a task-accuracy benchmark.
<!-- accuracy-results:end -->

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Independent baseline and PR worktrees use the same common base above. Conditions: Kimi-K3, 8× B300 (B30Z/SM103), TP8/EP8, MegaMoE with default real expert routing, ISL 65,536, OSL 1, concurrency 1, chunk 65,536, BF16 recurrent state, FP8 KV, `NCCL_SYM_CTAS=16`, default CE AllGather, MegaMoE reserved SMs=2. CUDA graphs, radix caching, overlap scheduling, custom SP collectives, and AR fusion are disabled. Only the PR arm enables the existing bank shard carry switch.

Each independent restart receives 4 warmup requests and two 16-request measured blocks. Baseline and PR are measured twice in an interleaved baseline/KDA/bank sequence. No profiler or hot-path diagnostic code is attached. Throughput is total input tokens divided by total measured duration; P50/P99 are recomputed from all raw formal requests in each row.

The original explicit `fake` dispatch fails on the common base because Kimi-K3 does not provide expert placement metadata. Both arms therefore use the default real routing. These results are not combined with the earlier prototype's fake-dispatch measurements.

<!-- performance-results:start -->
| Configuration | Requests | Input tok/s | P50 TTFT (s) | P99 TTFT (s) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| baseline R1 | 32 | 35,164.43 | 1.863768 | 1.873641 |
| bank R1 | 32 | 36,691.76 | 1.785341 | 1.802436 |
| baseline R2 | 32 | 35,200.97 | 1.859663 | 1.895896 |
| bank R2 | 32 | 36,623.06 | 1.785267 | 1.840323 |
| baseline pooled | 64 | 35,182.69 | 1.861480 | 1.886303 |
| bank pooled | 64 | 36,657.38 | 1.785341 | 1.829465 |

Across 64 formal requests per arm, input throughput changes by **+4.19%** and P50 TTFT falls by **76.138 ms**. All formal requests succeed with zero cache hits and zero retractions. These measurements describe the complete PR relative to the common base; they do not isolate the incremental review edits.
<!-- performance-results:end -->

## Checklist

- [x] Preserve the existing feature gate and parallelism restrictions.
- [x] Reuse the existing NCCL fallbacks and extend registered tests.
- [x] Avoid custom fusion preparation on the NCCL terminal path.
- [x] Complete exact-revision real-routing model regression and serving measurements.
- [ ] Run upstream GPU CI after maintainer approval.
